pdf_index.anonymized_output_policy: Preserve inherited validation status and original receipts. Copied bytes and relocation mappings are recorded in merge provenance.
pdf_index.is_anonymized_semantics: True only when a verified anonymized PDF and completed receipt are linked by this index; false means no verified copy is linked.

provenance.receipt_policy: Original project-relative receipt paths and content remain unchanged.

C1.justification: V1 presents MLCF for integration and explicitly leaves optimal allocation to future work. V3 makes variance-bound-optimal allocation and the variational-inference extension completed contributions, adding neural-network performance claims in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion. These substantially broaden the paper's central contribution beyond its retained convergence claim.

C2.justification: V3 explains when its optimized variance bound can improve on CF and why minimizing that bound need not give the best small-sample allocation. It discusses practical RKHS-norm estimation and newly identifies dependence on fidelity hierarchies and coarse–fine coupling. Existing smoothness and cubic-cost caveats remain, with additional discussion of variational-inference computational costs.

D1.justification: V1's appendix mainly supplies kernels, costs, and sample allocations. V3 adds kernel derivatives, hyperparameter selection and regularization guidance, explicit solver constructions, Lotka–Volterra transformations and prior parameters, and neural-network optimizer and sampling details (Appendices C–D). These substantially expand reproducibility information; the added descriptions do not establish changes to the retained experiments' underlying implementation.

E1.justification: V3 retains the boundary-value ODE and ecological posterior-integration tasks, while adding a two-dimensional uniform-distribution synthetic problem, a first-order initial-value ODE illustration, and Bayesian neural-network regression on wine-quality-red. The latter introduces variational optimization and predictive evaluation beyond the original integration tasks.

E2.justification: The original ODE and Lotka–Volterra comparator memberships are retained. The new neural-network comparisons add Fujisawa and Sato's MLMCRG gradient-recycling estimator alongside MC and two-level MLMC (Figures 5–6 and 8–11). Applying CF and MLMC to the new integration examples otherwise extends existing comparators.

E3.justification: V3 introduces synthetic allocation protocols and neural-network evaluations using ELBO, test log-likelihood, multiple network widths, and different gradient-sample budgets and schedules. Original differential-equation budgets and allocation tables remain unchanged. Figure 4's IID labels conflict with the retained MCMC descriptions, so they do not establish an actual sampling-protocol change.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained QMC/LHS/IID comparison, v3 tests MLCF-derived versus MLMC-derived allocations, illustrates variance reduction at individual levels, and examines kernel choice and gradient-sample schedules for neural networks (Figure 2 and Appendix D.5, Figures 8–11). These add substantial evidence about allocation and implementation sensitivity.

E5.justification: V1 already reports repetition counts and displays error distributions through boxplots; the original 100-run and 50-run counts are retained. V3 additionally reports neural-network learning curves as averages with standard deviations over 10 runs (Figures 5–6). This adds an uncertainty-reporting format without establishing increased replication of the original studies.

E6.justification: V3 adds allocation-comparison results, illustrative integration errors, and neural-network ELBO/log-likelihood curves with supplementary sensitivity results. The allocation comparison favors MLMC-derived allocation at small budgets and MLCF-derived allocation at the largest budget. The retained ODE boxplots also show revised error distributions, while preserving the broad MLCF advantage (v1 Figure 1; v3 Figure 3).

M1.justification: The original standard and simplified MLCF estimators remain. V3 adds variance-bound-based sample allocation and the MLCFRG extension, which treats variational-inference iterations as levels and introduces recursive gradient updates (Section 3, Equations 6 and 8–9). These materially extend the procedure.

P1.justification: The introduction is substantially rewritten around motivation, prior-method limitations, and explicit contributions. Background receives a clearer subsection hierarchy, the conclusion is rewritten, and appendices are reorganized into preliminaries, proofs, implementation, and experiments. The Stein-kernel formula and simplified estimator move into appendices rather than disappearing.

P2.justification: V3 adds a multi-panel illustration, allocation and integration plots, six neural-network learning-curve figures, and two allocation tables. Original plots are reformatted and repositioned; original tables become Tables 3–4 with corrected level headers. The document adopts a different preprint layout. Figure 4 introduces IID legend labels inconsistent with its MCMC description.

R1.justification: V3 substantially expands positioning toward machine-learning integration and variational-gradient estimation, including Fujisawa and Sato, Shi and Cornish, and literature on estimating RKHS norms. It retains the earlier contrasts with multilevel Bayesian quadrature and problem-specific control variates. Publication updates to existing Sun et al. references are not new works.

T1.justification: V3 adds an optimal-allocation theorem, a budget-dependent variance-bound derivation, comparisons with the CF bound, and a recursive variational-gradient proposition with proofs (Section 3; Appendices B.3–B.5). It also formally replaces the hyperrectangle domain assumption with the interior cone condition. The original unbiasedness and convergence results remain.

improvement.justification: V3 resolves v1's explicitly deferred allocation question through a derivation and direct empirical comparison. The variational-inference extension, sensitivity experiments, and substantially fuller implementation details improve methodological completeness and testability. Neural-network efficiency evidence remains limited to iteration-based comparisons, and Figure 4 introduces inconsistent sampling labels, but these shortcomings do not outweigh the substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MLCF research, retaining the base estimator and original differential-equation experiments. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: V3 retains the original empirical studies and adds synthetic integration, an illustrative ODE experiment, and Bayesian neural-network variational-inference results, including appendix sensitivity experiments.

before.justification: V1 reports original integration-error experiments for a boundary-value ODE and Bayesian Lotka–Volterra inference, with 100 and 50 repetitions respectively (Section 4, Figures 1–2).

C1.justification: v1 centers its contribution on Atari/MuJoCo performance and concludes superiority over DT, Transformer-XL, and TAP. v3 makes training procedures and success in explicitly memory-dependent environments central contributions, while qualifying classic-environment performance as better or comparable. This substantially changes the scope and emphasis of the principal claims.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive explanations for environment-dependent memory benefits, including minimal memory-token contributions in fully observable MuJoCo and differing dependence on past actions across Atari games. It explains curriculum learning through T-Maze's sparse decisive actions and interprets contrasting memory-intervention outcomes as requiring further study. The earlier short-sequence limitation remains; the MuJoCo discussion shifts from overlap/smoothness toward return handling.

D1.justification: v3 substantially expands reproducibility information with new-task configurations in Table 5, VizDoom trajectory collection details, curriculum shuffling, and return-target calibration for Table 6. The reported repository location changes. v1's explicit statement that model weights are public is no longer present; this establishes a disclosure change, not that weights became unavailable.

E1.justification: v3 retains the four Atari games and nine MuJoCo dataset/environment combinations. It adds VizDoom-Two-Colors, requiring object selection after a color cue disappears, and modified T-Maze, requiring recall of an initial directional hint. These introduce explicit memory-dependent task coverage absent from v1.

E2.justification: v3 adds a uniform-random policy to the VizDoom comparison in Table 1. The established comparator families remain: DT, CQL, and TAP. v1's Atari DT-XL comparator matches v3's RATE- by procedure and all four scores; DT30/DT90 and DT-3/DT-7 introduce configurations of DT rather than new comparator families.

E3.justification: v3 introduces lifetime and success-rate evaluation, DT context-length controls, and variable-horizon T-Maze protocols. For retained MuJoCo experiments, the reported memory-token count changes from 15 to 5, and inference gains segment-wise return resetting. Atari DT scores are now attributed to the original DT paper rather than the local reproduction described in v1. These establish reported setting/procedure changes, without proving which experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v3 adds curriculum controls, recall-versus-horizon analysis, memory replacement with noise, additive-noise and first-segment-memory interventions, VizDoom return-conditioning tests, and a trajectory case study (Sections 5.1–5.2, Figures 3–5, Table 6). v1's MuJoCo overlap/fixation ablation in Table 3 disappears. The earlier Atari sensitivity sweeps and attention analyses remain in Appendices C–D.

E5.justification: v3 extends existing uncertainty reporting with standard errors for the new tasks and uncertainty values for previously reported MuJoCo DT means. T-Maze specifies 10 runs over 100 seeds; VizDoom interventions specify three runs over 100 seeds. The default evaluation statement changes from v1's three seeds with 10 Atari episodes each to 100 episodes per seed, while Appendix D retains 10. These are reporting changes, not evidence that every retained result was rerun.

E6.justification: v3 adds extensive memory-task results: at three T-Maze segments, RATE-3 achieves 1.000 success rate versus DT-3's 0.491 (Table 2). Retained benchmark entries also change: RMDT/RATE Breakout is 123.8 ± 35.6 versus 132.8 ± 33.2; Medium-Expert Walker2d is 84.7 ± 9.4 versus 108.1 ± 0.1; DT Qbert is 7830 ± 2660 versus 2215.8 ± 1523.7. Changed protocols and provenance preclude interpreting these as established same-setting gains. The old MuJoCo overlap results are removed.

M1.justification: The Transformer-XL backbone and recurrent read/write memory tokens remain. Beyond renaming, v3 adds episode-start sampling for memory-dependent tasks, a cumulative trajectory-length curriculum for T-Maze, and resetting the target return at each MuJoCo segment. These substantively extend training and inference beyond v1's random-subsequence training and documented overlap/memory-fixation procedure.

P1.justification: v3 renames the paper/model, changes the author list, and substantially rewrites the abstract, introduction, contributions, and conclusion. Background moves to Appendix A, attention analysis to Appendix C, and existing Atari ablations to Appendix D, reorganizing the main narrative around memory-dependent training and evaluation.

P2.justification: v3 adopts a two-column main layout, condenses the original method illustrations into two schematics, and adds the VizDoom timeline and curriculum/memory-intervention plots. It introduces and restructures result tables, expands the hyperparameter table, and removes the MuJoCo overlap table. Existing attention maps and Atari sensitivity plots are relocated and reformatted rather than newly introduced.

R1.justification: v3 expands positioning around memory-based RL through Working Memory Graphs, TrMRL, and AdA, including explicit architectural and tokenization comparisons with AdA. It adds a broad first-attempt novelty statement and references supporting the new environments. The standalone CQL reference in v1 is removed even though CQL remains evaluated. These changes exceed bibliographic or citation-style editing.

T1.justification: v3 adds limited mathematical specification of the curriculum datasets Q_S as unions of trajectory sets q_i and a parameter-overhead relation involving head dimension and memory-token count (Section 4.2). The existing MDP, return, and attention mathematics is retained, largely relocated to Appendix A. No theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v1 supports its central memory claim mainly through classic benchmarks, token-removal comparisons, and attention maps. v3 addresses the important absence of explicitly memory-dependent evaluation with disappearing-cue and delayed-hint tasks, curriculum controls, and memory interventions (Tables 1–2, Figures 3–5). These substantially strengthen the evidence for memory use and reveal its limits, while the classic-benchmark claims become better qualified. Removing the MuJoCo overlap study and changing benchmark protocols reduce continuity, but the improved alignment between the central claim and its experimental evidence provides a substantial net gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same recurrent-memory transformer research, despite the RMDT-to-RATE renaming and expanded scope. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison.

after.justification: v3 reports original VizDoom-Two-Colors and T-Maze experiments, curriculum and memory-intervention results, and Atari/MuJoCo evaluations.

before.justification: v1 reports original RMDT evaluations on Atari and MuJoCo, memory and segment ablations, and attention-map analyses.

C1.justification: v4 recasts the central contribution around MRV-controlled information retention and explicitly claims better or comparable performance against Mamba-based state-of-the-art models. v3's separate headline contributions concerning training procedures and interpretable memory properties are no longer presented that way. The broad claim that memory helps memory-intensive tasks while preserving standard-benchmark performance remains.

C2.justification: v4 explains long-horizon failure through information loss during repeated memory updates and motivates MRV as its remedy. Curriculum learning is reframed as beneficial rather than necessary for solving T-Maze. New discussion addresses inherited A2C color bias, weak Memory Maze training data, and the offline/online comparison boundary. Detailed attention-map interpretations disappear, while the short-sequence limitation remains.

D1.justification: Beyond v3's hyperparameter table and general encoder descriptions, v4 provides optimizer/MRV settings, convolution configurations, additional collection and sampling instructions, and Appendix F's A100 hardware, GPU-memory usage, training times and parameter counts. The stated code location changes from an anonymous repository to AIRI-Institute/RATE on GitHub. These substantially expand reproducibility information without independently verifying repository availability.

E1.justification: v4 adds Memory Maze navigation, Minigrid.Memory with active clue acquisition and credit assignment, and the two-state Action Associative Retrieval task. It also evaluates ViZDoom with the pillar absent from the episode's beginning. The original T-Maze, ViZDoom, four Atari games and nine MuJoCo dataset/environment combinations remain.

E2.justification: v4 adds DMamba and MambaDM comparison results to both Atari and MuJoCo tables, retaining DT and the MuJoCo CQL/TAP comparators. The Atari RATE-without-memory comparator is removed. ViZDoom Figure 3 adds an online A2C reference, retains Random and DT90 under the name DT, and drops DT30; the text explicitly qualifies comparison with online A2C.

E3.justification: The reported ViZDoom dataset changes from 1,024 trajectories to 5,000 trajectories of length 90, and v4 specifies matching DT/RATE training fragments instead of v3's differing sampling starts. Table 5 changes ViZDoom from three layers/one head/five memory tokens to six/eight/fifteen, and MuJoCo memory tokens from five to fifteen. T-Maze configurations and inference horizons are revised. New tasks introduce additional protocols, including reward-filtered Memory Maze sampling and AAR training at length 90 with validation at 180.

E4.justification: v4 adds comparisons of five MRV designs against no MRV, Minigrid component ablations, AAR diagnostics, and ViZDoom pillar-removal and temporal-window analyses. Curriculum and noise-replacement tests are revised, while target-return sensitivity is retained in a redesigned comparison. v3's attention-map analyses, Atari segment-count/memory-size studies, and first-segment/additive-noise memory interventions are removed rather than relocated.

E5.justification: v4 specifies six runs over 100 seeds for ViZDoom Figure 3; v3's appendix ViZDoom study specifies three runs over 100 seeds. v4 adds ten-run averaging and correlation estimates for AAR. Conversely, v3's explicit T-Maze run counts and standard-error descriptions are not retained in v4's corresponding Figure 5 and Table 3. These are changes in reported statistical protocols, without establishing an increase in runs for an unchanged experiment.

E6.justification: RATE scores change throughout the Atari and MuJoCo tables: Breakout changes from 132.8 ± 33.2 to 119.8 ± 15.9, and Medium Hopper from 65.6 ± 2.2 to 77.4 ± 1.4. The corresponding DT/CQL/TAP values remain unchanged. v4 also reports revised T-Maze/ViZDoom findings and new task and MRV results, including Memory Maze rewards of 1.91 ± 0.10 for RATE versus 1.45 ± 0.23 for DT. Revised models and settings prevent interpreting these as uniform same-setting gains.

M1.justification: v3 passes transformer-produced memory embeddings to subsequent segments. v4 inserts a trainable Memory Retention Valve (MRV-CA-2), using previous memory as queries and updated memory as keys and values before recurrent reuse (Section 3). This substantially changes the memory-update procedure. Segment training, curriculum learning and the MuJoCo return-reset strategy already existed in v3.

P1.justification: The introduction and related work are extensively rewritten. Background moves from Appendix A into Section 2, related work moves after the experiments, and detailed environment/training descriptions move into appendices. Ablations are reorganized around three questions. These are substantial narrative and structural changes beyond the scientific additions; author order and affiliations also change.

P2.justification: v4 replaces the two-column main-text layout with predominantly single-column text and wrapped figures. The architecture diagrams are redesigned to include MRV; ViZDoom timelines and several tables give way to new plots. Attention maps and Atari sensitivity figures disappear, while environment illustrations, AAR diagrams/scatterplots and MRV schematics appear. Benchmark tables gain comparator columns and colored ranking highlights.

R1.justification: v4 introduces substantial positioning against state-space models, including Decision S4, DMamba and MambaDM, and expands long-context and online/model-based RL coverage. Much of v3's general vision, audio, multimodal and robotics survey is removed. The claim of being the first memory-transformer adaptation for RL action generation is narrowed explicitly to the offline-RL setting.

T1.justification: v4 adds an explicit POMDP formalization, a probability-based condition for memory in AAR (Equation 7), and mathematical specifications of MRV and its gated variant. Existing offline-RL definitions and curriculum formulas are largely retained. The additions concern formal definitions and update rules; neither version develops a theorem-and-proof analysis.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially strengthens evidence addressing v3's documented long-horizon memory decay: its controlled MRV comparison reports success rates of 0.90 versus 0.61 without MRV at 900 steps after training to 150 (Table 3). Additional memory/credit-assignment tasks, stronger comparators and implementation/resource documentation improve validation and reproducibility. These gains outweigh the removed attention-map and Atari sensitivity analyses, although reporting flaws remain: Appendix C claims best MuJoCo results in 5/9 cases despite only two highest-mean rows, and Figure 5(b) falls below the stated 50% noise-ablation success rate.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Recurrent Action Transformer with Memory (RATE). All 15 pages of v3 and 18 pages of v4, including equations, figures, tables and appendices, support reliable comparison despite substantial revisions.

after.justification: v4 reports original evaluations of revised RATE, including Memory Maze, Minigrid.Memory, Action Associative Retrieval and Memory Retention Valve ablations.

before.justification: v3 reports original RATE evaluations on ViZDoom-Two-Colors, T-Maze, Atari and MuJoCo, alongside memory ablations and appendix attention-map analyses.

C1.justification: v4's headline comparative contribution concerns superiority over counterparts without memory. v5's Introduction and Conclusion broaden this to strong memory-augmented and recurrent baselines, and foreground interpolation/extrapolation and compensation for training-data bias. This substantially expands the claimed competitive scope, although the basic RATE proposal and classic-benchmark versatility claim remain.

C2.justification: v5 distinguishes the importance of memory embeddings in sparse tasks from cached states in continuous environments and adds a mechanism interpretation connecting embeddings to red-pillar bias compensation. Curriculum learning changes from substantially beneficial in v4 to unnecessary or slightly harmful for RATE under v5's revised setup. The short-sequence limitation is replaced by concrete limitations concerning effective-context selection, per-step memory updating, and unknown memory capacity.

D1.justification: v5 newly documents dataset generation and sample counts, cache lengths, learning rates, AdamW coefficients, and RATE's disabled decoder feed-forward block. Reported RATE/DT GPU memory for ViZDoom and Memory Maze changes from 10/30 GB to 24/37 GB. Code access instructions change from a direct repository link to a project website. Conversely, v4's attention-mask and gradient-detachment discussion is omitted. These are substantial reproducibility-documentation changes.

E1.justification: All benchmark families, including AAR, are retained. Memory Maze training data change from the supplied random-object-navigation trajectories described in v4 Appendix C to Dreamer-generated trajectories in v5 Appendix B. Minigrid evaluation extends from the roughly 60-cell range plotted in v4 Figure 5(d) to 91x91 grids in v5. These revise coverage within existing tasks.

E2.justification: Beyond v4's DT-centered comparisons and Minigrid component ablations, v5 explicitly evaluates RMT and TrXL in ViZDoom, T-Maze, and Memory Maze. Table 1 adds DLSTM, DGRU, and DMamba comparisons on memory tasks; Table 5 adds OracleDT. CQL joins the Atari comparison although already present for MuJoCo. The displayed A2C reference is removed from the ViZDoom results.

E3.justification: Reported settings change substantially. ViZDoom health loss changes from 5/32 to 10/32 per step and survival reward from 0.01 to 0.02; Minigrid training size changes from 13x13 to 31x31. Tables 5 and 8 revise training budgets, batch sizes, dropout, memory-token counts, MRV head counts, and Memory Maze embedding dimension from 128 to 64. New oracle and noise controls introduce additional protocols, while ViZDoom lifetime reporting is dropped. These documented revisions do not establish which experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v5 adds an OracleDT control testing performance with privileged task information, ViZDoom corruption tests separating memory embeddings from cached states, graded noise sensitivity, and sweeps over cache length, memory-token count, MRV heads, and activation functions (Section 5; Appendix F). Curriculum comparisons expand to DT, RATE, RMT, and TrXL under the three-segment setup. The existing five-way MRV architecture ablation is retained.

E5.justification: v5 Appendix E, Table 9 newly specifies run counts, inference seeds, and uncertainty conventions across the suite, including 10 runs/100 seeds for T-Maze and 3/100 for Minigrid and MuJoCo. v4 already reported corresponding information for ViZDoom, Memory Maze, Atari, and AAR. This extends statistical disclosure without establishing increased run counts or introducing significance tests.

E6.justification: Numerous comparator, oracle, and ablation results are added. Memory Maze RATE/DT rewards change from 1.91 ± 0.10/1.45 ± 0.23 to 7.64 ± 0.41/6.83 ± 0.51 under revised data and settings, preventing a same-setting gain interpretation. All four RATE Atari entries change; Breakout changes from 119.8 ± 15.9 to 111.0 ± 2.9. AAR RATE training/validation correlations change from 0.85/0.71 to 0.97/0.80. Curriculum findings reverse under the revised setup. MuJoCo task scores and the MRV configuration table remain unchanged, with MuJoCo means added.

M1.justification: The proposed RATE procedure retains segmented trajectory processing, recurrent memory embeddings, cached hidden states, and cross-attention MRV updates. Algorithms 1–2 primarily reformulate the existing method. Appendix D newly discloses disabling RATE's decoder feed-forward block, but does not establish that this implementation differed in v4; this is documentation rather than a demonstrated method revision.

P1.justification: Section 3 is substantially rewritten around algorithm descriptions. AAR moves from the main experimental narrative into Appendix C, curriculum learning moves into Appendix F.2, and the appendices are reorganized with a new DT explanation and results-reporting section. Extensive paragraph editing, terminology standardization, and a switch to author-date citations accompany this restructuring.

P2.justification: v4's ViZDoom Figures 3–4 become the expanded Figure 3, and its combined Figure 5 is redistributed into separate benchmark and ablation displays. v5 adds comparison tables and noise/sensitivity figures, enlarges and relocates AAR plots, and substantially revises colors, legends, training-range shading, table structures, and page layout. These visual changes extend well beyond numerical updates.

R1.justification: v5 adds a short RNN/DLSTM subsection and citations for DLSTM, CQL, Dreamer, and DQN, while removing references to Performers, Q-learning Decision Transformer, and Elastic Decision Transformer. It also drops v4's claim to be the first attempt to adapt memory transformers for offline-RL action generation. The broader transformer, SSM, and memory positioning remains.

T1.justification: v5 Section 5 introduces the conditional mathematical assertion R[OracleDT] >= R[RATE] >= R[DT], interpreting oracle information as perfect memory. v4 contains no corresponding bound, and v5 supplies no proof. The existing AAR memory criterion and MRV-G equations survive in Appendices C and F.3; reorganized pseudocode and notation do not constitute new theory.

improvement.justification: v5 addresses an important weakness in v4: the central memory-environment evidence relied mainly on comparison with DT. Direct tests against competing memory and recurrent models, together with targeted controls and sensitivity analyses, substantially strengthen assessment of RATE's contribution. Expanded implementation/run documentation and concrete limitations improve transparency. The broader superiority wording and unproved OracleDT bound overreach some evidence, but these shortcomings do not outweigh the substantial gains in experimental support. Higher Memory Maze scores under changed settings are not themselves evidence of improved paper quality.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RATE study. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching across revisions and relocations.

after.justification: v5 retains original empirical evaluations and reports additional memory-model comparisons, OracleDT controls, and noise and hyperparameter ablations.

before.justification: v4 reports original RATE experiments on memory-intensive environments, Atari, MuJoCo, and Action Associative Retrieval, together with memory-component, curriculum-learning, and MRV ablations.

C1.justification: The claimed novelty of a provably exact, fixed-dimensional polynomial-time algorithm remains. However, the stated runtime guarantee changes from O(N^D) to O(N^(D+1)), and the abstract adds claims of optimal out-of-sample accuracy and empirically demonstrated polynomial runtime reductions from upper-bound filtering.

C2.justification: v1 primarily interprets exact training accuracy through interpretability and practical usefulness. v2 adds a VC-bound argument linking exact optimization to generalization, interprets cross-validation as supporting superior test performance, and explains pruning behavior. Section 4.2 newly discusses the SDP memory/runtime tradeoff and why compiler optimization alone cannot overcome scaling limitations.

D1.justification: v1 provides Haskell code and proposes optimized C++ comparisons as future work. v2 explicitly states that its reported experiments use an efficient C++ translation of that code. Appendix B's routines and the existing repository reference remain unchanged; detailed compiler or hardware settings are not supplied.

E1.justification: v2 replaces Blood transfusion with Voicepath in the UCI evaluation and adds synthetic datasets in dimensions 1–4 for computational experiments. Habermans, Caesarian, Cryotherapy, and Acute inflammations remain; the latter is renamed Inflammations. Cross-validation on these retained datasets changes the protocol rather than dataset coverage.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains SVM, logistic regression, and Fisher's linear discriminant, called LDA in v2. The new cross-validation table uses the same comparator set. Expanded discussion of MIP, branch-and-bound, and other methods does not introduce reported comparisons against ICE.

E3.justification: v2 adds ten-fold cross-validation with separate training and test errors. New timing protocols vary dataset size across dimensions 1–4 with the upper bound disabled, then sweep the bound on synthetic datasets with optimal error approximately 0.1N or 0.2N. These are added evaluation designs; changes to retained experiments' preprocessing or splits are not established.

E4.justification: v2 adds runtime scaling analysis across sample sizes and dimensions in Figure 2, and sensitivity analysis of the existing viability bound in Figure 3. The latter tests how tightening the bound reduces runtime and examines its plateau at loose bounds. Neither analysis appears in v1 or its appendices.

E5.justification: v2 Table 2 introduces mean classification errors and standard deviations across ten cross-validation folds, whereas v1 reports only individual error counts and percentages. This adds uncertainty reporting without introducing independently repeated cross-validation, seed information, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: Table 1 changes Cryotherapy errors from 6 to 4 for ICE and 9 to 4 for logistic regression, Habermans logistic-regression errors from 77 to 73, and Caesarian SVM/logistic-regression errors from 21 to 22. v2 also adds cross-validation, Voicepath, and runtime results while removing Blood transfusion results. Settings are insufficiently documented to interpret the revised counts as verified same-setting gains.

M1.justification: v2 Section 3.2 introduces selection of a maximum-margin representative of the optimal hyperplane's equivalence class for out-of-sample prediction. The core ICE enumeration, loss, viability pruning, and Haskell routines in Section 2 and Appendix B remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The overall section order, detailed algorithm exposition, and most appendix prose remain intact. Editing expands the abstract and motivation, updates the title and author list, corrects wording, and organizes the expanded experiments and discussion into Sections 3.1–3.3 and 4.1–4.2. Most substantial expansion introduces scientific content rather than rewriting retained exposition.

P2.justification: v1 has one table and no figures. v2 adds a search-tree illustration, runtime scaling plot, two-panel upper-bound sensitivity plot, and cross-validation table. Table 1 is relocated after the algorithm exposition and reformatted with percentages before counts, revised headers, and bold best results.

R1.justification: The brief prior-work discussion expands into Section 4.1, covering surrogate losses, exact clustering and trees, MIP classifiers, and scoring systems. v2 explicitly identifies Nguyen and Sanner's similar polynomial search algorithm while distinguishing its missing correctness proof. The Alexanderson and Wetzel reference disappears, leaving an unresolved citation in Appendix A.

T1.justification: v2 Section 3.3 adds a runtime derivation and revises the worst-case bound from v1's O(N^D) to O(N^(D+1)). Section 1 adds an i.i.d. VC-dimension generalization bound. Appendix A largely retains the correctness argument, while correcting the general-position definition from linear to affine subspaces.

improvement.justification: v2 replaces the overstated O(N^D) runtime claim with O(N^(D+1)) analysis and supporting timing experiments, addressing a central weakness in v1's efficiency claim. Cross-validation with variability reporting and fuller related-work positioning substantially strengthen validation. The new claim of optimal out-of-sample accuracy exceeds what the bound and Table 2 establish, including ties and substantial fold variability, but the correction and empirical validation provide substantial net gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ICE research. Their text, equations, tables, figures, correctness appendix, and Haskell linear algebra appendix are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original UCI classification and cross-validation results in Tables 1–2, plus synthetic runtime and upper-bound sensitivity results in Figures 2–3.

before.justification: v1 Table 1 reports original UCI classification experiments comparing ICE with SVM, logistic regression, and Fisher's linear discriminant.

C1.justification: v1 already claims effective, efficient unlearning without remaining data. v2 adds an explicit claim to be the first remaining-data-free method to outperform state-of-the-art methods using remaining data, alongside claims of sequential-unlearning resilience and easy hyperparameter tuning. The abstract, introduction, and conclusion thus expand the claimed novelty and practical capabilities.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations of sequential failures as knowledge recovery, knowledge residue, and utility breakdown, and connects input sensitivity to generative classifier interpretations and privacy. It acknowledges weaker random-subset competitiveness of remaining-data-free methods. Conversely, v1's concluding limitations about unexplained utility preservation and imperfect contribution estimation disappear, although v2 still describes the sensitivity surrogate as approximate.

D1.justification: Appendix C adds training schedules, optimizers, batch sizes, frozen batch-normalization instructions, baseline implementation sources, and extensive hyperparameter settings and search ranges. Hardware changes from RTX 2080Ti to RTX 4090. Much of this is newly disclosed information rather than demonstrated changes to earlier procedures. v1's promise to release MU-Mis code is absent; v2's implementation links identify baseline sources.

E1.justification: v2 adds Tiny ImageNet, SVHN, and the Lamp subclass evaluation while retaining the earlier datasets and task families. It also introduces sequential deletion of five distinct classes or five related subclasses. These scenarios add the requirement that previous forgetting survive subsequent unlearning requests, which v1 does not evaluate.

E2.justification: v2 retains v1's five comparators, with Blindspot renamed Bad Teacher (BT), and adds Boundary Expand, EU-k, CF-k, SCRUB, DUCK, SalUn, NG, RL, JiT, and SCAR in reported comparisons. Boundary Shrink also enters subclass comparisons, where v1 excluded it. This substantially broadens the evaluated comparator set.

E3.justification: Random-subset deletion changes from 100 CIFAR-10 samples to 10%. v2 adds VGG-16 and ImageNet-initialized ViT configurations, test accuracy, average-gap and output KL-divergence metrics, and sequential-request evaluation procedures. Reported MU-Mis learning rates also differ from v1's stated range. These are substantive evaluation changes, separate from newly disclosed implementation details.

E4.justification: v2 adds sequential-unlearning robustness analyses examining recovery of forgotten knowledge and accumulated utility damage, plus learning-rate and stopping-threshold studies in Figures 4–7 and 9. The attention-map and pairwise-gradient analyses are retained. The loss ablation is revised: v1's two-stage TC-then-OC experiment is removed, as is its Appendix A.2 trajectory comparing forgetting-data and remaining-data sensitivity gaps.

E5.justification: v1 presents point estimates without specifying repeated-run counts or uncertainty. v2 introduces means and standard deviations over five independent trials in Table I and carries this reporting format into other benchmark tables. This is a substantial change in statistical reporting; v1 supplies no prior run count from which an increase in repetitions could be established.

E6.justification: Benchmark results are extensively revised and expanded. For CIFAR-20 Sea, MU-Mis forgetting accuracy changes from 97.66 to 81.00 ± 2.95, while the retrained reference changes from 97.05 to 80.93 ± 2.20 (v1 Table 4; v2 Table II). New architecture, dataset, sequential-unlearning, and hyperparameter results add substantial findings. Changed protocols and reference models prevent interpreting these revisions as same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The basic sensitivity-gap objective remains, but Algorithm 1 replaces v1's loss-change stopping criterion with a criterion tracking recovery of irrelevant-class sensitivity relative to its initial value and minimum. Appendix C-D also introduces dynamic loss reweighting, using kappa=80 for Tiny ImageNet and early sequential subclass requests. These alter termination and optimization, rather than merely documenting the existing method.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related-work discussion, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around remaining-data-free unlearning. v1's unified Method section becomes separate analysis and proposed-method sections; experiments and appendices are reorganized, and the Broader Impacts section is removed. The title and author block also change. This is substantial narrative restructuring.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a different document template and replaces compact benchmark tables with broader tables containing additional metrics, comparator groupings, and uncertainty displays. v1 Figures 3–4 are combined and expanded into v2 Figure 3; attention maps move from Figure 6 to Figure 8, and the gradient histograms become Appendix Figure A2. New sequential and hyperparameter plots substantially change the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v2 adds a dedicated remaining-data-free related-work subsection positioning MU-Mis against JiT and SCAR. It substantially expands connections to influence estimation, sequential-unlearning evaluation, input curvature, memorization, privacy, and generative interpretations of classifiers. These change the research positioning beyond citation formatting or publication-metadata updates.

T1.justification: The central contribution/residual decomposition is retained. v2 explicitly states approximations neglecting probability derivatives and changes in the training-dependent gradient mapping, distinguishes infinitesimal self-influence from leave-one-out memorization, and adds an MLP/ReLU derivation in Section III-B, Eqs. (6)–(7). These are limited mathematical extensions and refinements within the existing approximate theoretical framework.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's limited evaluation, absent uncertainty reporting, and sparse reproducibility information through broader comparisons, sequential-request tests, five-trial statistics, and Appendix C. These make the central utility and efficiency claims much more assessable. Removing the explicit limitations paragraph and using broad superiority language despite weaker random-subset results in Table A5 are drawbacks, and the theory remains approximate. Nevertheless, the empirical scrutiny and reproducibility documentation constitute a substantial net quality improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MU-Mis and provide readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Despite substantial expansion and reorganization, the retained and revised content can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 reports original benchmark comparisons, sequential-unlearning experiments, hyperparameter studies, ablations, and diagnostic analyses in Section V and Appendices A–B.

before.justification: v1 reports original unlearning experiments, timing comparisons, loss ablations, attention maps, and sensitivity analyses in Section 4 and Appendix A.

C1.justification: The central claim that problem-oriented pairs improve code optimization remains. However, v1's main contribution of overcoming correctness bottlenecks through model merging is replaced by anchor verification mitigating the 'optimization tax.' Correctness improvement becomes an explicit central contribution alongside optimization ratio and speedup.

C2.justification: V2 replaces merging and curriculum-learning explanations with interpretations about structural diversity, data efficiency, and reliable test outputs from slow code. Its limitations replace the natural-language-to-efficient-code research question with unresolved full correctness. One new interpretation overstates PCO's optimization-ratio advantage: Tables 2 and 4 report DeepSeek-V3 refinement gains of 12.16 percentage points on PCO versus 16.04 on PIE, although the speedup gain is larger on PCO.

D1.justification: V2 adds LLAMA-FACTORY and vLLM usage, model-version and base-versus-chat details, explicit anchor-verification and comparator prompts, and a concrete code-access URL. Reported hardware changes from four to eight A100 GPUs, and LoRA targets change from q_proj/v_proj to all. V1's average test-case counts and performance-conditioned-generation documentation are omitted.

E1.justification: Both versions train and evaluate on CodeNet/PIE-derived C++ competitive-programming code with execution-time optimization as the task. PCO continues the problem-oriented reconstruction of PIE. Changed pair selection, counts, and partitions remain within this coverage; no additional domain, language, or independent benchmark is evaluated.

E2.justification: The correctness-improvement comparisons drop Curriculum-Learning and add Direct Test Generation, while retaining the self-correction comparison family as Self-Debugging. Prompt comparisons also remove GPT-3.5 and CodeLlama 34B. V2 adds Qwen2.5-Coder comparisons against PIE fine-tuning controls, substantially revising the evaluated comparison set.

E3.justification: V1 selects problem-oriented pairs with greater than 90% runtime reduction; v2 selects top-speedup pairs while matching PIE's pair count per problem. Training sets change from 56,086/14,051 pairs to 77,967 each, and the test set changes from 1,422 samples across 80 problems to 978 across 41. Model configurations and LoRA targets also change. New refinement experiments cap methods at one iteration, with three generated inputs or cases for test-based methods.

E4.justification: V2 adds CFG graph-edit-distance analysis, semantic-embedding visualization, training-data percentage experiments, and three anchor-verification case studies. It also examines refinement benefits on PIE versus PCO. V1's merge-weight sensitivity study and failure-category breakdown disappear. The original optimization-type analysis and four illustrative code comparisons are retained, with the latter relocated to Figures 15–18.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seeds, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests. BEST@1/BEST@8 remains a candidate-selection protocol rather than uncertainty estimation. The human and GPT-4 sampling counts remain 100 and 1,000 pairs, respectively.

E6.justification: Many retained-model results are replaced: DeepSeek-Coder 33B's problem-oriented BEST@8 results change from 71.03% optimized and 4.812× speedup in v1 to 74.87% and 6.67× in v2, under changed settings. V2 adds anchor-verification results, including 58.90% to 71.06% optimized, 5.22× to 6.08× speedup, and 61.55% to 74.54% correctness with DeepSeek-V3 refinement. V1's merging and error-breakdown results are removed.

M1.justification: V1 addresses correctness bottlenecks by merging models separately fine-tuned on user-oriented and problem-oriented pairs using Merge-Linear or Merge-Slerp. V2 replaces this with anchor verification: generate test inputs, execute the original slow code to obtain reference outputs, and refine optimized code using execution feedback. This substantially changes inference.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and dataset-construction explanation are extensively rewritten. Previously separate experimental-setting, results, and analysis sections are reorganized into Section 3, followed by the anchor-verification section. Appendices are substantially reorganized, with training details, prompts, and retained examples moved into a new structure.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn as submission trajectories, and the optimization-type pie charts become separate human and LLM bar charts. V2 adds structural, semantic, data-efficiency, verification-framework, prompt, and case-study displays, plus comparison tables with delta columns. Dataset statistics move to the appendix, and retained code examples become Figures 15–18.

R1.justification: V2 introduces substantial positioning against generated-test and execution-filtering approaches, citing CodeT, B4, and SelfCodeAlign to motivate anchor verification. Model-soup and curriculum-learning positioning disappears. References also expand to newer code models, code-efficiency research, and tools supporting the new analyses.

T1.justification: V2 Section 3.1 adds explicit combinatorial pair-count expressions under assumptions about numbers of problems, users, and submissions, supporting an additional scaling argument. V1 describes trajectories, pairs, and filtering thresholds without this counting argument. No substantial theorem or proof development is added.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens support for the central claim by matching training pair counts per problem, addressing v1's unequal data-size and problem-coverage comparison, and adding structural and data-efficiency analyses. Anchor verification is documented concretely and tested against self-debugging and direct test generation across three backbones, providing stronger evidence for its correctness mechanism. Some new PIE/PCO interpretations overstate the reported optimization-ratio gains, but the improved controls and methodological evidence provide a substantial net benefit. Changed splits prevent treating higher cross-version scores as directly comparable performance gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same problem-oriented code-optimization work, although v2 substantially revises its second contribution. All pages, including equations, tables, figures, and appendices, were available for inspection.

after.justification: V2 reports original fine-tuning and anchor-verification experiments, structural and semantic analyses, data-efficiency experiments, and appendix case studies.

before.justification: V1 reports original prompting, fine-tuning, model-merging, optimization-type, and error-analysis results, including Tables 2–4 and Figures 3 and 5.

C1.justification: The two central contributions and their principal performance claims remain. v3's abstract additionally asserts that optimization is more challenging than code generation, while its introduction and conclusion elevate the existing data-scarcity argument into a more explicit contribution. This modestly expands the framing without redefining the work.

C2.justification: v3 attributes PCO's gains primarily to the pairing perspective rather than selection, and verification gains to accurate executed outputs. It adds interpretations concerning transferable edit patterns, semantic failure modes, diminishing sampling returns and execution overhead. Section 4 and Appendix L substantially expand applicability discussion and qualifications concerning complex codebases and extremely slow anchors.

D1.justification: v3 adds the largest model's 48 GPU-hour fine-tuning cost, Python profiling/data-size information and physical CPU specifications. It removes v2's public-code statement and repository link, and omits the previously stated 1,000-pair GPT-4 analysis sample size. Existing training hyperparameters and prompts largely remain; the missing link does not establish that the code itself became unavailable.

E1.justification: v2 evaluates C/C++ competitive-programming optimization. v3 adds Python versions of PIE and PCO constructed from CodeNet, evaluating both fine-tuning and verification across this additional language (Section 4 and Appendix J). This substantially broadens actual coverage; the original C/C++ coverage remains.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds GPT-4o and DeepSeek-V3 as CoT optimization baselines; v2 used them as refinement backbones only. v3 also adds sampling controls and a two-step LLM-output Comparison Group in its ablations. The original PIE, Self-Debugging and Direct Test Generation comparison families remain.

E3.justification: The original C++ splits, metrics, compiler and two-epoch fine-tuning setup remain. New experiments introduce Python profiling with cProfile, matched random-selection controls, 40% GED-stratified training subsets, three/five refinement iterations, BEST@2 through BEST@7, and physical-hardware timing on 20 pairs. These substantially expand the evaluation design rather than revise the retained experiments.

E4.justification: v3 adds controls separating pairing perspective from speedup selection and executed outputs from LLM-generated outputs, plus iteration sensitivity, GED-stratified ablations, analysis of 100 failures, BEST@k scaling, runtime overhead and hardware validation. Figure 11 adds an edit-pattern transfer case study. The original percentage analysis and appendix verification cases are retained.

E5.justification: v3 Appendix P specifies averaging execution times over ten runs per hardware-tested pair and reports a Pearson correlation analysis. v2 has no corresponding repeated-timing study. This does not establish increased runs for the retained experiments, whose seed variability, confidence intervals and significance tests remain unreported.

E6.justification: Most original scores remain, including Table 2's 71.06% optimization, 6.08× speedup and 74.54% correctness. Table 1 changes PCO Qwen2.5-Coder-32B optimization from 58.89% to 58.90%. Substantial new entries include PCO-Random's 49.55% optimization (Table 6), Python verification's 95.35% correctness (Table 9), and five-iteration verification's 78.43% optimization (Table 4). These additions represent new comparisons/settings, not same-setting gains between versions.

M1.justification: The proposed method retains cross-user, runtime-ordered optimization pairs, supervised fine-tuning and the same three-stage Anchor Verification procedure. v3 explicitly identifies PCO-Top-Speedup as the original PCO. New sampling controls and iteration experiments test the existing approach without replacing its core procedure.

P1.justification: v3 substantially revises the abstract, contribution statements and explanatory narrative, adds an explicit roadmap, and reorganizes the results and analyses. Related work and limitations move into appendices, and a dedicated Generalizability section is introduced. This changes the document's organization beyond simple renumbering.

P2.justification: v3 changes the two-column document to a single-column ICLR layout and redistributes retained plots, prompts and code examples. It adds ten analysis tables and the edit-pattern Figure 11, expands Table 1 and introduces green highlighting. The original dataset statistics and PIE verification tables remain as Tables 5 and 14.

R1.justification: v3 adds references including GPT-4o, Qwen2, DeepSeek-Coder-V2 and BigCodeBench, while omitting WizardCoder. Its bibliography substitutes the DeepSeek-R1 report for the earlier DeepSeek-V3 report despite retaining DeepSeek-V3 experiments. Positioning relative to PIE and execution-feedback research remains substantially unchanged; moving related work to Appendix B is structural.

T1.justification: The pair-count formulas and their assumptions are retained from v2 Section 3.1 in v3 Section 2.1. No new theorem, proof or substantive formal revision appears. The added speedup rationale and prefix-sum case explanation do not change the mathematical framework.

improvement.justification: v2's PCO-versus-PIE comparison combines perspective and top-speedup selection. v3's matched random-selection control addresses this central attribution gap, while Table 3 tests the importance of executing test inputs. Python replication, failure analysis and measured runtime/hardware evidence further strengthen the paper's empirical support. The removed code-access link is a drawback, and main-result uncertainty remains unreported; hardware validation also covers only 20 pairs. These limitations do not outweigh the substantial improvement in evidence for the central explanations and practical applicability.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PCO and Anchor Verification research. Text, equations, figures, tables and appendices support reliable comparison, and retained material can be matched across restructuring and renumbering.

after.justification: v3 retains these empirical results and adds controlled ablations, Python experiments, failure analysis, runtime measurements and physical-hardware validation.

before.justification: v2 reports original fine-tuning and verification experiments in Tables 1, 2 and 4, alongside structural, semantic, human and LLM analyses.

C1.justification: v1 emphasizes prediction-based regularization and quantified 23% efficiency and 8% performance improvements in robotic manipulation. v2 drops those percentages, broadens the central claims to manipulation and locomotion, and claims competitiveness with model-based methods. Body-schema adaptation, previously discussed through qualitative examples, becomes an explicit main contribution.

C2.justification: v2 adds an explanation of how the agent-feature bottleneck discourages modeling unrelated dynamics. It hypothesizes that transferred hyperparameters and pixel-level reconstruction of changing backgrounds explain Distracting DMC failures, proposes contrastive learning as future work, and discusses computational overhead. The limitations involving fixed babbling and correlated agent/object motion were already present in v1.

D1.justification: v2 documents the 2048-dimensional projection, recurrent MLP normalization and activations, and simulator-derived SEAR masks, and changes the listed code repository. However, it omits Appendix A's detailed layer specifications, training tables, BAIR split, hardware, VRAM, and execution-time information. Some defaults move into the main text, but much reproducibility detail is lost.

E1.justification: v2 retains BAIR and the ten main Meta-World tasks, adds five previously untested Meta-World tasks, and includes Stick Push in the main 16-task comparison; Stick Push already appeared in v1's horizon ablation. Figure 7 additionally evaluates six Distracting DMC and three Hurdle DMC tasks, introducing different embodiments, locomotion, background distractions, and obstacles.

E2.justification: v2 adds Dreamer-v3 to the evaluated DrQ-v2 and SEAR comparator set (Figures 6–7). This introduces a model-based comparison absent from v1's experiments and supports a substantially broader comparative assessment.

E3.justification: RL defaults change from 50,000 to 25,000 babbling steps and from a 40-step to a 10-step prediction horizon. The aggregate evaluation changes from steps needed to reach 90% of best performance to performance at common threshold-crossing steps, averaged over 85%, 90%, and 95% thresholds. Ablations switch to Door Open episode reward. Hurdle aggregation membership remains unclear: Figure 1 labels two tasks, while Figure 7 plots three.

E4.justification: v2 adds gradient-based visualization of scene versus agent features and ablations of agent-feature dimensionality and babbling duration, while revising the existing loss-weight and horizon sweeps. Distracting and Hurdle DMC also test perceptual and control challenges absent from v1. BAIR prediction, unseen-trajectory generation, and Door Open/Hammer case studies already existed.

E5.justification: v1 reports three random seeds with best-to-worst ranges; v2 reports five runs with means and standard deviations. This refines an existing repeated-run uncertainty practice without adding confidence intervals or significance tests. Exact seed identifiers listed in v1's Table 3 are no longer provided.

E6.justification: v1's ten-task numerical summary and learning curves are replaced and expanded with revised curves and new aggregate results. For example, v2's Figure 1 reports Meta-World scores of 0.61 for DrQ-v2-EF versus 0.36 for DrQ-v2, but Distracting DMC scores of 0.41 versus 0.44. These are results under revised methods and protocols, not directly comparable gains over v1.

M1.justification: v1 separately encodes visual context and future proprioceptive states, combining reconstruction and scene-similarity losses. v2 splits a visual encoding into scene and agent features, recurrently predicts agent features from commanded actions, and reconstructs a sampled future frame without the similarity loss. This substantially changes inputs, architecture, and training objectives (Section 3).

P1.justification: The paper is retitled, the approach and RL background are substantially rewritten, and dataset-specific experimental sections become separate setup, disentanglement, and RL-evaluation sections. The conclusion gains distinct limitations and future-work discussions, while Appendix A and the checklist disappear. This substantially reorganizes the narrative.

P2.justification: v2 replaces the opening cartoon with feature visualizations and aggregate charts, redraws the architecture, expands and rearranges learning-curve panels, and consolidates ablations into Figure 8. The BAIR and unseen-trajectory displays are combined in Figure 5. All three v1 tables are removed, alongside a substantial template and layout change.

R1.justification: v2 removes the dedicated controllable-video-generation discussion, including Genie and UniSim, and expands positioning around visual RL and world models through TD-MPC2, Masked World Models, and newer robot-centric representation work. SEAR remains the closest prior method, while comparisons with model-based approaches and claims about supervised methods' embodiment limitations become more prominent.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulation changes through recursive agent-feature definitions and removal of v1's explicit slow-scene assumption and similarity-loss definition. v2 also revises the stated Bellman target to use the minimum of two target critics. These are changes to the model and objective formalization; neither version supplies theoretical guarantees or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's acknowledged narrow validation across agents, action spaces, and tasks. Feature-gradient evidence and component ablations better support the representation claims, while the expanded comparisons expose meaningful failure boundaries under distractions. Five-run evaluation also strengthens the empirical basis. Losing Appendix A's detailed settings and leaving Hurdle aggregation unclear weakens reproducibility and transparency, but the gains in validation and diagnostic evidence outweigh these losses.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Ego-Foresight by the same authors. All text, equations, tables, and figures support comparison, including v1's Appendix A and checklist. The complete v2 PDF ends with references and contains no appendix.

after.justification: v2 reports original prediction and feature-visualization results, learning curves across Meta-World and DMC tasks, and component ablations in Section 4.

before.justification: v1 reports original BAIR video predictions, Meta-World learning curves and numerical results, and hyperparameter ablations in Section 4.

C1.justification: The three-part decomposition and BA-LoRA contribution remain. V7 narrows the introduction's account of LoRA vulnerability to noisy or imbalanced adaptation without explicit regularization, presents the RoBERTa/T5 comparison as hypothesis-consistent evidence, and replaces the conclusion's broad state-of-the-art and safe-deployment claims with more bounded performance and robustness claims.

C2.justification: V7 explicitly acknowledges architecture and pre-training-objective confounding in the RoBERTa/T5 comparison (3.2.2, D.2, D.6), previously described as controlled. It removes the interpretation of MATH and GSM8K as creativity and robustness proxies, qualifies universal cross-model superiority, and adds explanations of minority collapse and capability retention. Teacher reliability, covariance decorrelation and ethical limitations receive more careful qualifications.

D1.justification: V7 documents how teacher and student NLU logits use a shared classification head, explains validation-based coefficient selection, and supplies practical calibration and tuning guidance. It clarifies aggregated GPU memory and Full Fine-tuning's out-of-memory status. Code disclosure changes from a promised release upon acceptance to reported public access to experiment scripts, substantially expanding reproducibility information.

E1.justification: V7 adds Wikitext-2 language-modeling evaluation to assess preservation of pre-trained capabilities after adaptation (C.7). Existing NLG, GLUE and imbalanced-MNLI coverage remains. GLUE-X disappears from the ethics statement, but v6 provides no corresponding experimental results or protocol establishing a removed evaluation.

E2.justification: Figure 2 adds Full Fine-tuning to the convergence comparison. New appendix comparisons include an entropy-regularized BA-LoRA variant and the unadapted LLaMA-2-7B reference. Comparator membership in the main benchmark tables remains unchanged; changing the stated NLU baseline count from ten to eight corrects prose.

E3.justification: New supplementary protocols evaluate global and minority-class silhouettes in pre-projection logit space, minority recall, and left-to-right Wikitext-2 test perplexity (C.6–C.7). The established benchmark training configurations remain substantially unchanged. Newly described validation-based tuning and shared classification heads are implementation disclosures, without evidence of revised earlier experiments.

E4.justification: C.5–C.7 add targeted tests of covariance versus entropy regularization, minority-class separation and recall, and preservation of pre-trained language-model behavior. These substantially extend the evidence addressing the proposed mechanisms beyond v6's ablations and visualizations. Figure 4 also revises sensitivity results; existing model-family and rank sweeps are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions retain three seeds (42, 1024, 2024) and the existing tables' plus/minus reporting. V7 introduces shaded bands around Figure 2's loss curves without defining whether they represent run variability, confidence bounds or smoothing. Consequently, a change in statistical uncertainty reporting cannot be established reliably.

E6.justification: New results include entropy-variant MNLI accuracy of 90.41, minority recall of 61.7 for BA-LoRA versus 26.4 for PiSSA and 5.8 for LoRA, and Wikitext-2 perplexities of 5.68, 7.12 and 5.42 for BA-LoRA, PiSSA and the pre-trained model. BA-LoRA's NLG average is corrected from 25.90 to 26.18 without changing constituent scores. Other averages and Figure 4 sensitivity points also change, including the selected consistency weight becoming a local MATH peak rather than a dip.

M1.justification: Equation 10 changes the NLG diversity loss from minus the mean of sum p log p to plus that mean, making minimization encourage entropy as intended. This corrects a consequential sign within the retained three-regularizer framework. The PDFs do not establish whether implementation changed or experiments were rerun.

P1.justification: V7 polishes and qualifies existing prose, condenses the PiSSA explanation, expands related-work and ethics discussion, and adds appendix subsections. The main section sequence and much existing exposition remain intact. Conference headers, contact information, acknowledgments and discussion numbering also change.

P2.justification: V7 adds Tables 11–14, redraws Figure 2 with Full Fine-tuning, revised legends and shaded bands, and replaces Figure 4's two shared-scale panels with four metric-specific panels. Existing tables are reformatted or relocated. Figures 1, 3, 5 and 6 retain their underlying graphics.

R1.justification: Related work substantially expands comparisons with C-LoRA, Bayesian PEFT and representation-learning approaches. V7 explicitly relates its regularizer trio to the already cited label-noise framework of Chen and colleagues, distinguishing output-space regularization from feature-space and parameter-space approaches. Appendix B.3 also develops the distinction from MiLoRA; these are substantive positioning changes beyond bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: V7 corrects the mathematical sign of the entropy objective and adds asymptotic computational-cost expressions for all three regularizers in NLU and NLG (C.8, Table 14). The existing initialization and other loss formulations remain substantively intact; no substantial theorem or proof framework is introduced.

improvement.justification: V7 resolves important correctness and evidentiary weaknesses: it fixes the entropy-loss sign and erroneous averages, adds direct minority-class and capability-retention tests, and acknowledges the confounding behind its central noisy-pretraining comparison. Clearer connections to preceding methods and expanded reproducibility information further strengthen the paper. Architectural confounding remains unresolved and Figure 2's bands are undefined, but the gains substantially improve the reliability and support of the retained contribution.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same BA-LoRA research. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and figures, support a reliable comparison. Extraction difficulties in some graphics were resolved through visual inspection.

after.justification: V7 retains these original results and adds regularization-objective comparisons, minority-class measurements and Wikitext-2 perplexity evaluations in Appendix C.

before.justification: V6 reports original BA-LoRA benchmark results, regularizer ablations, imbalance analyses and computational measurements, although some baseline scores are sourced from prior publications.

C1.justification: V1 foregrounds perturbation suppression, a fail-safe backbone, and temporal binary training. V2 makes an explicit corrective gradient path addressing STE's alleged blind spot central to its contribution, alongside the affine shortcut, LLM efficiency frontiers, and the claim that larger aggressively quantized models can outperform smaller higher-precision models at favorable efficiency.

C2.justification: V2 substantially changes the stability explanation toward error-dependent gradients, normalization analogies, and low-variance numerical failures. It adds interpretations concerning outlier localization, activation/weight precision allocation, and scaling. V1's explicit reshaping/ridge-overhead limitation disappears, while v2 introduces qualifications about energy-proxy omissions, including data movement and quantization overhead.

D1.justification: V2 adds PyTorch/A100 and JAX/TPU execution details, distinguishes simulated quantization from native low-precision inference, and supplies shortcut reference code. The core quantization/reconstruction snippets remain substantially equivalent. The earlier explicit block-reshaping matmul example is replaced by a shortcut snippet that assumes an additional helper function.

E1.justification: V2 substantially expands coverage with autoregressive language-model experiments on Shakespeare, OpenWebText, and C4. ImageNet classification and both WMT translation directions remain in A.2.7–A.2.8; their relocation does not constitute removed coverage.

E2.justification: V2 adds evaluated BitNet and ParetoQ comparators in the nanoGPT/GPT-2 experiments and substantially expands direct STE comparisons. BitNet was discussion-only in v1. The earlier ImageNet and WMT literature-comparison sets remain, while the multiplicative-mask sparsification baseline disappears with v1's Table 6 experiment.

E3.justification: New protocols include 124M-parameter GPT-2 training for 25k steps, Gemma 1B training on 6.5B C4 tokens with context length 512, and a 26B-token model-scale comparison. V2 also introduces C4 accuracy and arithmetic-energy-proxy evaluations and revises sparse-storage accounting to include sign and position bits. Retained ImageNet/WMT protocols are substantially unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 adds extensive tests of reconstruction versus STE, affine versus linear quantization, centered versus uncentered Hadamard transforms, FP4 versus INT4, and Gemma sparsity/efficiency trade-offs. The old block-size and lambda sweeps remain. V1's WMT sparsity sweeps and its unsuccessful multiplicative-perturbation experiment are removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports random seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, significance tests, or experimental uncertainty estimates. V2's additional tables and curves continue the point-estimate reporting practice.

E6.justification: V1 Tables 1–5 and 7–8 retain their numerical results as v2 Tables 7–13. V2 adds substantial results, including A1W1 affine SCQ-128 accuracy of 0.3751 versus STE's 0.3397 (Table 1), and sparse Gemma3-4B accuracy of 0.4517 versus Gemma3-1B BF16's 0.4494 (Table 6). These are new comparisons, not improvements over matching v1 runs. V1's WMT sparsity result tables are removed.

M1.justification: The core detached-error quantization and ridge-regression reconstruction remain, including the bias-free variant already present in v1's supplement. V2 adds a centered-Hadamard option with mean correction (A.2.3) and an affine-matmul shortcut using two rank-one corrections (Section 5), extending the computational procedures beyond v1's four-term expansion.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, motivations, and much of the method narrative are extensively rewritten around STE's blind spot and LLM efficiency. Related work and the earlier benchmark sections move into the appendix, while normalization and efficient matmul receive dedicated main-text sections. This is substantial rewriting and restructuring.

P2.justification: V2 replaces the original Figure 1 panels with new loss, affine-comparison, and efficiency-frontier displays, and adds scaling plots and ablation charts. Retained benchmark tables are relocated and reformatted, the WMT sparsity tables disappear, and reference code becomes appendix snippets. The document also changes from two-column to single-column layout.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands positioning around ParetoQ, QuEST, STBLLM, and rotation-based quantization, adding corresponding citations and comparisons of their approaches. It also changes the method's positioning from v1's 'forward implementation of the STE' to a claimed non-straight-through approach. This exceeds relocation of the original related-work section to A.1.

T1.justification: V2 adds the affine-matmul shortcut theorem and proof, a centered-Hadamard identity, and an asymptotic complexity analysis (Section 5, A.2.3, A.4). V1's explicit convergence/continuity propositions and perturbation-sensitivity derivation are no longer developed, although the ridge objective, closed-form reconstruction, and mean-collapse limit remain.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses v1's limited direct evidence for LLM applicability and comparative robustness through GPT/Gemma experiments and matched STE ablations, while retaining the established benchmarks. The shortcut proof and revised sparse-storage accounting materially strengthen the efficiency argument. These gains outweigh the removed WMT sparsity analyses, although stronger causal claims remain incompletely isolated, uncertainty reporting is still absent, and the energy results establish proxy-cost trade-offs rather than measured hardware savings.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ridge-regression-based quantization and sparsification framework. All 12 pages of v1 and 25 pages of v2, including appendices, are readable and support comparison despite extensive reorganization.

after.justification: V2 retains original ImageNet and WMT results and reports additional nanoGPT, GPT-2, and Gemma experiments, with numerical comparisons and training curves.

before.justification: V1 reports original ImageNet classification and WMT translation experiments, including quantization, sparsity, block-size, and regularization results.

C1.justification: V1's introduction explicitly limits its proved convergence contribution to one-dimensional Gaussians. V2 broadens this central contribution to Gaussian convergence under several settings, including the restricted multidimensional case. The identification of bidirectional IMF with IPMF and the conjecture of more general convergence remain.

C2.justification: V1 describes approximately equal CelebA target fit and groups MSE behavior mainly by solver. V2 interprets results through initialization-dependent target-fit and input-preservation tradeoffs, and explains why SDEdit couplings could begin closer to both desired marginals and an SB solution. General convergence remains an acknowledged limitation.

D1.justification: Appendix C.9 adds DDPM training specifications, SDEdit noising/denoising settings, the Stable Diffusion model identifier and prompt, guidance settings, resizing instructions, and implementation sources. Section 4.1 newly specifies three uniformly spaced intermediate times; v1 does not establish a different grid. Most existing implementation information moves from Appendix D to C.

E1.justification: Both versions use Gaussian transport, Gaussian-to-Swiss-roll translation, the same SB mixtures benchmark, colored-MNIST 3-to-2 translation, and CelebA male-to-female translation. SDEdit initializations retain the CelebA population and task; the changed Gaussian dimensionality is a setting revision within retained coverage.

E2.justification: Tables 1 and 2 retain the same comparison methods, including SF2M-Sink, the best-benchmark row, and the ASBM/DSBM initialization variants. The added SDEdit pipelines construct initial couplings within IPMF; they are not evaluated as standalone competing SB solvers.

E3.justification: Section 4.1 changes the Gaussian experiment from D=16 to D=128 at epsilon=0.3. Table 3 changes the stated initial DSBM training budget for CelebA Ind(p0,p0) from 20,000 to 100,000 gradient updates. V2 also introduces protocols for the SDEdit initialization experiments; these disclosures do not establish which existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 extends initialization analysis to learned image-translation couplings, testing their effects on target fit and input preservation using both solvers (Figures 5, 6, and 8). Figure 2 also adds separate optimality-matrix, mean, and covariance diagnostics beyond v1's aggregate KL curves, substantially expanding the evidence about how convergence proceeds.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-training-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Results remain point estimates and individual curves. The benchmark's Monte Carlo estimation descriptions, including 1,000 conditional samples and 10,000 target-distribution samples, are retained.

E6.justification: V2 replaces the Gaussian curves with results for D=128 and adds parameter-convergence outcomes. CelebA gains SDEdit results and revisions to existing curves: terminal DSBM-IMF MSE changes from approximately 0.42 to 0.18 (v1 Figure 7b; v2 Figure 8b), without explaining that revision. These are reported-result changes, not established same-setting performance gains. All numerical entries in Tables 1 and 2 remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The IPMF projection sequence and ASBM/DSBM fitting algorithms remain unchanged. V2 adds a concrete initialization component: constructing couplings through SDEdit using either a CelebA-trained DDPM or pretrained Stable Diffusion 1.5 (Appendix C.3). This extends initialization without redesigning the fitting procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, background, and experimental narrative undergo extensive rewriting. Contributions are reorganized, Gaussian proofs are restructured, experimental appendices C and D are consolidated, and broader impact moves into the main text. These are substantial editorial and structural changes beyond the added scientific content.

P2.justification: V2 converts the main text and references to two columns, adds the IPF/IMF/IPMF schematic, expands Gaussian diagnostics and CelebA displays, and restructures Table 3. The Swiss-roll figure moves to Appendix C with identical images, while colored-MNIST visuals are retained and rearranged. V2 also introduces the placeholder running header 'Title Suppressed Due to Excessive Size'.

R1.justification: V2 adds references supporting SDEdit, DDPM, latent diffusion, and matrix analysis, among others. It removes Ibe (2013) and Janati et al. (2020), including the latter's role in qualifying the earlier scalar Gaussian result. The central positioning as a unification of IPF and IMF is retained.

T1.justification: V1's scalar optimality coefficient and Gaussian-plan lemma become an optimality matrix and multidimensional Theorem 3.1.
