Theorem 3.2 extends exponential convergence to D>1 for discrete IMF with N=1 and sufficiently large epsilon. Appendix B adds matrix marginal bounds, Lipschitz analysis, and convergence proofs, while retaining the scalar analysis.

improvement.justification: The decisive gain is the extension from scalar-only convergence theory to a multidimensional analysis with explicit restrictions and supporting proofs (Section 3.2 and Appendix B), addressing a substantial part of v1's theoretical limitation. SDEdit experiments additionally connect initialization flexibility to practical image-preservation behavior. General convergence remains open, and unexplained revisions to existing CelebA curves limit empirical comparisons, but the stronger theoretical support and broader mechanism analysis provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same IPMF research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial rewriting and reorganization.

after.justification: V2 retains original experimental results and reports additional Gaussian diagnostics and CelebA experiments with SDEdit-based initializations in Section 4 and Appendix C.

before.justification: Section 4 and Appendix C report original Gaussian simulations, neural SB experiments, image translations, and quantitative evaluations. Explicitly borrowed benchmark rows are distinguished from the work's own results.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the BAMDP formulation, continuous MCTS and search-based policy-iteration contributions, together with performance claims on twelve D4RL and three tokamak tasks. The expanded comparisons provide additional support without materially redefining these core claims.

C2.justification: Appendix E.1 adds an interpretation of belief adaptation as model calibration and connects changing dominant ensemble members to prediction accuracy, while acknowledging the HalfCheetah-medium-expert likelihood exception. Appendix E.5 discusses the measured training-cost tradeoff. Earlier qualifications concerning supervised updates, warm-up training and history-free policies remain.

D1.justification: v2 supplies a specific codebase location and reproduction statements for the new comparisons; v1 referred to released code without providing a location. It also reports proposed-method runtimes on the specified hardware while retaining the detailed hyperparameter tables. Conversely, Algorithm 2 replaces an explicit value target with a less specific TD-loss description.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same twelve D4RL MuJoCo combinations and three simulated tokamak tracking tasks, including the same 725270-transition tokamak dataset. The added diagnostics and penalty experiments reuse this coverage.

E2.justification: v2 retains the earlier comparisons and adds MOBILE, CBOP, RAMBO, APE-V and MAPLE in Table 10. It reports author-run MOBILE results and CBOP reproductions, while distinguishing published baseline scores. This substantially broadens the comparison set beyond v1.

E3.justification: The original hyperparameter tables and principal evaluation settings are retained. New Appendix E.1 introduces offline transition-likelihood evaluation and rollout prediction MSE using 10000 starting states, controlled ensembles and behavior policies, and ground truth from simulator action replay. Table 10 additionally introduces a comparison matching BA-MCTS and MOBILE's world models and hyperparameters.

E4.justification: The existing zero-penalty ablation is retained as Table 9. v2 adds controlled tests of whether belief adaptation improves likelihood and prediction accuracy, a Hopper belief-trajectory case study, an alternative reward-penalty experiment, and an expanded computational-cost comparison. These substantially strengthen analysis of the method's mechanisms and tradeoffs.

E5.justification: The earlier three-seed mean/standard-deviation reporting and 95% confidence intervals are retained. Table 10 newly specifies seed identities 0, 1 and 2 for BA-MCTS/MOBILE and matching CBOP reruns. There is no reported increase in repetitions for the original experiments.

E6.justification: Original benchmark scores, reward ablations and learning curves are unchanged. New Tables 6–7 report likelihood and prediction-error results; Table 10 reports 80.25 for modified BA-MCTS versus 76.50 for MOBILE under their matched setup, plus CBOP reproduction results. Table 11 adds proposed-method runtimes. The 80.25 score uses a different penalty and setup, so it is not a same-setting improvement over v1's 74.45.

M1.justification: Section 4.3 and Algorithm 2 replace the explicit n-step target bootstrapped with search values by standard TD learning, and replace explicit uniform initialization with beliefs obtained from offline trajectories. Appendix E.4 also evaluates a variant using MOBILE's Q-target-disagreement reward penalty. These revise substantive components, although Continuous BAMCP remains stable. Short dataset-started rollouts were already documented in v1 Appendix C.

P1.justification: v2 substantially rewrites and condenses the introductory, background, related-work and methodological explanations. Evaluation is reorganized around six research questions and Sections 5.1–5.3, while appendix experiments are consolidated into E.1–E.5 and tokamak details move from G to D. This is extensive narrative and structural revision.

P2.justification: The main text changes from one column to two, with extensive changes to typography, headers and placement of displays. v2 adds Tables 6, 7 and 10 and the belief-adaptation Figure 3, and restructures the timing table to compare algorithms. Original plot images are retained and relocated; v1 Figure 3 becomes v2 Figure 4.

R1.justification: Section 3 adds substantive comparisons with offline meta-RL and model-based value expansion, including Dorfman, Choshen and Tamar, Feinberg, and Jeong; Appendix E.4 incorporates additional leading baseline literature. The earlier discussion of continuous BAMCP extensions, including Hoang and Vien, is removed. Much MuZero discussion moves to Appendix E.5 and is expanded.

T1.justification: The main BAMDP/Bellman equations and Appendix A's Lemma A.1 proof remain unchanged. v2 removes Section 2's explicit POMDP tuple and observation mapping, and adds the formal Q-target-disagreement penalty in Equation 7. These are limited formal changes without a new convergence theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: v1 supported its central model-accuracy argument mainly through policy returns; v2 adds direct, controlled likelihood and prediction-error evidence in Appendix E.1. The broader baseline comparison, matched MOBILE setup and transparent CBOP reproduction results in E.4 address important gaps in empirical validation. Runtime measurements and explicit code access further improve assessability. Algorithm 2's value-learning specification becomes less explicit, and the higher Table 10 score uses a modified configuration, but these qualifications do not outweigh the substantial gains in supporting evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same BAMDP-based offline reinforcement learning work. Their text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and can be matched despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds belief-adaptation diagnostics, evaluations with an alternative reward penalty, baseline reruns and runtime measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of BA-MBRL, BA-MCTS and BA-MCTS-SL on D4RL and three simulated tokamak tracking tasks, including reward-penalty ablations.

C1.justification: Weight-space discovery and multimodal applicability remain central. V3 adds prominent claims about operating without spurious-correlation counterexamples, scaling discovery to ImageNet-1k, exposing weaknesses across other classifiers, and regularization under perfect correlations. This substantially broadens v1's contribution centered on concept discovery and zero-shot bias prevention.

C2.justification: V3 explicitly separates its objective from measuring fairness, interprets synthetic controls as evidence against generation artifacts, and explains its absence of blonde-hair correlations. It removes v1's captioning, keyword-extraction, hierarchy and human-assistance caveats. Conversely, it acknowledges that manual checking restricted synthetic validation to a few discovered correlations.

D1.justification: V3 adds pseudocode, the exact Llama filtering model, an ImageNet filtering exception, the regularization coefficient, torchvision model/weight identifiers, and code-access information. Appendix C announces a later ImageNet-related data release; actual availability cannot be verified from the PDFs. V1's Nico++ construction details and cosine-annealing specification disappear. Algorithm 1 also introduces an index-versus-score ambiguity at lines 14–15.

E1.justification: Waterbirds, CelebA and CivilComments remain. V3 adds ImageNet-1k and synthetic test images combining depicted classes with discovered confounding concepts. It removes the custom four-class Nico++ evaluation, including its appendix results, and the Spawrious O2O-Hard example reported in v1's introduction.

E2.justification: V3 adds a quantitative Lg comparison on Waterbirds, absent from v1 Table 1 despite Lg appearing in its qualitative comparison. The new regularization experiment evaluates ERM, GroupDRO, random-concept regularization and Lg-based regularization against WASP-based regularization (v3 Table 3), substantially expanding the actual comparator set.

E3.justification: V3 introduces a protocol removing minority groups to enforce 100% spurious correlations, plus synthetic evaluation using 1,000 images per prompt, with/without-concept controls, softmax activations and prediction frequencies. The reported logit scaling also changes from a learned temperature in v1 to CLIP's temperature in v3. These are protocol changes, not merely additional documentation.

E4.justification: V1's final-minus-initial-weight scoring ablation disappears. V3 compares dynamic selection with top-30 and top-20% selection and tests modality-gap correction (Table 6). It also adds synthetic correlation-exploitation tests across classifier families and an ERM-versus-GroupDRO loss–concept correlation analysis after one training epoch (Appendix E, Figure 5).

E5.justification: V1 reports point estimates, whereas v3 introduces ± quantities for the accuracies in Table 3. V3 does not define these quantities or specify repeated-run counts or seeds, so this establishes added uncertainty reporting without establishing additional repetitions or significance testing.

E6.justification: The proposed method's reported zero-shot worst-group accuracies change from 55.3/75.6/53.7% to 50.3/73.1/53.2% for Waterbirds/CelebA/CivilComments (v1 Table 1; v3 Table 5). These accompany method changes and are not controlled same-setting regressions. Baseline values and concept rankings also change, while substantial ImageNet, regularization and loss-correlation results are newly reported.

M1.justification: The normalized linear-probe framework remains, but v3 adds Llama-assisted concept filtering, dynamic selection replacing the fixed top-15 cutoff, and negative-correlation scoring. It also introduces an SC-based regularization loss for mitigating learned correlations (Section 5.2, Equations 4–5). These change the procedure beyond renaming; Appendix C specifies that ImageNet filtering remains WordNet-only.

P1.justification: Beyond renaming ConceptDrift to WASP, v3 substantially rewrites the abstract, introduction and conclusion. Related work becomes Background before the method, the five-step presentation becomes initialization plus two stages with substeps, experimental setup is separated from evaluation, and the appendix is reorganized into sections A–E.

P2.justification: V3 adopts a two-column main layout and replaces the Waterbirds overview with an expanded ImageNet pipeline diagram. It adds synthetic-image illustrations, a threshold schematic and correlation plots, restructures the qualitative and zero-shot tables, converts prompt lists into a table, and adds extensive model-weight and concept-score tables. These are substantial visual and organizational changes.

R1.justification: V1's broad discussion of debiasing, fairness and invariant learning becomes a detailed taxonomy of error analysis, training-data analysis, manual interpretation and subpopulation-shift approaches. V3 adds substantive positioning against DrML, Singla and Feizi's work, and CoBalT, alongside modality-gap literature. Several earlier fairness and invariant-learning references are removed.

T1.justification: V1's Equation 2 and Appendix A derive and prove a cosine-similarity bound supporting the ranking rationale; v3 removes both the bound and its proof. V3 instead adds mathematical definitions for negative-correlation scoring, dynamic thresholding and SC regularization. Its positive-score minimum also includes all classes rather than explicitly excluding the target class. No replacement theoretical guarantee is provided.

improvement.justification: V1 mainly validates discoveries indirectly through zero-shot prompting and leaves cutoff selection unresolved. V3 introduces and evaluates adaptive selection, directly tests discovered correlations using synthetic controls (Tables 1–2), and adds regularization comparisons against random concepts and Lg under perfect correlations (Table 3). These substantially strengthen the empirical case. The gains outweigh meaningful drawbacks: removal of the supporting proof and limitations discussion, undefined ± reporting, and inconsistent cutoff pseudocode. Synthetic validation remains limited to a few manually checked correlations.

A1.justification: The same authors and class-initialized linear-probe/concept-ranking framework establish continuity despite the rename from ConceptDrift to WASP. Both PDFs, including figures, equations, tables and appendices, are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: V3 reports original synthetic ImageNet evaluations, fully spurious training experiments, zero-shot results, ablations and an appendix loss-correlation analysis.

before.justification: V1 reports original zero-shot classification results and ablations in Tables 1–2, plus extracted concepts for Waterbirds, CelebA, Nico++ and CivilComments.

C1.justification: v1's abstract, contributions, and conclusion emphasize latent geometry, early stabilization during training, and noise-image distance mappings. v2 instead centers reduced latent diversity in smooth regions, the concentration of approximation errors in early inversion steps, and consequences for interpolation and editing. Training-stability findings remain in Appendix G but cease to be headline contributions.

C2.justification: v1 already observes large inversion errors on smooth surfaces. v2 develops a substantive explanation involving reduced latent variance toward zero and early-step approximation errors, then connects these properties to manipulation failures and possible mitigation. It also acknowledges curved denoising trajectories and qualifies the obtuse-angle interpretation for the expanded model set. Some interpretations remain overgeneralized: Figure 5's LDM FID curves do not exhibit the deterioration described in its general caption.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-availability link, a model configuration table, checkpoint provenance, conditioning details, and latent dimensions. Appendices B–D document angle estimation, smooth-region masks with threshold 0.025, and the storage, replacement, and normalization of noise predictions. These substantially expand reproducibility information; most original training hyperparameters remain in Appendix G.

E1.justification: v1 studies unconditional generation and inversion on CIFAR-10, ImageNet, and CelebA. v2 retains these domains and adds image interpolation, class-conditioned generation, and text-conditioned editing with changed prompts. Its DeepFloyd IF experiments use Recap-COCO-30K prompts and a LAION-A-trained model, substantially extending the represented inputs and task requirements.

E2.justification: Neither version quantitatively benchmarks competing inversion algorithms; Renoise and Null-text inversion remain cited rather than evaluated comparators. Added ADM configurations, DiT, and DeepFloyd IF are models being investigated. The prediction-replacement variants are ablations, while Gaussian noise remains the reference throughout.

E3.justification: Correlation evaluation changes from top-10 pixel correlations over 2,048 samples to top-20 absolute correlations within 8x8 patches over 10,000 samples. Mean angles become constrained histogram-based estimates, and the stated assignment sample count changes from 1,000 to 2,000. New experiments introduce 50-step sampling, guidance scale 1, interpolation and prompt-swapping protocols, and additional quality, diversity, and alignment metrics. Appendix G describes training from scratch where v1 describes fine-tuning; this reporting change does not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds quantitative comparisons of smooth and non-smooth regions, isolates inversion error by timestep, and tests how replacing early predictions affects correlations, reconstruction, interpolation, and editing. It also extends assignment analyses to inverted latents. Most training analyses move to Appendix G, but v1's 50-nearest-neighbor coverage analysis and the CIFAR-10 training-angle panel are removed.

E5.justification: v2 adds angle-distribution histograms and replaces mean-angle summaries with constrained modal estimates. However, it omits v1 Section 4.1's explicit statement that training results average three models trained with different seeds. Both versions retain plus/minus reporting and shaded bands; v2 does not establish increased replication or introduce significance testing.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive regional-error, latent-assignment, interpolation, editing, and intervention results. For example, its new Table 12 reports DiT interpolation FID of 19.68 for standard latents and 17.51 after replacing five inversion steps. CIFAR-10 latent correlation changes from 0.462 in v1 Table 1 to 0.382 in v2 Table 2 under a different metric and sample count, so this is not a comparable performance improvement. Original noise-assignment entries survive in Table 11a, while v1's distance-versus-step entries are removed.

M1.justification: The underlying DDIM sampling and inversion algorithms remain unchanged. However, v2 Section 5 introduces a diagnostic adaptation that replaces selected early inversion predictions with stored outputs from the original sampling trajectory. This is a limited procedural modification requiring ground-truth access, rather than a new general inversion solver.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, experimental narrative, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Background and related work are merged, experiments are organized around explicit research questions and conclusions, and retained training analyses move into Appendix G. The title and DDPM/ADM terminology are also revised.

P2.justification: v2 switches from a single-column to a two-column layout, transposes the correlation table, expands and colors assignment tables, and redraws geometric displays. New visuals include an overview diagram, inversion-error schematic, regional masks, timestep-error plots, interpolation panels, and radar charts. Retained training plots and image grids move to the supplement, while some original panels disappear.

R1.justification: v2 replaces much of the semantic-feature and internal-latent-space survey with substantially expanded inversion, editing, and interpolation literature, including EDICT, LEDITS++, BELM, and NoiseDiffusion. It also qualifies the optimal-transport positioning by citing conflicting results from Kim and Milman and Lavenant and Santambrogio, rather than simply extending the earlier optimal-transport interpretation.

T1.justification: v2 introduces a formal constrained histogram-based triangle estimator in Appendix B and masked, normalized inversion-error definitions in Appendix D. The background also revises sigma_t to include a square root. The deterministic DDIM equations remain equivalent, and neither version develops formal convergence or correctness proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the explanation and practical relevance of v1's geometric observations. Regional measurements, isolated timestep errors, and interventions using stored ground truth connect inversion discrepancies to their origin and downstream effects (Sections 3.3–5 and Appendices C–F). Detailed procedures further improve reproducibility. These gains outweigh reporting weaknesses, including overgeneralized interpolation claims, unexplained zero IF CLIP entries in Table 7, and the omitted three-seed disclosure. The intervention evidence supports diagnosis, while its ground-truth requirement limits claims of a practical remedy.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DDIM inversion study, with matching authors, core variables, experiments, and retained figures. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison despite substantial revision.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical findings and adds regional inversion-error measurements, interpolation and conditional-editing evaluations, and controlled prediction-replacement experiments in Sections 3–5 and the appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original pixel-correlation measurements, geometric analyses, noise-image assignment accuracies, and training-dynamics experiments in Section 4 and Appendix A.

C1.justification: The central claims about smooth-region correlations, early inversion errors, reduced manipulability, and the forward-diffusion fix remain. v4 adds an explicit abstract and introduction claim that existing inversion methods do not fully resolve the problem, incorporating this comparison into its stated contributions.

C2.justification: v4 develops the variance-recovery rationale and interprets competitors' reconstruction, editability, and speed tradeoffs. It adds an argument that the extra reconstruction error at 4% replacement is perceptually negligible, without a direct perceptual study, and removes v3's statement that DiT edits align similarly with source and target prompts. Existing low-step failure conditions and the CelebA exception remain.

D1.justification: The new comparison reports solver configurations, ReNoise step/iteration settings, and function-evaluation counts. Estimated reproduction cost increases from 95 GPU hours in v3 Appendix C to 110 in v4 Appendix D. Conversely, the explicit 10,000-sample count for Table 2 disappears. Hardware information, pseudocode, and the code-access URL are retained.

E1.justification: The datasets and task domains are retained, including CIFAR-10, ImageNet, CelebA, Recap-COCO-30K, and ImageNet-R-TI2I. The added SDXL experiment uses the existing prompt domain and image-editing task; it expands model settings rather than establishing new dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: New Section 4.3 and Table 7 evaluate Pix2Pix-Zero, three ReNoise configurations, and first- and second-order DPMSolver inversion against DDIM and the proposed fix. v3 discusses related inversion methods but provides no corresponding empirical comparison with these competitors.

E3.justification: v4 introduces an SDXL evaluation using 2,000 generated images, roughly 50 function evaluations across different solver and ReNoise configurations, and reconstruction PSNR and inversion-time measurements. Appendix F adds replacement fractions from 0.1% to 4% at 1,000 steps, while Figure 4 adds a prediction-spread recovery metric. These are added protocols, not evidence that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Figure 4(b) newly tests whether early inversion predictions recover sampling-prediction diversity, and Table 9 tests the fix across replacement fractions at 1,000 steps. Figure 5 extends the fix's interpolation analysis across five existing models and the full path. Conversely, v3's global-variance analysis, DiT midpoint replacement-fraction table, and 20% editing-ablation rows are removed; the cumulative-error table is retained in Appendix J.

E5.justification: Both versions use selected plus/minus summaries without introducing new repeated-run counts, seed disclosures, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The added tables extend this reporting convention. Figure 4's standard-deviation ratio measures prediction diversity rather than uncertainty in an estimate.

E6.justification: v4 adds the SDXL comparison, 1,000-step fix results, and interpolation curves for 4% forward replacement. Existing DiT target-alignment values change from 0.689/0.568 in v3 Table 10 to 0.681/0.662 in v4 Table 6, matching values already in v3's appendix; these are reporting corrections, not demonstrated performance gains. Removed entries include global latent variances, IF triangle angles, and portions of the replacement-fraction ablations.

M1.justification: Equation (5) and Algorithm 1 retain the same procedure: apply forward diffusion to an early timestep, then complete DDIM inversion. The additional models and replacement-fraction experiments do not introduce a new algorithmic component.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contribution list, and conclusion are substantially rewritten. The analytical narrative is condensed, triangle results and cumulative-error reporting move to appendices, conditioning information is consolidated in Appendix G, and the fix's rationale moves before its evaluation. Section 3 becomes 'Analysis,' and an LLM-usage disclosure is added.

P2.justification: v4 changes the document template and substantially revises several displays: Figure 3 loses its LDM panel, Figure 4 gains the prediction-spread panel, and Figure 5 gains forward-replacement curves. Figure 7 corrects its DreamSim label and replaces the SSIM display with existing LPIPS results. New comparison and sensitivity tables accompany several table removals and relocations.

R1.justification: v4 adds citations for DPM-Solver, SDXL, and adversarial robustness, and more explicitly positions its analysis and fix against shortcomings of prior inversion work in Sections 3.1 and 4.3. Most related-work discussion remains; citation-style and publication-metadata updates do not constitute additional research-positioning changes.

T1.justification: Figure 4(b) introduces a recovery diagnostic defined as the ratio of inversion-prediction to sampling-prediction standard deviations. This is a limited mathematical-definition addition. The DDIM derivations, triangle optimization, mask definitions, and appendix error formulas remain unchanged, with no new theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: Section 4.3 and Table 7 address an important gap in v3: the fix lacked empirical comparison with competing inversion algorithms. The new evidence makes its reconstruction, editability, and runtime tradeoff assessable. Figure 4(b), expanded interpolation results, and Appendix F strengthen mechanism and efficacy support, while DiT corrections improve consistency. Some ablation detail is lost, IF alignment inconsistencies persist, and perceptual negligibility remains untested, but the overall gain in support for the practical contribution is substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DDIM inversion study. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and can be matched despite restructuring and renumbering.

after.justification: v4 retains original empirical results and adds inversion-method comparisons using SDXL, prediction-diversity analysis, and experiments applying the fix with 1,000 inversion steps.

before.justification: v3 reports original measurements of latent correlations, reconstruction, interpolation, and editing, plus appendix experiments on noise-image mappings and diffusion-model training.

C1.justification: v1 emphasizes the lowest training time and memory footprint against its compared methods. v2 narrows the central claim to resource efficiency among planar representations and competitive costs overall, foregrounding compatibility with image models. It also promotes the existing macro-only setting as ULW with the lowest per-scene memory requirement. This substantially redefines the contribution's scope.

C2.justification: The macro-only setting changes from an ablation illustrating quality degradation to an explicitly useful memory-quality tradeoff. v2 interprets SPARF texture errors through LPIPS and examples, and adds a specific limitation concerning inherited pretrained-VAE biases. v1's explicit suggestion to reduce the initial scene subset as future work is dropped.

D1.justification: v2 identifies Nerfstudio implementations for the single-scene baselines and documents CodeNeRF (MSIG)'s frozen-network, latent-code optimization in Appendix C. The project-page address changes with the method name. Core training hyperparameters remain identical between v1 Tables 7–8 and v2 Tables 13–14.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates ShapeNet Cars and Basel Faces. v2 retains these and adds training/evaluation on ShapeNet Furniture, Speakers and Sofas, substantially broadening represented object categories while retaining the many-view novel-view synthesis task.

E2.justification: The five previous baselines remain. v2 adds 3D Gaussian Splatting, CodeNeRF, the adapted CodeNeRF (MSIG), and SPARF-32/SPARF-128 to reported comparisons. These additions substantially expand the comparison to methods specifically relevant to learning many scenes.

E3.justification: The main NVS comparison changes from 50 sampled scenes per dataset to four per dataset: 16 ShapeNet scenes and four faces. Retained ablations and stage comparisons still use 50. Reported timing changes from four NVIDIA L4 GPUs to a single L4 basis. v2 also introduces CodeNeRF (MSIG)'s 1000-scene initial subset and adds LPIPS to the ablation evaluation; these changes do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: The existing component ablations and stage-specific quality checks remain, with the macro-only ablation renamed ULW. v2 adds a limited comparison of 500 versus 1000 initial scenes for CodeNeRF (MSIG) in Appendix C and targeted SPARF texture-failure examples in Appendix D.

E5.justification: Neither version reports seeds, repeated-run counts, error bars, confidence intervals or significance tests. Both provide point metrics averaged across sampled scenes. The changed scene sample size and added per-scene tables do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive aggregate and per-scene results for the expanded comparison, including SPARF-128's 0.82-minute training time versus Fused-Planes' 8.96 minutes in Table 1. Changed samples and timing conditions preclude interpreting headline differences as same-setting gains. Stage-specific scores are retained, while the matched ablation table adds LPIPS and changes Tri-Planes SSIM from 0.9512 to 0.953.

M1.justification: Fused-Planes retains v1's micro-macro decomposition, shared base planes, latent/RGB/autoencoder objectives and two-stage optimization. The ULW variant matches v1's macro-only ablation with zero micro features; its promotion and renaming do not establish a new procedure. Algorithm 1 is substantively unchanged.

P1.justification: The title, abstract and introduction are substantially rewritten around Fused-Planes and multi-scene inverse graphics. Related work is reorganized into multiple subsections, the experimental narrative is rebuilt around baseline categories, and appendix organization expands. These changes substantially alter the narrative beyond terminology replacement.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column main layout, redraws Figure 1 around per-scene costs with planar/non-planar distinctions, and restructures the main comparison table. It expands scaling plots and qualitative comparisons, adds per-scene tables and image grids, and introduces texture-failure close-ups. The architecture diagram is largely retained with revised labels and caption.

R1.justification: Section 2 expands substantially into discussions of shared representations and a taxonomy of single-scene, feed-forward and many-scene approaches, supported by a new appendix overview. New positioning against CodeNeRF, SPARF and C3-NeRF accompanies an explicit shared-planar-representation novelty claim. The renamed IG-AE citation refers to the same previously cited work.

T1.justification: The mathematical decomposition, rendering definitions, losses, optimization objectives and common-distribution assumption are retained. Resource formulas are restated using per-scene rates and shared-overhead notation within the same affine scaling model. No new theorem, proof or substantive mathematical derivation appears.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the evidence and positioning behind the central efficiency contribution. Adding SPARF and CodeNeRF exposes important competing resource advantages and supports narrowing v1's broad lowest-cost message to planar representations. Additional object categories, per-scene results and failure examples improve scrutiny. The reduction from 50 to four scenes per dataset in the main comparison, without uncertainty estimates, limits generalization; nevertheless, the expanded relevant comparisons and better-calibrated contribution resolve an important weakness of v1.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same micro-macro planar representation and two-stage latent-space training framework, despite the renamed paper and method. All pages, including equations, figures, tables and appendices, are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: Section 4 and Appendices B–D report original evaluations across four ShapeNet categories and Basel Faces, including expanded baseline comparisons, CodeNeRF sensitivity results and SPARF failure examples.

before.justification: Section 4 and Appendices A–B report original novel-view synthesis results, resource measurements, component ablations and stage-specific evaluations on ShapeNet Cars and Basel Faces.

C1.justification: The general claim of improvements across structure, fitness and function remains. v2 adds headline claims of practical antibody-loop improvement and improvement of 19% of BFVD structures, making these case studies central contributions. Its state-of-the-art fitness claim now rests on ProSST plus ProteinTTT rather than SaProt plus TTT.

C2.justification: v2 adds benchmark saturation as an explanation for smaller gains in larger models and interprets the existing hyperparameter grid as having two effective degrees of freedom. It also qualifies MSA customization through the MSA Transformer degradation finding and discusses large-database feasibility. The original perplexity explanation and overfitting/failure-mode cautions remain.

D1.justification: v1 promises a Python package; v2 Appendix D reports package availability and supplies usage and extension code, interfaces, and fuller hardware specifications. Appendix E and Table A3 add model/MSA configurations and disclose the early all-token, unnormalized loss used for starred fitness experiments. This substantially improves implementation documentation without establishing changes to retained experiments.

E1.justification: v2 adds SAbDab antibody CDR and antigen structure evaluation, plus large-scale viral-protein prediction using BFVD. These introduce distinct biological populations and specialized structural targets beyond the retained ProteinGym, MaveDB, CAMEO, TPS, DeepLoc and setHard coverage.

E2.justification: The fitness comparison removes TranceptEVE S/M/L and GEMME and adds ProSST. Structure comparisons add HelixFold-Single; Appendix B evaluates MSA Transformer, and BFVD comparisons include AlphaFold2 predictions. TerpeneMiner becomes EnzymeExplorer with the same described model and results, so that rename does not constitute a new comparator.

E3.justification: New protocols include 32-sequence MSA Transformer inputs, length-filtered SAbDab/BFVD evaluations, CDR-specific scoring, and 20 adaptation steps for BFVD. Retained benchmark splits remain unchanged. The masked-prediction baseline is now described as masking amino acids before the PLM rather than embeddings before the folding block (v1 Appendix A.2.3; v2 E.1.3), without establishing that its unchanged results were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds antibody and viral-protein case studies, MSA-subsample sensitivity findings, confidence-versus-reference-accuracy analyses, and CAMEO performance-versus-step curves. It replaces v1's ESM3 timing analysis with an ESMFold runtime analysis separating confidence-selection overhead. The original hyperparameter grids and per-protein analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Five-seed standard-deviation reporting for retained benchmarks is unchanged. v2 adds a paired t-test across fitness assays with p < 0.05, 95% confidence intervals from 1000 bootstrap samples for SAbDab, and explicit median/interquartile-range runtime summaries. These extend statistical reporting in specific comparisons.

E6.justification: Retained benchmark scores are unchanged, but v2 adds substantial results: ProSST improves from 0.5068 to 0.5087 Spearman, HelixFold-Single from 0.4709 to 0.4839 TM-score, and SAbDab LDDT improves for 115/175 CDRs and 487/814 antigens. MSA results and confidence-based BFVD outcomes are also new. These are added comparisons, not performance gains between versions under the original settings.

M1.justification: The single-sequence adaptation procedure, SGD optimization, LoRA and confidence-based selection are retained. v2 Appendix B adds ProteinTTT_MSA, which optimizes the existing loss over homologous sequences. This is an optional extension rather than a redesign of the core method.

P1.justification: v2 changes the title and terminology to ProteinTTT/customization and extensively rewrites the introduction, related work, method exposition and discussion. Structure evaluation precedes fitness; the perplexity discussion and detailed function evaluation move into appendices. The appendices are comprehensively reorganized with a contents page.

P2.justification: v2 redraws Figure 2, adds an architecture inset, antibody/BFVD figures, an MSA table, and new step-dependence and confidence plots. The ESM3 timing figure is removed and a different ESMFold timing figure appears. Existing function/perplexity displays move, while comparison tables are expanded or reformatted.

R1.justification: The research context is substantially refocused toward customization and practical antibody/viral applications. v2 adds recent fine-tuning and test-time learning work, including Schmirler et al. and Hübotter et al., alongside ProSST, SAbDab and BFVD references. It removes several earlier MSA/family-adaptation examples and Tranception/TranceptEVE references. Samusevich 2024/2025 is an update of the same cited work.

T1.justification: v2 Appendix B introduces the MSA-averaged objective and homologous-sequence distribution in Equation 4. The original masked-modeling loss, pseudo-perplexity argument and log-odds scoring mathematics are retained. Additional parameter notation and confidence-selection formalization mostly restate existing procedures; no new proof is supplied.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens practical applicability evidence beyond v1's selected CAMEO targets and standard benchmarks, especially through SAbDab comparisons against experimental structures and additional model/MSA evaluations. Code examples, hardware and loss disclosures, and added statistical analyses also materially improve reproducibility and evidential support. The BFVD 19% claim remains chiefly confidence-based, and some cross-reference and step-count inconsistencies persist, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial new validation and documentation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same per-protein test-time adaptation work despite the changed title. The complete main texts and appendices are readable, and retained methods, experiments, tables and figures can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds model comparisons, MSA adaptation experiments, and SAbDab antibody and BFVD viral-protein case studies.

before.justification: v1 reports original fitness, structure and function prediction experiments in Tables 1–3, with dataset analyses and additional experimental results in the appendices.

C1.justification: The abstract and new Contributions subsection broaden the stated application scope from minimal closed-form Wahba cases to related rotation-optimization problems, illustrated by residual and axis-prior uses in Sections 3.1–3.2. The central SU(2) derivations and two learning representations remain the principal contributions.

C2.justification: Appendix F adds explanations linking 2-vec to balanced gradients and QuadMobius to a stable intermediate representation followed by predictable projection gradients. It also discusses double-cover and redundancy problems in direct SU(2) prediction. Removing the NeRF experiment removes its specific overfitting interpretation; existing singularity and computational-cost qualifications largely remain.

D1.justification: Appendix G.1 supplies architectures, pretraining, dropout, training budgets, batch sizes, camera-loss weights, hardware, and checkpoint-selection details for the new benchmarks. G.2.2 newly identifies the retained synthetic network's source and T4 hardware, without establishing a hardware change or rerun. B.3.2 documents zero-division handling. NeRF implementation details disappear with that experiment.

E1.justification: v3 removes the NeRF synthetic lego experiment and adds object orientation from ModelNet10-SO3 images, inverse kinematics using human motion-capture poses, and joint camera-pose prediction on Cambridge Landmarks. Appendix F also introduces dropout-corrupted and outlier-contaminated input scenarios. Synthetic Wahba coverage is retained.

E2.justification: The established solver and learning baseline sets remain; Fast Quat is renamed Fast 2 Vec, still citing Markley (2002). Appendix F adds projection-only and eigendecomposition-only comparisons in Table 3 and a qualitative comparison with direct SU(2) prediction. Extending existing baselines to new benchmarks does not itself change their membership.

E3.justification: New protocols include ModelNet angular-accuracy thresholds and category-specific training budgets, joint-position losses for inverse kinematics, and joint rotation/translation training with checkpoint selection for camera pose. Appendix F specifies 1,000-input diagnostic studies and a 10,000-input component study. The retained synthetic experiments preserve their original generation and training design.

E4.justification: Appendix F adds gradient-balance analysis for 2-vec versus Gram-Schmidt, dropout sensitivity at different QuadMobius stages, gradient analysis under 10% outlier contamination, and component ablations separating projection and eigendecomposition. These investigate mechanisms and robustness beyond the retained noise-level and learning-configuration comparisons.

E5.justification: Two-point solver reporting expands from median error alone in v1 Table 2 to 5th, 50th, and 95th percentiles in v3 Table 5, adding empirical dispersion summaries. The million-trial and 10,000-timing-measurement counts remain unchanged. Neither version reports confidence intervals or uncertainty across repeated training seeds.

E6.justification: v3 adds benchmark and diagnostic results while removing the NeRF results. For example, its new King's College comparison reports mean angular errors of 2.631 degrees for QMAlg and 3.204 for QCQP. General Wahba results, all 24 learning configurations, and representation timings remain numerically unchanged. Two-point tail percentiles are newly reported; these changes do not establish same-setting performance gains between versions.

M1.justification: The Wahba solvers, exact-alignment procedures, 2-vec, and QuadMobius mappings are retained. v3 Eq. (26) algebraically combines the normalizations in v1 Eq. (48). The new residual and axis-prior passages describe applications of existing constraints without establishing a changed core estimator.

P1.justification: The narrative is substantially reorganized: mathematical background moves to Appendix A, rotation recovery to C.1, exact-alignment procedures to D, and synthetic learning experiments to G.2.2. A Contributions subsection and rewritten Sections 3 and 5 foreground applications and learning benchmarks. Derivation explanations are also substantially expanded.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column layout. v3 adds a conceptual diagram, benchmark tables, an inverse-kinematics display, gradient/dropout plots, and an ablation table. NeRF images and their table disappear; solver tables move and expand. The original learning curves are retained as Figure 6.

R1.justification: v3 adds references supporting axis-prior applications and new evaluation tasks, including Chandrasekhar, Magner and Zee, Chen, Kendall, Liao, and Walch, while removing the NeRF reference. Positioning relative to Gram-Schmidt, SVD, QCQP, and classical Wahba solvers remains substantially intact.

T1.justification: Appendix B.2 adds derivations of 2-vec and both QuadMobius mapping formulas. Appendix B.3.2 derives the polar-factor derivative through a Sylvester equation, whereas v1 explicitly omitted that derivation. The original metric, nearest-unitary, and two-point solution proofs are retained.

improvement.justification: v1 supported learning applicability mainly through synthetic points and one NeRF scene. v3 substantially strengthens that evidence through object images, real motion-capture inverse kinematics, and real camera-pose evaluation. Appendix F adds meaningful component and robustness investigations, while B.2–B.3.2 fills derivational gaps. These gains outweigh removal of the NeRF example, although absent training-seed uncertainty and insufficiently clear separation of checkpoint selection from testing still limit confidence in performance rankings.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SU(2)-based rotation-estimation work. All pages, including appendices, are readable, and methods, proofs, figures, and retained results can be matched despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v3 retains original synthetic results and reports additional object-orientation, inverse-kinematics, camera-pose, and representation-analysis experiments in Section 5 and Appendices F–G.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic Wahba simulations, neural-network learning experiments, NeRF camera-orientation experiments, and timing measurements in Section 5 and Appendix D.

C1.justification: V4 removes the prominent quantified speedup claims, including up to 1.47×, and shifts the abstract, contribution summary and conclusion toward LLM pretraining and image classification. The central one-line optimizer modification and convergence-preservation claims remain.

C2.justification: V4 adds interpretations concerning learning-rate robustness and Lion's stability, and Appendix F acknowledges masking/scaling costs and discusses distributed communication. It removes v3's model-size-gap interpretation and general resource-limitation paragraph, softens post-training universality to potential applicability, and adds a specific larger-scale C-Muon limitation. The central masking explanation and no-free-lunch qualification remain.

D1.justification: V4 documents extensive search grids and selected hyperparameters in Tables 5–6, additional C4 settings, Mini-ImageNet learning rates and distributed implementation/timing information. It removes v3's code-access link and A100/GH200 experiment-to-hardware mapping. The retained MAE hyperparameters move from v3 Table 4 to v4 Table 8 without changing.

E1.justification: V4 adds educational-web pretraining on FineWeb-Edu and supervised Mini-ImageNet classification. It replaces the six GLUE tasks with ARC Easy/Challenge, HellaSwag, LAMBADA, OpenBookQA, PIQA and MMLU. C4, the toy problem, instruction-tuning, RLHF and ImageNet-1K reconstruction remain, with the latter experiments relocated to appendices.

E2.justification: V4 adds evaluated LaProp and MARS comparisons against their cautious variants in Table 4, plus Muon versus C-Muon in Appendix E.3/Figure 9. AdamW and Lion remain in the C4 comparison, and GD/GDM remain in the toy experiments.

E3.justification: The main C4 evaluation changes from 60M–1B models trained for 10K steps with sequence length 256 to a 100M model trained for 50 billion tokens with sequence length 1024, larger batches and learning-rate sweeps. New FineWeb-Edu scaling uses 130M–1.2B models, 1× Chinchilla budgets, sequence length 4096 and separate hyperparameter searches (Tables 2, 5–6). These are revised or new experimental designs.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained toy-mask and sparsity analyses, v4 adds practical learning-rate sensitivity and gradient-clipping comparisons, a linear-decay scheduler test, and a 60M batch-size sweep (Table 1, Figures 5–8, Table 7). V3's separate shared-hyperparameter toy plot, Figure 2, disappears, although its discussion remains.

E5.justification: V4 Table 3 adds ± uncertainty values to downstream scores, whereas v3 Table 2 reports point scores alone. The uncertainty statistic and repeated-run or seed counts are not specified, so this establishes added uncertainty reporting rather than an increase in experimental repetitions.

E6.justification: V3's C4 scaling and GLUE result tables are replaced by substantially different reported evaluations. V4 Table 1 reports AdamW/C-AdamW perplexities of 18.965/18.684 at learning rate 0.01; Table 4 reports Mini-ImageNet accuracies of 72.11/73.52. C-AdamW scores higher on five of seven new downstream tasks. Scheduler, batch-size, Muon and timing results are added, while post-training and MAE curves are retained. These are new or reconfigured experiments, not same-setting v3-to-v4 performance gains.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1–3 retain the alignment mask, normalization, momentum updates and weight-decay procedures. The additional cautious optimizer instances apply the existing generic rule; v4 does not introduce a distinct update component, objective or architecture.

P1.justification: The empirical narrative is substantially reorganized: Section 3.2 is rewritten, image classification becomes a main subsection, and the previous post-training and MAE subsections move to Appendices E.4–E.5. Experimental appendices are reorganized into dedicated sections B–F, with corresponding abstract and conclusion edits. Most theory prose remains intact.

P2.justification: The main text changes from a two-column format to a single-column ICLR layout. Training-curve displays are removed, retained toy figures and heatmaps are relocated, and new search, scheduler, Muon and tabular displays substantially reshape the presentation. Post-training/MAE figures move to the appendix. V4 also introduces visible mathematical typesetting defects and clipped proof lines on page 18.

R1.justification: V4 adds CADAM as concurrent online-learning work and citations supporting the new optimizers, datasets, scheduling and evaluation benchmarks. It removes the GaLore/OSD discussion and the GaLore and GLUE references. The broader positioning around simple Adam-like modifications and Hamiltonian analysis remains.

T1.justification: The Hamiltonian framework, assumptions, Theorems 2.1–2.4 and Appendix A derivations, proofs and inner-product-mask results remain substantively unchanged. V4 introduces notation/typesetting defects, including stray v prefixes and a malformed bracket in Example A.1, without a substantive revision of the mathematical reasoning.

improvement.justification: V4 substantially strengthens the central optimizer comparison through learning-rate sweeps, separately tuned scaling comparisons and scheduler/batch-size checks (Tables 1–2, 5–7). These address an important weakness of v3's fixed-learning-rate LLM evidence: whether gains depend on favorable tuning or training conditions. Removed code/hardware disclosures, mathematical typesetting regressions and inconsistencies between tuning/throughput claims and reported values are drawbacks. Nevertheless, the more controlled empirical evidence substantially improves the paper's credibility and usefulness.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Cautious Optimizers work. Their main texts, figures, tables, equations and complete appendices support comparison, including matching relocated experiments and proofs. V4's typesetting defects do not prevent identifying the substantive changes.

after.justification: V4 reports original C4 and FineWeb-Edu pretraining, downstream benchmark, Mini-ImageNet classification and robustness results, alongside retained post-training and MAE experiments.

before.justification: V3 reports original toy-optimization, C4 pretraining, GLUE evaluation, instruction-tuning, RLHF and ImageNet-1K MAE results.

C1.justification: Both versions claim a first distractor-free generalizable 3DGS framework, improved training robustness, inference artifact suppression and generalizable mask prediction. The rewritten abstract and introduction preserve these contributions and their scope.

C2.justification: V3 newly argues that geometric consistency matters more than precise segmentation boundaries and explains why relaxed or angle-weighted mask fusion can admit harmful distractors. It also discusses residual distractors in evaluation targets and expands the existing common-occlusion limitation with an explanation involving absent completion capabilities and concrete failure examples.

D1.justification: Appendix A supplies previously unavailable image resolution, 10K-iteration training budget, PyTorch/CUDA versions, RTX 3090 hardware, synthetic distractor frequency and coverage, and baseline integration details. It specifies, for example, that NeRF-HuGS uses SAM/COLMAP but excludes Nerfacto. These are new disclosures, without establishing changes to existing experiments.

E1.justification: On-the-go, RobustNeRF and COCO-augmented Re10K/ACID remain the dataset coverage. Appendix B.10/Table 7 additionally document Statue evaluation without access to clean references and with partially clean references, extending the explicitly tested input conditions beyond v2's stated mixed evaluation pool.

E2.justification: V3 adds Mvsplat+HybridGS to Table 1 and MVSgaussian on Arcdetriomphe to Table 12. Table 7 adds standalone scene-specific comparisons, including NeRF-W and HA-NeRF, while Table 3 adds a published SLS single-scene result. These substantially broaden the reported comparator set.

E3.justification: V3 supplies additional protocols for single-scene training and controlled reference cleanliness (Table 7), real-to-synthetic inference versus synthetic fine-tuning on separate training scenes (Table 10), and resource profiling across resolutions and reference counts (Table 8). The principal N=4, K=8 and PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS setup remains.

E4.justification: V3 adds reference-versus-query accuracy across training checkpoints, segmentation removal/SAM2 comparisons, feature-consistency and clustering alternatives, relaxed and angle-weighted mask fusion, resource scaling and illustrated failure cases. These examine several previously untested design questions. V2's reference-count ablation and parameter plots are retained through relocation.

E5.justification: Neither PDF reports repeated-run or seed counts, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. V3's checkpoint comparison reports point estimates rather than run-to-run uncertainty.

E6.justification: Matched headline results remain unchanged, including DGGS's 21.74 mean PSNR in Table 1. V3 substantially expands result entries through new comparators, ablations, resource measurements and single-scene results. Table 10 newly reports 26.51 PSNR for real-to-synthetic DGGS and 29.66 after synthetic fine-tuning; these are different settings, not version-to-version performance gains.

M1.justification: Section 4 retains reference-based mask prediction, segmentation refinement, auxiliary supervision, reference scoring and selective Gaussian pruning. The added SAM2 and mask-fusion variants are experimental analyses of this retained design.

P1.justification: V3 rewrites the abstract and opening introduction, moves experimental setup from Section 5.1 into Appendix A, simplifies several subsection hierarchies and reorganizes the experimental narrative. It also adds reproducibility and acknowledgement sections and structured supplementary discussion.

P2.justification: V3 adds Tables 5–12 and additional qualitative and failure displays. V2's Table 4 moves to Table 13, Figure 9 becomes appendix Figure 10, and Figure 6's mask panels are split between Figures 6 and 12. Main tables are reformatted and the document adopts ICLR typography and headers.

R1.justification: The bibliography adds six works, including SAM2, DINOv2, COLMAP and a 3DGS survey. These mainly support implementation and supplementary discussion. The related-work taxonomy and positioning against scene-specific distractor removal remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulation is retained. V2's mask-fusion Equation 6 becomes inline mathematics and subsequent equations are renumbered. No substantive formal definitions, assumptions, derivations or proofs are added.

improvement.justification: For the supplied PDFs, v3 substantially strengthens the paper's evidential support and reproducibility. Tables 5–6, 9 and 11 directly examine central reference-rendering, segmentation and fusion assumptions; Table 10 adds quantitative synthetic evidence; Appendix A fills important implementation and data-construction gaps. Some added variants remain briefly specified and uncertainty reporting is unchanged, but the gains materially improve how readers can assess and reproduce the work.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DGGS work, with readable and directly matchable methods, equations, figures and main results. However, v2 ends at the references despite citing an appendix, whereas v3 includes Appendices A–C. Earlier supplementary material therefore cannot be checked; additions below refer to content newly supplied in v3.

after.justification: V3 retains those original results and reports further segmentation, mask-fusion, reference re-rendering, synthetic-transfer and single-scene experiments.

before.justification: V2 reports original DGGS reconstruction experiments, fine-tuning results and component ablations in Tables 1–5 and Figures 5–10.

C1.justification: v2 makes diagnosis beyond known candidate variations, continuous vision-language exploration, superiority over RL/VLM baselines, and demonstrated policy improvement central contributions. v1 primarily claims proactive vulnerability mapping and presents retraining as a potential application; its conclusion leaves substantially enlarging the action space to future work.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations for semantic guidance, embedding separation and joint fine-tuning, plus an explicit limitation for environments far from known examples. It also introduces FSI-based robustness interpretations. A new unresolved tension appears: v1 associates uniform action probabilities with indiscriminate vulnerability, whereas v2 Figure 8 labels a uniform distribution as ideal zero failure, without reconciling these interpretations.

D1.justification: v2 adds UR5e setup information, RL comparator configurations, VLM video preparation using 15 frames per trajectory pair, five-shot prompting details, and explicit action-to-language mappings with resize dimensions. It also adds a project-page pointer. Conversely, v1's layer-by-layer NatureCNN description and several PPO parameters are no longer supplied. These are documentation changes; the pointer alone does not establish code availability.

E1.justification: v1 reports simulated manipulation with displayed results centered on cube/table color and table-size perturbations. v2 adds physical UR5e object pickup, Square, Threading and Pick & Place evaluations, and explicit unseen-object/environment tests. Lighting, robot/gripper appearance and object-shape variations broaden the tested conditions (Tables I, III–IV; Figure 18). Lift-like demonstrations and stacking already appear in v1.

E2.justification: v1 characterizes robot policies without benchmarking competing diagnosis methods. v2 Table I directly compares RoboMD with A2C, SAC, Qwen2-VL, Gemini 1.5 Pro, GPT-4o and GPT-4o with five-shot in-context learning. These are newly evaluated diagnosis comparators; the retained BC, BCQ and related policy profiles concern policies under test.

E3.justification: v2 adds ground-truth success/failure pair ranking accuracy, including an evaluation using 100 unseen pairs, instead of relying primarily on displayed action probabilities. New designs include matched-timestep RL exploration comparisons, multiple fine-tuning conditions, FSI, and embedding MSE/Frobenius-distance evaluations. These are added evaluation protocols; the PDFs do not establish that retained profiles were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's illustrative perturbation case and alternate displays of failure profiles, v2 tests RL exploration diversity, loss and image/text backbone choices, kNN neighborhood sensitivity, representation-training dynamics, and joint versus sequential fine-tuning conditions (Figures 6, 9, 14–16; Table V). These analyses investigate design choices and robustness rather than merely redisplaying existing results.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run or seed counts, confidence intervals, standard deviations, error bars or significance tests for its experiments. Entropy and FSI describe failure distributions, rather than statistical uncertainty in the reported estimates.

E6.justification: v2 retains all six original entropy values in Table II and two radar profiles in Figure 7, while omitting the other detailed profiles. It adds extensive accuracy, ranking, embedding-quality and fine-tuning results. For example, Table I reports PPO accuracies of 82.3%, 84.0% and 76.0% for Lift, Square and Pick Place. These are newly reported evaluations, not same-setting performance gains over v1.

M1.justification: v2 extends discrete PPO failure search with a ViT–CLIP/MLP embedding, BCE/contrastive training, continuous action search with embedding-distance and repetition penalties, density-based ranking, and failure-guided fine-tuning (Sections III-B–D). These are substantive components beyond renaming. The stated discrete success reward also changes from -100/horizon in v1 to -Csuccess*t in v2.

P1.justification: The title, framework name, abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten. The separate failure-analysis section is incorporated into a reorganized methodology covering candidate diagnosis, generalization, ranking and improvement. Experiments are reorganized around explicit research questions, and the appendices are substantially restructured. This exceeds terminology changes or prose added solely to describe new experiments.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column layout, redraws the framework overview, and adds embedding diagrams, benchmark tables, physical-robot illustrations and analysis plots. v1 Figure 2 moves to appendix Figure 13. Two earlier radar plots are incorporated into Figure 7 alongside a new physical-robot plot, while the original stacked bars, heatmap and individual bar-chart displays are removed.

R1.justification: v2 substantially repositions the contribution around generalizing failure search beyond fixed candidates, distinguishing it from standard VLM queries, brute-force evaluation and uncertainty estimation. It adds references including REFLECT, generalization-gap and scaling studies, ViT, CLIP, Diffusion Policy and MimicGen, while dropping references such as Octo and Open X-Embodiment. Many earlier failure-analysis and safety references remain.

T1.justification: v1's discrete MDP/PPO/softmax formulation is extended with a mathematical embedding objective, distance-penalized continuous reward, Gaussian action-density comparisons and nearest-embedding reliability measure (Sections III-B–C). v2 also defines the weighted Failure Severity Index in Section IV-B. These substantially extend the formal construction, although no calibration or generalization theorem is added.

improvement.justification: v1 mainly displays the diagnostic agent's action probabilities without benchmarking diagnosis accuracy or demonstrating policy repair. v2 adds ground-truth ranking comparisons, physical-robot evidence, controlled embedding ablations and actual manipulation success rates after fine-tuning (Appendix Figure 14), substantially strengthening validation of usefulness and design choices. Reporting remains imperfect: Table I's GPT-4o average does not match the arithmetic mean of its task scores, Figure 8's zero-failure interpretation remains unsupported by normalized action probabilities, and repeated-run uncertainty is absent. These limitations qualify but do not outweigh the substantial improvement in empirical support.

A1.justification: The PDFs describe the same research framework, renamed from RoboFail to RoboMD and substantially extended. The retained discrete method and matching results establish continuity. Both documents, including their figures, equations, tables and appendices, support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds diagnostic accuracy benchmarks, physical-robot results, embedding ablations and policy fine-tuning outcomes in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original simulated perturbation experiments, failure profiles and entropy values for six robot policies in Figures 2–6, including appendix visualizations.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction replace the 300% greater-gain headline with up to 100% and extend the stated empirical support to nuScenes and Waymo. The central contributions—joint rendering-based pre-training, curvature sampling and prototype learning—and the potential-scaling claim remain.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the new experiments as evidence of broader task applicability and robustness to random seeds. The prototype visualization interpretation narrows from learning semantic understanding to representing scene parts. Existing qualifications about noisy assignments and untested large-scale pre-training remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds Swin encoding, LiDAR-depth projection and derivative-implementation details, eight-H100 hardware, approximately 45 minutes per pre-training epoch, and 108/252 downstream epochs. Existing learning-rate and masking details move to the supplement. However, the image-checkpoint source citation becomes unresolved; code and models remain promised rather than newly available.

E1.justification: v2 adds Waymo 3D object detection and Semantic KITTI LiDAR semantic segmentation, substantially extending both dataset and task coverage. nuScenes detection and the supplementary ONCE transfer experiments are retained.

E2.justification: The nuScenes comparison in Table 1 expands from random initialization and UniPAD to include ALSO, OCC-MAE, SLidR and PPKT. These are evaluated comparators, spanning additional pre-training approaches, rather than citation-only additions.

E3.justification: New protocols include Waymo's 798/202 scene split, CenterPoint fine-tuning with 1% labels, and Level-1/Level-2 mAP and mAPH evaluation. Supplement Section 2.1 adds Cylinder3D segmentation evaluated with mIoU. Existing convergence-matched fine-tuning remains; the newly stated nuScenes epoch count is additional documentation.

E4.justification: Supplement Section 2.2 adds a study explicitly testing robustness to random seeds through repeated fine-tuning of random initialization, UniPAD and CLAP. The component ablation, reduced-label analysis, ONCE transfer analysis and curvature/prototype visualization examples are retained.

E5.justification: v1 provides no run-count or dispersion reporting. v2 discloses a common fixed seed for main experiments and reports means and standard deviations across five nuScenes fine-tunings for three initializations. This adds uncertainty reporting for the central comparison, but not the full expanded evaluation.

E6.justification: v2 adds baseline, Waymo, segmentation and repeated-run results. Examples include CLAP's 62.87% Waymo Level-1 mAP and 34.28% segmentation mIoU versus UniPAD's 31.88%. Retained nuScenes, scaling, ablation and ONCE scores are unchanged, but Table 1 corrects UniPAD's gain from +0.72 to +1.12. The new segmentation gain annotation is inconsistent: 31.88 minus 28.23 is 3.65, not the reported 3.55.

M1.justification: Section 3.3 changes sampling weights from the component average of the curvature quantity to its L2 norm, changing the stated sampling distribution. The joint pre-training pipeline and its EM, swapping-prediction and Gram-regularization components remain.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten, contributions are reorganized, and Section 3.4 is renamed Prototype Learning with EM presented before swapping prediction. The supplement expands from two sections into implementation details, several experimental subsections, visualization and social-impact discussion. These constitute substantial narrative restructuring.

P2.justification: Table 1 gains comparator rows, a Waymo table is added, and retained tables move and receive new numbering. Figure 2 revises prototype labels and corrects the Gram-regularization target; other figures retain their examples with resizing. The supplement acquires review headers, line numbers and separate table/figure numbering.

R1.justification: v2 explicitly distinguishes CLAP's cross-modal scene-part prototypes from SwAV's image-category prototypes. It adds references for the new baselines, Waymo, Swin, convergence-related work and differential geometry, while MMDetection3D, ONCE and the detection-survey bibliography entries disappear. The overall research positioning remains joint multimodal pre-training.

T1.justification: Section 3.3 replaces the component-average construction described as mean curvature with a norm-based quantity described as geodesic curvature, explicitly defining the sampling weight as the L2 norm and adding a geometry reference. This is a localized mathematical-definition revision; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's narrow comparative evaluation through four additional pre-training baselines, Waymo detection and a segmentation task. The five-run analysis strengthens evidence that the central advantage is stable, and the UniPAD gain correction improves accuracy. These gains outweigh the unresolved appendix citations, sparse segmentation settings and new gain-annotation error, although those defects limit reproducibility and polish.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CLAP, and all 13 pages of each, including the supplementary material, are readable. Methods, equations, tables and figures can be matched reliably. Unresolved appendix citations in v2 reduce traceability but do not prevent comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds Waymo detection, Semantic KITTI segmentation, additional baseline evaluations and repeated nuScenes fine-tuning results.

before.justification: v1 reports original nuScenes detection experiments, component ablations, reduced-label evaluations and ONCE transfer results in the supplement.

C1.justification: The abstract and central training-free uncertainty-estimation and active-learning contributions remain. v2 adds an explicit claim that Bayesian methods have not previously been employed for VLM uncertainty quantification. Its cosine-approximation contribution bullet now specifies Gaussian embeddings rather than broadly referring to probabilistic embeddings.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly identifies Gaussian feature distributions and restriction to Bayesian projection layers as limitations, and interprets the new Hessian and EuroSAT analyses. It removes v1's specific warning about variance overestimation at high cosine similarity and its detailed generative-VLM outlook. The proxy-training-data mismatch limitation remains.

D1.justification: v2 adds construction/prediction pseudocode, an explicit probit prediction formula, and runtime-measurement details including V100 hardware, batch size one, and three warmup steps. It drops v1's specific PCME++ checkpoint and adapter-training dataset information. The fine-tuning hyperparameters, general GPU information, and code-access link remain.

E1.justification: v2 adds CIFAR-10, UCF101 action recognition, SUN397 scene recognition, and zero-shot ImageNet-R evaluation. DTD evaluation disappears, while EuroSAT leaves the benchmark tables but gains a before/after active-learning case study. OfficeHome coverage otherwise persists; v2's three-domain pool description conflicts with its appendix's four-domain description, so removal of the real-world domain is not established.

E2.justification: TTA is newly evaluated against BayesVLM in the CLIP and SigLIP comparisons. ProLIP mean embeddings are newly compared with ProbCosine in Table 3. The existing PCME++ comparison is retained separately in Table 11 rather than alongside CLIP and BayesVLM as in v1 Table 1.

E3.justification: v2 adds a reported ViT-L-14 zero-shot configuration, EuroSAT evaluation with 200 support points, a Hessian minibatch sweep, and timing/GFLOP protocols. Its main text revises Hessian samples from 30k to 327k and the tau search limit from 50 to 200. Those later values already appeared in v1 Appendix D, so these revisions do not establish increased experimental budgets or reruns.

E4.justification: New analyses examine predictive error versus entropy before and after EuroSAT active learning, Hessian-trace stability versus sample count, and computational overhead. These test calibration behavior and practical estimation costs absent from v1. The corruption example, Monte Carlo approximation check, and k-NN distance ablation are retained, sometimes relocated.

E5.justification: v2 Figure 10 introduces means and plus/minus one standard deviation over 10 random LAION subsets; runtime measurements are averaged over 1000 runs. The existing test-set standard errors and paired t-test at p = 0.05 remain. There is no documented increase in repeated training runs.

E6.justification: Numerous zero-shot entries change: CLIP-base BayesVLM ECE moves from 0.79 to 1.91 on Food-101 and from 2.69 to 1.77 on CIFAR-100; temperature-scaled SigLIP's Flowers-102 ECE changes from 62.79 to 6.28. v2 also adds extensive comparator, model, diagnostic, and cost results. These are revised reports, not established same-setting performance gains given the protocol ambiguities.

M1.justification: Both versions use projection-layer Laplace/KFAC posteriors, Gaussian cosine-similarity approximation, probit predictions, and targeted BALD/EPIG with online Laplace updates. ProbCosine names the existing approximation; Algorithms 1–2 document the existing procedure rather than establish a new method.

P1.justification: The introduction is extensively rewritten, background is separated from the proposed method, and the cosine approximation is integrated into BayesVLM under the ProbCosine name. Experiments receive a dedicated setup subsection and question-led organization; the conclusion is shortened and appendices are reorganized. These exceed renumbering or isolated wording edits.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is substantially redrawn as a full-width overview. v2 adds a method-family comparison table, two algorithm blocks, EuroSAT and Hessian plots, and runtime/GFLOP tables. Zero-shot tables are expanded and separated by model, while the approximation-quality figure moves to the appendix. Existing active-learning and corruption plots are largely retained.

R1.justification: The introduction shifts from few-shot support-set selection toward four uncertainty-estimation desiderata and a new comparison of method families in Table 1. New discussion and citations cover TTA, ensembles, dropout, Dirichlet uncertainty learning, and Bayesian language-model adaptation, while much of the earlier foundation-model and few-shot framing is removed. The explicit first-Bayesian-VLM claim further changes positioning.

T1.justification: v2 corrects the text-side Kronecker-factor definition to use the text encoder psi instead of phi (v1 Equation 24; v2 Equation 22). It also removes v1's inconsistent main-text online-update equations while retaining the square-root-weighted appendix formulation. The principal Laplace and cosine-similarity derivations otherwise remain.

improvement.justification: v2 supplies previously missing quantitative support for central practical claims through Hessian-stability analysis and measured runtime/GFLOP comparisons (Figure 10; Tables 7–8). TTA and ProLIP evaluations strengthen validation, and explicit algorithms improve procedural clarity. These are substantial gains despite reporting weaknesses: some performance summaries exceed the tables' findings, and OfficeHome-domain and large-versus-huge model descriptions remain inconsistent.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same BayesVLM work. All 21 pages of v1 and 22 pages of v2, including appendices, equations, tables, and figures, support comparison. Internal reporting inconsistencies do not prevent comparison of the available material.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds evaluations including TTA and ProLIP comparisons, EuroSAT error analysis, Hessian-estimation sensitivity, and computational costs.

before.justification: v1 reports original zero-shot classification, active-learning, corruption, approximation-quality, and distance-metric ablation results in the main text and appendices.

C1.justification: The central benchmark, DSL, and neuro-symbolic-superiority contributions remain. v3 adds a 'first open-ended' novelty claim and explicitly frames its validation/test design as assessing unseen-composition generalization. Its abstract updates the headline result to 37.0% and a 10× advantage, while the introduction retains 27.9% versus 2.60%.

C2.justification: v3 develops substantial new interpretations concerning contextual complexity, TTG scalability, diminishing refinement returns, and conflicting preferences. It attributes some translation failures to constraint deletion and offers hypotheses about Chinese-language exposure, extending v1's mainly qualitative diagnosis. The original limitations concerning Chinese-language specificity and limited human data are retained in Appendix A.
