D1.justification: v3 adds detailed environmental-constraint semantics, DSL tutorials and preference implementations, solver configurations, questionnaire instructions, recruitment/payment information, and a multistage annotation workflow. These substantially extend v1's existing API, concept-function, and prompt documentation. It also removes the project-webpage pointer and adds CC-BY-NC 4.0 licensing and a release-upon-publication statement.

E1.justification: v3 adds Human-1000, collected through WJX and evaluated on novel constraint compositions beyond the retained Human-154 set. It also evaluates masked-POI contextual reasoning and fifteen paired-preference scenarios. These broaden task requirements and query coverage beyond merely increasing sample counts; the underlying ten-city sandbox remains unchanged.

E2.justification: v3 Table 3 adds evaluated TTG with oracle constraints and LLM-Modulo with an oracle verifier to the Easy and Human-154 comparisons. v1 compared Act, ReAct, and NeSy variants. Appendix H.3 additionally reports preliminary Reflexion results. ReAct becoming ReAct (zero-shot) is a naming clarification.

E3.justification: v3 reports DeepSeek-V3 and Qwen3-8B instead of the earlier backends and adds Llama3.1-8B and Mistral-7B, although Appendix H.2 retains older model names. New protocols include TTG's POI subsampling, hourly discretization and 15-minute limit, LLM-Modulo's 64K context restriction, anonymized syntax matching, and paired-preference rank aggregation. NeSy's five-minute search limit remains unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's translation examples, syntax-refinement analysis, and single-preference ablation, v3 adds constraint-distribution and context-size analyses, literal versus semantic POI reasoning, seen versus unseen DSL matching, TTG runtime analysis, and LLM-Modulo error trajectories. Appendix H adds paired-preference trade-offs, categorized POI errors, and pure-LLM failure cases.

E5.justification: v3 Section 4.2 newly reports error-count summaries such as 3.2 ± 0.8 and 5.1 ± 1.2 and describes error reduction as statistically insignificant. v1 lacks corresponding uncertainty reporting. However, v3 does not specify what these spreads represent or identify the statistical test; neither version documents repeated-run counts or random seeds.

E6.justification: v3 adds Human-Test, TTG, LLM-Modulo, and additional model results while removing Table 3's Medium result block. Human-154 DeepSeek FPR changes from 27.9% to 37.0% under a different stated backend, so this is not a controlled same-model gain. The retained preference figure also changes values, including PEQ daily attractions from 0.93 to 0.79 and transport time from 41.9 to 26.9.

M1.justification: The proposed DSL, 35 concept functions, and NeSy procedure remain: NL2DSL translation with syntax-guided reflection, followed by LLM-guided backtracking search. Algorithm 1 and the preference-driven search procedure match across versions. Expanded explanations and additional comparator evaluations do not establish a revision to the proposed planner.

P1.justification: The introduction and benchmark-construction narrative are extensively rewritten or condensed, a Benchmark Characteristics section reorganizes the argument, and the appendices gain a contents listing and substantial topical restructuring. Existing material is also expanded into tutorials and metric explanations. The title changes from 'Real-World' to 'Open-Ended,' alongside author and affiliation edits.

P2.justification: v3 changes the predominantly two-column layout to one column and substantially restructures Table 3. It adds cost, reasoning, refinement, preference, and formulation displays. The sandbox map is removed, while v1's translation-failure Figure 4 is retained as v3 Figure 9 in the appendix. Existing DSL examples are consolidated into a dedicated figure.

R1.justification: v3 substantially expands positioning through TTG and LLM-Modulo comparisons, NaturalPlan and LongProc discussion, and detailed contrasts with TravelPlanner's contextual demands and constraint diversity. Relevant citations and Appendix E are added. Much of the original related-work appendix remains; the updated Hao reference represents an existing cited work rather than a new contribution.

T1.justification: v3 Appendix K adds an adapted MILP formulation for TTG, with parameter and decision-variable definitions, mathematical constraints, and variable/constraint-size calculations in Tables 14–18. This substantially expands the formal mathematical content beyond v1's DSL definitions and search pseudocode. The additional explanations of existing evaluation metrics alone would not warrant this label.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens v1's limited human-query evidence and comparator coverage through a separate 1,000-query test, TTG/LLM-Modulo evaluations, quantitative failure analyses, and detailed annotation documentation. These make the benchmark's challenges and evaluation more assessable. The gains outweigh the removed Medium results and reporting inconsistencies, including the claim that DeepSeek leads every subset despite Table 3 showing Easy FPR of 60.6% for GPT-4o versus 52.6% for DeepSeek.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ChinaTravel, retaining the same ten-city sandbox, compositional DSL, and NeSy planner. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v3 reports original benchmark experiments, including Human-Test results and additional comparison methods in Table 3, alongside reasoning, refinement, and preference analyses in the main text and Appendix H.

before.justification: v1 Table 3 reports original experiments on Easy, Medium, and Human queries. Figures 5–6 report syntax-refinement and preference-ablation results.

C1.justification: The central claim that contact-based joint optimization improves human and scene reconstruction, including the EMDB state-of-the-art claim, remains. v2 adds the specific claim that web-pseudo-label training outperforms EMDB-ground-truth training and softens JOSH3R's claimed superiority over optimization-free methods to accuracy 'on par' with traditional approaches. General compatibility and multi-human support were already claimed in v1, so their greater prominence is not wholly new scientific scope.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations of focal-length error propagation, contact-noise resistance through masking/depth filtering and robust penalties, and the differing effects of depth versus human-initialization noise. Appendix H also argues that scene-scale correction suffices for JOSH3R's scene prediction. Existing limitations concerning poor initialization and invisible or absent contacts, together with the training-domain explanation for JOSH3R's performance, are largely retained.

D1.justification: v2 Appendices B and H substantially revise the implementation documentation, including optimizer settings, loss weights, the 0.2 m contact-depth filter, initialization construction, and JOSH3R architecture/training details. The web-source description changes from 13 videos to 20 hours while retaining clip/frame counts. v2 newly states code/model availability and discusses releasing preprocessing/evaluation scripts, although its abstract and reproducibility statement differ about release timing; actual availability cannot be verified from the PDFs.

E1.justification: The principal EMDB, SLOPER4D, RICH, and pedestrian-web-video coverage remains. v2 additionally uses EMDB to train a JOSH3R comparator, evaluates JOSH3R on RICH, and adds corrupted-initialization and withheld-intrinsics scenarios on SLOPER4D. The retained 3,175 clips and approximately 460,000 annotated frames do not establish expansion of the web training corpus.

E2.justification: v2 introduces the reimplemented SynCHMR* as its principal direct 4D reconstruction comparator, adds PromptHMR-Vid to the extensive EMDB comparison, and compares against EMDB-trained JOSH3R. The MASt3R* and MonST3R* human-motion comparator rows in v1 Table 1 disappear from the corresponding comprehensive human-motion comparison in v2 Table 4, although these methods remain in scene comparisons. These are substantive comparator changes beyond renaming.

E3.justification: v2 adds jitter, foot sliding, and foot floating metrics, plus noise and estimated-intrinsics evaluation protocols. Appendix B explicitly excludes SLOPER4D seq009 from scene evaluation, unlike v1's stated six-sequence evaluation. Reported optimization changes from 500/200 iterations at learning rates 0.07/0.014 to 1,000 iterations at 0.05. JOSH3R's batch size changes from 64 to 32, augmentations change, and its local-pose source changes from SMPLer-X to HMR2.0. These reported setting changes do not independently establish which experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds initialization-variant comparisons, fixed-versus-optimized intrinsics ablations, web-pseudo-label versus EMDB-ground-truth training analysis, and tests perturbing 20% of depth, contact, or human initializations. The cumulative JOSH ablation in v1 Table 3 is replaced by component-removal experiments in v2 Table 2. The hinge-factor analysis and all three JOSH3R component ablations from v1 Appendix D are removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or statistical significance tests. v2's random perturbations define robustness conditions rather than an uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: Many results are added or revised. For example, TRAM's SLOPER4D W-MPJPE changes from 4157.5 in v1 Table 1 to 1285.3 in v2 Table 4, while JOSH's RICH W-MPJPE changes from 132.5 to 184.3. JOSH's EMDB 68.9 WA-MPJPE and 174.7 W-MPJPE remain unchanged. New physics, initialization, robustness, and training-source results substantially expand the evidence. Scene-score changes involve the seq009 exclusion and cannot be interpreted as same-setting gains. v2 also contains unresolved discrepancies, including JOSH3R's SLOPER4D RTE of 8.8% in Figure 7 versus 10.4% in Table 3.

M1.justification: v2 optimizes human pose and shape alongside transformations, replaces the hinge contact penalties, changes the static-contact constraint, and adds temporal smoothness, keypoint reprojection, depth filtering, and focal-length-coupled depth updates. The two-stage optimization in v1 Appendix A becomes a single-stage procedure. JOSH3R is also redesigned: v1's mask embeddings and optional local-joint features give way to ROI-pooled human/scene tokens, interacting decoders, and explicit human, scene-scale, and relative-transformation heads in v2 Appendix H.

P1.justification: The introduction, preliminaries, method explanation, and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten and reorganized. Related work moves from v1 Section 2 to v2 Appendix A; experiments are structured around direct 4D comparison, initialization variants, and scalable training. JOSH3R's architectural discussion is consolidated in the appendix, and ethics and reproducibility statements are added.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column presentation. The JOSH overview and JOSH3R architecture diagrams are redrawn, comparison and training-source bar charts and qualitative displays are added, and tables are reorganized around paired initializations and additional metrics. Several existing displays are retained and moved, including v1's dense-scene comparison and web-label examples, which become v2 Figures 6 and 9.

R1.justification: v1 states that no method directly supports 4D human-scene reconstruction. v2 instead recognizes SynCHMR, HSR, and the work of Luvizon et al. and Liu et al., positioning JOSH against their sequential reconstruction procedures. It also discusses Müller's multi-view joint reconstruction and adds newer work including PromptHMR. This substantially revises the novelty comparison and relevant research context, beyond moving related work or updating citation formatting.

T1.justification: The underlying geometric setup and trajectory-composition equations remain. v2 revises the mathematical definitions of the contact penalties and human regularizer in Eqs. 5–8, replacing v1 Eqs. 4–6, and introduces the focal-length/depth rescaling relation. These are bounded changes to the formal optimization formulation; neither version develops theorems, proofs, or theoretical guarantees.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the central empirical case: its matched-initialization SynCHMR* comparison, physical-plausibility metrics, and initialization/noise analyses address important gaps in v1's support for coherent, general-purpose joint reconstruction. Recognizing competing 4D methods also makes the novelty positioning more credible. Material drawbacks remain: JOSH3R component ablations disappear, Figure 7 conflicts with Table 3, and excluding seq009 narrows scene evaluation and prevents direct comparison of scene-score changes. These limitations weaken specific conclusions, but the evidence supporting the main JOSH contribution is substantially more informative.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same JOSH/JOSH3R research. Their main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial revision and reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original reconstruction experiments and reports additional initialization comparisons, physical-plausibility measurements, robustness tests, and training-source comparisons.

before.justification: v1 reports original JOSH and JOSH3R evaluations on EMDB, SLOPER4D, and RICH, including reconstruction results, runtime measurements, and component ablations.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and discussion retain the central claims about unlabeled-data self-consistency, strict properness, preserved amortization, and robustness beyond training distributions. Removing the proof-of-concept wording does not materially redefine these claims; the added experiment supplies support for their existing scope.

C2.justification: Section 4.2 adds explanations of regression-model vulnerability to inadequately represented covariates and the motivation for differencing time series. It interprets the new results as robustness without artificial misspecification. Existing qualifications about learned likelihoods and expensive density evaluation remain.

D1.justification: v3 supplies Eurostat source identifiers, the observation period and predictors, parameter priors, and flow/LSTM architecture and optimizer settings for the new application. The Gaussian implementation details move to Appendix A.2 essentially unchanged. No experimental code release or hardware information is added.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates synthetic normal-means problems only. v3 retains this coverage and adds posterior inference for an autoregressive model using 2004–2019 passenger traffic from 15 European countries to the USA, with household debt and GDP predictors. This substantially expands the represented data and modeling scenarios.

E2.justification: Standard NPE remains the baseline, and the Gaussian experiments retain their analytic posterior reference. v3 additionally evaluates Stan as the reference estimator in the air-traffic comparisons; v1 only discusses MCMC references conceptually.

E3.justification: The Gaussian protocols are retained. The new air-traffic evaluation introduces differenced time series with covariates, training with real data from 4, 8, or 15 countries, and absolute posterior-moment errors and Wasserstein distances against Stan averaged across countries. Appendix A.4 specifies its distinct network configuration and training settings.

E4.justification: The five Gaussian sensitivity studies are retained in Appendix A.3. The air-traffic study extends the investigation of unlabeled-data availability to M = 4, 8, and 15 countries, with parameter- and country-specific posterior comparisons in Appendix A.5.

E5.justification: v3 adds explicitly defined central 50% and 95% posterior credible intervals in Figures 2 and 5–7, extending v1's contour and error-bar reporting. These describe posterior uncertainty; neither version specifies independent training-run counts, seeds, or uncertainty for the reported metric averages.

E6.justification: The Gaussian sensitivity curves are retained, while v3 adds substantial air-traffic results. For M = 8, Table 1 reports beta mean error of 0.152 for NPE versus 0.030 for NPE+SC, and Wasserstein distance of 0.161 versus 0.054. Gains are not universal: at M = 4, log(sigma) standard-deviation error increases from 0.049 to 0.057 (Table 2). These are new comparisons, not improvements to previously reported Gaussian scores.

M1.justification: The semi-supervised objective and variance-based self-consistency loss remain unchanged. The added air-traffic application introduces a limited architectural adaptation: an LSTM summary network for time series, whereas v1's Gaussian experiments use a Deep Set when summarization is needed.

P1.justification: v3 substantially reorganizes the manuscript: proofs and detailed Gaussian settings move into dedicated appendix subsections, the case-study section becomes two applications, and the appendix gains separate setup and results sections. Captions and passages are condensed, and the work-in-progress notice is removed.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redesigned from twelve contour panels into seven selected panels in one row. The original sensitivity figures move to Appendix A.3. v3 adds three numerical tables and four air-traffic figures, including a main-text extract of the fuller appendix comparisons.

R1.justification: v3 adds Frazier et al.'s work on statistical accuracy, Habermann et al.'s Amortized Bayesian Multilevel Models, and three Eurostat sources. The related-work discussion and positioning against existing robustness approaches remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: v3 adds the mathematical specification of the air-traffic autoregressive model and its independent parameter priors in Equations 8 and 20. The four strict-properness propositions, their assumptions and proofs, and the analytic Gaussian posterior remain unchanged; the first two proofs move to Appendix A.1.

improvement.justification: v1's broad real-data robustness claims were supported entirely by a controlled Gaussian example. v3 addresses that important evidence gap with an actual time-series application, Stan references, country-level posterior comparisons, and sensitivity to available unlabeled data, while retaining the earlier experiments and proofs. This substantially strengthens empirical support for applicability. Limited comparator breadth and absent training-run uncertainty remain unresolved, so general robustness is still not established.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same self-consistency approach to amortized Bayesian inference. Their complete text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching across relocations.

after.justification: v3 retains those experiments and adds original posterior-inference results on European air passenger traffic, reported in Section 4.2 and Appendix A.5.

before.justification: v1 reports original Gaussian-model experiments comparing neural posterior estimation with and without self-consistency, including several sensitivity analyses in Figures 1–3.

C1.justification: v4 extends the stated empirical scope to high-dimensional time-series and image applications, with robustness reported for several hundred parameters rather than the previously tested 100. It removes v3's explicit assertion that no existing ABI approach achieves comparable robustness. The central unlabeled-data, self-consistency and strict-properness contributions remain intact.

C2.justification: v4 interprets MNIST edge-localized uncertainty as meaningful ambiguity and patchy baseline uncertainty as spurious. The Discussion removes the extrapolation suggesting no major curse of dimensionality, extends the density-evaluation limitation to score-based diffusion and narrows the joint-learning challenge to very high-dimensional likelihoods. The learned-versus-known likelihood accuracy qualification remains in Section 4.1.

D1.justification: Appendices F and H add detailed simulator, numerical-integration, network, preprocessing and training recipes, including MNIST blur settings and self-consistency weight scheduling. New Appendix J documents hardware for all four studies and approximately 100 minutes for the longest MNIST training experiment. Hardware for the retained studies is newly disclosed, rather than demonstrably changed.

E1.justification: v4 adds simulated Hodgkin–Huxley neuron dynamics with seven parameters and 200-dimensional time-series observations, plus Bayesian denoising of 784-pixel MNIST digit-zero images under prior misspecification. These substantially extend the domains and inverse problems beyond the retained normal-model and air-traffic studies.

E2.justification: The retained comparisons still evaluate inference with versus without self-consistency, using analytic posteriors for the normal model and Stan for air traffic. The new studies extend the existing NPE/NPLE comparisons without self-consistency to additional tasks. Jointly learned likelihoods were already evaluated in v3; new citations do not introduce evaluated competitors.

E3.justification: New protocols include Hodgkin–Huxley training on 32,768 simulations with 1,024 unlabeled observations and predictive-bias evaluation over 1,000 out-of-simulation datasets. MNIST uses 12,000 simulated training pairs, a 400/580-image self-consistency/test split and 500 posterior samples per evaluated image. Appendices F and H specify task-specific architectures and training schedules. The previously stated normal-model and air-traffic settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v4 adds neuron posterior-predictive checks on in-distribution and shifted data, predictive-bias histograms and individual failure cases in Figures 4 and 11–13. MNIST analyses examine robustness to prior blur misspecification through reconstruction, uncertainty-map and posterior-sample comparisons in Figures 5 and 14–15. The original dimensionality, unlabeled-data, summary-network and likelihood ablations are retained.

E5.justification: v3 already displays normal-model error bars; v4 newly identifies them as ±1 standard deviation over 10 refits on new training data. New Table 4 reports cross-country standard errors for air-traffic posterior mean and standard-deviation biases at M = 4, 8 and 15. This expands statistical documentation without establishing an increase in run counts.

E6.justification: New results report lower neuron predictive bias with self-consistency for almost all evaluated datasets and smoother MNIST reconstructions with more coherent uncertainty maps. Retained air-traffic tables also contain small numerical revisions: Table 1 changes the alpha posterior-mean biases from 0.078/0.013 to 0.079/0.014 for NPE/NPE+SC. The earlier figures and their underlying results are retained.

M1.justification: The semi-supervised objective, variance-based self-consistency loss and joint posterior/likelihood estimation approach remain unchanged in Section 2. The new studies instantiate this framework with task-specific networks and training settings; they do not introduce a new inference algorithm or loss component.

P1.justification: The abstract, contribution framing and Discussion are substantially rewritten, case-study explanations are condensed and limitations receive an explicit paragraph. The appendix hierarchy changes from A.1–A.5 to separate lettered appendices. Most methods and proof prose remain stable. A new cross-reference error points Section 4.3's out-of-simulation discussion to Figure 11a, which depicts an in-simulation example.

P2.justification: All seven earlier figures are retained under corresponding numbering. v4 adds neuron predictive plots, image reconstruction and posterior-sample grids, and the air-traffic standard-error table. New Figure 2 redisplays two existing appendix MMD analyses in the main text. These additions substantially expand the visual presentation, alongside caption and placement changes.

R1.justification: v4 removes the meta-learning framing and the Finn and Hospedales references. It adds citations concerning unsupervised domain adaptation, MNIST, studentising flows and score-based diffusion. Section 3 otherwise preserves the positioning relative to adversarial regularization, post hoc correction, generalized Bayesian inference and labeled calibration approaches.

T1.justification: Formal additions are limited to the new experimental model: Appendix F specifies the Hodgkin–Huxley priors and membrane/gating differential equations, including Equations 21–26. The self-consistency Propositions 1–4, their assumptions, the qualification concerning jointly approximate densities and the existing proofs remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v3's broad robustness argument rests on a Gaussian toy problem and one air-traffic model. v4 substantially strengthens its empirical basis with nonlinear neuron dynamics and high-dimensional joint posterior/likelihood image inference, addressing limited validation in more complex settings. Refit documentation, standard-error reporting and implementation/resource details also improve transparency. The new MNIST evidence remains qualitative and neuron figure references need correction, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in validation and reproducibility.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same self-consistency approach to amortized Bayesian inference. The text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable. v3 Appendices A.1–A.5 match v4 Appendices A–E, enabling reliable comparison despite the added studies.

after.justification: v4 retains those empirical results and adds original Hodgkin–Huxley simulations and MNIST denoising experiments in Sections 4.3–4.4 and Appendices F–I.

before.justification: v3 reports original normal-model simulations and analysis of European air-traffic data, including comparisons against analytic posteriors and Stan in Section 4 and Appendices A.3–A.5.

C1.justification: The central claims remain semi-supervised ABI using unlabeled observations, strict properness, preserved amortization, and robustness beyond both training distributions. V5's more explicit wording about the analytic posterior and distribution independence restates properties already asserted in v4.

C2.justification: Expanded Section 2.3 and new Appendix B substantially clarify that robustness concerns inference under the specified, potentially misspecified model, rather than correction of that model. They explain SC-only optimization instability, the complementary role of supervised training, and loss-weight stabilization. Appendix D.1 discusses competitors' different posterior targets, while the Discussion adds a proposed combination with importance sampling.

D1.justification: V5 adds a code-access link, a reproducibility statement, practical proposal and loss-weight guidance, and implementation details for the new comparisons, including the VAE encoder architecture. Original network specifications, hardware information, and the detailed MNIST warm-up schedule were already present and are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same normal-model, air-traffic, Hodgkin-Huxley, and MNIST digit-zero tasks and distribution-shift scenarios. The added comparisons reuse existing coverage; their different simulation counts and model configurations concern evaluation settings.

E2.justification: V5 adds NPE-MMD, NPE-DANN, and NNPE to the normal-model comparison (Appendix D.1, Figure 8). It also evaluates a known-likelihood VAE and Schmitt et al. (2024)'s simulation-only self-consistency approach on air traffic (Appendix F.1, Table 2). V4 lacked these evaluated competitors.

E3.justification: V5 adds distinct comparison protocols: the normal-model comparison uses a shared 30-output DeepSet, 40 epochs, and a reported 1,028 simulations; the air-traffic comparison uses 40,960 simulations, including online NPE training and matched simulation counts across competitors. These supplement the retained original protocols rather than establish that the original experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix F.1 adds controls testing whether larger simulation budgets or self-consistency evaluated only on simulations explain robustness, helping isolate the contribution of unlabeled real data. The original dimensionality, unlabeled-data size/location, likelihood, summary-network, and neuron robustness analyses remain.

E5.justification: V5 Table 1 newly reports standard errors for air-traffic Wasserstein distances; v4 Table 4 reported standard errors only for posterior mean and standard-deviation biases. Existing ten-refit standard-deviation error bars are retained, and the new normal-model comparison follows that same practice.

E6.justification: V5 adds the Figure 8 comparator curves and Table 2/Figure 12 air-traffic results. For example, the new air-traffic comparison reports alpha Wasserstein distances of 0.010 for online NPE+SC, 0.080 for online NPE, 0.068 for Schmitt et al. (2024), and 0.065 for VAE. These are newly reported results under new protocols, not performance improvements over v4 runs. The consolidated Table 1 also adopts v4's appendix NPE mean-bias values for delta and log(sigma), which differed slightly from v4's main table.

M1.justification: The proposed simulation-based loss plus unlabeled-data self-consistency loss, density estimators, and inference procedure are retained. V5 expands explanations of proposal selection and loss weighting; the MNIST weight schedule was already documented in v4 Appendix H.

P1.justification: V5 substantially expands explanatory exposition through a new FAQ and additional Methods discussion, rewrites introductory passages, and condenses the MNIST narrative. It moves air-model background into the setup appendix and adds a reproducibility statement. These changes materially reshape the explanation and distribution of information, although the main section order remains.

P2.justification: V4 Tables 1–4 are consolidated into v5's appendix Table 1, and v5 adds Table 2 and Figures 8 and 12. Existing figure content is retained, with caption revisions, relocation, and enlarged neuron-example displays on separate pages. The overall visual format remains similar.

R1.justification: V5 adds focused references supporting the KL-variance argument, VAE comparison, Stan attribution, and importance-sampling outlook. It expands positioning against simulation-only self-consistency and domain-adaptation methods with different posterior targets. The existing related-work discussion and overall semi-supervised ABI positioning remain.

T1.justification: V5 Appendix B adds a formal definition of model misspecification and a mathematical approximation connecting KL divergence to self-consistency-ratio variance through a second-order Taylor expansion, attributed to Köthe (2023). Propositions 1–4 and the existing Appendix A proofs remain substantively unchanged.

improvement.justification: V4's empirical comparisons largely establish gains over plain NPE/NPLE. V5 substantially addresses the missing competitive and control evidence through robustness baselines, a known-likelihood VAE, simulation-only self-consistency, and larger-simulation controls in Appendices D.1 and F.1. Clearer target interpretation and added reproducibility guidance further strengthen the paper. Comparisons remain limited to two case studies and include differing inference targets, but these acknowledged limits do not outweigh the substantial evidential improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same self-consistency approach and four case studies. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, and moved or renumbered equations, figures, and tables can be matched reliably.

after.justification: V5 retains those original results and adds robustness-method comparisons and air-traffic control experiments in Appendices D.1 and F.1.

before.justification: V4 reports original normal-model simulations, European air-traffic analysis, Hodgkin-Huxley experiments, and MNIST denoising results in Section 4 and the appendices.

C1.justification: Headline guarantees now expose input dimension and finite-model separation, including O(sqrt(d_u N p)) instead of O(sqrt(N p)). The introduction removes the model-based versus model-free complexity contribution and foregrounds frequentist posterior-sampling guarantees. Section 2 additionally claims optimality up to logarithmic factors.

C2.justification: v2 leaves non-realizability to future work; v3 explains conditional applicability when a suitable model is uniformly closest across the state-action space. It also qualifies logarithmic regret when candidate models are nearly indistinguishable and interprets the pendulum results as successful control despite multiple approximate models.

D1.justification: Appendix B.2 newly documents pendulum equations, physical parameters, candidate-generation ranges, costs, discretizations and MPC implementation using IPOPT through CasADi. It also reports runtime. The earlier MATLAB, linear-controller, recursive-estimation and laptop details are retained; no code-access change is reported.

E1.justification: v2 evaluates only a 20-state, five-input linear system. v3 retains this coverage and adds nonlinear pendulum-on-cart swing-up with state and input constraints and 500 candidate models excluding the true dynamics, substantially expanding both task and environmental coverage.

E2.justification: The retained linear experiments use the same optimal true-model controller reference. The pendulum experiment extends this oracle-reference comparison to control using the true pendulum dynamics. The expanded related-work citations do not introduce additional evaluated learning baselines.

E3.justification: The pendulum study introduces a distinct protocol with 0.02-second simulation steps, constrained MPC over 50 steps at 0.04-second discretization, and input perturbations. Separately, the retained parametric linear experiment changes its stated epsilon from p/T to sqrt(p/N); the PDFs do not establish that this experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix B.2 adds a targeted misspecification case study examining control, parameter errors and posterior behavior when the true model is absent. This provides illustrative robustness evidence beyond the retained linear model-count sensitivity analysis, without a systematic comparison across misspecification levels.

E5.justification: Both versions report averaging Figure 3's regret over 40 independent realizations. v3 adds no repeated-run counts for the pendulum, empirical confidence intervals or significance tests. Its model-posterior plots concern model selection rather than uncertainty across experimental runs.

E6.justification: Figures 4–5 add pendulum control, estimation and posterior trajectories, alongside approximately 60 ms per iteration. Figure 4's caption reports swing-up after about 80 steps versus 60 with true dynamics, while Appendix B.2.1 says 40 additional steps, leaving the exact delay inconsistent. The stated linear convergence and scalability findings remain.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1–4 retain posterior-weighted model selection, periodic switching, Gaussian excitation and greedy covering. The MPC example instantiates the existing freedom to choose feedback policies. Corrected normalization indices align the pseudocode with v2's existing loss definition.

P1.justification: The introduction and related-work appendix undergo substantial rewriting and thematic reorganization. Appendix B gains a linear/nonlinear hierarchy, and detailed S2 algorithm explanation moves from Section 3.2 to Appendix D. These narrative changes extend well beyond local copyediting.

P2.justification: v3 adds pendulum plots in Figures 4–5 and a geometric illustration of misspecification assumptions in Figure 6. Figures 1–3 are retained and relocated. These additional displays substantially expand the visual presentation, alongside conference formatting and page reflow.

R1.justification: The introduction and Appendix A substantially reposition the work within posterior-sampling reinforcement learning and Hedge, expanding discussion of Osband, Ouyang, Xu and related research. New comparisons address Bayesian versus frequentist guarantees, mixing versus excitation assumptions, and Decision-Estimation Coefficient and Bellman-based complexity frameworks.

T1.justification: New Appendix G introduces assumptions and loss-gap derivations for non-realizable model classes, changing the benchmark to policies associated with a suitable closest model. The theorem statements and excitation assumptions also revise dimensional and separation-factor accounting, and Section 2 adds an online-regression lower-bound argument.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses important gaps: v2 supported its nonlinear applicability empirically only with linear simulations and deferred misspecification. Appendix B.2 now demonstrates constrained nonlinear control, while Appendix G separately develops conditional misspecification analysis. Clearer theoretical dependencies and research positioning further improve assessability. These gains outweigh the inconsistent swing-up timing and unexplained epsilon revision accompanying retained linear plots.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work and three theoretical settings. Their complete main texts, equations, algorithms, figures and appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial expansion and reformatting.

after.justification: The linear simulations remain, and Appendix B.2 adds original nonlinear pendulum simulations reporting control trajectories, parameter estimation, model probabilities and runtime (Figures 4–5).

before.justification: Appendix B reports original linear-control simulations for Algorithms 1 and 3, including a model-count study averaged over 40 independent realizations (Figures 1–3).

C1.justification: The headline contribution expands from a scalable value-approximation solver with multigrid to exploiting atomic equilibrium structure across value learning, model-free MARL, and MPC. The abstract, introduction, and conclusion newly emphasize reduced game-tree complexity and rapid 22-player football solving. The original atomic-support claim remains central.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive applicability qualifications about stochastic dynamics/observations preventing precise belief control and leaving the proposed operators as lower bounds. It adds a conjecture connecting PPO/MMD failures to boundary equilibria and interprets football behavior through concealment and defensive tactics. v1's explanation of higher dual approximation errors is removed.

D1.justification: New appendices document MPC policy parameterization and football state/control construction, semi-implicit integration, contact dynamics, costs, and initial lineups. New runtime hardware is identified as an M1 Pro MacBook. The PDF's code pointer changes from the conf_sub branch to iclr, while the detailed hard-constraint safety-model formulation is removed.

E1.justification: v3 adds a 22-player football environment with smooth contact and two private offensive objectives, substantially extending task and population coverage. v1's dedicated collision-constrained and 3D Hexner demonstrations are no longer reported, although some corresponding parameter descriptions remain in v3 Appendix G.

E2.justification: The original Figure 3 comparator sets are retained: CFR+, MMD, CFR-BR-Primal, JPSPG, and DeepCFR in their respective experiments. The new MARL comparisons in Figure 5 add evaluated PPO and R-NaD baselines and a model-free MMD comparison, substantially expanding comparator coverage.

E3.justification: New MARL protocols use 100-action discretizations and normal-form policy evaluations every 8192 steps. New MPC experiments optimize from fixed initial states using known dynamics and explicit rollout trees. These differ substantially from whole-state-space value approximation; the retained Figure 3 settings and DeepCFR hyperparameter table remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Figure 5 adds comparisons of atomic and discrete policy representations within both PPO and MMD at one and four stages, directly testing the structural contribution. MPC and football trajectory/belief case studies add analyses of concealment behavior. The existing multigrid comparison remains.

E5.justification: Both versions estimate retained action errors using 100 trajectories and report concealment time as 0.60 ± 0.06 seconds over 50 trajectories. Added curves continue the existing shaded-band presentation without newly specifying experimental seed counts, confidence-interval definitions, or significance tests.

E6.justification: New results report substantially smaller errors for atomic PPO/MMD policies, approximately five-minute Hexner MPC solving, and approximately 30-minute football solving. The retained Figure 3(d) JPSPG error at t=0.75 changes from roughly 35 to 18 without a stated protocol revision. Constrained and 3D trajectory results disappear. Multigrid runtime-table differences are only rounding.

M1.justification: The core CAMS value approximation and multigrid procedure remain. Sections 5.2–5.3 add CAMS-DRL, with learned action prototypes and mixture probabilities optimized using PPO/MMD, and CAMS-MPC, with differentiable rollout-tree minimax optimization. v1 Appendix I's safety-region penalty formulation is omitted.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, contribution narrative, and substantial portions of the main exposition are rewritten. The theory is reorganized around primal-dual reformulations followed by convergence, methods are divided into three learning/control regimes, and the appendices are extensively reordered, expanded, and pruned.

P2.justification: The opening figure is redesigned around game trees and football; MARL and MPC figures are added; repeated-game illustrations, constrained trajectory panels, and the 3D figure are removed. Figure 3 changes from a 2-by-2 arrangement to one row, several retained displays move, and the main text changes from two columns to one.

R1.justification: v3 repositions the contribution around structural knowledge for MARL and control, engages with Rudolph et al. (2025) and reports conflicting policy-gradient findings, and adds Hamilton–Jacobi regularity and football references. It removes the extended CFR/MMD/FTRL complexity survey and associated citations from v1 Appendix F.

T1.justification: v3 replaces v1 Appendix A's Taylor/stationarity argument with Appendix C's semiconcavity, viscosity, consistency, and non-expansiveness lemmas. Appendix B adds an explicit convex-envelope proof. Assumption A2 strengthens dynamics regularity to C1 with bounded derivatives, A5 drops prior knowledge of the NE, and the Hamiltonian running-cost sign changes. The baseline-complexity derivations are removed and football control-affine reasoning is added.

improvement.justification: Figure 5 provides direct tests of atomic versus discrete representations within both PPO and MMD against known equilibria, substantially strengthening v1's evidence beyond its custom value-approximation solver. The documented MPC and football applications further demonstrate practical utility. These gains outweigh the lost constrained and 3D demonstrations, although football equilibrium quality remains supported qualitatively and statistical reporting remains limited.

A1.justification: Despite the changed title and organization, both PDFs describe the same CAMS and primal-dual differential-game research. Both contain 32 readable pages, including complete appendices, with sufficient text and visual evidence for comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains original CAMS experiments and adds policy-learning comparisons, MPC results, and an 11-vs-11 football simulation in Section 6 and Appendices H–I.

before.justification: v1 reports original Hexner-game simulations, baseline comparisons, trajectory errors, multigrid runtimes, and constrained and 3D demonstrations.

C1.justification: The central contributions—variance-preserving initialization, learnable activation families, and polynomial mappings—remain. Performance claims are narrowed from outperforming traditional activations to successful training and matching or exceeding them. The abstract and conclusion now explicitly claim usefulness for fine-tuning, extending the previously proposed application with empirical support.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations connecting Tropical activations to convex conjugacy and decision-boundary geometry to polynomial, periodic, and max-plus structure. It qualifies Fourier/Tropical gains on CIFAR-10 as inconclusive. A dedicated limitations section reports 30–90% slower GPU training and claims inference-speed parity, while v1's explicit low-precision degree-three restriction is removed.

D1.justification: Appendix L/Table 7 adds a detailed CIFAR-10 recipe covering TIMM, four GPUs, batch size, AdamW, learning rate, scheduling, normalization, augmentation, and clipping. Appendix O specifies frozen and trainable parameters for transfer learning. Runtime information and implementation scaling are also revised. The torchortho code-and-weights availability claim is retained.

E1.justification: ImageNet-1k classification and OpenWebText language modeling are retained. v2 adds CIFAR-10 training, ImageNet-to-CIFAR-10 transfer learning, and noisy two-dimensional classification scenarios including moons and circles (Sections 4.1, 4.2, 4.5; Appendices L, M, O). These substantially extend the evaluated data and task requirements.

E2.justification: SiLU becomes an evaluated GPT-2/OpenWebText baseline in Table 2 and Figures 14–15; previously it was only discussed or cited. The new CIFAR-10 comparison also includes ResNet50 with ReLU alongside ConvNeXt-T with GELU (Table 8). This is a limited comparator expansion, with GELU retained throughout.

E3.justification: v1 reports extremal benchmark scores, whereas v2 specifies reporting at fixed epochs or iterations. v2 also describes the main Fourier experiments as using the proposed initialization, replacing v1's GELU-fitting setting. New protocols include 300-epoch CIFAR-10 training and transfer learning with only the final linear layer and activation coefficients trainable. Unchanged ablation scores linked to revised initialization theorems do not establish that those ablations were rerun.

E4.justification: The four original degree, initialization, learnability, and clamping ablations retain their numerical results. v2 adds qualitative decision-boundary diagnostics across noisy datasets, a Tropical-Laurent quadratic-fitting illustration, and a brief factorial-versus-power-law stability comparison (Appendices M and H; Remark 3.15). These are limited supplementary extensions to the retained ablation evidence.

E5.justification: v1 mentions fixed seeds without specifying run counts or reporting uncertainty. v2 specifies three seeds, adds uncertainty to the main tables, and plots means with minimum-to-maximum shading. This establishes expanded reporting, not a known increase from a specified earlier run count. The uncertainty definition remains inconsistent: Sections 4.3–4.4 say standard deviation, while Tables 1–2 say standard error.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 replace the earlier numerical summaries: Hermite ImageNet Top-1 changes from 82.34% to 82.18 ± 0.1270%, and GPT-2 validation perplexity from 18.39 to 18.80 ± 0.1905. Changed initialization and aggregation prevent interpreting these as same-setting performance changes. v2 adds SiLU results, FLOP estimates, CIFAR-10 scores, decision-boundary findings, and fine-tuning curves. Tables 3–6 retain their scores, and v1 Figure 7 survives as v2 Figure 16.

M1.justification: v2 replaces the Hermite and Fourier power-law initialization schemes with factorial-scaled series and new coefficient initializations. Fourier initial frequencies change from kπ/√3 to k, and Tropical outputs acquire a √2/n scaling. These procedural changes appear in Section 3 and Algorithms 1, 5, and 6. Tropical Rational activation and Hermite interpolation already existed in v1.

P1.justification: v2 substantially reorganizes existing material: detailed moment derivations and the polynomial-mapping discussion move into appendices, while initialization theorems become the main methods narrative. The abstract is rewritten, the title shortened, the complexity discussion condensed into a separate section, and experiments reorganized around additional subsections and a dedicated limitations section.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one. The MLP schematic moves to an appendix, and existing Hermite/Fourier fitting plots are merged into paired panels. Tables 1–2 replace initialization/learnability columns with computational-cost information and uncertainty displays. New configuration and results tables, decision-boundary panels, training curves, and fine-tuning plots substantially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v2 adds Glorot and Bengio (2010), Gao et al. (2025), Krizhevsky et al. (2009), and Wightman (2019), while removing Hendrycks and Gimpel (2016) and Pandey and Phukan (2020). Attribution of variance-preserving initialization and the approximation-theory discussion are refined. The extensive positioning against earlier activation work and KANs otherwise remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: The Hermite/Fourier moment calculations and initialization theorems are substantially revised around factorial series (Appendices C–D). v2 adds a Tropical initialization theorem and proof, a convex-conjugate definition, and a three-layer-collapse statement to the relocated polynomial-mapping proposition. The revision also introduces a mathematical inconsistency: Appendix D Eq. 67 omits the factor 1/2 implied by Eqs. 56 and 66.

improvement.justification: Replacing extrema-only reporting with fixed-checkpoint, three-seed summaries and visible run variation substantially strengthens the main empirical evidence. The transfer-learning experiment tests a previously proposed application, while explicit runtime costs and narrower performance claims improve assessment of practical value. These gains outweigh v2's conflicting SD/SE labels, unclear linkage between retained ablation scores and revised initializations, and the localized Fourier-proof factor error.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same activation-function research. All pages, including v1 Appendices A–J and v2 Appendices A–O, are readable; corresponding methods, results, and figures can be matched despite substantial restructuring.

after.justification: v2 reports original benchmark experiments and ablations, plus CIFAR-10 training, decision-boundary comparisons, and transfer-learning results.

before.justification: v1 reports original ImageNet-1k and OpenWebText experiments, numerical ablations in Tables 3–6, and activation-fitting results.

C1.justification: The central unbiased bridge-based MI claim remains, but the empirical contribution broadens from synthetic benchmarks to demonstrated superiority on protein embeddings in the abstract, introduction, and discussion. The introduction also strengthens its image-performance claim from comparable or superior to superior, extending the scope and strength of the main practical claims.

C2.justification: V2 interprets epsilon=1 as a robust default, argues robustness to network size, and recommends lower-variance Gaussian starting distributions and the uniform-based entropy formula where applicable. Existing Cauchy and limited-data limitations remain after relocation; the Cauchy qualification softens from theoretical inapplicability to absence of a guarantee.

D1.justification: Appendices C.2–C.4 add NVF/JVF implementation sources and CPU timings, MINDE image training and estimation settings, and protein filtering, normalization, architecture, regularization, and computational details. These substantially expand reproducibility information while largely retaining the original synthetic-benchmark implementation details.

E1.justification: V2 retains the synthetic MI benchmarks and adds paired 1024-dimensional ProtTrans5 embeddings from A. thaliana and H. sapiens (Section 5.3). Appendix B.3 also introduces actual entropy-estimation evaluations on 10-dimensional exponential and uniform distributions, substantially extending domain and task coverage.

E2.justification: V2 adds NVF and JVF to the low-dimensional comparisons in Tables 1 and 9. MINDE-C and MINDE-J newly participate in the image comparison (Figure 1 and Table 6); their presence in v1 was confined to the low-dimensional benchmark.

E3.justification: New protocols include 8000/2000 training/test splits for entropy, 100-epoch protein training, matched U-Net training budgets for image MINDE comparisons, MAE summaries, and hyperparameter sweeps. V2 Table 9 also changes the stated test count from 10,000 to 100,000, although Section 5.1 and Table 1 retain 10,000. This reporting inconsistency does not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds InfoBridge volatility sweeps on images and proteins, a U-Net parameter-count study, and entropy analyses comparing starting distributions and estimation formulations. The existing AE+WKL bottleneck study expands from dimension 4 to dimensions 4, 5, and 8, with divergence reported for dimension 8.

E5.justification: The original low-dimensional seed counts and image confidence-interval practices remain. V2 adds standard-deviation summaries, explicitly single-run entropy experiments, and mostly single-run ablations averaging the last five training measurements. Table 4 reports their mean and standard deviation; the source of Table 8's protein MAE standard deviations is less clearly specified.

E6.justification: Retained low-dimensional values match between v1 Table 4 and v2 Table 9. V2 adds baseline, entropy, protein, and ablation results: image MAE is 0.38 for InfoBridge versus 0.56 for MINDE-C, while protein MAE is 0.04 versus 9.29 (Tables 6 and 8). Low-MI AE+WKL dimension-4 estimates shown as negative in v1 Figure 3 appear at zero in v2 Figure 5, without an explanation of this change.

M1.justification: The core bridge-matching losses, shared binary-conditioned network, and MI inference procedure remain unchanged despite algorithm renumbering. V2 removes the optional endpoint-conditioned pointwise-MI estimation procedure from v1 Appendix A.3. Its new entropy experiments use an estimation procedure already described in v1.

P1.justification: Most existing prose is retained with local rewrites and corrections. Practical optimization now precedes generalizations, experiments receive numbered subsections, limitations move to Appendix A, and the appendices are reorganized. Citation style and author information also change.

P2.justification: The main text and references switch from two columns to one, and the algorithms are reordered and stacked. Comparison tables gain method categories, Figure 1 gains baseline curves, and new protein, entropy, ablation, and summary displays appear. V1 Figure 2's identical generated-image panels move to appendix Figure 4; the bottleneck plot gains curves and a revised vertical range.

R1.justification: V2 adds references for FlowMI, ProtTrans, the Lee–Rhee benchmark construction, Light Schrödinger Bridge, and multivariate information. Four PMI-application references disappear with the removed PMI appendix. The related-work taxonomy and fundamental positioning relative to MINDE remain largely unchanged.

T1.justification: V2 removes the entire pointwise-MI decomposition and derivation from v1 Appendix A.3, including Equations 21–22. The MI, KL, entropy, and interaction-information results remain. V2 also explicitly qualifies Theorems 4.1 and B.1 with regularity assumptions and narrows the uniform-entropy corollary's support condition from containment in S to equality with S.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses an important validation gap by directly comparing with MINDE on images, adds evidence from protein embeddings, and tests sensitivity and the previously theoretical entropy extension. Removing v1's always-nonnegative PMI formula also removes a conflict with its potentially negative log-ratio definition. These gains outweigh the new sample-count inconsistency and limited replication of some analyses. Image-superiority wording still needs qualification: Table 6 gives AE+WKL with known intrinsic dimensionality lower MAE than InfoBridge, 0.26 versus 0.38.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe InfoBridge and retain identifiable core methods, theoretical results, and experiments. The complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables, and figures, support reliable comparison.

after.justification: Section 5 and Appendices B–C retain original experiments and add protein-embedding evaluations, entropy-estimation experiments, and hyperparameter analyses.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendix B report original InfoBridge experiments on low-dimensional distributions and synthetic images, alongside an AE+WKL bottleneck analysis.

C1.justification: The abstract, hypotheses, and conclusion broaden the demonstrated contribution from gender-feature learning and gender debiasing to feature learning and behavior modification involving gender, race, and religion. v3 also drops the unqualified monosemantic characterization from the title and principal contribution statements. The claimed state-of-the-art gender result with INLP is retained.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations of unseen-class encodings and explains weaker race/religion rewriting through noisy attribute data, tokenization, and targeting only one class pair. It introduces limitations concerning simultaneous multi-axis debiasing and multi-token causal targets. These substantially qualify applicability beyond v2's gender proof of concept. CrowS exclusion also receives a new measurement-validity rationale.

D1.justification: v3 documents race/religion corpus construction, casing and token rules, training and validation budgets, and SuperGLUE task implementations. Reported LLaMA training hardware changes from two to three A100 GPUs. Conversely, v2's dataset publication statement and Table 5 dataset-access identifiers disappear. Code and gender-model links remain; the removed disclosure does not establish that the datasets became unavailable.

E1.justification: v3 adds Wikipedia-derived race and religion training/evaluation data, corresponding StereoSet and SEAT coverage, and eight SuperGLUE tasks. It also evaluates classes unseen by each pair-specific encoder. CrowS evaluation is removed, and the neutral corpus is revised to exclude race/religion attributes as well as gender terms.

E2.justification: The retained gender comparisons use the same seven baselines: CDA, DROPOUT, INLP, RLACE, LEACE, SELFDEBIAS, and SENTDEBIAS, with the same hybrid combinations. The new race/religion comparisons reuse subsets of these methods. GRADIEND BPI/FPI/MPI correspond to the renamed Female/Male, Female, and Male variants.

E3.justification: v3 introduces balanced downsampling for encoder evaluation and removes accuracy and mean-absolute-encoding metrics. GLUE training changes from three epochs without intermediate validation to evaluation twice per epoch and selection by loss. New race/religion protocols specify 70/20/10 splits, 2,500 training steps, and token filtering. SuperGLUE introduces additional task procedures, while removing CrowS changes the aggregate bias ranking.

E4.justification: v3 adds substantial analyses of how pair-trained encoders represent an unseen third class and gradients from other class pairs (Figures 3 and 5). Figures 7–13 extend feature-factor/learning-rate sensitivity analysis to race and religion. The existing gender name-overfitting analysis and profession-prediction cases are retained, not newly added.

E5.justification: Both versions retain 1,000 bootstrap samples, 95% confidence intervals, and three-seed gender training and GLUE reporting. v3 newly specifies one GRADIEND training run per race/religion configuration and task-preserving bootstrap sampling for MultiRC and ReCoRD. These are limited statistical extensions, not increased replication of the retained experiments.

E6.justification: v3 adds extensive race/religion and SuperGLUE outcomes and removes CrowS and several encoder-result columns. Retained entries also change: GPT-2 GRADIEND's SS becomes 59.09 instead of 59.55 in Table 12, and RoBERTa GRADIEND's GLUE becomes 82.47 instead of 75.13 alongside the revised checkpoint protocol. The summary base LMS changes from 82.50 to the correct seven-model mean, 87.46; this is an aggregation correction, not a performance gain.

M1.justification: The core procedure remains factual-gradient encoding through a scalar tanh bottleneck, MSE prediction of gradient differences, and an affine decoder whose output is added to model weights. v3 applies this pairwise procedure to additional feature classes; the generalized terminology and experimental scoring adaptations do not establish a new core algorithm.

P1.justification: The introduction and methodological narrative are substantially rewritten around general feature learning. Metrics move largely into the appendix, experiments are reorganized by bias type, and the appendices gain a structural overview and separate encoder/decoder/comparison sections. Terminology changes throughout, including counterfactual/orthogonal and BPI/FPI/MPI versus BalancedBS/FemaleBS/MaleBS.

P2.justification: v3 redesigns the encoder plots, adds race/religion distribution figures, and expands the main comparison table into three bias-specific blocks. The gender heatmaps are consolidated into Figure 6, while new race/religion heatmaps and benchmark tables are added. The main gender heatmap loses two panels that remain available in the appendix, and the document adopts a different visual template.

R1.justification: v3 adds references supporting feature representations, broader bias research, SuperGLUE, religious-text interpretation, and criticism of CrowS. It also explicitly distinguishes GRADIEND's weight rewriting from activation-based sparse autoencoders and discusses Li et al.'s attention-based analysis. These refine the positioning while retaining the established feature-learning and debiasing literature.

T1.justification: v3 formalizes a feature with d >= 2 classes and separately selected factual/orthogonal class pairs. Appendix C.3 extends the custom probability definitions to attribute sets, class-membership indicators, and multi-token terms. The encoder–decoder equations, bias-score product structure, and derivation of the 2-alpha-times-decoder-bias symmetry difference remain unchanged; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v3 tests the non-gender applicability that v2 left largely conjectural and documents informative failures and applicability limits. SuperGLUE broadens capability checks, GLUE checkpoint selection addresses v2's acknowledged overfitting concern, and summary language-score aggregation is corrected. Dataset-access identifiers are lost, and some prose becomes inconsistent with the results: Section 5.4.1 implies GRADIEND plus SENTDEBIAS ranks second, while Table 2 places it fifth. These weaknesses temper, but do not outweigh, the substantially stronger evidence about what GRADIEND can and cannot achieve.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GRADIEND research, retaining the core architecture and identifiable gender experiments. Text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial expansion and reorganization in v3.

after.justification: v3 retains original gender experiments and adds original race/religion evaluations and SuperGLUE results, with detailed outcomes in the appendices.

before.justification: v2 reports original encoder evaluations, bias-changing experiments, baseline comparisons, and generalization analyses across seven transformer models, including detailed appendix results.

C1.justification: The training contribution broadens from specifically linear-regression NCL to monotonic-regression NCL, explicitly treating linear regression as its default instance. The main intrinsic-verifier and hMCTS contributions, task scope, and headline claims of approximately 88% Maze and 43% Sudoku success remain unchanged.

C2.justification: V4 adds interpretations of reduced single-sample performance as a scalability tradeoff, dense verification, structured negatives, and local constraints producing global ranking alignment (5.2 and Appendix D). Appendix F discusses quantified computational tradeoffs, and the contrastive-loss description changes from global to local minima. V3's standalone limitations paragraph is retained in Appendix I.

D1.justification: Appendix B.6 newly explains one-hot encoding, continuous denoising and argmax decoding; Appendix F adds memory and inference-time information. Appendix L explicitly states availability of datasets and pretrained checkpoints alongside code, whereas v3 already linked the same repository. These are additional disclosures, not established changes to the existing implementation.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same Maze size-generalization and SAT-Net-to-RRN Sudoku settings. The added experiments use the existing 15×15 Maze task; they introduce no new dataset, task or input-environment scenario.

E2.justification: V4 substantially expands comparisons with a learned external verifier for VFScale BoN, sparse and dense ground-truth verifiers for full VFScale hMCTS (Tables 10–11), and QRNCL, RBNCL and FTNCL loss variants (Table 12). V3's Original, DDPM and existing oracle comparisons remain.

E3.justification: Existing splits, training configurations, success metrics and matched-NFE comparisons are retained. Additional protocols compare verifiers on identical BoN candidates, measure Kendall tau across denoising steps 0–9, and profile peak memory and per-sample inference time (Tables 10, 19, 22–23). These supplement the original evaluation.

E4.justification: V4 adds analyses of verifier quality and reward density, alternative monotonic constraints, adaptive switching, permutation versus Gaussian negatives, and ranking alignment across denoising steps (Appendix D). V3's noise-scale, inner-loop and fixed-switch sensitivity studies remain, substantially expanding the questions tested.

E5.justification: V3 reports no run counts or uncertainty estimates. V4 introduces means and standard deviations over ten random seeds for key Maze comparisons (D.5/Table 18), plus mean and standard-deviation rank correlations (Table 19). This establishes new statistical reporting, not an increase from a documented earlier run count.

E6.justification: Earlier tabulated results are retained, while v4 adds substantial comparison, ablation, ranking and resource results. For example, Table 10 reports N=81 Maze success of 0.6562 with intrinsic versus 0.3203 with learned external verification; Table 18 newly reports N=81 hMCTS success of 0.8422±0.0147. These supplement rather than replace v3's headline scores.

M1.justification: The default linear loss, KL regularizer, backbone and Algorithm 1 remain unchanged. V4 adds optional adaptive BoN-to-MCTS switching based on branch-energy variance (D.3) and quadratic, rank-based and fixed-transformation loss variants (D.2). These extend components without replacing the core method.

P1.justification: V4 makes localized introduction and method rewrites, revises loss terminology, moves the experimental overview to Appendix B.1, and organizes appendix analyses into named subsections with a contents page. It adds acknowledgment and disclosure statements while retaining the main section sequence and much existing prose.

P2.justification: V4 substantially expands tables displaying verifier comparisons, variants, uncertainty, rankings and computational costs, and redraws Figure 2's intermediate states as continuous predictions. Existing plots and case studies remain with relocations, label updates and conference-format reflow. Table 21 redisplays training times already reported in v3's prose.

R1.justification: The same 28 cited works and principal positioning relative to energy-based reasoning and externally verified diffusion scaling are retained. Updated titles, venues and author-year citation formatting do not introduce new related work.

T1.justification: The displayed core objectives, denoising equations, Appendix A consistency definition and linear-regression derivation are preserved apart from notation. V4's local-to-global discussion offers hypotheses and empirical evidence, without new formal assumptions, guarantees or proofs. Kendall tau is an added evaluation metric.

improvement.justification: V4 addresses important evidential gaps through ten-seed uncertainty estimates, direct verifier controls, and tests of alternative losses and negative sampling (Appendix D). Processing details and measured resource costs also improve reproducibility and assessment of computational tradeoffs (B.6/F). Some new claims that search success establishes global alignment exceed what the empirical tests demonstrate, but the substantial gains in validation and transparency outweigh this weakness.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe VFScale. Their main texts, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite v4's expansion and reorganization.

after.justification: V4 retains those original experiments and adds verifier comparisons, method variants, repeated-seed results, ranking analyses and computational measurements.

before.justification: V3 reports original Maze and Sudoku experiments, including generalization, training ablations, inference comparisons and sensitivity analyses.

C1.justification: V1 broadly presents CLEF as counterfactual generation preserving causal consistency. V2 distinguishes conditional generation from counterfactual prediction under assumptions and adds integration with causal predictors and performance under high confounding as core contributions (Introduction and Conclusion). Original immediate, delayed and zero-shot generation claims remain.

C2.justification: V2 specifies when sequence editing admits a causal interpretation, including identification assumptions and the absence of intervening treatments except the queried treatment. It newly interprets performance without balancing loss as evidence of balanced temporal representations (Sections 3.3 and 5.4). The original limitations and diabetes interpretations are largely retained or relocated.

D1.justification: V2 adds simulation/preprocessing instructions and CRN/CT integration details, including the attachment point, training objective and source hyperparameter configurations (Appendices C.3–C.4 and D.2–D.5). It also specifies Huber δ=1 and states that potentially sensitive patient data/model weights are not shared. Original hardware, hyperparameter grids and repository information remain.

E1.justification: V2 retains WOT, WOT-CF, eICU, MIMIC-IV and the diabetes cohorts. It adds tumor-growth counterfactual prediction under single-sliding treatment and random treatment scenarios, plus semi-synthetic MIMIC-III-CF trajectories with known counterfactual outcomes (Appendices C.3–C.4).

E2.justification: The original comparators remain. V2 additionally evaluates five causal prediction comparators: Counterfactual Recurrent Network with GR, CDC or no balancing loss, and Causal Transformer with CDC or no balancing loss (Appendix D.2; Figures 5 and 13–16). These comparisons are absent from v1.

E3.justification: New protocols include multi-step RMSE evaluation, confounding levels γ=0–4, tumor trajectory splits of 10,000/1,000/1,000, and a 60%/20%/20% split of 1,000 MIMIC-III-CF patients. The new ICU protocol specifies hourly aggregation, imputation, normalization and sampled treatment trajectories (Appendices C.3–C.4). Original experimental settings are retained.

E4.justification: V2 retains the original FFN/SimpleLinear ablations, SPECTRA analyses and diabetes interventions. It adds controlled analyses of confounding strength and prediction horizon, and tests whether CLEF benefits from balancing losses in CRN/CT (Section 5.4; Figures 5 and 13–16).

E5.justification: V1 already displays error bars and ± values without defining their estimation. V2 specifies three seeds for retained benchmarks, identifies 95% confidence intervals and Table 2 standard deviations, and reports five seeds for new causal benchmarks. These disclosures do not establish additional runs for retained experiments.

E6.justification: The original result plots and Table 2 numerical entries are retained. V2 adds RMSE results across confounding levels and prediction horizons for tumor and ICU counterfactuals (Figures 5 and 13–16). For example, Figure 5 shows lower RMSE with CLEF-CT plus CDC at γ=3–4 in the newly evaluated single-sliding treatment setting.

M1.justification: The original four-component CLEF architecture is retained. V2 adds CLEF-CRN and CLEF-CT by appending CLEF's GELU activation and multiplicative concept decoder to those models' outcome predictors; these extensions use factual-outcome MSE training (Appendix D.2). This substantively extends the procedure to counterfactual outcome estimation.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contributions and conclusion are extensively rewritten; the title and CLEF acronym expansion change. New causal-method/results subsections and expanded appendices reorganize related work, experimental details, limitations and broader impact. These changes substantially alter the narrative and document structure.

P2.justification: V2 changes the main text from two columns to one column with wrapped figures, rescales and relocates displays, moves Table 1 to the appendix and simplifies Table 2 row labels. New counterfactual plots replace the main generalization overview and add Figures 13–16; generalization evidence remains in Appendix Figures 11–12.

R1.justification: Section 2 and new Appendix A substantially expand positioning around longitudinal causal inference and digital twins, adding CRN, CT, potential-outcome and g-computation literature. V2 discusses excluded causal baselines and positions CLEF as an extension to existing causal prediction architectures, beyond v1's sequence-editing and concept-learning framing.

T1.justification: V2 adds a potential-outcome conditional mean formulation, Assumption 3.4, formal consistency/positivity/sequential ignorability assumptions, and a G-computation identifiability corollary (Section 3.3; Appendix B). Definition 3.1 also explicitly places treatment shortly before outcome measurement. V1 lacks this causal identification framework.

improvement.justification: V1's broad counterfactual claims lacked explicit identification assumptions and comparisons with longitudinal causal predictors. V2 substantially strengthens their basis through clearer conditional-versus-causal framing, known-counterfactual tumor/ICU benchmarks, and confounding/balancing analyses (Section 3.3, Section 5.4 and Appendix B). Uncertainty reporting also becomes interpretable. The new claim that prediction accuracy demonstrates balanced representations remains insufficiently established, but the clearer scope and stronger empirical validation provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CLEF, with matching core architecture, original datasets and retained results. Their text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite retitling and substantial reorganization.

after.justification: V2 reports original sequence-editing and patient case-study results, plus counterfactual prediction experiments on synthetic tumor growth and semi-synthetic ICU trajectories in Section 5.4 and Appendix E.

before.justification: Sections 5.1–5.5 and Appendix C report original benchmarking, simulated cellular trajectories, patient generalization experiments and diabetes case studies.

C1.justification: The central contributions remain controllable temporal-concept editing and counterfactual generation. v3 broadens claimed validation to sales, replaces headline maximum editing improvements of 36.01%/65.71% with average improvements of 16.28%/26.73% against matched non-CLEF counterparts, and adds a conclusion claim of generally faster convergence at comparable complexity. These refine the claims without redefining the contribution.

C2.justification: v3 substantially expands the interpretation of temporal concepts: it explains the multiplicative decoder's handling of measurement scales, argues why intermediate forecasts can accumulate noise in irregular ICU trajectories, and interprets treatment-prediction diagnostics as evidence about representation balance. Appendix F newly acknowledges possible decoder linearity restrictions and failure with missing or zero final observations, supplementing the retained hierarchical-concept and causal-guidance limitations.

D1.justification: v3 supplements the existing implementation documentation with exact total/trainable parameter counts, runtime and checkpoint tables, GPU memory/utilization figures, and M5-specific hyperparameters. Appendix C.1.1 also explicitly documents distinct counterfactual conditions, different subsequent cell sets, and trajectory uniqueness. These add technical disclosure; the code location and restrictions on sharing sensitive patient data and weights remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v3 adds M5 Walmart sales trajectories, extending evaluation beyond biological and clinical domains to product-price-conditioned sales prediction (Appendix C.5; Figures 4, 8–9). This introduces a substantially different application domain. The seven previous benchmarks remain; M5 evaluates observed trajectories, not ground-truth counterfactual outcomes.

E2.justification: The original Transformer, xLSTM, MOMENT, VAR, and five CRN/CT comparator configurations remain. v3 adds LowR decoder variants to immediate and delayed editing comparisons (Tables 7–8) and introduces SimpleLinear as a model comparator in both diabetes intervention studies (Tables 13–14), where v2 compared patient groups without that model control.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include the California/Texas/Wisconsin training/validation/test split for M5, LowR ranks 4/8/16, insertion of three intermediate forecast steps, separate edited/unedited-variable errors, and treatment-prediction BCE diagnostics. Table 1 also changes the reported WOT-CF sample count from 2,546 to 2,560. Existing patient splits, tumor simulation settings, and previously specified benchmark hyperparameters are retained.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained FFN, generalization, confounding, and intervention analyses, v3 tests preservation of unedited variables, alternative decoder structures, error accumulation from intermediate forecasts, and treatment predictability of representations.
