It also adds computational/convergence comparisons, SimpleLinear intervention controls, and individual patient trajectories (Tables 2–5 and 7–16). These substantially expand the examination of CLEF's mechanisms and behavior.

E5.justification: Both versions report three seeds for conditional-generation experiments, five for counterfactual benchmarks, 95% confidence intervals in figures, and standard deviations in the generalization table. Added tables continue repeated-run and variation reporting. Figure 6's added three-seed statement repeats information already supplied for that experiment in v2 Figure 17; no increased run count or new statistical test is established.

E6.justification: v3 adds substantial numerical and qualitative results for M5 and the new analyses. For example, Table 7 reports immediate M5 MAE of 1.306±0.032 for xLSTM versus 0.845±0.006 for CLEF-xLSTM with FFN=1. WOT-CF results in Figures 6 and 17 are updated, and the abstract's maximum zero-shot improvement changes from 63.19% to 62.84% alongside the revised sample. These are not established same-setting gains over v2. The generalization table and most existing clinical/counterfactual plots remain unchanged.

M1.justification: CLEF's sequence encoder, condition adapter, temporal concept encoder, multiplicative decoder, and forecasting procedure remain unchanged. Huber loss and counterfactual MSE/balancing objectives already appear in v2. LowR decoders and intermediate-step variants are introduced as experimental ablations, without replacing the proposed CLEF procedure.

P1.justification: v3 extensively revises the abstract, opening motivation, dataset overview, several results passages, and conclusion. It reorganizes Appendix D, moves the Huber explanation and intervention formalism into appendices, relocates Broader Impact as an Ethics Statement, and adds a Reproducibility Statement. These constitute substantial editorial and structural revision beyond the added scientific content.

P2.justification: Figure 4 changes from a horizontal arrangement to two rows with added M5 panels; Figures 8–9 gain M5 panels and share a page. Counterfactual plots are redrawn, and new resource, diagnostic, ablation, and patient-trajectory tables substantially expand the displays. Conference typography, headers, figure sizing, and placement also change, while many older plots are retained and relocated.

R1.justification: v3 adds focused distinctions from positional biological sequence design and reinforcement learning in Appendix A.3, citing Stanton, MGhari, Jain, and Oh, among others. It also adds M5, concept-intervention distribution-shift, and diffusion-game-engine references, while dropping the FDA animal-testing motivation/source. The principal positioning around sequence generation, counterfactual estimation, and concept learning remains.

T1.justification: The substantive causal assumptions, conditional-mean assumption, and G-computation corollary are retained. Definition 3.2 restates the existing temporal-concept ratio through its multiplicative relationship, and the Huber formula moves to Appendix D.1. No new proof, theorem, or substantive formal guarantee is introduced.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens scrutiny of CLEF's central promises through direct preservation measurements, decoder and intermediate-step ablations, and model controls for diabetes simulations (Tables 5, 7–9, 13–14). These address gaps in v2's reliance on aggregate accuracy and patient-group comparisons. Broader domain testing, quantified computational costs, and explicit decoder failure conditions further improve assessability. Treatment-invariance diagnostics remain mixed and do not establish general causal validity, but this limitation does not outweigh the substantial validation gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CLEF research work. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite reformatting and added material.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical evaluations and adds sales forecasting, decoder ablations, representation diagnostics, computational measurements, and patient-level analyses.

before.justification: v2 reports original sequence-editing experiments, simulated counterfactual predictions, generalization evaluations, and diabetes patient case studies in Sections 5.1–5.6 and the appendices.

C1.justification: v3 explicitly claims to be the first framework addressing suboptimal demonstrations in skill-based meta-RL through both exploration-guided refinement and relabeling, and adds an accelerated-convergence claim in the introduction. The central contributions and claims of robust adaptation through skill refinement and maximum return relabeling remain.

C2.justification: v3 adds a reward-model stability argument, identifies potential bias from differing task reward scales and suggests per-task standardization (Section 5.4 and Appendix F.4). Its limitations replace v1's qualitative description of comparable per-iteration computation with a measured 16% overhead. The meta-test fine-tuning limitation is retained.

D1.justification: v3 adds baseline repository links, reports training runtime, documents resetting the high-level buffer during reinitialization and offers a temperature-selection guideline. Its reproducibility statement says anonymized SISL code accompanies supplementary material, although availability cannot be verified from the PDFs. Existing architecture, hardware and hyperparameter details are retained.

E1.justification: The four environments and their task definitions remain unchanged. Within Kitchen, v3 adds random-action corruption and medium-quality or uniformly random demonstrations, extending the evaluated data conditions beyond expert and Gaussian-corrupted demonstrations (Appendices D.3-D.4).

E2.justification: Table 1 retains SAC, SAC+RND, PEARL, PEARL+RND, SPiRL and SiMPL. The new robustness comparisons reuse SPiRL and SiMPL; no external comparator is added or removed from a corresponding retained experiment. New component-removal variants are ablations.

E3.justification: v3 substantially extends the evaluation design with Kitchen dataset-size controls at 50%, 25% and 10%, random action replacement at 25%, 50% and 100%, and expert/medium/random comparisons. It also evaluates reward-model MSE and runtime. Existing task splits, training budgets, horizons and tabulated hyperparameters remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 adds robustness studies of data scarcity, unstructured corruption and demonstration quality, plus reward-model accuracy across noise levels and quantitative state-action coverage analysis. Appendix G.4 separately ablates RND and high-level policy reinitialization. The earlier buffer, prioritization-temperature and KL-coefficient ablations and skill visualizations are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions specify five random seeds and standard deviations shown through shaded regions and table uncertainties. The additional results follow this reporting practice; no increased run count, confidence interval procedure or significance test is introduced.

E6.justification: All 64 mean/standard-deviation pairs in Table 1 are unchanged. Substantial new results appear in the appendices: SISL achieves 3.28±0.15 with 10% Kitchen expert data and 1.68±0.18 with random data. Removing reinitialization yields 0.41±0.11 versus full SISL's 3.48±0.07 at Gaussian noise σ=0.3. Reward-model errors, coverage percentages and runtime measurements are also newly reported.

M1.justification: PRISM's exploration policy and buffer are renamed as SISL's skill-improvement policy and buffer. The objectives, prioritization, periodic skill deployment, high-level policy reinitialization and meta-test procedure remain equivalent. The additional buffer-reset description in Appendix G.4 is newly disclosed detail, without evidence that the procedure changed.

P1.justification: Beyond renaming PRISM to SISL, v3 extensively rewrites the contribution and methodology narrative around decoupled policies and self-improvement. It reorganizes appendix analyses, retains pseudocode only in the appendix, condenses environment descriptions, moves limitations into the main text and adds reproducibility and LLM-use statements.

P2.justification: The main text changes from a two-column ICML layout to a single-column ICLR layout. Figures 2 and 3 are redrawn, environment and learning-curve panels are rearranged, and retained analyses and algorithms are relocated. Five result tables are added: D.1-D.3, F.1 and G.1.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds targeted references, including Kipf et al., Rana et al. and Schmidt et al., and explicitly distinguishes reward-free skill learning from offline-to-online RL. It also excludes Yu et al. (2024b) and Wu et al. from its skill-learning category. Reset-related citations are added in G.4, while several exploration/self-supervision references are removed.

T1.justification: Equations (1)-(7) and the appendix loss definitions remain mathematically equivalent after notation changes and reordering. Neither version supplies formal theorems or proofs that are added or removed. New stability and curriculum explanations are informal interpretations.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the central robustness claim beyond v1's Gaussian-corruption experiments through scarce-data, random-corruption and medium/random-demonstration tests. New RND/reset ablations and runtime measurements address important validation and computational-cost gaps. One added explanation is inconsistent: F.4 says the reward-model buffers contain no offline data, whereas Section 4.2 initializes the prioritized buffer from offline data. Despite this weakness, the expanded controlled evidence provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, renamed from PRISM to SISL. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, and the methods, equations, tables and figures can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v3 retains these original results and adds data-quality and data-size experiments, reward-model measurements, runtime measurements and component ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments on Kitchen, Office, Maze2D and AntMaze, including benchmark returns, learning curves, ablations and skill visualizations.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the central claims of higher-order guided generation, faster score-matching convergence, tighter reconstruction bounds and competitive molecular/generic graph generation. Listing cell complex filtering separately in the four-part contribution list reframes a contribution already introduced in v1.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations for retaining spectral diffusion despite broadly comparable generation quality and for selecting guides according to dataset structure. Appendix F.3 discusses higher-dimensional sparsity, computational overhead and overfitting risk; Appendix G adds barriers to extending guidance to motifs, higher-order cells and cavities. The weaker benefits on Ego-small were already recognized in v1 and are retained.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies the EMD kernel for existing generic benchmarks, expands baseline-result provenance, provides SBM construction parameters and molecular-analysis instructions, and states that experimental code accompanies the supplementary material. Hardware, molecular preprocessing and the public code URL are retained. Conversely, v1's explicit explanation of formal-charge extensions to GraphAF/GraphDF is omitted.

E1.justification: v2 adds the SBM dataset, comprising 200 synthetic community-structured graphs with 44–187 nodes, while retaining QM9, ZINC250k, Community-small, Ego-small and Enzymes. This extends the existing generic graph-generation task to a larger synthetic graph population.

E2.justification: Molecular Table 1 adds GraphArm, MiCaM, SPECTRE, GSDM, CatFlow and DeFoG, substantially broadening comparisons with motif, spectral and flow-based alternatives. Generic Table 2 adds SPECTRE, and the new SBM comparison includes GRAN and GruM. GraphAF/GraphDF reporting is consolidated: v2's rows largely correspond to v1's +FC entries, while the separate standard rows disappear.

E3.justification: The existing molecular sampling budget of 10,000 and original benchmark settings are retained. The added SBM experiment uses a separate protocol with TV-based MMD and an additional Spec. metric; new analyses use matched hyperparameter search spaces for diffusion-domain variants and Morgan fingerprints with UMAP. Corrected validity remains reported in Appendix Tables 9–10 despite leaving the main table.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained cell/peripheral/noise ablations, v2 adds adjacency-versus-Laplacian diffusion experiments in Table 6, higher-order structure counts in Table 8, a qualitative report of worse molecular generation with 2-simplex guides, and molecular-distribution comparisons in Figure 8. These substantially expand the evidence concerning diffusion-domain choice, guide selection and distributional fidelity.

E5.justification: v1's molecular tables provide point estimates without a stated experimental run count. v2 reports three-run means and standard deviations in Tables 9–10, with asterisks identifying baselines lacking reported deviations. This substantially expands uncertainty reporting, but does not establish that the number of runs increased.

E6.justification: v2 adds baseline, SBM, timing, diffusion-domain, structure-count and distributional results. Existing reported values also change: HOG-Diff's ZINC250k FCD goes from 1.533 to 1.633, and QM9 uniqueness from 97.01 to 97.10. ZINC250k noise/peripheral-guide FCD changes from 1.665/1.541 in v1 Figure 4 to 2.665/2.641 in v2 Table 3; GraphEBM's QM9 NSPDK changes from 0.003 to 0.030. HOG-Diff's original generic Table 2 scores remain unchanged. These revisions do not establish same-setting performance improvements.

M1.justification: The core framework, spectral score network, loss and sampling pseudocode are retained. However, v1 Appendix D.2 describes GOU bridges in every subprocess, whereas v2 Appendix C.4 specifies a VP SDE for the final forward-diffusion interval. Since v2 Algorithm 2 still applies GOU-bridge updates throughout, the PDFs do not resolve whether this is a procedural change or a newly disclosed implementation exception.

P1.justification: The introduction is substantially rewritten around higher-order interactions and molecular structures. The method is reorganized into Sections 3.1–3.3, spectral motivation moves into Appendix C.2, and the background and related-work appendices are merged and reorganized. Extensive prose editing accompanies the terminology change from denoising network to score network and the added reproducibility and limitations sections.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to predominantly single-column pages with wrapped figures. Figure 2 gains a lifting panel, and v1 Figure 4 is separated into v2 Figure 4 and Table 3. Molecular tables are expanded and redistributed, while new timing, ablation, SBM, structure-count and uncertainty tables, a UMAP figure and SBM sample visualizations substantially extend the displays.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning around hierarchical and fragment-based generation, including HiGen, HierDiff and MiCaM, and discusses HypDiff, CatFlow and DeFoG. It adds broader topological-learning and molecular-design motivation and corrects HypeBoy's characterization to representation learning rather than direct hypergraph generation. Dymond is relocated, and Hygene's publication update represents the same cited work.

T1.justification: v2 Proposition 2 revises cell filtering to select closures of cells with a specified dimension p, replacing v1 Definition 3.1's unspecified cell membership. Section 2 also corrects the terminal conditional-density statement from equality to 1 to a Dirac-delta limit. The convergence and reconstruction proofs, including the Brownian-bridge derivation, are retained despite renumbering.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical support by adding relevant motif, spectral and recent flow baselines, directly testing diffusion-domain choice, reporting three-run uncertainty and evaluating larger SBM graphs. These address important validation gaps in v1 and make the method's strengths and applicability easier to assess. Guide-selection explanations and explicit computational limitations further improve transparency. The unresolved VP-stage description versus sampling pseudocode limits methodological clarity, but does not outweigh these substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe HOG-Diff by the same authors. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and can be matched across the reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original HOG-Diff experiments and adds SBM generation, diffusion-domain ablations, sampling-time measurements and molecular-distribution analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original molecular and generic graph-generation results in Tables 1–2, topological-guide ablations in Figure 4, and generated samples in the appendix.

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution list broaden the empirical claim to scalability and superior pairwise and higher-order metrics across eight benchmarks. The central contributions—explicit topological guidance, coarse-to-fine diffusion bridges, faster score-matching convergence and tighter reconstruction bounds—retain their previous meaning.

C2.justification: v3 interprets curvature results as evidence of recovering the topological backbone and attributes performance gains to higher-order preservation. It expands the computational-feasibility argument and explains approximate atom-type signals as motivation for endpoint perturbations. Existing limitations concerning topology-poor graphs and expensive richer filters remain; adaptive filtering order is added as future work.

D1.justification: v3 adds disclosure of masked endpoint perturbations, MOSES scaffold evaluation, GuacaMol round-trip preprocessing and descriptor-based scoring, plus concrete preprocessing and training times. Hardware and the core implementation description remain unchanged. The direct repository link becomes a project-page link, and the supplementary-code statement is removed; the PDFs cannot establish the external resources' actual availability.

E1.justification: v3 adds MOSES and GuacaMol, expanding from six to eight benchmarks. These introduce large lead-like and ChEMBL-derived molecular populations, including MOSES scaffold-generalization evaluation and GuacaMol molecules with up to 88 nodes. All six earlier datasets, including SBM, remain.

E2.justification: Comparator membership changes across several experiments: Cometh is added on QM9; RefineGen replaces DiGress in the standard SBM comparison; DisCo appears on MOSES and GuacaMol, and GraphINVENT on MOSES. DeepGMG disappears from the generic graph comparison. GraphEBM remains in the full appendix molecular tables, so its omission from main Table 1 is a display relocation.

E3.justification: New evaluation protocols include curvature-based persistence-landscape distances across eight datasets, MOSES scaffold-separated evaluation, GuacaMol preprocessing and normalized FCD/KL scores, and SBM validity–uniqueness–novelty evaluation. The original QM9/ZINC250k sampling protocol and generic-graph EMD/TV settings are retained. Renaming the two validity columns does not change their definitions.

E4.justification: New Section 4.3 directly tests multiscale topological preservation through curvature filtrations. Figure 3 adds generation-trajectory comparisons with GDSS and DiGress, while Appendix D.2 adds empirical preprocessing scalability and training-time comparisons. The earlier diffusion-domain ablation, filter-choice analysis and chemical-space visualization remain; Table 13 additionally contextualizes structural counts with node and edge counts.

E5.justification: Both versions report three-run means and standard deviations for QM9/ZINC250k and mark baselines lacking deviations with asterisks: v2 Tables 9–10 correspond to v3 Tables 8–9. Added rows and revised deviation values do not introduce a new reporting practice. No increased run count, seed specification, confidence interval or significance-testing procedure is documented.

E6.justification: Substantial additions include curvature distances, MOSES FCD 0.94, GuacaMol results, computational timings and SBM V.U.N. 0.83. Most original headline scores remain unchanged. However, ZINC guide-ablation FCDs change from 2.665/2.641/1.633 to 1.665/1.541/1.533 for noise/peripheral/cell guides without explanation; v3's cell value conflicts with 1.633 elsewhere. Appendix QM9 uniqueness also changes from 97.10 to 97.14, alongside revised standard deviations.

M1.justification: The CCF curriculum, GOU/VP diffusion processes, Laplacian representation, score network, objectives and Algorithms 1–2 are retained. Appendix C.2 newly mentions masked Gaussian perturbations of intermediate molecular node features, but does not establish that this represents an implementation change rather than newly disclosed training detail.

P1.justification: The introduction is substantially rewritten, with historical discussion redistributed into Related Work. Appendices D–F are reorganized, including moving the extended molecular results from F.4 to F.1 and separating efficiency and dataset discussions into subsections. Metric explanations and the conclusion are rewritten, and limitations also appear in the main text. This exceeds routine copyediting.

P2.justification: Figure 1 gains performance radar plots, and Figure 3 combines large-molecule result panels with comparative trajectories; the former Figure 3 is retained as appendix Figure 10. New displays include the curvature table, training-time table, filtering-cost plot and MOSES table. Molecular table columns and highlighting are redesigned, while SBM and structural-count tables gain columns.

R1.justification: The literature is updated with Cometh, DisCo, RefineGen, GraphINVENT, curvature filtrations, the added benchmarks and recent topological-learning work; several older citations are removed. The positioning around explicit higher-order guidance remains substantially unchanged. GLAD's workshop-to-conference reference update concerns the same work and does not constitute a new research relationship.

T1.justification: Theorem 4 changes from a bound over [0, tau1] containing E(tau1) to an accumulated K-stage reconstruction bound. Appendix A.3 adds Lemma 6 concerning function-class inclusion and optimal score losses, unrolls stage-wise error propagation, and introduces coefficient-domination and total-loss comparisons. These substantially revise the mathematical argument; the bridge derivation and Theorem 3 are largely retained.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens evidence for the central higher-order-guidance premise through direct multiscale topology evaluation, and tests molecular scale and scaffold generalization beyond v2's coverage. Measured preprocessing and training costs also make applicability more assessable. These gains outweigh localized reporting weaknesses, including the inconsistent ZINC cell-guide FCD and the retained no-slowdown assertion despite slower QM9 and Community-small training in the new Table 5.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe HOG-Diff by the same authors. Their readable text, equations, tables, figures and complete Appendices A–G support reliable comparison despite substantial additions and renumbering.

after.justification: v3 retains original experiments and adds molecular benchmark results, curvature-filtration evaluations, comparative generation trajectories and computational timing measurements.

before.justification: v2 reports original molecular and generic graph generation results, guide and diffusion-domain ablations, and sampling-time measurements in Section 4 and Appendices D–F.

C1.justification: The central non-asymptotic JE/AIS complexity claims remain. V2's abstract and contributions additionally claim empirical effectiveness and superiority over AIS in handling multimodality, and describe the action lower bound as quantitatively explaining mass teleportation.

C2.justification: V2 adds comparisons between sampling and normalizing-constant estimation complexities, including an explanation of their different discretization requirements. It interprets the action lower bound through mass teleportation and the experiments through mode coverage. The conclusion newly identifies limited practical interpretability of action; the existing tightness uncertainty and drift-estimation tradeoff remain.

D1.justification: Appendix I adds target parameters, reference-integration instructions, algorithm hyperparameters, score-estimation sample counts, and metric software details. Algorithm 2 also explains how to generate its correlated Gaussian noises. Conversely, v1's detailed TI parameter derivation is removed. Reproduction of MMD remains problematic: Appendix I.3 lists a zero bandwidth and a normalized kernel inconsistent with the reported MMD magnitudes.

E1.justification: V2 introduces actual evaluations on a modified Müller Brown distribution and an unequal-weight, four-component Gaussian mixture, both in two dimensions. V1 contains no empirical coverage; its Gaussian-mixture counterexample is theoretical.

E2.justification: Table 1 introduces measured comparisons of TI and AIS against RDMC, RSDMC, ZODMC, and SNDMC on both targets. These methods were discussed in v1, but none participated in a reported empirical comparison there.

E3.justification: Appendix I introduces a comparison budget of 50,000–60,000 oracle calls per generated sample and evaluates Z-hat/Z plus Gaussian-mixture MMD and Wasserstein-2 distance. Settings include 60,000 AIS steps and 50 RDS time steps with T=5 and δ=0.005. V1 has no corresponding experimental protocol.

E4.justification: Figures 2–3 and Appendix I add qualitative mode-coverage diagnostics by overlaying generated samples on target-potential contours. These support analyses of inadequate mode exploration by TI/AIS. No component ablations or sensitivity sweeps are introduced.

E5.justification: V2 introduces empirical mean±standard-deviation reporting across 1,024 rounds, each averaging 1,024 independent trajectory estimates, and reports numerical-integration uncertainty for the Müller Brown reference constant. V1's variance bounds and median-trick discussion are theoretical rather than experimental uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: V2 adds all numerical results in Table 1 and sample findings in Figures 2–3. For the Gaussian mixture, Z-hat/Z is 0.2042±0.0008 for AIS, 1.0001±0.0850 for RDMC, and 0.9973±0.0834 for SNDMC. Results also reveal substantial variability, including Müller Brown RSDMC at 1.2885±12.7843. These evaluations have no v1 experimental counterpart.

M1.justification: V2 makes a localized but consequential correction to the RDS estimator: Algorithm 2's final work update changes +(T−δ)d to −(T−δ)d, consistently with Theorem 5. This changes the returned estimate. The AIS procedure and four RDS score-estimation approaches otherwise remain; those approaches already appeared in v1 Appendix E.5.

P1.justification: V2 substantially reorganizes the narrative: much of v1's standalone preliminaries moves to Appendix A or the RDS section, while the problem-setting section gains motivating examples and a highlighted aim. Contributions, related work, the RDS discussion, and the conclusion are restructured. These changes extend beyond inserting experimental content.

P2.justification: V2 adds a six-method results table and two six-panel figures displaying samples against potential contours. The existing proof diagram remains Figure 1 but is resized and positioned before its explanatory sketch. A highlighted problem statement and substantial reflow further change the presentation.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands positioning through a new discussion of sampling beyond isoperimetry, computational hardness, and the relationship to Guo et al. (2025). It adds mass-teleportation literature and acknowledges an independently developed related proof in Chemseddine et al. (2025), alongside additional neural-sampling references. Publication updates to retained works are separate bibliographic edits.

T1.justification: V2 changes the AIS initialization complexity term from d^(3/2)/ε² to d^(4/3)/ε² while removing v1 Lemma 19 and its detailed Appendix H.2 proof. It changes Assumption 2 to exact stationarity at zero and extends the action lower bound to all r≥1. Appendix E corrects the RDS likelihood-ratio derivation, restores a missing dimension factor in the OU total-variation bound, and changes the SNDMC Hessian lower bound from βI to −βI. The principal action-dependent JE/AIS rates remain.

improvement.justification: The corrected RDS work sign in Theorem 5, Algorithm 2, and Appendix E.3 removes a systematic multiplicative error in the proposed estimator, resolving an important correctness defect. Repeated-run experiments and implementation details provide useful additional validation. These gains outweigh reduced self-containment of the TI guarantee and weaknesses in the new empirical reporting, particularly the inconsistent MMD specification and broad accuracy claims despite large RSDMC variability.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same JE/AIS/RDS research work. Their main text, equations, algorithms, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: V2 reports original normalizing-constant estimates and sampling results for two multimodal distributions in Table 1, Figures 2–3, and Appendix I.

before.justification: V1 reports theoretical results and proofs, including an analytical Gaussian-mixture example, but no original experimental or simulation outcomes.

C1.justification: Both versions advocate low-rank collapse as the diagnostic perspective, claim better correspondence with performance degradation, and establish rank convergence under stated weight and activation assumptions. The nonlinear-setting qualifier added to v3's abstract matches the novelty restriction already stated in v1's introduction; expanded experiments support the retained contributions.

C2.justification: New Appendix B explains that large rank does not guarantee good classification and that metric–accuracy correlations become uninformative when oversmoothing is alleviated. Appendices D and F further distinguish asymptotic untrained behavior from trained networks and clarify failures under residual connections and certain GCN activation settings. These substantially qualify applicability.

D1.justification: v3 newly specifies default dataset splits, the synthetic graph and initialization recipe, DropEdge's removal probability of 0.5, and the residual-update equation. These are focused reproducibility additions. The default-split statement is additional disclosure, without evidence that retained experiments changed splits.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained Cora, Citeseer, and Pubmed datasets, v3 evaluates Squirrel, Chameleon, Amazon Ratings, Roman Empire, and OGB-Arxiv, substantially extending coverage to heterophilic and large-scale graphs. Appendix D also introduces a synthetic Barabasi-Albert graph scenario.

E2.justification: The diagnostic comparators remain standard and normalized Dirichlet energy, standard and normalized projection energy, and MAD, alongside effective and numerical rank. The added datasets and architectural controls retain this comparator set.

E3.justification: v3 adds a controlled 300-layer evaluation using identity weights or weights sampled from U(0, 0.05) and U(0, 0.1), plus new architectural conditions involving BatchNorm, DropEdge, and residual connections. The retained trained-network protocol still uses width 32, eight depths from 2 to 24, and NAdam with learning rate 0.01.

E4.justification: New Appendix D tests how weight magnitude and activation choice affect asymptotic metric convergence. Appendix F extends the existing bias, LayerNorm, and PairNorm analyses with BatchNorm, DropEdge, and residual connections, testing whether metric–accuracy relationships survive interventions that alleviate oversmoothing.

E5.justification: Both versions report averaging metrics and accuracy over 10 separately trained GNNs. v3 adds no confidence intervals, significance tests, seed disclosures, or uncertainty bands; the retained plots are identical.

E6.justification: v3 adds extensive correlation results and synthetic convergence outcomes, including negative rank–accuracy correlations for residual networks whose accuracy remains stable. Some retained entries also change: the GCN+LeakyReLU+PairNorm accuracy ratio changes from 0.8252 in v1 Table 2 to 0.8556 in v3 Table 4, while its correlation coefficients remain unchanged. These revisions do not establish a same-setting performance improvement.

M1.justification: The proposed numerical-rank and effective-rank diagnostics retain their definitions and application to feature representations. Additional network components are experimental conditions. Appendix C discusses possible computational shortcuts without establishing an adopted change to the diagnostic procedure.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much of the prose remain intact. v3 edits background and contribution wording, consolidates the energy theorem presentation, renames the nonlinear subsection, reorganizes experimental material across appendices, and updates author ordering and acknowledgements. The expansion mainly supplies scientific content rather than pervasive rewriting.

P2.justification: v3 replaces the two-column main-text layout with a single-column format, substantially restructuring equation and table placement. The toy table becomes Figure 1 with a side caption; the main correlation display shifts to dataset comparisons, with architectural results reorganized into appendix tables. New tables are added, while the existing plots are retained and resized.

R1.justification: v3 adds references supporting GCN attribution, heterophily, beneficial smoothing, DropEdge, and newer oversmoothing analyses, including Kipf and Welling, Keriven, Rong and colleagues, and Roth. The LayerNorm reference to Ba and colleagues disappears. The central positioning relative to energy-based and rank-based research remains intact.

T1.justification: The principal rank-decay theorems and proofs are retained. Limited mathematical revisions include removing the assertion that the Lyapunov exponent is nonnegative in Appendix A.2. New Appendix C supplies asymptotic computational-cost analysis for the diagnostics and full or truncated SVD. Consolidating the earlier energy lemma and theorem is primarily reorganization.

improvement.justification: v1's empirical support largely covered three homophilic citation datasets. v3 substantially strengthens validation through heterophilic and large-scale datasets, controlled weight experiments, and architectural interventions. Its explicit limitations explain when the central rank–accuracy association fails, improving interpretation as well as coverage. These gains outweigh a small reporting inconsistency: the OGB-Arxiv GCN accuracy ratio is 0.0939 in Table 1 but 0.0957 in Table 3.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same rank-based investigation of GNN oversmoothing. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support comparison, including matching material relocated between versions.

after.justification: v3 retains original experiments and adds results across further datasets, synthetic networks, and architectural variants in Tables 1–4 and Appendices D–G.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments comparing oversmoothing metrics with classification accuracy, including Cora results in Section 6 and Citeseer and Pubmed plots in Appendix B.

C1.justification: The abstract and three principal contributions retain the same claims: unified spatial-signature modeling, a practical robustness metric, agreement with ranking stability, and analytical insight into semivalue-dependent robustness. The expanded evidence does not redefine these central contributions.

C2.justification: v3 interprets learning-algorithm variation as another source of ranking instability and connects Rp to practical top-k selection stability. Its conclusion now includes selected multiclass metrics within scope while retaining exclusions for non-linear-fractional binary metrics and regression in the multiple-valid-utility scenario. The principal geometric interpretation remains unchanged.

D1.justification: A new reproducibility statement reports a supplementary code package with scripts for all tables and figures. v3 also documents new dataset sources, learner configurations, sample sizes, and direction-sampling budgets. However, multiclass training is inconsistently specified as L-BFGS in A.1 and SGD in Tables 12, 17, and 18.

E1.justification: v3 adds regression on DIABETES, CALIFORNIA HOUSING, and AMES, and multiclass classification on DIGITS, WINE, and IRIS. Section 4.2 and Appendix A.6 also provide actual utility trade-off evaluations, whereas v2 experimentally concentrates on the binary multiple-valid-utility scenario.

E2.justification: Shapley, (4,1)-Beta Shapley, and Banzhaf remain the evaluated semivalue comparators in corresponding experiments. The same set is extended to new settings. The logistic-regression/MLP experiment varies the learning context, while overlap and Jaccard provide additional evaluation metrics.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce 300/100 training/test samples for regression, ridge and multiclass MLP learners, 1,000 Monte Carlo direction samples for higher-dimensional evaluations, and top-k measurements at k=10,20,50. Appendix A.8 additionally holds accuracy fixed while varying the learning algorithm. The original binary protocol is retained.

E4.justification: v3 adds empirical checks of the cross-size covariance assumption on BREAST and TITANIC (A.5), learning-algorithm sensitivity at fixed accuracy (A.8), and comparisons between Rp and top-k selection stability (A.9). The existing affine-surrogate validation remains in B.1.

E5.justification: Table 8 newly reports means with 95% confidence intervals over five seeds. Table 19 explicitly includes variation from both MLP initialization/optimization and semivalue approximation. Existing results retain five Monte Carlo trials and standard errors; an increase in their run counts is not reported.

E6.justification: All matched original result tables retain their numerical entries, but v3 Tables 8–20 add substantial results. These include exceptions to Banzhaf's usual advantage: the new three-utility CREDIT experiment reports R500 of 0.15, 0.16, and 0.11 for Shapley, Beta Shapley, and Banzhaf respectively (Table 15).

M1.justification: The spatial-signature construction, Rp definition, two-dimensional computation, and higher-dimensional Monte Carlo procedure are retained. The latter already appears in v2 Remark B.6. The multiclass decomposition instantiates the existing general construction with class-wise utilities without changing its computation steps.

P1.justification: v3 condenses the affine-surrogate discussion and conclusion, moves the Kendall connection into B.4, foregrounds alignment analysis in Section 3.3, and splits evaluation by scenario. Citation and author formatting also change. The abstract, introduction, and much existing appendix prose remain substantially intact.

P2.justification: v3 adds experiment and analysis Tables 8–20 and eight three-dimensional spatial-signature figures (12–19). Existing tables and two-dimensional figures are retained with relocation or renumbering. The conference template changes headers and author layout, and Figure 4 is substantially reduced in display size.

R1.justification: v3 adds references supporting the new datasets, including De Cock, Efron, and Fisher, and replaces the earlier Jia et al. nearest-neighbor citation with Wang et al. (2024a) on weighted nearest neighbors. The substantive positioning relative to prior data-valuation and robustness research remains stable.

T1.justification: v3 adds a Hoeffding error and sample-complexity bound for the existing Monte Carlo estimator (B.5), deterministic top-k overlap/Jaccard bounds with proofs (B.8), and multiclass utility decompositions (C.5). The general K-dimensional embedding and correlation decomposition already existed in v2; Proposition 3.3 largely promotes that existing analysis.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses an important validation gap: v2 motivates utility trade-offs and higher-dimensional applicability but experimentally focuses on binary multiple-valid utilities. New regression, multiclass, and trade-off evaluations, assumption checks, top-k analyses, and a Monte Carlo error bound substantially strengthen support and practical relevance. Conflicting multiclass optimizer descriptions limit reproducibility of that portion, but the broader validation gains remain substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete Appendices A–D are readable and support reliable matching despite additions and reorganization.

after.justification: v3 retains those original results and adds regression, multiclass classification, higher-dimensional utility, learning-algorithm sensitivity, and top-k stability experiments.

before.justification: v2 reports original semivalue experiments on eight binary-classification datasets, including rank correlations, robustness scores, and empirical validation of the affine utility approximation.

C1.justification: The central contributions remain low-to-high-fidelity transfer learning and two sequential schemes, with the retained claim of up to two orders of magnitude fewer high-fidelity simulations. V3's introduction extends the explicit efficiency claim from comparison with NPE to comparison with both NPE and TSNPE. Its more prominent naming of the sequential variants does not constitute a new original contribution.

C2.justification: V1 discusses shared features, simulator similarity, dimensionality, and ensemble overhead. V3 substantially develops this interpretation: Section 4.4 and Appendices B/J distinguish shared information from representational coherence and argue that posterior distance alone does not predict transfer success. Appendix K grounds the existing ensemble-cost caveat in measured tradeoffs, while the discussion adds guidance about when acquisition is worthwhile and the unresolved allocation of budgets across fidelities.

D1.justification: V3 expands v1's basic architecture and preprocessing description with software versions/licenses, Adam optimization, batch size 200, learning rate 0.0005, validation fraction, stopping patience, hardware, parallelization, and measured training costs (Appendices D/G/K). Appendix F.1.1 documents the MF-ABC implementation and settings. Section 6 promises code and data release upon publication; it does not establish present availability.

E1.justification: V3 retains all three original tasks and adds SLCP parameter inference, epidemiological SIR inference, and Gaussian Blob image inference using different image resolutions across fidelities. These substantially expand the represented domains, posterior structures, and observation types. Appendix B additionally evaluates noisy and coordinate-reversed OU observations.

E2.justification: V3 adds standalone TSNPE to the OU comparison (Figure 2) and MF-ABC to OU2, OU3, and OU4 (Figure 8), where v1 Figure 3 uses NPE as the baseline. MF-ABC was previously cited but not evaluated. Sequential multifidelity methods also enter the neuron comparisons in Figures 3B and 13.

E3.justification: V3 adds MMD and NRMSE evaluations, importance-resampling reference posteriors for SLCP/SIR, image preprocessing, and controlled perturbation protocols. It introduces per-observation sequential neuron evaluation and revises reported evaluation sizes. For example, spiking-network evaluation uses 1,000 observations in v1 Figure 5, versus 10,000 in v3 Figure 3, while v3 Appendix D.1 states 262,008. These documented changes and inconsistencies preclude exact matched-setting comparisons for affected results.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained pretraining-budget, parameter-dimensionality, calibration, and predictive analyses, v3 adds controlled noise/representation perturbations (Appendix B), MF-ABC threshold sensitivity and posterior diagnostics (F.1.1), joint low/high-fidelity pretraining experiments (H.3), posterior-distance analysis (J), and simulation-versus-training cost analysis (K). These directly investigate transfer effectiveness, alternative initialization, baseline sensitivity, and practical efficiency.

E5.justification: Ten-initialization averages and 95% confidence intervals already appear in v1. V3 adds explicit single-initialization reporting for costly non-amortized evaluations, mean and standard deviation for posterior distances (Table 3), and five-run timing summaries with standard deviations for L5PC (Table 4). This expands statistical documentation without establishing increased replication of the original experiments.

E6.justification: V3 adds benchmark accuracy curves, sequential neuron results, posterior-distance measurements, and computational-cost tables. It newly reports little acquisition benefit on SLCP/SIR and no clear advantage from joint pretraining. The reported neuron high/low-fidelity simulation-time ratio changes from approximately seven to four, without establishing matched hardware conditions. Conversely, the original firing-rate fractions of 66.4%, 94.2%, and 95.6% are retained in Figure 3F.

M1.justification: The original MF-NPE, MF-TSNPE, and acquisition-based algorithms retain their objectives and core procedures. V3 adds an explicit extension that transfers weights through multiple fidelity levels (Appendix L) and a CNN-embedding adaptation for image observations (Appendix E.6). These are limited extensions of the existing approach.

P1.justification: V3 reorganizes the results around a general benchmarking section, moves the detailed OU exposition into appendices, replaces the related-work subsection structure with thematic Background paragraphs, and extensively reorganizes the supplementary material. The abstract and method exposition are revised, acquisition-bias discussion moves to Appendix M, and reproducibility, acknowledgments, and LLM-use statements are added. This substantially changes the narrative structure.

P2.justification: V3 changes the main text from two columns to one, redraws the method schematic with neuron examples, and rebuilds the benchmark plots with additional metric panels. Original neuroscience figures and the firing-rate table are combined into Figure 3, while posterior and predictive displays move into appendices. New perturbation, image, sensitivity, posterior-distance, and cost displays constitute substantial visual redesign beyond renumbering.

R1.justification: V3 replaces the model-misspecification/ROPE discussion with substantially expanded positioning around simulation-efficient SBI, surrogate approaches, and concurrent multifidelity work by Thiele, Hikida, and Saoulis and colleagues. It also adds transfer-learning theory references and qualifies the earlier statement that transfer learning's potential for SBI had not been realized. These changes materially update the research context.

T1.justification: V3 Appendix C adds an explicit large-sample derivation connecting the NPE loss to expected posterior KL divergence, whereas v1 states related properties without this derivation. Appendix B adds mathematical definitions for controlled perturbations and information-invariance reasoning. These are limited formal additions; they do not establish a new transfer-learning convergence-rate guarantee.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens the evidence behind the efficiency claims. Evaluated TSNPE and MF-ABC comparisons address important comparator gaps in v1, while distinct benchmarks, controlled transfer analyses, and total-cost accounting make generality and practical efficiency more assessable. Expanded implementation details further improve reproducibility. Conflicting evaluation counts in Figure 3 and Appendix D.1 remain a material weakness, and code release is still deferred, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical support and explanation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same multifidelity inference work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching retained algorithms and experiments across substantial reorganization.

after.justification: V3 retains original empirical results and adds SLCP, SIR, and image experiments, controlled transfer-learning analyses, baseline comparisons, and computational-cost measurements.

before.justification: V1 reports original simulation experiments on the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process, a multicompartmental neuron, and a recurrent spiking network, including posterior accuracy, calibration, and predictive checks.

C1.justification: The central claims of few-shot force learning, OOD generalization, and forward/backward planning persist. v3 extends the stated contribution to vision-based physical reasoning and shifts the abstract's contrast from high-dimensional latent representations toward discrete transitions versus continuous explicit force fields.

C2.justification: v3 replaces the symbolic-input limitation with boundaries concerning varying friction/elasticity, deterministic environments, and rigid bodies. It adds explanations of NFF prediction failures and SlotFormer encoding failures. Solver interpretation changes from Euler's cross-scenario advantage to Heun3's stronger accuracy, with Euler justified through cost and stability (Appendix C).

D1.justification: Appendices A.3 and B.1 document PHYRE sampling, masks, recorded velocities, image resolution, convolutional channels, DeepONet size, solver step, learning rates, batching, and trajectory segmentation. Most existing state-based hyperparameters are retained. The new checklist promises code and data release after publication; it does not establish present availability.

E1.justification: v3 adds vision-based PHYRE ball-placement tasks with diverse object geometry and unseen templates. It also adds imperfect-observation scenarios through noisy N-body training trajectories and I-PHYRE states extracted from RGB images. These extend coverage beyond v1's state-based evaluations.

E2.justification: GCN joins IN and SlotFormer in the existing I-PHYRE and N-body prediction comparisons (v3 Table 1). DQN and RPIN enter the reported PHYRE planning comparison (Table 3). GPT-4o, human, and random-planning comparisons already appear in v1's appendix and are retained.

E3.justification: Appendix A.2 changes N-body central masses from fixed 5 to sampled ranges, revises cross-scenario masses and radii, replaces nine-body tests with eight- and ten-body systems, and extends evaluation horizons to 150 steps. PHYRE introduces fold-1 evaluation, 12,000 training trajectories, mask preprocessing, and AUCCESS. Noise and parallel planning-time experiments add further protocols.

E4.justification: v3 adds a DeepONet-versus-MLP ablation, noise and perception robustness tests, planning-time analysis, and NFF/SlotFormer failure cases. It removes v1's latent-dimension ablation, UMAP analysis, and dedicated SlotFormer overfitting curve. Integration-method analyses are revised; the controlled force-response analysis is retained as Figure A1 rather than newly added.

E5.justification: v3 reports prediction estimates with SEM in Table 1, replacing v1 Figure 5's median/quartile/outlier boxplots. The new timing experiment specifies three repetitions. Conversely, v1 Figure 7's explicit five-random-seed ablation disclosure is absent from v3. Existing planning uncertainty reports remain; these changes do not establish increased run counts.

E6.justification: New PHYRE results report AUCCESS of 49.22 for NFF, 36.58 for RPIN, 30.96 for DQN, and 21.04 for SlotFormer (Table 3). Noise, timing, and component-ablation results are added. N-body prediction and solver results change under revised conditions, precluding same-setting performance comparisons. Existing N-body, I-PHYRE, and GPT-4o planning tables retain their values.

M1.justification: v3 introduces a visual NFF adaptation using sparse convolutions on object masks, force and torque prediction, and mask translation/rotation to generate frames. PHYRE planning adds a pretrained TimeSFormer success classifier (Section 4.4; Appendix B.1). The state-based DeepONet and ODE pipeline already existed in v1 and remains substantively unchanged.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much shared prose remain intact. v3 retitles the paper, updates the author block, refines terminology and explanations, shortens planning exposition, moves impact text into Discussion, reorganizes appendices, and inserts a conference checklist.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one, with redesigned framework and transition diagrams. Prediction boxplots and the ablation figure are replaced by tables; trajectory panels are rearranged and the force-response figure moves to the appendix. New PHYRE, robustness, timing, and failure-case displays substantially revise the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v3 adds positioning against static-field approaches, event-attended graph ODEs, and physics-informed methods requiring known equations, citing Kofinas, Yuan, and Chu. It also adds GCN and TimeSFormer references and removes Dohare's continual-learning citation. The broader physical-reasoning and continuous-dynamics positioning remains.

T1.justification: The force-field formulation, second-order dynamics, forward/backward integration, and appendix metric definitions retain their mathematical substance. Planning equations are compressed into inline expressions. The added standard AUCCESS formula documents an evaluation metric; neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens validation by addressing part of v1's symbolic-input limitation through documented visual modeling and imperfect-perception tests. The neural-operator ablation, planning-time measurements, and explicit failure cases better support and delimit the central claims (Section 4.5; Appendices D, E, G). These gains outweigh the loss of latent-dimension and overfitting diagnostics. Mask supervision, lost seed disclosure, and unclear PHYRE baseline training counts between Figure 5 and Table 3 still limit interpretation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same NFF research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial additions and changed experimental conditions.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds PHYRE experiments, noise tests, planning-time measurements, and failure analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original trajectory prediction, planning, force-field visualization, and ablation results on I-PHYRE and N-body simulations.

C1.justification: v2 adds first-time weight-space processing of hash-based NeRFs as a central contribution. Its introduction and conclusion qualify unseen-architecture generalization to variants within training families, replacing v1's broader arbitrary-architecture language. Single-architecture performance claims also shift from matching or exceeding prior methods to superiority/state-of-the-art performance.

C2.justification: v1 presents LC as preferable for strong architectural invariance; v2 favors LR+C because LC weakens class separation. New interpretations discuss hash-table subclusters, sensitivity to table size, and Objaverse retrieval failures. The stated main limitation changes from missing hash-based validation to training and quantitative evaluation concentrated on ShapeNetRender.

D1.justification: Appendices A/B/D add exact graph attributes, hash hyperparameters, and NerfAcc implementation information. Reported hardware changes from RTX 3090 to RTX A6000. Core encoder/decoder and training hyperparameters, training-time estimates, and the planned code release remain. Conversely, v1's explicit cosine retrieval distance and NeRF input frequency-encoding widths are no longer specified.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates ShapeNetRender objects represented by MLPs and tri-planes. v2 adds hash-based NeRF inputs and ObjaNeRF/Objaverse queries against ShapeNetRender galleries, introducing a distinct data distribution and retrieval scenario. The separate quantitative class-level retrieval evaluation in v1 Appendix A is removed.

E2.justification: nf2vec and Cardace et al. remain the evaluated external comparators in corresponding single-architecture classification experiments: v1 Tables 2/4 and v2 Tables 3/5. No new external baseline is evaluated. The contrastive-only variant remains evaluated in v2 Appendix C.

E3.justification: Multi-architecture training changes from BOTH to ALL, with three representations per object and revised pair sampling. v2 adds hash depth, width, level-count, and table-size test configurations, plus cross-dataset retrieval with no matching instance in the gallery. Class-recall evaluation disappears. Appendix B retains the original ShapeNet splits, training epochs, batch sizes, and optimizer settings.

E4.justification: v2 adds hash-level/table-size sensitivity tests and cross-dataset retrieval robustness cases, including the LR versus LR+C ObjaNeRF comparison in Figure 9. The three-loss latent-space analysis is revised for three families. The separate seen-versus-unseen MLP t-SNE analysis in v1 Figure 5 and Appendix C is removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. Both present point estimates and qualitative visualizations.

E6.justification: Multi-architecture results are replaced under changed training conditions. For example, MLP-to-TRI LR+C recall@1 is 41.2% with BOTH training in v1 Table 5 and 30.6% with ALL training in v2 Table 10; these do not establish a controlled performance decline. Retrieval favors LC in v1 and LR+C in v2. Single-architecture MLP/TRI results remain unchanged, hash results are added, and class-level retrieval scores disappear.

M1.justification: Section 3 adds a parameter-graph conversion for multi-resolution hash tables using table-entry and feature nodes. Training changes from fixed MLP/tri-plane pairs to randomly selected pairs among three architectural families. The GMN encoder, nf2vec decoder, and underlying rendering and SigLIP loss forms remain.

P1.justification: Beyond the title change, v2 substantially reorganizes the exposition: existing MLP/tri-plane graph descriptions move to Appendix A, Section 3's loss motivation is condensed, architecture descriptions are consolidated, and LC results receive a dedicated Appendix C. The introduction, conclusion, and qualitative-analysis narrative are substantially rewritten.

P2.justification: The main text switches from two columns to one. Figures 1–2 incorporate hash inputs; architecture Tables 1/7 and detailed graph Figure 5 are added. Result tables gain reorganized rows/columns and family-based highlighting, while retrieval montages are redesigned and expanded. The class-retrieval table and unseen-MLP t-SNE display are removed.

R1.justification: The existing GMN, nf2vec, and contrastive-learning positioning remains. v2 adds focused references on hash-based NeRFs, ObjaNeRF/Objaverse, and NerfAcc, and explicitly distinguishes its hash-table graph construction from the constructions borrowed from Lim et al. This extends the retained research positioning rather than replacing it.

T1.justification: v2 Appendix A adds a mathematical graph-size comparison: the hash representation requires N(T+F) nodes and NTF edges, versus O(N(R^3+F)) nodes and O(NR^3F) edges for explicitly represented voxel grids. This supplies a new complexity argument absent from v1, without adding a broader theorem or proof framework.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses v1's stated main limitation—untested hash-table NeRFs—with a concrete graph construction, complexity justification, and substantial classification, retrieval, and architectural-variation evidence. It also better qualifies the scope of generalization. These gains materially strengthen the central contribution despite removing class-level retrieval scores, the unseen-MLP visualization, and some reproducibility details. Objaverse evidence remains qualitative, and changed training conditions prevent interpreting revised scores as controlled performance gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GMN-based NeRF representation-learning work despite the changed title. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: Section 4 and the appendices report original classification, retrieval, and loss-comparison results, including hash-based NeRF experiments and ObjaNeRF retrieval examples.

before.justification: Sections 4.1–4.3 and the appendices report original latent-space analyses, classification experiments, and instance-level and class-level retrieval results.

C1.justification: v1 presents three main contributions: the taxonomy, MIKASA-Base, and MIKASA-Robo. v2's introduction and conclusion add released offline datasets as a fourth contribution and broaden the empirical conclusions to online, offline, and VLA agents. The original three contributions remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds action chunking as a possible memory shortcut and interprets limitations of SAC, TD-MPC2, and VLA agents. Its new limitations section qualifies VLA conclusions because fine-tuning was computationally constrained and identifies longer dependencies and meta-RL as remaining extensions. Table 1 also changes RotateStrict's memory classification from Object to Spatial.

D1.justification: v2 adds package installation instructions and updated examples, dataset schemas and collection procedures, reported access to PPO checkpoints and collection scripts, VLA controller and fine-tuning specifications, and single-NVIDIA-A100 hardware information (Appendices A, B, D, and G). These substantially extend v1's environment examples and task documentation.

E1.justification: v2 adds expert-demonstration datasets actually used for offline training across all 32 robotic tasks, plus language-paired demonstrations for five VLA tasks (Appendices B and D). These training datasets are absent from v1's online experiments. The underlying robotic tasks and MIKASA-Base environment inventory remain unchanged.

E2.justification: Beyond v1's PPO-MLP and PPO-LSTM, v2 evaluates SAC-MLP and TD-MPC2 in selected dense-reward comparisons, RATE, DT, BC, CQL, and Diffusion Policy across all 32 offline tasks, and Octo-small and OpenVLA on five tasks. Participation is documented in Figures 5 and 9 and Tables 4 and 6.

E3.justification: v2 introduces RGB-only offline training with sparse rewards and 1,000 successful trajectories per task. VLA experiments use 250 demonstrations, 50,000 training iterations, end-effector control, and specified context and action-chunk settings. Revised online plots also change displayed training horizons and label some ordinates Return instead of Success Rate; whether this reflects a metric change or relabeling is unclear.

E4.justification: v2 Table 4 adds an OpenVLA action-chunk sensitivity comparison, K=4 versus K=8, across five tasks, examining whether chunking compensates for missing observation history. The existing observation-mode, reward-density, architecture, and task-difficulty analyses are retained.

E5.justification: v1 already reports mean ± SEM from three training runs with 16 evaluation seeds; v2 retains this description in Appendix F. v2 additionally specifies 100-episode VLA evaluation, three runs with 100 episodes per run for offline results, and seeds 1–100 in Appendix G. The general 100-episode description is not reconciled with the retained 16-seed account, so an across-the-board rerun cannot be established.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial online, offline, and VLA results. Table 6 reports RATE at 0.92±0.01 on ShellGameTouch and Diffusion Policy at 0.68±0.02 on InterceptMedium; all five offline methods report zero success on the nine capacity/sequential tasks. Table 4 reports OpenVLA RememberColor3 success of 0.21±0.00 for K=4 and 0.59±0.04 for K=8. These are new comparisons, while the original PPO oracle-solvability findings remain.

M1.justification: The four memory categories, two-tier MIKASA-Base design, and MIKASA-Robo task procedures and reward structures are retained. The additions evaluate existing agent families and supply demonstration datasets; they do not introduce a new proposed learning algorithm or memory component.

P1.justification: Substantial rewrites affect the MIKASA-Base motivation and design narrative, related-work discussion, contribution list, and conclusion. Section 6 is reorganized around online, offline, and VLA evaluations; concrete robotic examples and a standalone limitations section are added. The detailed task appendices remain largely verbatim despite renumbering.

P2.justification: v2 adds radar Figure 6 and VLA, instruction, and offline-results Tables 4–6, expands selected learning curves with additional baselines, and redraws the sparse-reward plots. v1's recommended-task Table 4 is removed. Typography, table coloring, and figure placement also change, while the appendix task illustrations are retained.

R1.justification: v1 says no dedicated robotic-manipulation memory benchmark is known. v2 acknowledges concurrent MemoryBench and positions MIKASA-Robo through broader memory categories, task coverage, and efficient parallelization (Sections 2 and 6). It also adds FetchBench to Table 3 and references supporting the expanded offline RL and VLA evaluations.

T1.justification: The POMDP definition, expected-return objective, correlation-horizon condition, and mathematics in the retained task descriptions are unchanged. Neither version adds original theorems or proofs relative to the other.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens benchmark validation beyond v1's two PPO backbones through diverse online, offline, and VLA evaluations. Documented demonstration datasets expand the benchmark's practical usefulness, while action-chunk sensitivity tests and explicit fine-tuning limitations improve interpretation. These gains outweigh reporting weaknesses: the 16-seed and 100-episode descriptions remain unreconciled, and revised plots mix Return and Success Rate labels, limiting precise comparisons.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MIKASA study and provide readable text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices. Retained material can be matched despite renumbering, layout changes, and expanded evaluations.

after.justification: v2 retains original PPO experiments and adds SAC, TD-MPC2, offline RL, and VLA evaluations in Sections 6.2–6.4, Tables 4 and 6, and Appendix F.

before.justification: v1 Section 6.3 and Appendix D report original PPO-MLP and PPO-LSTM experiments, including learning curves under full-state and visual observations with dense and sparse rewards.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution statements, and conclusion retain the same claims about FIM-based mathematical step expansion, NuminaMath-FIM, and improved reasoning performance. The broader applicability findings are introduced in the analysis rather than changing these central contribution statements.

C2.justification: v3 interprets the new experiments as evidence of cross-domain applicability and discusses imperfect PRM judgments and excessive filtering. It adds boundaries concerning executable code, already-detailed R1-like traces, and nonlinear reasoning structures, plus discussion of existing performance regressions. However, Appendix B still states that evaluation is exclusively mathematical, contradicting Section 4.7.

D1.justification: Appendix J documents the verifier model, its application during merging, and the exact removal fractions. Section 4.7 identifies the new model configurations and training-data roles. Existing hardware, hyperparameters, decomposition rules, and RL details remain unchanged; the new reproducibility statement mainly points to existing documentation.

E1.justification: Section 4.7 extends the earlier mathematical coverage with general-reasoning FIM training data and LogiCoT expansion. Evaluation adds BBH, GPQA Diamond, MMLU Redux, LogicBenchBQA, and HellaSwag, substantially broadening the domains actually tested.

E2.justification: The Llama and Qwen prompt-fill comparators remain identical in Table 4 and v2 Table 7/v3 Table 9. Table 5 retains DPO, Step-DPO, RFT, and PPO. New domain experiments retain original-versus-expanded data controls; PRM-filtered variants constitute ablations.

E3.justification: v3 introduces human validation using 100 randomly sampled examples evaluated by two authors against a PRM threshold of 0.8. It also adds filtering experiments removing the lowest-scoring 10%, 20%, or 30% of generated steps and transfer experiments using additional downstream Qwen configurations. Existing SFT, RL, and decoding settings are retained.

E4.justification: New analyses test human–PRM consistency, sensitivity to PRM filtering, transfer beyond mathematics, and FIM training outside mathematics. Appendix L adds worked examples showing two expansion iterations and similarity filtering. Earlier distillation, iteration, model-size, training-data-quality, and RL analyses remain.

E5.justification: The stated main evaluation practice remains averaging 16 sampled answers per question at temperature 0.7. v3 adds no seed reporting, confidence intervals, significance tests, or other uncertainty-reporting procedures; the human agreement percentage is a new evaluation result.

E6.justification: Earlier numerical results are retained, including v2 Table 10/v3 Table 13. New Tables 6–7 report cross-domain results; Table 6 gives BBH accuracy of 36.54% versus 52.05% for Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B trained on original versus expanded data. Table 12 reports MATH accuracy of 22.76% without filtering, 24.12% with 10% filtering, and 21.66% with 30% filtering. Human–PRM agreement is reported as 94%.

M1.justification: The core FIM construction, training loss, and similarity-based insertion procedure remain unchanged. Appendix J adds an optional verification component that uses PRM scores to remove low-scoring generated steps before insertion. ReasoningFimer applies the existing FIM procedure to different training data.

P1.justification: Most existing prose is retained with limited wording corrections. Related work moves from the main text to Appendix C, appendix material is reorganized, and acknowledgements, ethics, reproducibility, and LLM-usage statements are added. The header changes from preprint to ICLR 2026 publication.

P2.justification: v3 adds three result tables, Tables 6, 7, and 12, and extensive boxed examples in Appendix L comparing original and successive expansions. These displays use color and strikethrough to distinguish inserted and filtered steps. Existing figures and tables retain their content, with several relocated.

R1.justification: v3 adds benchmark references for BBH, GPQA, MMLU Redux, LogicBench, and HellaSwag. The substantive related-work discussion is retained in Appendix C. The added introduction citation to Bavarian et al. references a work already cited in v2.

T1.justification: The FIM mapping, random-step decomposition, and insertion equations retain their mathematical content; v3 adds equation numbering. No new theoretical assumptions, propositions, proofs, or formal derivations are introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 relied on PRM scores for direct step-correctness assessment and left nonmathematical applicability untested. v3 adds human validation, a filtering sensitivity study, and two complementary cross-domain evaluations, substantially strengthening evidence about reliability and applicability. Explicit applicability limits and worked examples also aid scrutiny. These gains outweigh the sparse documentation of new-domain training and the contradictory, unrevised math-only limitation in Appendix B.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MathFimer research. Their complete text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and can be matched despite section moves and additions.

after.justification: v3 retains those results and adds cross-domain evaluations, human assessment of generated steps, and PRM-filtering experiments.

before.justification: v2 reports original fine-tuning evaluations, step-expansion ablations, PRM analyses, and reinforcement-learning results, including Appendix F.

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion retain the same contributions: hierarchical fragment-level generation, stochastic fragment bags, efficient sampling, improved property control, and NPGen. The introduction reformats these claims into contribution bullets without materially changing their meaning or scope.

C2.justification: v3 develops v2's brief novelty weakness into an explicit fidelity–novelty trade-off and controllable sampling discussion. It adds interpretations of latent necessity, rare-fragment recovery, inference-bag estimator variance, and possible EMA stabilization. It also clarifies that NP-likeness evaluation targets distributional fidelity rather than maximization. These substantially expand the interpretation of component behavior and evaluation.

D1.justification: v3 adds detailed architecture and training tables for the autoencoder, flow model, and discriminator (Tables 13–15), fragment-vocabulary counts, frozen-autoencoder training disclosure, and metric implementation details. However, UMAP fingerprint/settings information from v2 Figure 8 disappears, and Table 14's fragment-type/edge loss weights conflict with the retained equations in A.2.4.

E1.justification: ZINC250k already supported docking-conditioned generation in v2; v3 additionally evaluates unconditional distribution learning and reconstruction on it (Tables 4 and 6). MOSES, GuacaMol, NPGen, molecular-property conditions, and protein targets are retained, so coverage expands within the existing molecular domains.

E2.justification: v3 adds a retrained SAFE-GPT-20M comparator on MOSES (Table 1; D.4). Its new ZINC250k comparison also introduces evaluated methods absent from v2's comparisons: GraphDF, GDSS, GSDM, GruM, SwinGNN, and GGFlow. Existing benchmark comparator sets are otherwise retained.

E3.justification: New protocols include 25,000-sample unconditional ZINC250k evaluation with NSPDK, random-versus-encoded latent reconstruction, separate training/inference bag-size sweeps with detailed balance excluded, and a two-temperature sampling grid. FA7/PARP1 plots replace lambda_B=0.1 with 0.0 and 0.2. These expand evaluation design without establishing reruns of retained headline benchmarks.

E4.justification: Beyond v2's reconstruction, unseen-fragment, sampling-step, and conditioning studies, v3 adds latent necessity testing (Table 7), rare-fragment recovery (Figure 10), bag-size sensitivity (Figure 11), and novelty/fidelity temperature analysis (Table 10). Docking analyses additionally report generated-score distributions and FA7/PARP1 MAE–validity curves.

E5.justification: v3 newly documents the statistical estimator for NP-likeness KL divergence: Gaussian KDE, a shared 1,000-point grid, and numerical stabilization (B.4). This is added estimator documentation, not evidence of a changed calculation. Three-run averaging and the NPGen standard deviations remain unchanged; no increase in runs is reported.

E6.justification: Matched headline scores remain unchanged, including MOSES FCD 0.58 and NPGen FCD 1.34. Substantial new results include ZINC250k validity 99.81%, NSPDK 0.0002, and FCD 0.630; NPGen random-latent reconstruction accuracy 34.4% versus 97.4% with encoded latents; and temperature-controlled novelty of 94.5% versus the default 87.1%, with FCD increasing from 0.58 to 0.91. Docking curves are also replaced under revised guidance settings.

M1.justification: The core autoencoder, joint discrete/continuous flows, and fragment-bag guidance remain. v3 introduces optional temperature scaling of fragment predictions and bag sampling probabilities (C.6). It also revises the reported Blossom matching weights from log probabilities to logits (A.1). These are localized inference refinements.

P1.justification: v3 substantially rewrites and condenses the method and NPGen exposition, introduces contribution bullets, reverses the conditioning/efficiency subsection order, and reorganizes the appendix blocks. Method explanations expand, while citation style, headings, and author information also change. This exceeds routine copyediting.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn with a decoder/Blossom panel. The existing UMAP moves into a main-text NPGen overview with annotated molecules, and existing timing results gain a chart. New ablation and hyperparameter displays are added, while docking plots are expanded and rearranged. Appendix F's molecular examples are retained with renumbering and layout changes.

R1.justification: v3 adds SAFE-GPT positioning, references supporting novelty/fidelity and long-tail discussions, and sources for additional ZINC250k comparators. It removes the general DDPM, score-SDE, and QED references. The central positioning against restricted-vocabulary fragment diffusion remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Most DFM, continuous-flow, diffusion-bridge, and detailed-balance mathematics is retained or relocated. v3 revises the matching objective's weights to logits and explicitly states its degree constraint (A.1), and corrects the conditional-fragment marginalization index to sum over molecules (A.3). No substantial new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses important gaps in v2's validation of its central components through controlled latent-vector and bag-size experiments, while detailed architecture/training tables substantially improve reproducibility. Broader comparisons and explicit novelty-control analysis make the evaluation more informative. Conflicting loss weights, incorrect metric-direction arrows in Table 4, and lost UMAP settings limit reporting precision, but these defects do not outweigh the stronger component validation and technical documentation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe FragFM and NPGen. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial reorganization.
