after.justification: v3 retains original experimental results and adds ZINC250k benchmarking, latent-vector ablation, fragment-bag sensitivity, and novelty-control experiments.

before.justification: v2 reports original FragFM generation, reconstruction, conditional-generation, and sampling-efficiency results, including experiments in Appendices D and E.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution bullets, and conclusion retain the same central claims about FragFM's hierarchical framework, scalable fragment bags, NPGen, sampling efficiency, and property control. The added evidence does not redefine those stated contributions.

C2.justification: Section 5.2 qualifies NPGen superiority to graph-based models and acknowledges SAFE-GPT's stronger distributional alignment but lower novelty. V4 also adds interpretations concerning decoder fidelity, synthesis-oriented fragment bias, chemically organized embeddings, and the modest diversity cost of stronger guidance. Existing novelty and scaffold-vocabulary limitations remain.

D1.justification: V4 adds a code/data availability statement and repository link, NPGen baseline training recipes, explicit jointly trained property-regression objectives, and labeled-data-use disclosure. Table 16 corrects swapped loss-weight labels to fragment type 1 and edge 5, matching Equation 25 already in v3, and clarifies 384 as the fragment bag size.

E1.justification: Both versions use MOSES, GuacaMol, ZINC250k, and NPGen, with the same molecular-property and protein-docking targets. New retrosynthesis, fragmentation, diversity, and embedding analyses examine retained molecular populations rather than introduce new dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: V4 adds MolHF and MolGrow to MOSES Table 1; SAFE-GPT, MolHF, and DeFoG to NPGen Table 2; and MolHF to ZINC250k Table 5. SAFE-GPT and DeFoG already appeared elsewhere in v3, but their NPGen participation is new. These additions substantially broaden the relevant comparison families.

E3.justification: V4 extends evaluation with a 25,000-molecule AiZynthFinder protocol measuring solved routes and reaction steps, internal-diversity measurement, and fragmentation/decoder controls. Appendix B.2 corrects the stated split from 85:5:15 to 80:5:15 while retaining identical counts. Appendix A.4 changes reported GuacaMol/NPGen node/edge stochasticity parameters from (10,2) to (2,20). These revisions do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V4 adds RECAP/rBRICS fragmentation ablations (Section 5.5), retrosynthetic accessibility analysis (C.2), random-decoder inference ablation (C.3), guidance-versus-diversity analysis (C.8), and learned-fragment embedding analysis (F.2). These test additional robustness, component-role, and chemical-organization questions. V3's random-latent, fragment-generalization, long-tail, bag-size, and temperature analyses are retained.

E5.justification: V3 Table 5 and v4 Table 6 both report NPGen means and standard deviations over three runs. Added baseline rows follow that existing practice. Three-run averaging elsewhere is retained, without new confidence intervals, significance tests, or seed-reporting procedures.

E6.justification: Existing FragFM benchmark scores remain, but substantial results are added. In NPGen Table 2, new SAFE-GPT results give FCD 0.15 versus FragFM's retained 1.34, with novelty 73.5% versus 95.4%, changing the distributional ranking. New Table 9 reports FCD 0.90 with a random decoder versus 0.58 normally. V4 also removes the extra 500-step DiGress row reporting 84.8% validity and FCD 1.37 from v3 Table 11.

M1.justification: The autoencoder, Blossom decoding, stochastic fragment bags, joint discrete/continuous flows, and dual guidance remain the same. Newly explicit regressor objectives document existing components. Equation 30 repairs the retained Gaussian-guidance derivation; the PDFs do not establish an underlying algorithm change.

P1.justification: V4 retains the main section sequence and most prose while adding focused subsections, rewriting the NPGen results discussion, and correcting language and terminology. It also revises author/affiliation formatting and adds conference headers and acknowledgments. The narrative is extended rather than substantially reorganized.

P2.justification: V4 adds ablation Tables 3 and 9, retrosynthesis Figure 10, diversity Figure 20, and embedding Figures 25–27. Benchmark tables expand with comparator rows and graph/sequence labels, and ZINC250k metric-direction arrows are corrected. Existing plots and molecular examples are also resized or relocated. These changes substantially expand the visual evidence beyond renumbering.

R1.justification: New Section 2.3 positions FragFM against MolGrow, MolHF, and hierarchical 3D generation, distinguishing chemically defined fragments from implicit graph coarsening. References also add fragment-generation, AiZynthFinder, RECAP, and rBRICS works. The broader positioning remains intact; DiGress's 2022-to-2023 citation change updates the same work.

T1.justification: Equation 30 changes all three guidance exponents from positive to negative squared-error gradients, restoring consistency with the preceding Gaussian-likelihood derivation. The flow, diffusion-bridge, and detailed-balance mathematics otherwise remains intact. New Equations 35–36 explicitly document objectives for the existing property regressors.

improvement.justification: V4 substantially strengthens empirical credibility. The expanded NPGen comparison exposes SAFE-GPT's fidelity/novelty tradeoff and supports a more qualified interpretation. New fragmentation and decoder controls, retrosynthetic evaluation, and diversity analysis address important gaps in validating the proposed design and its practical tradeoffs. Mathematical and reporting corrections improve reproducibility. Although retrosynthesis remains a computational proxy and core scores are unchanged, the conclusions are materially better tested and calibrated.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FragFM framework and NPGen benchmark. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices A–F support reliable comparison after matching relocated and renumbered content.

after.justification: V4 retains these original experiments and adds baseline evaluations, fragmentation and decoder ablations, retrosynthetic analysis, and embedding and diversity analyses.

before.justification: V3 reports original molecular-generation benchmarks, conditional-generation experiments, reconstruction tests, and sensitivity analyses in Section 5 and Appendix C.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction replace the precise 102.8% relative-improvement headline with nearly twice the aggregate score, and the introduction removes the claim of evaluating 12 times more tasks than previous baselines. The four principal contributions, distribution-shift motivation, and sample-efficiency and adaptation claims otherwise remain.

C2.justification: v3 adds explanations that online collection and imagined rollouts mitigate occasional retrieval errors, and attributes difficult Meta-World tasks to long horizons, small objects, and strict success criteria. It also introduces broad robustness interpretations, although Figures 12 and 14 expose failures without guidance or with entirely irrelevant retrieval. Appendix D's substantive limitations are retained.

D1.justification: v3 supplies a project code-and-dataset access link, specifies the Dreamer policy-update version followed, discloses the smaller original DreamerV3 baseline configuration, and corrects the behavior-cloning code's return typo. Hardware, runtime estimates, and hyperparameter tables remain largely unchanged. Conversely, the explicit Meta-World Gaussian-noise grid in v2 is shortened to a maximum noise level of 2.0.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same DMControl and Meta-World coverage: 72 tasks, six embodiments, and 60k offline trajectories. The additional studies reuse existing tasks and data while varying retrieval composition, configurations, or training budgets. The Ant/Quadruped wording change accompanies the same continual-adaptation task sequence.

E2.justification: v3 adds an evaluated iVideoGPT-align comparison, including Assembly, which was absent from v2's iVideoGPT comparison panels (Appendix A.2, Figure 10). The original comparator sets remain. UDS-RLPD denotes the UDS-plus-RLPD combination already used in v2; DreamerV3-Align chiefly introduces a model-size control.

E3.justification: Appendix A adds substantial evaluation controls: iVideoGPT fine-tuning on the authors' dataset with behavior-cloning initialization, no reward shaping or demonstration pre-filling, and a 200k-step comparison; a DreamerV3 model-size match; retrieval precision at 250/500 trajectories; and guidance-schedule and retrieval-contamination sweeps. Selected difficult tasks also receive longer training budgets. The original benchmark budgets and Appendix J hyperparameters remain.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained component, OTS, and world-model fine-tuning ablations, v3 adds retrieval accuracy analysis (Table 2), guidance-schedule sensitivity (Figure 12), task-irrelevant retrieval injection (Figure 14), baseline-capacity sensitivity (Figure 15), and extended-budget analysis of difficult tasks (Figure 16). These investigate previously untested questions about retrieval reliability, robustness, and performance bottlenecks.

E5.justification: v2 states three seeds per task. v3 Appendix I and Figures 17–19 report five seeds for NCRL and three for the baselines, although the main text and compute estimate retain three-seed statements. Mean/confidence-interval reporting already existed; v3 additionally displays uncertainty bands for the full per-task benchmark curves.

E6.justification: Many benchmark estimates change alongside the revised seed reporting: Assembly success changes from 0.20 to 0.44, Soccer from 0.67 to 0.16, and mean DMControl return from 631.10 to 617.73. DreamerV3's reported Meta-World mean at 1M steps changes from 0.900 to 0.656 despite unchanged task entries. v3 also adds extensive control and robustness results, including failure with 100% task-irrelevant retrieval in Figure 14. These are updated estimates and additional settings, not established method-level performance gains.

M1.justification: The RSSM architecture, retrieval, rehearsal, and policy-switching procedure remain matched. However, v3 replaces the single-KL loss expression with separately weighted, stop-gradient dynamics and representation losses, and changes the actor objective from expected critic value to the lambda-return. The PDFs do not establish whether these reflect implemented training changes or corrections and expanded documentation of the existing method.

P1.justification: v3 consistently renames GSA to NCRL and generalist world models to task-agnostic world models, edits introductory and methodological explanations, and condenses the main related-work section while retaining detail in Appendix C. It also moves the ethics statement and adds reproducibility and LLM-usage statements. The overall methods–experiments–conclusion organization remains recognizable.

P2.justification: v3 adds a retrieval-precision table, five comparison/analysis figures, and three extensive per-task learning-curve figures. Existing plots receive revised sizing, labels, legends, and axis ticks, and the document adopts ICLR formatting. Earlier appendix figures are retained under renumbering: v2 Figures 10–12 correspond to v3 Figures 11, 13, and 20.

R1.justification: v3 adds citations to Kakade and Langford, Mereu et al., and the DMControl and Meta-World benchmark papers, while removing the TRPO reference used by the earlier proof. Table 1 changes RLPD's training-stability classification from negative to positive. The broader research positioning remains; much of the expanded appendix review preserves material from v2's main related-work section.

T1.justification: Appendix B.2 replaces v2's alpha-coupling argument and uniformly positive guide-advantage assumption with an explicit mixed policy and an expected-advantage bound containing a distribution-shift penalty, invoking Kakade and Langford. The forgetting proposition becomes an explanation. This substantially revises the formal support, although v3's prose condition for positive improvement does not match the sign required by Equation 11.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens empirical credibility by adding aligned iVideoGPT and matched-capacity DreamerV3 comparisons, addressing important comparison gaps in v2. Retrieval diagnostics, stress tests, and full per-task curves with five NCRL seeds reported make the central mechanisms and performance limits more assessable. These gains outweigh remaining weaknesses: ambiguous seed reporting, robustness prose that understates Figure 14's failure boundary, and the inconsistent positivity condition in Appendix B.2. The improvement rests on stronger validation and transparency, rather than higher reported scores.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work, with GSA renamed NCRL in v3. The complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices A–K are available and readable, supporting a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains original benchmark and adaptation results and adds original aligned-baseline comparisons, retrieval evaluations, sensitivity tests, and extended-training experiments in Appendix A.

before.justification: v2 reports original reinforcement-learning experiments across 72 tasks, continual adaptation, and component ablations, including Figures 3–11 and Appendix I.

C1.justification: The central critic-chunking contribution remains, but v3 adds target-network-free locomotion training and quantified low-UTD/sample-efficiency claims prominently in the abstract and introduction. Its conclusion qualifies v1's 'no existing method' novelty assertion to 'few prior methods.' The earlier cover's sparse Box-Pushing state-of-the-art positioning is also qualified as competitive in v3 Section 5.3.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive explanations involving target reuse, fresh-window sampling, and fixed-horizon boundary effects. It identifies sparse-reward instability under hard refresh and weaker locomotion performance associated with action masking (Sections 4.4–5.5 and Appendices E/G). v1's discussion of entropy-induced distribution shifts and overfitting after entropy removal is no longer retained.

D1.justification: v3 expands pseudocode, replay/masking and embedding specifications, hardware/timing information, baseline provenance, and task-specific settings. It newly documents terminal-only success and aggregation procedures, and promises code, scripts, and models upon acceptance. The earlier mean-to-covariance policy description disappears, without establishing whether its implementation changed.

E1.justification: v3 retains the 50 Meta-World tasks and dense/sparse Box-Pushing, while adding five Gymnasium MuJoCo tasks: Ant, HalfCheetah, Hopper, Walker2d, and HumanoidStandup. This extends evaluation from manipulation to locomotion and substantially broadens environmental coverage.

E2.justification: v1's principal comparisons include PPO, gSDE, GTrXL, SAC, and CrossQ. v3 adds TCP, BBRL, and TOP-ERL to the retained manipulation comparisons (Figures 3, 8, and 9), and TD3 to locomotion evaluation. New critic comparisons include GRU, LSTM, and chunk-conditioned MLP variants.

E3.justification: Meta-World T-SAC curves extend to 20M interactions in v1 but use a stated 5M budget in v3; reported UTD changes from 0.25 to 1. Box-Pushing position tolerance changes from ±5 mm to ±5 cm, and the dense-task discount changes from 0.98 to 0.99. New locomotion evaluation specifies deterministic policies and 152 evaluation episodes. The PDFs do not establish whether the tolerance revision reflects a correction or changed experiments.

E4.justification: v1's covariance augmentation, policy normalization, entropy-removal, and SAC-variant ablations disappear. v3 instead directly tests attention, residual blocks, causal masking, supervision horizons, policy chunking, window multiplicity, and recurrent critic alternatives (Figure 5). Appendix E adds hard-refresh instability and direct return-averaging controls, substantially changing the questions investigated.

E5.justification: v1 shows shaded IQM curves and mentions eight runs for one ablation without specifying a general uncertainty procedure. v3 explicitly reports 95% bootstrap confidence intervals, default seed counts, four-seed ablation/sparse-task exceptions, and baseline-specific counts (Section 5.1 and Appendix I). This substantially improves statistical reporting; it does not establish that retained experiments received additional runs.

E6.justification: Reported dense Box-Pushing success changes from 92% in v1 Table 1 to 96.8% in v3 Section 5.3, while sparse success remains 58%. Changed tolerances and training settings prevent interpreting this as a same-setting gain. v3 also reports revised Meta-World curves, new locomotion and ablation outcomes, TOP-ERL's 70% sparse success, and 99.5% dense success for the policy-chunking adaptation.

M1.justification: The prefix-conditioned Transformer critic and gradient-averaged loss remain. v3 adds a locomotion variant using cached bootstrap targets and a periodically refreshed frozen critic snapshot instead of continuous Polyak updates (Section 4.4). It also introduces an evaluated policy-chunking adaptation of T-SAC (Section 5.5.3), changing policy outputs.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, method exposition, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. v3 separates related work from preliminaries, relocates the algorithm into an appendix, reorganizes references and supplementary sections, removes the original contribution cover and future-work discussion, and adds reproducibility and LLM-use statements.

P2.justification: v3 redesigns the overview as a critic diagram plus aggregate results, adds a detailed critic schematic, and removes v1's compact performance table. Benchmark and ablation displays are substantially reworked, with new timing, locomotion, recurrent-network, and replay-mask figures. Hyperparameter tables gain comparator columns; existing environment illustrations are retained and relocated.

R1.justification: v3 substantially broadens positioning around target-network alternatives, action chunking, and return averaging, adding discussions of Vincent et al. (2025), Fellows et al. (2023), Li et al. (2025), and Daley et al. (2024), among others. It develops a sharper comparison with TOP-ERL's episodic policy, trust-region machinery, and interaction requirements.

T1.justification: v1 Appendix B derives an undiscounted, independent-reward averaging variance. v3 substantially extends this to discounted and correlated rewards/bootstrap values, gradient-variance lemmas, horizon-weight optimality, and target-reuse/sparse-reward derivations (Appendices C, D, and G). These are substantive mathematical additions, although Appendices C and D give conflicting variance-ratio limits for fixed discount below one.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens empirical attribution and reproducibility: v1 mainly ablates policy modifications and omits TOP-ERL from reported comparisons, whereas v3 directly tests critic components, recurrent alternatives, and return averaging, adds relevant episodic baselines, and documents uncertainty and experimental provenance. These address important weaknesses in support for the central contribution. Conflicting variance-limit claims in Appendices C/D weaken the theoretical expansion, and changed Box-Pushing tolerances prevent attributing higher scores to algorithmic improvement, but the empirical and documentation gains remain substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe T-SAC and retain matching core methods and manipulation benchmarks. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices support comparison. Identifiable protocol changes require qualifications when comparing scores.

after.justification: v3 reports original T-SAC benchmark and ablation results, including locomotion experiments and comparisons of target-update and return-averaging strategies, in Sections 5.2–5.5 and Appendices A and E.

before.justification: v1 reports original T-SAC benchmark results and ablations on Meta-World ML1 and dense/sparse Box-Pushing in Section 4, Table 1, and Figures 2–4.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction expand the contributions from Gaussian Point Loss and two-stage post-image adaptation to coordinated pretraining, Post-Interaction and Mid-Interaction learning. v2 newly emphasizes pretraining responsiveness under distribution shift, adaptation benefiting the current image, and robustness against overfitting. The central goal of handling unseen modalities and pathologies remains.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations for class-restricted CCG and its distinct role during Mid-Interaction adaptation, including why Dice–Focal-only updates can learn incorrect regions. It explicitly discusses satisfactory pseudo-label quality, PI's diminishing benefit after many clicks, and source-performance loss and recovery (Sections 2.3–3.3; Appendix A.11). These substantially extend v1's two-stage rationale and applicability discussion.

D1.justification: v2 adds guidance-map construction, uniformly sampled training click counts, detailed pseudocode and GPU/CPU latency information. However, it omits v1's Adam optimizer and learning rates, most dataset sizes, removal of 232 G1020 images and PAPILA's first-expert annotation choice. These are substantial documentation changes; omitted settings do not establish changed execution. Both versions still promise code and models upon publication.

E1.justification: The five fundus and four brain MRI datasets remain, but evaluated scenarios change substantially. v2 adds mixed-domain image streams, erroneous user-click inputs and returning to the source domain after adaptation elsewhere (Table 9, Table 11, Appendix A.11). Conversely, the TBI-T2 and TBI-SWI evaluations shown in v1 Figure 2 are absent from v2.

E2.justification: v2 adds automatic U-Net comparisons in Figure 2 and cross-entropy pseudo-labeling and entropy-minimization alternatives in Tables 15–16. It also adds Med-SA to the fundus and pathology comparisons and IA+SA to the MRI modality and pathology comparisons, where they were absent in v1. Med-SA matches v1's Medical SAM Adapter; ICNN* matches ISFCNN*.

E3.justification: The reduced-click BRATS-T1/T1c experiment changes from three clicks in v1 to five in v2 Table 4. New protocols include 50-click adaptation, mixed streams with 25 images per domain, hardest-first ordering and specified wrong-click schedules. Appendix A.9 introduces average clicks to reach 80% Dice, capped at 20. The earlier G1020 evaluation on a separate 20% holdout during adaptation is removed.

E4.justification: v2 substantially expands analysis to pretraining CCG, individual PI/MI loss terms, class restriction, Gaussian weighting, hyperparameter sensitivity, noisy clicks, poor pseudo-labels and source-domain recovery. It also adds qualitative segmentation examples. Some earlier controls disappear: v1 Figure 3's computation-matched Stage 1 ×2 comparison, Stage 2-only variant and G1020 adaptation-over-time analysis are not retained.

E5.justification: v1 Table 1 explicitly states that TSCA and OAIMS results average three runs; v2 drops that statement from the corresponding table. v2 specifies three different seeds for Table 6 and newly reports individual seed outcomes demonstrating instability at sigma=0 in Appendix A.8. This changes uncertainty disclosure without establishing an overall increase in repeated runs.

E6.justification: The retained fundus rows match after mapping OAIMS to PI, but retained MRI results change. In Table 2, reported BRATS-T1 Dice at ten clicks changes from 45.3 to 62.5 for the frozen backbone and from 72.2 to 78.9 for OAIMS/PI. v2 additionally reports 88.0 for PI+MI and extensive new robustness, ablation and efficiency results. Unspecified optimization details limit interpreting revised rows as controlled cross-version performance gains.

M1.justification: v1 updates model parameters after completing interactions on each image. v2 retains this two-stage procedure as Post-Interaction adaptation and adds Mid-Interaction adaptation: each corrective click supplies a pseudo-label for updating the preceding prediction, followed by prediction with updated weights (Section 2.4; Algorithm 1). This substantially changes learning and inference. Renaming GPL to CCG and ISFCNN* to ICNN* does not itself constitute a new method.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and method exposition are extensively rewritten. Methods are reorganized into overview, pretraining, CCG loss and adaptation subsections; experiments gain a clearer subsection hierarchy, while simulation details move into an expanded appendix. GPL/CCG and ISFCNN*/ICNN* terminology changes accompany this substantial narrative restructuring.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is substantially redrawn to display pretraining and both adaptation processes. Table 1 combines formerly separate disc/cup rows into paired cells. The earlier TBI and G1020 plots disappear, while v2 adds automatic-versus-interactive curves, segmentation overlays, click-progression examples, a sensitivity plot and numerous structured analysis tables. The page template and table styling also change.

R1.justification: v2 adds U-Net and segmentation-review/validation citations and positions OAIMS against pseudo-label self-training and entropy minimization in Appendix A.10. It drops the Sambaturu and image-specific fine-tuning Wang references and their dedicated introductory discussion. The principal positioning relative to IA+SA and TSCA remains, making this a localized expansion.

T1.justification: The Gaussian-weight definition changes from a fixed 10-pixel coordinate cutoff in v1 Section 2.2 to 3 sigma in v2 Equation 1, giving nine pixels at the retained sigma=3. This is a non-equivalent mathematical refinement. Neither version supplies theoretical guarantees or proofs; the added standard Dice formula is explanatory.

improvement.justification: v1 largely supports learning from corrected predictions through benchmark results and a G1020 ablation. v2 directly tests unreliable pseudo-labels, erroneous clicks, component contributions and simpler self-training alternatives (Tables 5–11; Appendix A.10), substantially strengthening evidence for the central mechanism. Click-efficiency and latency measurements improve practical assessment. Removed controls and omitted optimizer/data-selection details are drawbacks, but the targeted validation gains outweigh these reporting regressions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe OAIMS for interactive medical image segmentation, with the earlier two-stage method identifiable within the expanded later framework. Text, equations, tables and figures support comparison. v1.pdf has no appendix; v2.pdf's Appendix A.1–A.11 is available and readable.

after.justification: v2.pdf retains original segmentation results and reports additional adaptation experiments, ablations, robustness tests, timing measurements and click-efficiency results throughout Section 3 and the appendix.

before.justification: v1.pdf reports original segmentation experiments with simulated user clicks on fundus and brain MRI datasets, including baseline comparisons and component ablations in Tables 1–3 and Figures 2–3.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion replace masking-centered contributions and the two original caption datasets with MAF, IF-caps, and structured data curation. Superior fine-grained instruction following and cross-modal regularization become headline claims. The overarching unified audio/music generation claim remains.

C2.justification: v2 explains benefits through masking-induced robustness, reduced information leakage, and video redundancy. v3 instead attributes improvements to suppressing cross-modal interference and textual supervision regularizing other modalities. Sections 5.3–5.5 additionally distinguish fidelity from instruction following and interpret performance through interaction between data curation and fusion.

D1.justification: v3 adds annotation schemas, augmentation examples, benchmark composition, and automated-judging specifications in Appendices A.1–A.3. It documents MAF's 60M parameters and Synchformer's 25-fps features. Appendix A.4.1 newly specifies 3,000 stylized VGGSound keyframes for the retained image experiment. Benchmark/evaluator release is newly promised; code and dataset availability still uses future tense.

E1.justification: v3 adds AudioTime training/evaluation and T2A-bench evaluation, extending coverage to explicit event counts, ordering, duration, and timestamps. IF-caps supplies structured instruction supervision over the existing audio/music sources. Inpainting, music completion, and image-to-audio coverage remain in the appendix.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds VATT and VAB specifically to VGGSound video-to-audio comparisons. The new instruction-following comparisons include Make-An-Audio2, and Table 3 evaluates AudioSetCaps as an external caption-source baseline. Comparator sets in the other retained experiments remain unchanged.

E3.justification: Reported batch size changes from 96 to 48 and training time from approximately 3.2k to 4k GPU hours; Table A.1 revises training composition and sample counts. New protocols include T2A-bench's four groups of 500 prompts and two-stage Gemini judging, plus AudioTime temporal metrics.

E4.justification: v2's mask-ratio sweep and no/feature/input-masking comparison disappear. v3 adds caption-source and augmentation comparisons in Table 3 and MAF, gate, and query ablations in Table 4. The unified-versus-specialist and modality-combination analyses are retained, moving from Figure 6 to Figure A.3.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates and average human ratings without repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty bars. The user-study plot is retained unchanged as v3 Figure A.2.

E6.justification: Table 1 revises AudioX results: AudioCaps T2A IS/FAD changes from 12.09/1.86 to 12.48/1.59, while VGGSound T2A IS changes from 20.27 to 19.58. These accompany changed architecture and training, rather than isolating a same-setting improvement. v3 adds instruction-following and curation/MAF results and removes masking results. Inpainting, completion, image-generation, and user-study outcomes are retained.

M1.justification: v2's input-masking and direct-concatenation design is replaced by Multimodal Adaptive Fusion, using gates, learnable queries, attention, and residual updates. v3 also adds Synchformer synchronization features. The captioning pipeline changes from Qwen2-Audio annotation to Gemini annotation followed by Qwen2-Audio augmentation.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, method narrative, ablation discussion, and conclusion are substantially rewritten. Related work is reorganized, Section 5.5 adds a discussion, and several task evaluations and modality analyses move into a reorganized appendix with extensive annotation and evaluation explanations.

P2.justification: v3 adopts a single-column conference layout, redraws the annotation and model diagrams, and replaces the capability panel with instruction-following charts. It adds word clouds, benchmark-distribution graphics, and new comparison/ablation tables. Retained task tables and user-study/modality plots move to the appendix, while the masking plot disappears.

R1.justification: The masking-focused related-work discussion is removed, while dataset and temporal-control positioning expands through works including AudioSetCaps, AudioTime, and Make-An-Audio2. The novelty argument shifts toward fine-grained supervision and controllability. Publication updates for retained works such as MMAudio and VidMuse do not constitute new research additions.

T1.justification: Appendix A.3 introduces mathematical correctness rules for the new benchmark accuracies: detecting all required categories, exact counts/order, and timestamps within a one-second tolerance. The diffusion equations (2)–(4) remain unchanged, and no theorems or proofs are added.

improvement.justification: v2 supported its caption-data contribution mainly through general benchmark performance. v3 adds direct caption-source comparisons, fusion-component ablations, and explicit instruction-following evaluations on two benchmarks (Tables 2–4), substantially strengthening evidence for its contributions. Appendix schemas and scoring rules also improve reproducibility. These gains outweigh reporting weaknesses, including unreconciled IF-caps clip-versus-caption totals and Appendix A.3's judge example discussing a wave crash despite a catapult prompt.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe AudioX. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, and retained methods, experiments, and figures can be matched despite substantial scientific revisions and reorganization.

after.justification: v3 reports original generation experiments, new instruction-following evaluations and data/fusion ablations, alongside retained empirical results in Appendix A.4.

before.justification: v2 reports original audio/music generation experiments, inpainting and completion results, masking ablations, and a human evaluation in Section 5 and the appendix.

C1.justification: Both versions claim language-guided adaptation to changing anomaly definitions, two regularization strategies, the 35,279-video PreVAD dataset and strong zero-shot generalization. v2 emphasizes the already-used weak supervision and adds targeted evidence without materially changing these central claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations of LAVAD's event-understanding failure and Qwen2.5-VL's localization limitations in Section 6.4. Appendix F explains the applicability of video-specific prompts, while Appendix A acknowledges limitations in temporal and multimodal modeling and benchmark coverage. These qualify the retained generalization argument.

D1.justification: Appendices B–E newly document substantial implementation and reproduction information: RTX4090 hardware, AdamW training for 40 epochs, batch size 64, architecture dimensions, sampling, synthesis parameters, curation models and prompts, annotator procedures and baseline adaptations. v2 also provides a repository address and specifies annotation/download-script release and usage restrictions; actual online availability is not established.

E1.justification: PreVAD training and the seven evaluation datasets are retained. v2 extends variable-definition testing from illustrative UCF-Crime cases to systematic category-subset scenarios on XD-Violence and MSAD. This is a bounded extension of test scenarios within the existing dataset coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B and HolmesVAU to the concept-drift comparison alongside VadCLIP and LAVAD. In the matched trashcan case, LAVAD and Qwen2.5-VL replace PEL as comparators alongside VadCLIP. The MIL baseline is also removed from Table 2.

E3.justification: Protocol 2 introduces evaluation under category subsets, relabeling excluded categories as normal and computing both frame-level AUC and AP. Appendix E specifies conversion of Qwen temporal predictions into binary frame scores. Appendix F additionally documents controlled changes to synthesis settings, prompting and training-data fractions; these extend the evaluation design.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained component ablations, v2 supplies quantitative concept-drift robustness results, synthesis sensitivity tests, prompting comparisons and a training-data usage analysis (Table 4, Tables D–E and Figure E). It also revises the trashcan case, removes the cattle-stealing example and supplies further diagnostic examples in Figures H–I.

E5.justification: v2 introduces averaging over five randomly sampled category subsets for drift@5, explicitly motivated by reliability in Appendix D.2. This adds scenario-level sampling and estimation, not repeated training runs. Neither supplied PDF reports training-seed variability, confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: The retained cross-dataset scores and main component-ablation values are unchanged. New Table 4 reports LaGoVAD AUC/AP of 0.857/0.371 on XD-drift@5 and 0.856/0.401 on MSAD-drift@5. Appendix F adds sensitivity and detailed ablation results. v2 also removes MIL's 49.50 UBNormal result and the explicitly marked ground-truth-segment CLIP and ActionCLIP classification rows.

M1.justification: The documented core procedure retains language-conditioned detection, CLIP features, temporal and fusion modules, two prediction heads and the same four losses. Appendix B supplies architecture details and synthesis pseudocode, but does not establish a change to the underlying method.

P1.justification: v2 adds 'under Weak Supervision' to the title, streamlines introductory and dataset prose, combines dataset and architecture ablation discussion, and reorganizes experimental setup around two protocols. The main section sequence and substantial passages remain recognizable; much of the expansion documents additional evidence and technical details.

P2.justification: The document switches from two-column to single-column layout and substantially reorganizes its displays. Figure 1 is redrawn, the radar plot moves into Table 2, and most earlier dataset panels merge into Figure 3 while the duration plot moves to Appendix Figure D. New comparison tables, diagrams and appendix figures substantially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v2 adds positioning against Follow the Rules, distinguishing its one-class and few-shot setting, plus references for Qwen models, HolmesVAU and implementation tools. Some earlier citations, including Mosaic/Cutout inspiration, disappear. The central positioning around user-defined anomaly changes remains intact.

T1.justification: The concept-drift formulation, conditional-distribution assumption, optimization objectives and loss mathematics are retained. Equation regrouping and Appendix B's repeated loss and procedural elaboration do not introduce a new theorem, proof or substantive mathematical revision.

improvement.justification: As supplied, v2 substantially strengthens the central concept-drift claim with a controlled quantitative evaluation, where v1 offered cross-dataset scores and illustrative cases. The appendices also make implementation, curation and sensitivity much more inspectable. A classification-reporting ambiguity remains: Appendix E describes abnormal-segment sampling while Table 3 retains v1's unmarked scores and drops its explicit ground-truth-segment rows. This does not outweigh the substantial gains in validation and reproducibility.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe LaGoVAD and PreVAD, and their supplied text, equations, tables and figures are readable. However, v1 ends at the references despite citing supplementary Sections B–F; v2 includes Appendices A–F. This limits comparison of appendix-only material, which can establish newly documented content but not necessarily newly performed work.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and reports additional concept-drift evaluations, sensitivity analyses and qualitative results in Section 6 and Appendix F.

before.justification: v1 reports original zero-shot detection and classification experiments, component ablations and qualitative concept-drift examples in Section 6.

C1.justification: v2 expands the central contribution from performance benchmarking to mechanistic interpretation and targeted compression. Its abstract and introduction add claims about final-layer up-projection importance, excessive compression of particular modules, and gains from selective protection. The parameter-count versus knowledge claim remains; the shorter-output finding persists in Appendix G but loses its headline contribution status.

C2.justification: v2 attributes important reasoning components primarily to distillation and interprets importance losses as excessive compression of gate projections and final-layer modules (Sections 4–5). It explains small MuSiQue protection gains through unchanged weight count. It also drops v1's API-security conjecture and newly uses degradation at 50% sparsity to justify excluding pruning from mechanistic analysis.

D1.justification: v2 adds an interpretation-code repository pointer and distinguishes AutoAWQ inference from original AWQ pseudo-quantization in Appendix D. It removes v1's explicit word-based response-length counting, API retry description, and MuSiQue sampling-pool provenance. Core inference platforms and decoding hyperparameters are retained.

E1.justification: Documented task coverage remains AIME 2024, FOLIO, Temporal Sequences, and closed-book MuSiQue. Their mathematical, logical, temporal, and knowledge-intensive multihop requirements are retained. The added model configurations and analyses of reasoning behaviors do not establish a new benchmark, domain, or input scenario.

E2.justification: v2 Table 1 adds evaluated AWQ, GPTQ, and GPTAQ variants for distilled models, plus ANY4/3 for the Qwen-32B, Llama-8B, and Qwen-7B groups. v1 Table 2 evaluated dynamic quantization, distilled models, and SparseGPT variants, with AWQ/GPTQ only discussed in the literature. v2 Table 4 additionally compares ordinary and selectively protected 3-bit AWQ.

E3.justification: v2 adds Llama-8B and Qwen-7B configurations and extensive 3-/4-bit quantization settings. New experiments quantize individual components using 3-bit round-to-nearest and compare AWQ with versus without 16-bit final-layer MLP restoration (Tables 3–4). Benchmark sizes, accuracy/EM/F1 metrics, closed-book answering, and the stated decoding parameters remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds analyses locating important modules and tracking importance shifts after distillation and quantization, including appendix heatmaps. Five component perturbations test whether importance predicts sensitivity, and selective protection tests whether restoring identified modules helps. The earlier sparsity sweep, response-length analyses, and collapse examples are retained rather than replaced.

E5.justification: v1 specifies one pass per benchmark. v2 Table 1 reports three-pass means for student-model results, while original R1 and dynamic quantization remain exceptions; Table 2 explicitly retains one-pass sparsity results. This adds repeated evaluation and averaging, but no seeds, dispersion estimates, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: v2 adds many quantization results and component-intervention outcomes. Its main-table Llama-70B and Qwen-32B averages become 81.8 and 82.2, versus v1's 80.7 and 83.0; these are three-pass summaries replacing single-pass entries, not demonstrated model improvements. New Table 4 reports 46.0 versus 52.57 average accuracy for ordinary versus protected 3-bit AWQ. The sparsity and response-length tables retain their numerical results.

M1.justification: v1 benchmarks existing compression methods. v2 adds an adapted component-level difference-of-means and attribution-patching procedure to estimate reasoning importance and compression effects (Sections 2.2–2.3). It also introduces a mixed-precision AWQ procedure that restores final-layer MLP weights to 16-bit (Section 5.2).

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Background and experimental setup are reorganized into Problem Formulation, and the results narrative separates performance, distillation effects, and quantization effects. Related work, implementation details, model comparisons, response-length analysis, and case studies move into expanded appendices. Author and affiliation text also changes.

P2.justification: v2 redraws Figure 1 to show the expanded pipeline, substantially expands the main comparison table, and adds six heatmap figures and two intervention tables. Dataset statistics and earlier response-length/collapse displays move to appendices; v1 Figure 2 becomes v2 Figure 8. Typography, table-caption placement, and boxed takeaway displays also change.

R1.justification: v2 substantially repositions the work around interpreting compression effects. It builds on Arditi and Syed, distinguishes its module-level analysis from Venhoff's layer-level work, and contrasts its up-projection finding with Shao and Wu's o-projection finding. It also adds recent compression and reasoning-model studies, while largely retaining the earlier general compression review in Appendix B.

T1.justification: v2 Sections 2.2–2.3 introduce mathematical definitions for behavior-specific steering vectors, their normalization, attribution-based importance, and relative importance shifts. They also introduce the minimal-shift hypothesis and reasoning for displaying only decreases. This formal framework is absent from v1; no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens v1's limited quantization comparisons and aggregate analysis through comparisons on the same model backbones and explicit component perturbation/protection experiments (Tables 1, 3–4). These provide a stronger empirical basis for compression recommendations, beyond simply reporting more scores. Important limits remain: protection is tested only on Llama-8B with additional precision, variance and annotation details are missing, and Figure 5 inconsistently names the compared model. These constrain broad causal and superiority claims but do not outweigh the substantial gain in empirical grounding.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DeepSeek-R1 compression study and provide readable text, tables, figures, equations, and appendices. Earlier experiments can be matched across renumbering and relocation, despite substantial additions in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds quantization comparisons, component-importance analyses, and selective quantization/protection experiments in Tables 1, 3–4 and Figures 2–7.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark evaluations, sparsity sweeps, response-length analyses, and model-collapse examples in Section 5, Tables 2–5, and Figure 2.

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion broaden the three headline findings from R1-distilled Llama/Qwen models to R1 and non-R1 families. The introduction and conclusion also extend the excessive-compression finding to pruning, expanding the claimed mechanistic contribution beyond distillation and quantization. The original headline numerical gains remain unchanged.

C2.justification: V3 adds substantive interpretations of RAG gains, model-specific importance patterns, pruning-analysis feasibility, and the selective-quantization exception, which it attributes to random perturbation. It also discusses hardware tradeoffs of nonuniform compression, unmatched dynamic-quantization calibration, and uncertainty from the small annotation-validation sample.

D1.justification: Documentation expands substantially: v3 specifies the 120 annotated instances with 30 per benchmark, annotation temperature and sequence exclusions, component-specific precision in the dynamically quantized model, and calibration-information limitations. It also documents AlphaPruning's use of SparseGPT and the RAG embedding model and top-ten retrieval procedure. Existing code-access information remains unchanged.

E1.justification: The four reasoning benchmarks are retained. Appendix L adds an actually evaluated retrieval-assisted MuSiQue scenario, supplying external knowledge to the models; v2 evaluates MuSiQue only closed-book and references other work's RAG results.

E2.justification: V3 adds AlphaPruning to Table 1 for R1-Distill-Llama-70B at 50% sparsity and Llama-8B at 30% and 50%. The previous comparator set remains; rows formerly labeled 'sparse' are identified explicitly as SparseGPT.

E3.justification: V3 adds substantial evaluation designs: annotation validation at temperatures 1 and 0.1, a GPT-OSS-distilled 4B model with its GPTQ variant, retrieval-assisted MuSiQue, and selective 4-/5-bit Llama and 3-bit Qwen tests. Existing benchmark sizes and generation settings remain unchanged; the newly disclosed 120-instance annotation dataset does not establish a revised sampling protocol.

E4.justification: New Appendices G–N investigate annotation stability, dependence on displaying only importance decreases, pruning effects, non-R1 generalization, base-model importance, knowledge provision through RAG, agreement with AWQ scaling signals, and the first-versus-final-layer quantization exception. These substantially extend validation of the central findings. V2's response-length analysis and collapse cases remain in Appendices O/P.

E5.justification: Appendix G and Table 6 introduce Spearman correlations and 95% confidence intervals for human annotation ratings, using ten instances sampled with replacement per behavior. This statistical reporting is localized to annotation validation; existing benchmark averaging and one-pass sparsity reporting remain unchanged.

E6.justification: Existing numerical entries in Tables 1–4 and the relocated response-length tables are unchanged. V3 adds AlphaPruning results, annotation ratings, non-R1 scores, RAG outcomes, and selective-quantization results. For example, Table 7 reports average accuracies of 71.1 and 63.2 for DistilGPT-OSS-qwen3-4B and its 4-bit GPTQ variant; Table 8 reports Llama-8B MuSiQue F1 of 4.43 closed-book versus 14.52 with RAG.

M1.justification: The steering-vector computation, attribution-patching importance scores, relative-importance normalization, and selective final-layer protection procedure remain unchanged. V3 applies this framework to additional models and compression settings without introducing a new proposed algorithm.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained. V3 makes local wording corrections, adds cross-references, acknowledgments, and conference headers, and inserts new appendix sections. The former Appendices G/H become O/P with their substantive text preserved.

P2.justification: V3 substantially expands the displays with new validation and evaluation tables and importance heatmaps in Figures 8–13. Figure 2 is enlarged and rearranged into stacked groups, and Figure 1 incorporates AlphaPruning. Existing response-length tables and the collapse illustration are relocated and renumbered, with their content retained.

R1.justification: New Appendix B.5 positions the importance analysis within module-wise compression, adding AlphaPruning, OWL, and Liu et al.'s principal-weight study. This is a targeted extension of the retained literature review and research positioning. OWL is discussed but not evaluated as a baseline.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions and equations for steering vectors, attribution importance, and relative importance are retained, as is the minimal-importance-shift hypothesis. V3 adds empirical validation and conceptual explanations, without new formal results, proofs, or derivations.

improvement.justification: V2 explicitly omitted mechanistic pruning analysis and lacked annotation-validation and non-R1 checks. V3 adds these, together with base-model and selective-quantization controls that substantially strengthen the central weight-importance argument. These additions address important validation gaps. The annotation sample remains small, and RAG comparisons do not fully isolate knowledge from reasoning, so some strengthened generalization and causal interpretations remain insufficiently supported.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and can be matched across the revision.

after.justification: V3 retains these original experiments and adds annotation validation, AlphaPruning evaluations, non-R1 experiments, retrieval-assisted evaluation, and further diagnostic results.

before.justification: V2 reports original compression benchmarks, sparsity sweeps, weight-importance analyses, and selective-quantization experiments, including Tables 1–4.

C1.justification: v1's central claims concern optimal precision control and substantial welfare influence. v3 retains these while adding central claims that LLM planners reproduce theoretical policy structure, accommodate non-Bayesian behavior, and exhibit strategic reasoning relevant to studying information mediators and their regulation (abstract, Sections 1.1 and 7).

C2.justification: v3 interprets policy deviations through central tendency and non-Bayesian updating, and attributes hybrid performance losses to applying Bayesian policies to different agents. Section 7 adds applicability boundaries for heterogeneous preferences, especially the unresolved biased case. The earlier information-parity, signal-symmetry, and observability constraints remain in Remark 2.

D1.justification: Compared with v1's brief JuliaPOMDP and trajectory-budget description, Appendix E specifies EXAONE Deep 32B, prompts for all three LLM roles, an explicit parameter grid, and programmatic profile/car-fact construction. JuliaPOMDP remains the numerical tool. The earlier 100-step horizon is not restated, and message-precision calibration remains undocumented.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates abstract binary-state social learning with Bayesian agents. v3 adds synthetic car-purchase scenarios with generated demographic profiles, car facts, natural-language messages, and non-Bayesian LLM agents, including good-car and bad-car trajectories in Appendix E.3.

E2.justification: v1 Figure 2 compares analytical optimal and myopic policies for both planner objectives; v3 Figure 2a compares LLM planners with analytical optimal planners. Figure 2c additionally includes Hybrid comparisons using analytical policies with LLM agents, alongside Analytical and LLM settings under both myopic and long-term objectives.

E3.justification: v3 introduces single-signal belief-update probes, measurement of LLM-reported beliefs and percentage policy deviations, and analytical/LLM/hybrid evaluation designs. Figure 2c explicitly conditions welfare comparisons on the true state B. These introduce substantial new evaluation procedures beyond v1's numerical trajectory study.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's aggregate welfare comparison and example policies, v3 investigates deviations from Bayesian updating in Figure 1b, policy discrepancies in Figure 2b, and analytical-policy robustness to LLM agents in Figure 2c. Appendix E.3 adds trajectory case studies examining resistance to information cascades.

E5.justification: v1 reports 1,000 trajectories per parameter combination and 125,000 per policy; v3 omits these replication counts without establishing that actual run counts decreased. Figure 1b introduces shaded bands, but their statistic and uncertainty level are unspecified.

E6.justification: v1 reports optimal biased/altruistic welfare changes of -26.34%/+96.97%. v3 Figure 2c replaces these summaries with state-B-conditioned comparisons, showing approximately -35%/+80% for long-term analytical planners and additional Hybrid/LLM outcomes. The conditions differ, preventing direct performance-change claims. Figures 1b, 2b, and 4 add belief-update, policy-deviation, and trajectory findings.

M1.justification: The underlying MDP remains, but v3 adds an operational LLM planner–oracle–agent procedure: the planner selects precision, and the oracle generates profile-specific messages for LLM decision-makers. Prescribed analytical controls also change through the corrected altruistic threshold and biased obfuscation policy.

P1.justification: The paper is retitled from Controlled Social Learning: Altruism vs. Bias to Steering the Herd: A Framework for LLM-based Control of Social Learning. The abstract, introduction, contribution narrative, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Related work becomes a standalone section, applications move to Appendix A, and proof material is reorganized into appendices.

P2.justification: The two-column presentation becomes single-column, and the original policy and welfare displays are substantially reworked into Figure 2's multipanel comparison. v3 adds a system diagram, belief-update plot, deviation histogram, decision-tree illustration, trajectory plots, and a parameter table.

R1.justification: v3 substantially expands positioning beyond social-learning control into information design, Bayesian persuasion, and LLM economic agents. Section 2 adds works including Kamenica and Gentzkow, Bergemann and Morris, and Dutting et al., explicitly distinguishing its repeated social-learning setting from framing-and-signaling research.

T1.justification: Appendices B–C supply extensive derivations and proofs beyond v1's sketches, including continuity and epsilon-optimality analysis. Theorem 1 changes the investment condition from beta(1) < C to beta(1) < C(1-p). Biased-policy results replace 1-b-epsilon with b-epsilon, recognize nonattainment, and weaken several bounds. Appendix D adds a formal extension to observable heterogeneous preferences.

improvement.justification: The decisive gains are substantially more checkable theory and corrections to important policy statements: v3 supplies previously omitted derivations, corrects the altruistic threshold, and addresses biased-policy nonattainment. LLM/hybrid analyses and disclosed prompts add useful empirical scrutiny. These gains outweigh remaining reporting weaknesses, including missing replication and precision-calibration details and Section 6.3's 40–50% welfare-loss claim exceeding Figure 2c's roughly 35% analytical result.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same authors' sequential social-learning framework with planner-controlled signal precision, despite substantial retitling and expansion. All pages, equations, and figures support comparison. v1 contains no appendix; v3 includes readable Appendices A–E.

after.justification: Section 6 and Appendix E report original LLM simulations and numerical comparisons, including belief updates, planner policies, welfare outcomes, and example trajectories.

before.justification: Section V and Figures 1–2 report original numerical evaluations and simulated trajectories comparing altruistic and biased planners, including measured welfare changes.

C1.justification: The abstract and first contribution shift from proposing a taxonomy of 13 functions to evaluating 12 principal score functions, modestly narrowing the headline contribution. The central claims about over 12% inactivity, AWFT underestimation, output-norm scoring and limited finetuning effects remain substantively unchanged.

C2.justification: v4 adds interpretations of dataset stability, AWFT's decline with growing context and the role of output projection. Appendix A.14 substantially clarifies applicability: AHON requires computing head outputs, so zeroing them does not itself save that computation, and multiple-choice interventions do not establish reliable generation. It also discusses routing and cache-compression possibilities.

D1.justification: v4 adds a stated code-repository location, exact FineWeb-Edu sequence identifiers, projected-output implementation details and descriptions of the added datasets. Existing PyTorch intervention steps, model dtypes and automatic batch-size guidance are retained. These are useful but localized reproducibility additions.

E1.justification: v2 evaluates intervention accuracy on MMLU and uses FineWeb-Edu for attention analyses. v4 adds PIQA physical commonsense reasoning and WinoGrande pronoun resolution across all 14 models, substantially broadening the evaluated task requirements beyond the original knowledge benchmark.

E2.justification: v4 Figure 7 adds circuit-based AHON and its layer-normalized variant to the MMLU comparison. Figures 2–3 exclude Last Token Head Output Norm (HN) from the overlap and ranking comparisons, although it remains in appendix intervention grids. AWFT and random-zeroing baselines are retained.

E3.justification: The existing 14-model, 5-shot MMLU and seven-threshold protocol remains. New designs include 0-shot PIQA, 5-shot WinoGrande, dataset-specific threshold calibration to identify 15% of heads for layer comparisons, and tracking growing prefixes of three FineWeb-Edu sequences of at least 512 tokens. These substantially extend the controlled evaluation procedures.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained overlap, distribution, scaling, finetuning and PCA analyses, v4 adds an output-projection ablation (A.1), cross-dataset layer profiles (4.4), examples identified by individual scoring rules (A.3), and context-dependent inactivity curves and masks (A.5). These investigate sensitivity to output definition, dataset and increasing context.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests for the intervention evaluations. The added experiments continue reporting point results and curves without uncertainty estimates; the score-distribution histograms are behavioral analyses.

E6.justification: MMLU Table 2 is unchanged, including average removable-head fractions of 4.61% for AWFT and 12.18% for Ours. v4 adds PIQA results of 10.01% versus 21.38% and WinoGrande results of 6.90% versus 14.45%, plus circuit-based, layer-wise and context-dependent findings. These are substantial additional results under distinct conditions.

M1.justification: The original scoring and dynamic head-zeroing procedures remain. Appendix A.1 adds implemented circuit-based AHON variants that score head contributions after output projection, changing the quantities used to select heads. Head normalization is retained in Appendix A.2 and intervention plots; its disappearance from the main text does not constitute method removal.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained. v4 standardizes score-function terminology, reframes Section 3, expands the normalization explanation and moves head normalization and short scoring-rule descriptions into the appendix. The new analyses receive dedicated subsections, while editing of retained material remains localized.

P2.justification: v4 adds layer profiles, circuit comparisons, example-head panels, two complete benchmark grids, context-length curves and inactivity masks, together with three result tables. It also simplifies Table 1, revises the main comparison matrices and replaces repeated legends in the full MMLU grid with a shared legend. These substantially change the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v4 adds references for PIQA, WinoGrande, transformer circuits, runtime neural pruning and mixture-of-depths. These extend discussion toward circuit interpretations and conditional computation. The main positioning relative to attention sinks, dormant heads and earlier head-pruning research remains largely unchanged.

T1.justification: v4 Appendix A.1 adds a formal definition of projected head contributions and derives the block decomposition of the output projection in Equations 2–3. It also explains why zeroing a fixed head removes its contribution under either output definition. The original scoring equations remain, and the added mathematical treatment is limited in scope.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially addresses v2's reliance on MMLU for intervention validation by adding two distinct tasks across all 14 models. The projection ablation and dataset/context analyses strengthen the evidence, while explicit computational and generation limitations improve the interpretation of retained claims. The gains concern validation and clarity rather than improved MMLU scores. Generalization remains bounded: AWFT still wins several rows in Tables 4–5, and generation is unevaluated.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study, with matching authors, core scoring methods and original experiments. The text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are available and readable, supporting a reliable comparison despite substantial additions in v4.

after.justification: v4 retains those original results and adds PIQA and WinoGrande evaluations, projected-output scoring comparisons, layer-wise analyses and growing-context experiments.

before.justification: v2 reports original MMLU head-zeroing experiments across 14 models, score-function overlap measurements, attention-score distributions and attention-pattern analyses.

C1.justification: The abstract and central contributions remain substantively unchanged: reward-guided optimization can promote unfaithful explanations, and causal-attribution augmentation can mitigate this behavior in controlled settings. Additional experiments support these existing claims.

C2.justification: v3 substantially expands applicability and mechanism discussion: the conclusion identifies controlled-setting limitations and difficulties constructing high-quality counterfactuals, while Section 5 explains D's label independence, C's proposed noise reduction, and avoidance of evaluator exploitation during training. Appendix F cautiously interprets mixed transfer evidence.

D1.justification: Appendix B.2 newly documents exact-match answer extraction, invalid-output handling, and BoN counterfactual sampling from 16 responses. v3 also explicitly separates evaluator use from training. Existing DPO hyperparameters, hardware, software packages, prompt templates, and code-access information are retained.

E1.justification: Math Book/AQUA-RAT and BiasQA/WINOGENERATED coverage is retained. v3 adds a limited software-reasoning transfer evaluation using 300 CodeMMLU Software Principles examples and Math Book-trained models (Appendix F, Table 4).

E2.justification: v3 adds RM_ALL, which appends disclaimers to every response, as an evaluated BoN comparator with both Skywork reward models (Appendix D, Figure 7). Existing base-model and default-RM comparisons remain.

E3.justification: v3 expands the evaluation design with full BoN/DPO experiments using Llama-3.2-3B, a blanket-disclaimer control, and cross-domain evaluation of Math Book-trained models. Appendix C also replaces classwise evaluator F1 reporting with macro-F1 and accuracy. Existing Llama-3.1-8B splits and training hyperparameters are retained.

E4.justification: v3 adds a mechanism-focused ablation testing whether disclaimer wording alone explains mitigation (Figure 7), evaluator agreement and error examples (Tables 2–3), and a transfer analysis (Appendix F). These substantially extend the diagnostic evidence beyond v2's evaluator validation and generation examples.

E5.justification: Both versions specify three experiments with different seeds and report means and standard deviations. The additional results follow this existing practice; no new confidence intervals, significance tests, or increased run counts are reported.

E6.justification: v2 Tables 1–4 retain their numerical values in v3 Tables 1, 5, 6, and 9. v3 adds extensive 3B results, RM_ALL curves, transfer results, and revised evaluator metrics. For example, new Table 10 reports 3B BoN@16 stereotype rates of 68.1% with SK-Gemma-27B RM versus 55.5% with RM_C; these are new configurations, not improved earlier scores.

M1.justification: Both versions use the same counterfactual prediction tests, strategies D and C, and disclaimer augmentation for BoN and DPO. v3 clarifies the evaluator's evaluation-only role and counterfactual sampling without establishing a change to the proposed procedure.

P1.justification: The seven-section main narrative and much of the results prose remain. v3 makes localized rewrites and explanatory reorganizations, particularly in the introduction and Sections 3.2 and 5, revises appendix organization, and adds an LLM-usage statement.

P2.justification: v3 changes the main text from a two-column workshop layout to a single-column conference layout. It combines the introductory diagram with a reward-distribution panel, moves the original full distribution figure to Appendix B, adds counterfactual explanatory diagrams and experimental displays, and substantially rearranges appendix tables and plots.

R1.justification: Section 6 adds comparison with Turpin et al. (2025), distinguishing pre-alignment generator training from alignment-stage RM augmentation and discussing possible complementarity. A CoT Monitorability paragraph and additional citations broaden context while retaining the original research positioning.

T1.justification: The prediction-disagreement criterion, unfaithfulness condition, and background BoN selection expression are retained. New diagrams and explanations introduce no substantive mathematical definitions, assumptions, derivations, or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 lacked a control testing whether disclaimer wording alone explained mitigation. v3's RM_ALL experiment (Figure 7) addresses this important gap, strengthening support for selective causal attribution. Second-generator experiments, evaluator error examples, and explicit counterfactual limitations further improve credibility. Transfer evidence remains preliminary and mixed, and classwise evaluator F1 detail is lost, but the stronger validation of the central mechanism provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work and contain readable main text, figures, tables, mathematical expressions, and appendices. Retained content can be reliably matched despite reformatting and renumbering.

after.justification: v3 retains those experiments and adds original results for another generator model, a disclaimer ablation, and CodeMMLU transfer evaluation.

before.justification: v2 reports original BoN and DPO experiments on Math Book and BiasQA, including numerical results and manual validation of its acknowledgment evaluator.

C1.justification: The central diagnosis, two-component i-LN contribution, and claims about restoration quality, feature stability, and low-precision robustness remain. v3 explicitly extends the introduction's applicability claims to real-world IR and presents theoretical insights as an additional contribution in the abstract.

C2.justification: v3 substantially expands the mechanism discussion: it explains cumulative outlier growth through residual paths, connects normalization bypassing to equal-statistics degeneracy, interprets SRFormer's permutation as partially holistic normalization, and discusses why gradient clipping fails while KLD sacrifices reconstruction fidelity. These extend the original bypassing and bias-alignment interpretations.

D1.justification: Beyond v2's brief settings paragraphs, v3 supplies a model-variant inventory, detailed architecture and optimization tables, degradation implementations, channel-entropy pseudocode, computational costs, and a code-repository link. This substantially improves implementation disclosure. Some inconsistencies remain: Table 5 describes HAT2 training as 300K iterations, whereas Table 14 specifies 500K.

E1.justification: The original training corpora, benchmark datasets, and four restoration tasks are retained. Appendix E.2 adds a complex synthetic degradation scenario for ×4 super-resolution, applying the Real-ESRGAN pipeline to DF2K training images and the same five SR test sets. This is a bounded extension of input conditions within the existing SR task.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains the original normalization comparator set. v3 adds LN with gradient clipping and LN with KL-divergence regularization as evaluated alternatives in Table 8, and compares SRFormer with LN versus i-LN in Table 7. These extend the comparisons without replacing the original comparison framework.

E3.justification: v3 introduces full-sized HAT experiments using 500K iterations for ×2 SR followed by 250K iterations of warm-start ×4 fine-tuning, an SRFormer configuration, and batch-size 2/4/8 tests. These substantially expand the evaluation design. The old HAT† results are retained under HAT2; newly disclosed settings for those existing experiments do not establish reruns.

E4.justification: v3 completes the component ablation by adding LN plus rescaling without spatial holisticness (Table 3). It extends RPE analysis across ablation variants, shallow/deep layers, and training stages (Figure 12), and adds gradient-clipping/KLD analyses, seed-stability tests, batch-size sensitivity, and additional qualitative cases. These address questions beyond the retained v2 analyses.

E5.justification: v2 does not document a repeated-seed evaluation protocol. v3 introduces multi-seed training trajectories in Figure 11 and five individual seed results with averages in Table 9. This substantially expands repeatability and variability reporting, although formal confidence intervals and significance tests are not supplied.

E6.justification: Table 2 and the previously reported ablation and low-precision scores are retained. v3 adds rescaling-only, full-sized HAT, SRFormer, regularization, and complex-degradation results; Table 9 reports average Urban100 PSNR of 21.95 for LN versus 22.14 for i-LN under the new degradation protocol. Some normalization-specific Set5 results disappear from Table 1. Table 6 prints Set14 ×2 SSIM as 0.8276 for i-LN versus 0.9274 for LN while bolding i-LN.

M1.justification: v2 Equations 3–5 and v3 Equations 2–3 specify the same method: joint spatial-channel normalization followed by rescaling attention/FFN outputs using the preceding normalization's standard deviation. The new theory, backbone experiments, and ablation variants do not revise the proposed i-LN procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are substantially condensed and rewritten. Related Work moves from Section 2 to Section 5, observations become a standalone section, and experiments are reorganized into ablation and LN/i-LN property sections. Terminology changes from spatial consistency to spatial holisticness, and indexed backbone names clarify model variants.

P2.justification: The original Table 3 is split into separate ablation and quantization tables, Table 1 loses its Set5 columns, and existing plots and panels are rearranged or reformatted. v3 adds numerous experimental and configuration tables, entropy pseudocode, multi-run plots, expanded RPE displays, and qualitative comparison panels. These are substantial display changes beyond renumbering or page-count growth.

R1.justification: The original IR-transformer and abnormal-feature positioning largely remains. v3 adds references to Real-ESRGAN, SRFormer, BasicSR, and rate-distortion/VAE research supporting its new experiments and regularization discussion. It also adds a specific interpretation of SRFormer's normalization behavior, without broadly redefining the paper's research position.

T1.justification: v2 provides normalization equations and intuitive motivation without formal propositions or proofs. v3 adds definitions of inter-pixel structure and structure preservation, propositions concerning LN and holistic LN*, and derivations in Appendix G. The new analysis explicitly concerns normalization before the learned affine transformation.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens reproducibility and experimental support through detailed configurations, a complete component ablation, full-sized model tests, and repeated-seed and batch-size analyses. These address important gaps in v2 concerning component contributions, scaling, and training reliability while retaining its original benchmark results. The gains outweigh the added reporting problems, including the HAT2 training-duration conflict and Table 6 SSIM/bolding inconsistency. The expanded 'real-world' evidence remains entirely synthetic.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same i-LN research work. Their text, equations, tables, and figures support reliable comparison. v2 ends with references and has no appendix; v3 includes Appendices A–G and detailed configuration tables, which were included in the comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains those original experiments and adds component ablations, regularization comparisons, repeated-seed analyses, and complex-degradation super-resolution results. The explicitly borrowed baseline scores in Table 6 do not negate the original results elsewhere.

before.justification: v2 reports original restoration experiments, normalization comparisons, feature-statistics analyses, ablations, and low-precision inference results in Tables 1–3 and Figures 1–10.

C1.justification: The central text-aligned tokenization contribution remains. However, v2's abstract adds comparative superiority on generated speech continuation, and its introduction adds precise speech editing and few-shot spoken QA as demonstrated capabilities. v1's explicit claim of substantially reduced computation during training and inference is no longer advanced in the introduction.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive limitations concerning latency and streaming, English-only evaluation, and missing robust turn-taking and instruction following. It interprets new QA results as preservation of text-model capabilities and listening results as evidence of perceptual reconstruction quality. v1's speculation that successful embedding modeling could permit eliminating quantization is removed.

D1.justification: Appendix A.4 newly documents Mechanical Turk sampling, 20 samples per method, more than 10 ratings per sample, MUSHRA reference conditions, complete human/GPT-4o instructions and transcription steps. Existing optimizer, hardware and epoch details are retained in relocated Appendix A.3. Conversely, v1's explicit Distil-Whisper aggregator initialization and two-decoder-block specification disappear. The resource pointer changes from a repository to a project website.

E1.justification: English Emilia and LibriTTS training coverage is retained. Beyond v1's reconstruction and likelihood-based benchmarks, v2 evaluates prompted speech generation, spoken question answering on Web Questions and LLaMA-Questions, and editing between utterances with the same transcript. Appendix Table 4 also adds SALMON background-domain and random-background scenarios.

E2.justification: Reconstruction comparisons add EnCodec and Mimi. The matched likelihood comparison adds TWIST 7B and removes pGSLM and ASR+LLM (v1 Table 2; v2 Table 4). New continuation comparisons include two cascade systems, while question answering compares Mini-Omni, Moshi, Llama-Omni and their corresponding text models.

E3.justification: Reconstruction WER switches from Whisper to HuBERT-Large; duration consistency switches from Whisper alignment with 25 ms tolerance to Montreal Forced Aligner with 50 ms tolerance. Emotion consistency is removed, while DNSMOS, ViSQOL and MUSHRA are added. LoRA alpha changes from 64 to 128. New continuation and few-shot QA protocols are introduced. v2's reconstruction prose names LibriSpeech, but Table 1 still names LibriTTS, leaving the actual corpus uncertain.

E4.justification: Section 4.1.2 and Figure 3 add a focused editing case study absent from v1.
