Swapping selected tokens between utterances with different speaking rates tests whether word-specific duration information transfers; alignment visualizations show changes concentrated in the exchanged words. This is a limited qualitative mechanism analysis.

E5.justification: v1 reports point estimates only. v2 adds uncertainty values to retained SALMON/StoryCloze results in Table 4 and reports values labeled standard deviations for reconstruction, continuation and QA in Appendix Tables 5–7. The estimation procedures are not explained sufficiently, and no training-seed counts or repeated-training evidence are supplied.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial continuation, QA, editing and background-consistency results. TASTE's reconstruction entries change from approximately 190 bps and 3.8% WER to 150 bps and 4.4% WER under revised evaluation conditions. Matched TASLM SALMON/StoryCloze point estimates are retained, but TWIST 1.3B's sSC/tSC scores change from 55.4/76.4 to 52.4/70.6 (v1 Table 2; v2 Table 4).

M1.justification: The core TASTE pipeline remains, but v2 adds an editing procedure that swaps selected word-aligned speech tokens before decoding (Section 4.1.2). The stated SLM objectives also change: Equation 6 omits v1's word-start loss mask, and Equation 8 explicitly includes text cross-entropy in the embedding objective. These equation revisions do not establish that training was rerun.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and substantial method passages are rewritten, with simplified notation and explanations. Related work, vocabulary alignment, training details and detailed benchmark descriptions move into dedicated appendix sections. The results narrative is reorganized around reconstruction, editing, continuation and question answering.

P2.justification: v2 adds a conceptual overview and an editing diagram with spectrograms, redraws the tokenizer schematic, and removes v1's dedicated vocabulary-alignment/SLM-variants figure. Reconstruction tables are redesigned with different columns and highlighting. Detailed likelihood results move to Appendix Table 4, while new continuation, QA and uncertainty tables substantially expand the displays.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning around speech representation learning and generative tokenization, adding works such as SUPERB, UniWav and Align-SLM while removing several earlier multimodal-LLM references. Appendix A.1 explicitly distinguishes TASTE from Chen and Rudnicky's prior text-speech attention for TTS. Much of v1's related-work section is retained through relocation.

T1.justification: v2 Equation 7 replaces v1 Equation 12's abstract KL expression with an explicit Gaussian expansion. Its printed first variance term is sigma rather than sigma squared, inconsistent with the stated sampling parameterization. This introduces a mathematical discrepancy beyond notation changes. Neither version contains theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v1 claims natural speech continuation but evaluates its SLMs through likelihood-based selection. v2 addresses this important evidential gap with direct generation tests using human and automated ratings, alongside perceptual reconstruction, editing and QA evidence. Evaluation instructions and explicit applicability limits further strengthen the paper. The conflicting reconstruction-corpus labels, new KL-formula discrepancy and unclear uncertainty estimation temper the improvement, but the substantially stronger evidence for the central generative capability outweighs these reporting weaknesses.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TASTE/TASLM research. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support comparison. Internal inconsistencies in v2 limit interpretation of particular settings, rather than material completeness.

after.justification: v2 reports original reconstruction, speech continuation, human listening, spoken question answering and speech-editing results in Tables 1–4 and Figure 3.

before.justification: v1 reports original speech reconstruction experiments and TASLM evaluations on SALMON and StoryCloze in Tables 1–2.

C1.justification: v2's abstract claims comparable SALMON/StoryCloze performance; v3 broadens this to outperforming pretrained SLMs on likelihood-based next-speech selection, despite unchanged scores. v3 also makes avoiding redundant textual information an explicit token-design principle. The central contribution remains text-aligned tokenization for joint spoken language modeling.

C2.justification: v3 adds explanations linking reconstruction WER to paralinguistic information and weak ViSQOL to the flow-based vocoder, interprets ASR robustness, and discusses SALMON background weaknesses. Its limitations additionally identify untested generalization to other generative tasks and unsupported overlapping speakers and non-lexical events. These substantially expand the scientific interpretation and applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: v3 newly specifies the shallow-layer choice l=6 and normalized embeddings with learned softmax fusion weights, and explicitly confirms ASR transcription use in the main experiments. Training hyperparameters, hardware, and access statements remain substantially unchanged. The earlier explicit tokenizer checkpoint specification and RVQ straight-through-estimator note are omitted.

E1.justification: Training datasets and the original reconstruction, continuation, SALMON, StoryCloze, and QA tasks remain. v3 adds reconstruction under white noise at 20, 15, 10, and 5 dB SNR (Table 8). Table 1's change from LibriTTS to LibriSpeech resolves v2's caption/prose inconsistency rather than establishing different dataset coverage.

E2.justification: v3 substantially expands the evaluated codec comparators through DAC, DM-Codec, and BigCodec in the new noise comparison (Table 8), alongside retained SpeechTokenizer, Mimi, and S3. The comparator sets in the original reconstruction, language-modeling, and QA tables remain unchanged.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include module and encoder-layer controls measured by S3 top-5 reconstruction accuracy, ground-truth versus ASR transcription controls, Parakeet replacing Whisper before GPT-4o scoring, and controlled white-noise reconstruction (Tables 4–8). These extend the evaluation protocol; the original training budgets, benchmark metrics, and human-evaluation sample counts are retained.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained editing case study, v3 adds component ablations, ASR-dependence and evaluator-sensitivity tests, noise robustness comparisons, attention-map inspection, and layer-wise representation analysis (Section 5.2.3 and Appendices A.1.1–A.1.4). These directly examine information retention, alignment, layer selection, and robustness.

E5.justification: v3 introduces canonical correlation analysis between Whisper layers and S3 embeddings, adding a statistical association analysis (Appendix A.1.3, Figure 6). Existing standard-deviation tables and human-rating counts are unchanged. No additional repeated runs, seeds, confidence intervals, or formal significance-testing procedure are reported.

E6.justification: The original benchmark scores and standard-deviation tables are retained, but substantial diagnostic results are added. Examples include module-wise top-5 accuracies of 0.98, 0.88, and 0.76 versus 0.65 for text-only (Table 4), Parakeet-based TASLM scores of 3.20/3.37 (Table 7), and TASTE's 11.1% WER at 5 dB SNR (Table 8). These are new conditions, not version-to-version performance gains.

M1.justification: The Whisper encoder, attention aggregator, RVQ quantizer, speech decoder, token/embedding language-modeling objectives, and word-level alignment algorithm are retained. Appendix A.5 specifies the previously described weighted-sum fusion; it does not establish a changed procedure.

P1.justification: The introduction and result interpretations are extensively rewritten. Related work moves from the appendix into the main text; results are reorganized into main and additional results; and the appendices are reordered. Ethics, acknowledgements, and an LLM-use disclosure are added, alongside conference-format and affiliation edits.

P2.justification: v3 adds five diagnostic tables and three figures containing attention maps and a layer-correlation curve. Table 1 gains a token-frequency column and expanded caption, Table 3 is placed beside the new ablation table, and existing figures and appendix tables are relocated or reformatted. Figures 1–3 retain their underlying visual evidence.

R1.justification: v3 adds supporting literature on newer joint SLMs, codecs, continuous-token modeling, ASR, and representation analysis, while removing some general representation-learning and subword-tokenization references. The central positioning against length-mismatched speech tokens and the distinction from Chen and Rudnicky's TTS cross-attention remain. Moving related work into Section 2 is principally structural.

T1.justification: Equations (1)–(8), the vocabulary-alignment algorithm, and the substantive mathematical assumptions are retained. Appendix A.5 writes out the already described weighted-sum implementation; it adds no substantive theoretical result, proof, or revised derivation.

improvement.justification: v2 largely supported its ASR assumptions and component choices through end-task results. v3 directly investigates these central dependencies through component ablations, transcription and evaluator controls, attention/layer analyses, and noise tests (Tables 4–8, Figures 4–6). Together with clearer applicability limits, this substantially strengthens validation of the retained method. The new analyses lack quantified uncertainty, and the abstract's broader superiority claim exceeds the unchanged SALMON evidence, but these weaknesses do not outweigh the substantial gain in empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe TASTE and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. The retained method and experiments can be matched reliably across the revisions and relocations.

after.justification: v3 retains these original results and adds component ablations, ASR checks, representation analyses, and controlled noise experiments.

before.justification: v2 reports original speech reconstruction, text-aligned editing, speech continuation, benchmark evaluation, and spoken question-answering results, including human listening tests.

C1.justification: The three central contributions—camera-agnostic representation learning, joint spectral/spatial SSL and cross-domain validation—remain. Section 6 replaces v2's broader priority claim of being the first work explicitly designed for spectral heterogeneity with the more specific claim to combining camera-agnostic spatio-spectral encoding and SSL.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive interpretations that spectral SSL prevents representation collapse and that learned features separate organ semantics from sensor identity. It also interprets embedding dimension as more useful than increasing representation count beyond eight. The discussion adds computational cost as a limitation and identifies spatial-resolution differences and additional sensor metadata as an applicability issue and possible remedy.

D1.justification: Appendix A.3 newly specifies satellite dataset composition, 78,000 pre-training iterations, NVIDIA H200 hardware, weight decay, and linear-probe optimization, epochs, augmentation and resolution adjustment. Other implementation settings and GPU-memory information are revised. Section 7 adds a reproducibility statement identifying public datasets and existing documentation; the pseudocode was already present in v2.

E1.justification: Satellite pre-training expands from HySpecNet-11k hyperspectral imagery to mixed EnMAP and Sentinel-2 data, adding SpectralEarth and BigEarthNet. Evaluation adds m-forestnet classification and m-SA-crop-type and m-cashew-plantation segmentation, including Landsat-8 coverage. Medical evaluation additionally uses real-world filter responses for synthesis and previously unseen simulated cameras.

E2.justification: DOFA is added to medical, automotive, satellite and computational comparisons; Early Fusion is added to the medical comparison in Figure 5. The SegMunich comparison removes ViT and ViT-22k. Its previously retrained SpectralGPT+ comparator remains under the shorter SpectralGPT+ name, rather than being a newly introduced baseline.

E3.justification: Satellite experiments switch from the small model to a base configuration with spatial embedding dimension 768 and expand pre-training from 11,483 to 808,001 images. Appendix A revises SSL channel processing, mask counts and proportions, batch size from 16 to 64, and final learning rate from 10^-5 to 10^-6. New protocols include linear probing, k-NN evaluation and class-removal controls; DOFA input resolution is doubled for linear probing.

E4.justification: v3 adds tests using real-world filter responses and withheld HSICity traffic-class annotations, plus spatial-only versus joint spectral/spatial SSL ablation (Table 3). Table 6 adds aggregation and embedding-dimension ablations while retaining the existing positional-encoding and representation-count results. Appendix E adds unseen-camera feature analysis using t-SNE and regression-based variance estimates.

E5.justification: The existing 95% confidence-interval reporting continues, without new seed or repeated-training-run counts. Appendix E adds a statistical estimation procedure: separate regressions on organ class and sensor identity, with R2 averaged across embedding dimensions to estimate explained variance.

E6.justification: HSICity HyperFree mIoU changes from 40.1 to 44.6; CARL and CARL-SSL remain 48.6 and 50.1, while newly added DOFA scores 49.6. SegMunich CARL-SSL changes from 50.7 to 50.9 under different model and pre-training conditions. The matched SpectralGPT+ Mine/dump entry changes from 48.2 to 38.2. Substantial new results include linear probing, transfer tests, SSL ablation accuracy of 22.1 versus 32.6, and organ/sensor explained variance of 61.6% versus 0.6%.

M1.justification: Sections 3 and Algorithms 1–2 retain the wavelength encoding, alternating attention, representation aggregation, teacher–student predictors and summed VICReg objectives. Query representations Q are renamed spectral representations S. Model scale and masking settings change, but no new algorithmic component or objective is introduced.

P1.justification: Related work, experimental descriptions, ablation discussion and the closing discussion are extensively rewritten. Query terminology changes throughout the method and pseudocode. The document adds a reproducibility section, a satellite implementation subsection, feature-analysis and LLM-usage appendices, and moves existing medical protocol details into Appendix D.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redesigned, Figure 5 gains comparator curves and changes its horizontal axis from subject counts to fractions, and Figure 6 adds a t-SNE visualization. New tables present method capabilities, transfer and SSL tests, linear probes, dataset composition and explained variance. Existing benchmark and ablation tables are reorganized and expanded, alongside widespread header, typography and float-layout changes.

R1.justification: Related work substantively incorporates DOFA, AnySat and Galileo, distinguishing camera-agnostic spatial methods from CARL's joint spectral/spatial approach. New Table 1 organizes positioning around four capabilities. Conversely, v3 removes explicit methodological links to Avilés et al.'s wavelength encoding and BLIP-2's query inspiration, changing attribution as well as citation membership.

T1.justification: The wavelength positional encoding, VICReg equations and synthetic-filter construction remain mathematically equivalent. Naming the two loss components and renumbering equations do not alter their definitions. The new regression analysis is empirical; neither version adds theoretical propositions or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 lacked direct ablation of its central spectral SSL contribution and offered limited evidence about the learned representations themselves. v3 substantially addresses these gaps through the SSL ablation, controlled transfer tests and unseen-camera feature analysis, while adding stronger comparators and broader downstream validation. These strengthen support for the existing scientific claims. Limited drawbacks remain: Table 3b's CARL class-drop deltas are not reconciled with Table 9, and some methodological attribution is removed. The overall evidential gains outweigh these drawbacks.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CARL and CARL-SSL, with matching architectures and identifiable corresponding experiments. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations and appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains original experiments and adds satellite classification and segmentation evaluations, controlled transfer tests, SSL ablations and feature analyses.

before.justification: v2 reports original medical, automotive and satellite segmentation experiments, architectural ablations and computational measurements.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and concluding discussion retain the same central claims: camera-agnostic spatio-spectral encoding, joint spectral/spatial self-supervision, and cross-domain robustness. Changing 'wavelength-aware' to 'camera-agnostic' within the first contribution aligns with its existing heading and surrounding claims. The expanded experiments support the retained contribution.

C2.justification: v4 adds explanations that channel subsampling preserves information through learned spectral relationships and acts as stochastic regularization against missing or shifted bands. It also connects expanded unseen-sensor results to the accuracy–compute tradeoff. Existing limitations concerning computational cost and spatial-resolution heterogeneity remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v4 newly documents public access to code and model weights through a repository identified in the abstract, materially extending the reproducibility information beyond v3's pseudocode and training recipe. Table 8 also supplies benchmark sensor, channel, wavelength, class, and task metadata. This assesses documented access; external resource availability was not verified.

E1.justification: Satellite evaluation expands from four to eleven benchmark entries. Additions include m-bigearthnet, m-eurosat, urban and rural LoveDA, WHU-OHS, Wuhan, and Beijing, extending evaluation to RGB imagery and unseen Orbita and Gaofen-5 hyperspectral sensors. The earlier datasets, including renamed m-cashew-plantation, remain. Medical, automotive, and pretraining coverage is retained.

E2.justification: v4 adds Galileo, Croma, Copernicus-FM, and SMARTIES to satellite linear-probe comparisons where applicable, including retained benchmarks. Table 10 adds SMARTIES to SegMunich fine-tuning and retains SatMAE, despite Appendix C's narrower baseline description. The computational comparison removes EVA-02, HyperFree, Hyve, and Spectral Adapter and adds Copernicus-FM and SMARTIES.

E3.justification: The FLOP comparison changes from standardized-depth/width encoders at 128×128×48 in v3 Appendix B to base-size models with a fixed 16×16 patch grid and 3/12/32/116 channels in v4 Appendix D. v4 also introduces average benchmark rank and a separate 16-channel training experiment. Table 8 reports 13 rather than 12 channels for the retained cashew and crop-type datasets; this revises reported inputs without establishing reruns.

E4.justification: v4 Appendix D extends the efficiency analysis across channel configurations and adds a targeted subsampling test: 16-channel training yields 68.8 versus 69.1 validation mIoU with roughly 75% fewer training FLOPs. The architectural ablations, SSL-loss ablation, medical heterogeneity tests, and t-SNE/feature-variance analysis are retained.

E5.justification: v3 Table 4 reports 95% confidence intervals for satellite linear probing; corresponding results in v4 Tables 4, 5, and 9 omit them. Confidence intervals remain for medical robustness, automotive segmentation, and SegMunich fine-tuning. Neither version specifies repeated-run counts, seeds, or a confidence-interval estimation procedure.

E6.justification: v4 adds extensive satellite results, including WHU-OHS mIoU of 21.7 for CARL versus 1.5 for each evaluated baseline and an average rank of 1.6. Added SMARTIES results exceed unchanged CARL scores on m-forestnet (49.8 versus 47.0) and SegMunich linear probing (39.1 versus 38.9). DOFA's cashew entry changes from 18.7 to 18.2 alongside revised reported channel counts. Computational results are replaced under different settings; CARL's fine-tuned SegMunich score remains 50.9.

M1.justification: The wavelength encoding, spectral self-attention/cross-attention architecture, aggregation, spatial encoder, masking objectives, and Algorithms 1–2 are retained. Channel subsampling already appears in v3 Appendix A.1; v4's 16-channel experiment changes an experimental setting without introducing a new method component.

P1.justification: v4 revises the satellite-results narrative, expands related-work explanations, rewrites the complexity discussion, and adds appendix subsections and acknowledgments. Satellite model labels are simplified, and headers change to conference-publication status. Most introductory, methodological, medical, automotive, ablation, and concluding prose remains substantially intact.

P2.justification: The satellite results presentation is substantially reorganized: v3 Table 4 becomes expanded tables separating seen and unseen sensors across the main text and appendix. Fine-tuning moves from main-text Table 5 to appendix Table 10, a dataset-description table is added, and the FLOP table gains sensor-specific columns and performance ranks. The six figures are retained, with limited diagram, caption, sizing, and placement adjustments.

R1.justification: v4 adds an expanded related-work appendix and substantially elaborates distinctions among channel invariance, wavelength awareness, spatial versus spatio-spectral encoding, and SSL strategies. Added works include Copernicus-FM, SMARTIES, Panopticon, TerraMind, Croma, OmniSat, and FlexiMo. This broadens and sharpens research positioning beyond citation or bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: v4 Appendix D adds explicit asymptotic reasoning distinguishing O(C²) spectral self-attention, O(CK) cross-attention, and O((HW)²) spatial attention from SpectralGPT's O((HWC)²) attention. v3 provides only qualitative complexity discussion and linear cross-attention scaling. The wavelength, loss, and synthetic-filter equations remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially strengthens evidence for the central camera-generalization claim by testing unseen real RGB and hyperspectral sensors against additional camera-agnostic competitors; v3's satellite evaluation covered Sentinel-2 and Landsat-8 only. The LoveDA and WHU-OHS results directly support this broader applicability. Expanded efficiency analysis and documented code/weight access also improve assessability and reproducibility. Dropped linear-probe confidence intervals and unexplained channel-count revisions weaken reporting, but the new evidence addresses an important limitation of the earlier validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CARL and contain readable methods, equations, experimental results, figures, tables, and appendices. Inspection of all 19 pages of v3 and 23 pages of v4 supports comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v4 retains these original results and adds satellite benchmark comparisons, revised computational measurements, and a channel-subsampling experiment.

before.justification: v3 reports original medical, automotive, and satellite experiments, architectural and self-supervision ablations, computational measurements, and feature-representation analyses.

C1.justification: v3 adds cognitively interpretable determinants of decoding performance as an explicit contribution in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion. Its prominent model contribution expands to commercial fine-tuning and zero-/few-shot reconstruction. The original claims about decoding text-specific goals and the difficulty of free-form reconstruction remain.

C2.justification: v3 introduces substantive interpretations involving resource-efficient reading, task adaptation, feature redundancy, fixation ordering, and the inferential character of OneStop questions. Reconstruction discussion now distinguishes model-specific benefits from eye movements and their limits on unseen texts. These extend v2's mainly aggregate performance and generalization discussion.

D1.justification: v3 supplies Gemini demonstration-selection prompts, GPT fine-tuning settings and model versions, and detailed LLaVA encoder layers. It corrects feature-table attribution and removes v2's conflicting candidate-loss training description. Code instructions now identify a named repository, and Appendix G.2.2 announces access to generated questions and annotations through generated_questions.csv.

E1.justification: The OneStop population, passages, and goal-decoding tasks remain unchanged. Appendix A adds SQuAD question–passage data for a comparative lexical-overlap analysis, providing limited additional dataset coverage while gaze-model evaluations remain on OneStop.

E2.justification: Reconstruction comparisons add DalEye-GPT, Gemini variants, DalEye-LLaVA, and GPT-4o-mini/LLaVA text-only controls. Arbitrary GPT-4o questions are replaced by arbitrary Gemini 3 questions (v2 Table 12; v3 Tables 14–15). v2's 'Llama 3.1 arbitrary question' is retained as Text-only Llama 3.1; selection comparators remain available in the appendix.

E3.justification: Question-word and category evaluation changes from Cohen's kappa to accuracy, and Gemini introduces zero-shot and regime-matched ten-example protocols. v3 also reports LLaVA LoRA rank 16 instead of 8 and early-stopping patience 7 instead of 8 epochs. These are reported setting revisions; rerunning is not established. The ten-fold splitting design remains.

E4.justification: v3 adds RoBERTEye feature-group ablations (Table 13), an eleven-predictor analysis linking decoding to reading behavior (Figure 4), and lexical-overlap checks (Appendix A). It expands the existing generation example across models (Table 16). v2's DalEye-Llama prompt/input sensitivity experiments are retained.

E5.justification: Reconstruction reporting changes from means with 1,000-bootstrap confidence intervals to mixed-effects intercept estimates and intervals accounting for paragraph/participant structure. v3 adds reconstruction significance comparisons and an eleven-test Bonferroni correction for the cognitive analysis. The ten cross-validation splits are retained.

E6.justification: Reconstruction results are substantially expanded and revised: DalEye-Llama's New Participant BLEU summary changes from 0.602 to 0.556, and Gemini few-shot newly reports QA accuracy 0.804 (v2 Table 12; v3 Tables 14–15). Changed metrics and estimation prevent treating revised scores as same-setting performance gains. RoBERTEye's aggregate selection scores remain 49.3%, 70.9%, and 57.3%.

M1.justification: v3 substantially extends generation beyond v2's fine-tuned models by adding DalEye-GPT and zero-shot/ten-example few-shot Gemini procedures, with regime-dependent demonstration selection (Sections 4.2 and C.1.2). The existing discriminative models and DalEye-Llama remain; DalEye-LLaVA is retained in the appendix.

P1.justification: The generative-model and reconstruction-results narratives are substantially rewritten, related work is condensed into three thematic discussions, and appendix organization changes. LLaVA and generative selection discussion move out of the main narrative, while prompt variations are regrouped with their results. Goal/question and text/item terminology is also standardized.

P2.justification: v3 adds the cognitive coefficient plot and overlap/ablation tables, redraws the reconstruction chart with expanded comparisons and revised axes, and expands v2 Figure 7 into Table 16. Selection tables are split or relocated, and the LLaVA diagram is revised and relocated.

R1.justification: v3 adds citations on perceived relevance, GazeXplain, synthetic gaze feedback, and supporting datasets/statistical tools. The central positioning against procedural reading-task classification remains unchanged. OneStop and LLaVA publication updates refer to retained works.

T1.justification: The task mappings and embedding/fusion mathematics retain their substance, with no new theoretical results or proofs. Appendix E expands the explanation of chance probabilities already presented in v2 Table 1; the new regression formulations concern statistical analysis.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens evidence about what gaze contributes and when decoding succeeds through feature ablations, cognitive analyses, additional text-only controls, and explicit dependence-aware reconstruction statistics. These address important explanatory and evidential gaps in v2. Replacing kappa with accuracy loses chance correction, and revised LLaVA settings remain incompletely reconciled, but the gains in experimental scrutiny and reproducibility outweigh these limitations.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same OneStop reading-goal decoding work. Their complete main texts, appendices, equations, tables, and figures support comparison, including material relocated in v3.

after.justification: v3 retains original experiments and adds generative-model evaluations, feature ablations, cognitive analyses, and dataset overlap measurements in Section 6 and Appendices A and G.

before.justification: v2 reports original goal-selection experiments, DalEye-Llama reconstruction results, and prompt/input comparisons in Section 6 and Appendix E.

C1.justification: The central contributions remain hierarchical motion representation, coherent parallel generation and scale-specific guidance. v2 strengthens the existing efficiency claim to state-of-the-art sampling efficiency and generation of over 2000 frames within two seconds in the introduction. This extends a retained contribution rather than redefining the research objective.

C2.justification: v1 describes explicit body-part conditioning as unavailable; v2 asserts and illustrates body-region guidance, while reframing the limitation as poor semantic interpretability across scales. It removes the parameter-scalability warning and interprets PM/guidance results through reconstruction-versus-interaction trade-offs and collision failures. Finger omission was already disclosed in v1; v2 emphasizes its expressive consequences.

D1.justification: v2 provides baseline adaptation recipes and newly specifies 200 autoencoder and 1500 diffusion epochs, while revising hardware from RTX 4090 to L40 and changing optimizer/scheduler details. It omits v1's parameter counts, wall-clock training durations, masking-rate formulas/examples and precise ten-joint, 100-dimensional cross-distance specification. Reproducibility documentation therefore changes substantially, with both additions and losses.

E1.justification: Both versions use DD100's 1.95 hours of paired dance/music spanning ten genres for leader- and music-conditioned reactive dance generation. Long-sequence generation is already evaluated in v1. The revised skeleton, guidance configurations and participant count change settings within retained coverage.

E2.justification: Table 1 expands from Duolando and InterGen to also evaluate GestureLSM, EDGE and TCDiff. v2 substantively adapts InterGen through music conditioning and independent dancer networks. The representation ablation changes from VQ-VAE to RVQ-VAE. Figure 9 also evaluates the expanded baseline set, while v1's user-study ground-truth comparison is absent.

E3.justification: v2 reports SMPL-based baseline retraining, adds MPJPE, MPJVE and inference-time evaluation, and marks diversity and beat metrics as targeting proximity to ground truth. The user study changes from 15 participants making binary choices to 20 participants providing five-point ratings on three criteria. Reported diffusion optimization changes from Adan with cosine scheduling to AdamW with a different learning rate and exponential decay.

E4.justification: v1 tests residual depths, removes BLC/dense-window training, and crosses guidance settings with PM removal. v2 drops the depth sweep and PM-by-guidance grid, tests training strides 16/64 and a latent-stitching control, and revises guidance analysis for two layers. Appendix Figures 6–8 add qualitative HFSQ/PM failure analyses and body-region guidance demonstrations.

E5.justification: v2 Figure 9 introduces error bars around mean perceptual ratings, whereas v1 reports preference percentages without uncertainty. The error bars' meaning and calculation are unspecified. Neither version reports training-run counts, random seeds or formal significance tests.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces ReactDance's FIDk/FIDg/FIDcd values of 41.61/10.95/8.24 with 5.57/7.63/14.17 under revised representation and training settings; these are not same-setting gains or losses. v2 adds MPJPE 132.99, MPJVE 15.68, inference time 1.75 seconds, and numerous baseline/ablation results. Figure 9 replaces preference percentages with naturalness/music/coordination ratings of 4.32/4.16/4.24.

M1.justification: Beyond renaming GRFSQ to HFSQ, v2 changes the representation from 25-joint SMPL-X global positions to 22-joint SMPL with root-relative reactor coordinates, adopts two residual stages instead of three, and adds foot-contact and relative-orientation losses (v2 Equation 7 versus v1 Equation 8). Upper/lower-body separation, progressive masking, BLC and LDCFG are retained.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, methods and experimental discussion are extensively rewritten. v2 changes the title and terminology, consolidates v1's fragmented and repeated ablation discussion, adds a related-work subsection, and organizes supporting material into an appendix. The narrative structure changes substantially.

P2.justification: v2 switches from two-column to single-column layout, replaces the opening and qualitative-comparison figures, revises and relocates shared architecture diagrams, and substantially restructures the tables. Appendix Figures 6–9 add ablation illustrations, body-region guidance examples and a perceptual-rating chart. These exceed numerical updates or renumbering.

R1.justification: v2 adds a dedicated long-motion discussion positioning BLC against MotionStreamer, priorMDM, EDGE and Lodge. It introduces DuetGen, GestureLSM, Co3Gesture and robotics/application references while removing substantial older solo/group-generation and quantization coverage. This materially revises research positioning beyond citation-format or publication-metadata updates.

T1.justification: The written quantization mathematics changes: v2 Equation 1 explicitly maintains cumulative residuals, and reconstruction includes scaling factors, replacing v1's recurrence over previous quantized outputs and unweighted sum. v2 also explicitly defines the autoencoder latent loss with stop-gradient operations. These are localized mathematical revisions; neither version provides theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v1's unquantified sampling-efficiency claim and narrow two-baseline evaluation are materially strengthened by v2's timing comparisons, reconstruction metrics and five explicitly adapted baselines. Revised controls, appendix failure analyses and the three-criterion perceptual study provide more informative evidence, while clearer methods and organization improve assessability. Some implementation details and previous ablations are lost, and the user-study error bars remain undefined, but these shortcomings do not outweigh the substantial gains in evidential support and clarity.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ReactDance and provide readable methods, equations, figures and experimental tables. All supplied material was inspected, including v2's appendix, Sections 6.1–6.5. v1 ends with references and contains no appendix. The substantial revision remains reliably comparable.

after.justification: v2 reports original DD100 comparisons, reconstruction and timing results, revised ablations, qualitative analyses and a perceptual study, including appendix results.

before.justification: v1 reports original DD100 benchmark results, component ablations, guidance experiments and user-study preference percentages in Tables 1–4.

C1.justification: The central contributions remain HFSQ for hierarchical motion representation, BLC for coherent parallel generation and LDCFG for multiscale control. Both versions claim high-quality long-form generation exceeding 2000 frames within two seconds. Frequency terminology and revised future-work framing do not materially change these headline claims.

C2.justification: v3 adds frequency-based decomposition, phase-agnostic decoder smoothing and scalar-grid explanations, together with interpretations of depth/cost trade-offs, hand denoising, conditioning roles and generalization. Some interpretations overreach: A.7 describes consistently improving jitter, although Table 6 reports 17.18 at stride 240 and 17.99 at stride 64.

D1.justification: v3 discloses fourfold temporal downsampling and independent per-layer condition dropout with probability 0.2. It also supplies relative training-cost information and a project-page pointer. The hardware, optimizers, learning rates, epoch counts and batch size in the training appendix remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained DD100 body-motion evaluation, v3 adds hand-motion modeling, reversed leader/follower roles and zero-shot reactions to FineDance solo-dance inputs (Appendices A.8, A.10–A.11). These expand output requirements and input conditions; the generalization outcomes are reported descriptively without embedded demonstrations.

E2.justification: The five main baselines remain GestureLSM, EDGE, TCDiff, InterGen and Duolando. Table 2 adds VAE and RVQ-VAE with progressive masking as tokenizer comparators. The old 'w/o HFSQ' results are retained under RVQ-VAE without masking, rather than replaced.

E3.justification: The original DD100 splits, 8-second clips, 30 fps and default stride 4 remain. v3 adds PFC and IPR evaluation, boundary-jitter measurement, separate reconstruction evaluation, residual-depth settings R=1–4, additional strides 1/240/360 and conditioning-removal controls. These substantially broaden the evaluation design.

E4.justification: v3 expands the tokenizer/masking analysis into reconstruction and generation comparisons, tests residual-depth scalability, and extends stride analysis to boundary continuity and training cost. Appendices A.8–A.11 additionally investigate hand-motion stability, conditioning roles, role swapping and distribution shift.

E5.justification: Figure 9 retains the same user-study means and error bars, with the same participant and comparison counts. Neither version specifies what those error bars represent, and v3 adds no seed counts, repeated-run reporting, confidence intervals or significance-testing procedures.

E6.justification: Existing main-table scores, retained ablation entries, guidance results and user-study ratings remain unchanged. v3 adds physical metrics, including ReactDance PFC 0.6039 and IPR 7.84%, plus reconstruction, depth, stride, hand-motion and conditioning results in Tables 2 and 5–8. Role-swapping and FineDance successes are newly reported qualitative findings.

M1.justification: HFSQ quantization, progressive masking, diffusion losses, BLC sampling and the LDCFG inference equation are retained. v3 newly documents independent layerwise conditioning dropout, but does not establish that it replaces a different v2 procedure.

P1.justification: Sections 3.4–3.5 receive focused rewriting into explicit mechanism and training/inference explanations, with smaller terminology and conclusion edits. The main section order and much retained prose remain stable. The appendix is relabeled from Section 6 to Appendix A and its outline and cross-references are expanded.

P2.justification: Table 1 gains physical-quality columns, Table 2 is substantially restructured into reconstruction and generation panels, and Tables 5–8 add displays for the new analyses. Figures 1–9 are retained, with relocation and page reflow; v3 also adds conference headers.

R1.justification: v3 adds citations to MoMask, generalized winding numbers and FineDance. It contrasts MoMask's residual vector quantization and serial generation with HFSQ, and refines the DuetGen comparison to conditional response diversity. The broader related-work organization and positioning remain.

T1.justification: Appendix A.7 newly defines boundary Jitter as mean L2 velocity change around block boundaries, using a 30-frame half-radius. This is a limited mathematical metric definition. Equations 1–9 otherwise retain their substance, including equivalent W-to-T notation in positional encoding; no proofs or theorems are added.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens evidence for the central design choices: Table 2 supplies a masking-matched RVQ comparison missing from v2, while Tables 5–6 test residual depth and directly connect boundary continuity to training cost. These address important gaps in component validation. Unexplained reconstruction MPJPE differences between Tables 2 and 5 (28.66 versus 24.32), overstated jitter monotonicity and video-dependent generalization evidence temper, but do not outweigh, those gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ReactDance work. All pages, including appendices, provide readable text, equations, tables and figures. Added video-linked demonstrations can be compared only through their descriptions in v3.

after.justification: v3 retains these original results and adds physical-quality measurements, expanded ablations, hand-motion results and reported generalization experiments.

before.justification: v2 reports original DD100 benchmark results, component and guidance ablations, qualitative comparisons and a 20-participant user study.

C1.justification: v3 claims API applicability but explicitly acknowledges a gap to attacking proprietary models. v4's abstract and introduction claim demonstrated success against Gemini-2.5-Pro, materially extending that scope. The lightweight BiasNet, attack formulation and response-quality metric contributions remain.

C2.justification: v4 removes the limitation concerning proprietary-model content monitors. It newly interprets stronger results on Gemini Pro as evidence that JULI benefits from more knowledgeable targets, and uses the BiasNet-only and benign examples to argue for knowledge extraction with preserved general abilities. Defense interpretations now emphasize API-compatible comparisons.

D1.justification: v4 adds a code-repository link, documents tokenizer reuse and sequential one-token API collection of training logits, and discloses sampling temperatures. The architecture, AdamW optimizer, 100 training pairs, 15 epochs, batch size and learning rate were already documented in v3.

E1.justification: v4 extends simulated API evaluation to actual Gemini-2.5-Flash and Gemini-2.5-Pro APIs, adds a deep-safety-alignment scenario, and includes benign instruction examples from databricks-dolly-15k. AdvBench, MaliciousInstruct, the hard AdvBench subset and LLM-LAT training data are retained.

E2.justification: FLIP and the Naive prefix attack join the retained benchmark and circuit-breaker comparisons. v4 also evaluates the longer-prefix Naive+ variant and adds LINT restricted to top-5 access to an API comparison. GCG, ED, WTS, LINT and Base remain in corresponding legacy comparisons.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include top-k token-hit measurements on 100 LLM-LAT pairs and a BiasNet-only control that removes the target-output residual during training and sampling. The circuit-breaker comparison replaces unrestricted black-box JULI with restricted API JULI. Score-equals-five count metrics are dropped; the existing training budget, dataset selection and human-rating design remain.

E4.justification: v4 adds token-availability analysis (Figure 2), projection-seed robustness (A.4), a BiasNet-only ablation and benign-response cases (A.8), deep-alignment tests (A.12), and prefix-length analysis (A.13). The KL-divergence, top-k sensitivity and transfer analyses already existed in v3.

E5.justification: Appendix A.4 newly reports an optimization-robustness experiment with five random seeds and individual results in Table A3. This does not establish repeated runs for all benchmark results. The human-rating correlation analysis is unchanged, and no confidence intervals or significance tests are added.

E6.justification: v4 adds substantial results, including Gemini-Pro scores of 4.19 Harmful Score and 3.19 Harmful Info Score in Table 2. It also revises retained entries, such as the Qwen hard-subset Base Info Score from 2.23 to 0.08 (v3 Table A5; v4 Table A9). Most legacy white-box means and transfer scores remain. Score-5 counts and some full-vocabulary black-box results disappear; replacement circuit-breaker API scores use stricter access and are not same-setting declines.

M1.justification: The documented training objective in Eq. 9 changes from scoring BiasNet's output alone to including the target-output residual. Section 4.2 also changes padding from the kth log probability to that value minus 10. BiasNet's architecture and additive decoding strategy remain. These reported revisions do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

P1.justification: The introduction replaces the contribution bullets with a substantially revised narrative emphasizing knowledge extraction and proprietary APIs. Section 5 separates open-weight and API evaluations and moves mechanism analysis later; the appendices are reorganized. Extensive prose editing accompanies metric renaming from GPT-4 Score and Info Score to Harmful Score and Harmful Info Score.

P2.justification: v4 adds the token-hit figure and several experimental tables, moves the main open-weight and top-k tables into the appendix, removes count columns, and restructures the circuit-breaker table around API compatibility. The overview and KL-analysis figures are retained, with the latter renumbered. Conference formatting also changes headers, typography and layout.

R1.justification: v4 adds references covering Gemini 2.5, FLIP, deep safety alignment and covert malicious fine-tuning, while removing the Toxicity Detection for Free citation. The introduction expands discussion of prompt-rewriting and encryption attacks, but the main related-work taxonomy remains.

T1.justification: Eq. 9 revises the mathematical training objective to include the target-output residual, and new Eq. 10 specifies the objective without that residual for the ablation. The probability definitions and prior-attack formulations remain unchanged. No theoretical guarantees or proofs are added.

improvement.justification: Actual Gemini API evaluations address v3's central gap between simulated API feasibility and demonstrated proprietary-model attacks. Added prefix and FLIP comparisons, restricted-access LINT, and mechanism and robustness controls substantially strengthen the evidence. Removing score-5 counts and the content-monitor limitation reduces transparency, and some notation and labels remain inconsistent, but these costs are outweighed by the stronger validation of the central claim.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe JULI and BiasNet. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support matching retained, relocated and revised material.

after.justification: v4 retains original experimental results and adds Gemini API evaluations, new baseline comparisons, seed experiments and mechanism ablations.

before.justification: v3 reports original jailbreak experiments on AdvBench and MaliciousInstruct, circuit-breaker and transfer evaluations, and a 120-response comparison with human ratings.

C1.justification: The central claims linking MF and IGB and associating optimal trainability with transient prejudice remain. V3 qualifies the introductory trainability statement to wide architectures and explicitly broadens the equivalence's stated applicability beyond MLPs under mean-field assumptions. Its new empirical contribution mainly supports the retained central principle.

C2.justification: V3 adds explanations involving softmax saturation and zero favoured-class gradients, Adam-mediated delayed learning in ordered phases, and residual architectures without phase distinctions. Its limitations shift from v1's emphasis on wide MLPs and finite-width breakdown to ordered infinite-width/data limits, absent feature learning and a proposed proportional data/parameter regime. These materially change the interpretation and applicability discussion.

D1.justification: V3 Appendix B and Table 2 add optimizer, regularization, learning-rate, batch-size, architecture and dataset-binarization details, plus residual scaling and the specific timm pretrained checkpoint. V1 mainly supplies simulation settings in captions. Reproducibility information expands substantially, although Table 2 duplicates a CIFAR10 ViT entry where Appendix B.3 distinguishes binary and multiclass tasks.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates synthetic Gaussian inputs and initialization gradients on CIFAR10. V3 adds supervised training on binarized Fashion MNIST, binarized CIFAR10 and multiclass CIFAR10, plus CIFAR100 fine-tuning of an ImageNet-21k-pretrained Vision Transformer (Section 6 and Appendix B). This substantially extends both dataset and task coverage.

E2.justification: MF and IGB remain the compared analytical descriptions in matched signal-propagation experiments. No competing initialization or optimization method is newly benchmarked. Residual MLPs and Vision Transformers are additional study architectures, while initialization-phase comparisons remain the experimental controls.

E3.justification: V3 introduces training and fine-tuning protocols, train/test accuracy and classification-frequency measurements, additional model configurations, and pretrained-weight scaling controls. It also revises the existing activation-drift error sweep: v1 Figure 5 uses weight variances 1.8–2.2 and bias variances 0/0.1, whereas v3 Figure 14 uses 1.5–2.5 and 0/0.1/0.2, retaining the width set.

E4.justification: V3 adds class-specific accuracy and gradient analyses, residual-network criticality checks, pretrained-weight perturbations, and variance/covariance concentration studies across widths (Appendices B, E and G). Conversely, v1 Appendix D's width-50 MF–IGB breakdown analysis and Figure 7's pooled-network gradient panels are removed.

E5.justification: V3 Appendix G newly specifies median-over-input gradient summaries, including medians restricted to favoured and unfavoured classes; v1 does not specify this estimator. The existing 90% MF interval practice is retained. Neither version specifies repeated training runs or seeds, and v3 does not explain the statistical meaning of its training-curve shading.

E6.justification: V3 adds train/test accuracy and classification-frequency outcomes (Figures 4–13), including rapid bias absorption near the EOC in vanilla MLPs and similar learning across initializations in residual MLPs. It also adds covariance-concentration and class-specific gradient findings and replaces the activation-drift error entries on a revised parameter grid. These are new or replaced results, rather than demonstrated same-setting performance improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The MF–IGB framework and Gaussian initialization approach already include nonzero biases and multi-node pooling in v1. V3 introduces no new proposed optimization or inference algorithm; its additional architectures and weight perturbations serve as experimental applications and controls.

P1.justification: V3 substantially reorganizes the narrative: the former Section 6 pooling discussion moves into Appendix F, training dynamics becomes the new Section 6, and the setup and contribution list are rewritten. A supplementary contents page, extensive notation guide and reorganized appendix subsections materially change navigation and exposition, beyond the title and terminology edits.

P2.justification: V3 adds extensive training and class-specific gradient panels, covariance-concentration figures and an experimental-settings table, while removing several earlier displays. Appendix result grids are enlarged and reorganized. Matching confirms that the pooling phase diagram is retained unchanged from v1 Figure 4 as v3 Figure 19; its relocation is not a new result.

R1.justification: V3 adds references supporting Transformers, Vision Transformers, ImageNet, generalization, Adam and timm, while removing the Roberts–Yaida–Hanin theory book and Li–Nica–Roy covariance-SDE reference associated with finite-width discussion. The central positioning relative to prior MF and IGB research remains.

T1.justification: V3 states an architecture-general equivalence theorem with explicit limit ordering, expands MF derivations, and adds extensive pooling calculations and proofs in Appendix F. It also replaces chi1 with tilde-chi1 in the variance-map derivative (v1 Equation 56; v3 Equation 66). These substantively extend existing theory, although new Lemmas F.7/F.9 label points as EOC despite preceding formulas giving chi1 below one, conflicting with Section 2.2's criterion.

improvement.justification: V3 directly addresses an important evidential gap: v1 inferred bias absorption and learning behaviour largely from initialization theory, whereas v3 measures bias alongside training and test performance across architectures and datasets (Section 6 and Appendix B). The accompanying protocols and diagnostic analyses make the central claim substantially more assessable. Removing the width-50 failure example and introducing notation, setting-label and pooling-EOC inconsistencies weaken parts of the revision, but the gain in direct training evidence and reproducibility information provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MF–IGB equivalence and initialization/trainability study, despite the revised title. The complete 27-page v1 and 48-page v3, including equations, figures, tables and appendices, support reliable comparison.

after.justification: V3 retains numerical validation and adds original training and fine-tuning results across MLPs, residual MLPs and Vision Transformers (Section 6 and Appendix B).

before.justification: V1 reports original network simulations, including MF–IGB correlation comparisons, finite-width deviations and CIFAR10 initialization-gradient measurements (Figures 2 and 5–9).

C1.justification: v1 claims demonstrated feasibility and leading performance on CARLA Town05 while leaving real-world effectiveness unexplored. v2 broadens its abstract, contributions and conclusion to multiple benchmarks, real-world applicability and claimed vehicle-deployment validation. It also omits v1's explicit claim to be the first work using probabilistic modeling for the continuous planning action space.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning multimodal candidate quality, traffic-density robustness, vocabulary coverage and transfer, and the distinction between similar open-loop accuracy and stronger closed-loop performance. The introduction replaces the richer-supervision rationale with simpler action ranking. The conclusion replaces the unexplored-real-world limitation with specific concerns about naive simulated agents and insufficient realism; Appendix A.3 discusses vocabulary-related latency.

D1.justification: v2 adds component-specific encoder details, vocabulary-sampling pseudocode and endpoint-distance selection, six-waypoint planning, feature dimension 256, 16 NVIDIA 4090 GPUs, and parameter/latency measurements. Appendix A supplies dataset composition and shared-backbone comparison details. These substantially expand reproducibility information, although v1's Town05 route counts and lengths are omitted. The GitHub address is retained.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates CARLA Town05 Long and Short. v2 retains these and adds Bench2Drive, NAVSIM, NAVSIMv2 and a 3DGS benchmark involving 2000 hours of real-driving training data and 337 reconstructed evaluation scenarios. Appendix A.2 also uses nuScenes trajectories to construct a vocabulary evaluated on NAVSIM, substantially extending represented data and environments.

E2.justification: Town05 Long Table 1 removes CILRS and LBC and adds Rao et al. (2024), DriveCoT and LeapVAD. Town05 Short, moved to v2 Table 9, adds LeapVAD while retaining its previous comparators. New benchmark comparisons additionally include DiffusionDrive, PRIX, GenAD and ETA, among others, substantially expanding the evaluated comparator set.

E3.justification: New evaluations introduce NAVSIM navtest PDMS, NAVSIMv2 extended metrics, eight-second 3DGS scenarios with collision/deviation metrics, and controlled density, vocabulary-size and training-data experiments. The Town05 data description also changes from three million frames sampled at 2 Hz to three million clips containing 1.6-second histories at 10 Hz. This is a reported setting revision, without establishing that retained results were rerun.

E4.justification: The original component ablation and qualitative examples are retained. v2 adds top-five candidate evaluation, traffic-density robustness, vocabulary and training-data scaling, deterministic versus probabilistic comparisons in open and closed loop, and vocabulary sampling/transfer analyses (Tables 6, 8 and 10–13). Appendix A.3 also adds reconstruction-quality and computational-efficiency analyses.

E5.justification: Both versions report performance point estimates without seed information, repeated-run counts, error bars, confidence intervals or significance tests. The expanded evaluations do not introduce uncertainty reporting for experimental performance.

E6.justification: The retained Town05 scores and component-ablation values are unchanged, including VADv2 driving scores of 85.1 on Long and 89.7 on Short. v2 adds substantial results, including NAVSIM PDMS 89.3, NAVSIMv2 EPDMS 85.8, Bench2Drive driving score 76.15 and 3DGS collision ratio 0.270 (Tables 2–5), plus new comparator, ablation and efficiency entries.

M1.justification: Section 3.3 changes the stated training target: v1 inserts the ground-truth trajectory into the vocabulary and downweights nearby negatives; v2 labels the nearest existing vocabulary trajectory and estimates empirical action frequencies from these assignments. This is a localized supervision revision. The scene-token architecture, trajectory vocabulary, Transformer planner and PID inference remain.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and related-work discussion undergo substantial rewriting. The scene encoder becomes a component-by-component explanation, terminology changes from environmental to scene tokens, and experimental discussion is reorganized across the main text and a new appendix. Author/header information also changes. The revision extends well beyond isolated wording edits.

P2.justification: The paper changes from a two-column layout to a single-column conference format and substantially reorganizes its displays. Town05 Short moves to Appendix A, the original qualitative Figure 3 becomes a compact four-panel Figure 4, and Figure 1 is reduced beside text. Numerous benchmark and ablation tables, an algorithm box and a standalone vocabulary visualization are added.

R1.justification: Related work is substantially revised to discuss Trajeglish, MotionLM, Diffusion Planner, DiffusionDrive and GoalFlow, alongside newer driving benchmarks and methods. v2 explicitly positions complete-trajectory tokens against single-step tokenization and iterative rollout, while condensing the earlier LLM survey and removing the sweeping first-work claim.

T1.justification: v2 Section 3.3 defines empirical action frequencies, derives the cross-entropy objective from KL divergence and supplies an explicit indicator-based conflict-loss equation. These are limited mathematical additions. The continuity assumption and probabilistic-field construction remain, and no theorem or proof-based guarantee is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important evidential gaps in v1 through direct deterministic-planner controls, multimodal and vocabulary analyses, and evaluations beyond Town05 using NAVSIM and reconstructed real-driving environments. These additions test the central planning argument more directly and broaden its empirical support; implementation disclosures also improve reproducibility. Repeated-run uncertainty remains absent, and on-vehicle deployment outcomes are referenced rather than shown in the supplied PDF, limiting the strongest applicability claims. Nevertheless, the added controlled evidence constitutes a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same VADv2 research, with clearly matchable methods and Town05 experiments. The supplied text, equations, tables and figures are readable. v2 includes Appendix A; v1 contains no appendix. Referenced external demonstrations and supplementary deployment results are outside this comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original Town05 results and adds Bench2Drive, NAVSIM, NAVSIMv2 and 3DGS evaluations, together with original analyses in Section 4 and Appendix A.

before.justification: v1 reports original CARLA Town05 Long/Short evaluations, component ablations and qualitative planning results in Tables 1–3 and Figure 3.

results.title: VADv2: End-to-End Vectorized Autonomous Driving via Probabilistic Planning

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central contributions: localized embeddings from a frozen backbone, efficient gradient decomposition, optional contextual regularization, and use across retrieval, captioning and generation. The added evidence does not redefine these claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations connecting convergence to semantic capture and later boundary refinement, alpha to the local/global tradeoff, and comparative scaling to better use of larger backbones. It also argues for overlapping-mask independence and multi-object relationship preservation. The original explainability-quality and small-object limitations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents explicit computational-graph detachment and configurations for the added runtime experiments. Conversely, it omits v1's project-page link and explicit LeGrad averaging/normalization description. Existing backbone weights, optimizer, default iteration count and positional-embedding interpolation details are retained.

E1.justification: Appendix G/Figure 8 adds qualitative generation cases using masks covering combinations of cartoon characters, extending the illustrated input scenarios. The seven quantitative benchmark datasets and established task families remain unchanged; medical and aerial imagery are discussed but not evaluated.

E2.justification: v2 Table 3 adds evaluated comparisons with MaskCLIP, CLIPSurgery and SCLIP across seven retained benchmarks and three backbone sizes. These comparisons were absent from v1, substantially expanding the comparator coverage while retaining the earlier baselines.

E3.justification: v2 adds controlled protocols tracking PascalVOC loss and accuracy through 100 iterations, sweeping alpha from 0 to 20 on RefCOCO, and measuring runtime at resolutions from 224 to 768 pixels with 10 masks and 10 iterations. The original benchmark metrics, backbone configurations and default optimization settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New Appendices D-G examine convergence and the stopping budget, runtime versus resolution, regularization sensitivity, and multi-object representation. These substantially extend v1's analyses. The earlier optimization visualizations, mask-quality, explainability-method and gradient-decomposition ablations are retained under matched sections and figures.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, standard deviations or significance tests. The added parameter sweeps and curves do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: v2 adds baseline scores, regularization sensitivities, convergence/runtime curves and multi-object outputs. Most original results remain unchanged, but Table 2 changes ViT-B/32 PascalVOC Acc@10 from 8.9 to 98.8. In the new Table 3, H/14 advantages over the best listed baseline, CLIPSurgery, are 25.5 points on VOC and 23.6 on COCO; the accompanying prose incorrectly states 31.7 and 32.8.

M1.justification: Both versions use a frozen backbone, a CLS-initialized token optimized against a query mask through explainability and Dice loss, optional cosine regularization, and gradient decomposition. The new explanations of overlapping masks and graph detachment do not establish a changed algorithm.

P1.justification: v2 polishes wording, condenses the methodological background and conclusion, makes experimental setup a separate subsection, and moves ablations before captioning and diffusion. Gradient decomposition is incorporated into Section 3.2. These are limited editorial reorganizations within the retained overall narrative.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 3 and 7 and Figures 5-8, redraws Figure 2 as a horizontal workflow, moves Figure 1 into the introduction, and regroups the main comparison and ablation tables. Existing qualitative figures and analyses remain, often relocated and renumbered. The visual changes extend substantially beyond pagination.

R1.justification: v2 adds CLIPSurgery, SCLIP and GradCAM++ references and expands its positioning against training-free dense-token aggregation. It removes the Efficient Self-Ensemble citation. Updates to LeGrad, FGVP and lambda-ECLIPSE bibliographic information concern existing works; the central novelty positioning remains stable.

T1.justification: Appendix I.1 adds a focused product-rule derivation supporting gradient decomposition, formalizing stop-gradient initialization and the token's zero derivative with respect to backbone activations. v1 states the independence and decomposition without this proof. The new derivation explicitly omits cosine-normalization terms.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of the unchanged method: Table 3 supplies missing direct training-free comparisons, while Appendices D-F quantitatively support the iteration budget and regularization choice and examine resolution costs. These address important evidence gaps in v1. Overstated baseline margins and removal of the project link detract from the revision, and the added proof remains limited by omitted cosine normalization, but the comparative and design-choice evidence is substantially stronger.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MaskInversion. All 16 pages of v1 and 20 pages of v2, including equations, tables, figures and appendices, support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds training-free baseline comparisons, hyperparameter analyses, resolution-scaling measurements and multi-object examples.

before.justification: v1 reports original retrieval and captioning experiments, mask-quality and runtime ablations, and qualitative generation results.

results.title: MaskInversion: Localized Embeddings via Optimization of Explainability Maps

C1.justification: The contribution expands from a six-subject examination benchmark to multilingual, multi-source benchmarking and analysis of generalization across languages and evaluator families. v2 additionally emphasizes specialized evaluator training and test-time scaling, replacing v1's emphasis on limited prompting and agent benefits. The central claim that automatic evaluators fall short of humans remains.

C2.justification: The explanation based on missed key information is retained, but v2 adds interpretations involving tie aversion, temperature-sensitive reasoning models, reward-model generalization, and overconfident RL convergence. Recommendations shift from broadly seeking semantic-sensitive metrics and additional disciplines toward trained evaluators, hybrid workflows, and explicit cost–quality tradeoffs.

D1.justification: v2 supplies filtering/paraphrasing prompts, expanded annotation instructions and compensation details, language-specific preprocessing and BERTScore backbones, and TTRL hyperparameters such as batch size 8, 32 rollouts, and learning rate 5e-7. It adds inference-time and API-cost tables, while removing several detailed agent-specific implementation recipes. Both versions already advertise code and data access.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates English translations of Chinese examination material covering six subjects. v2 evaluates Chinese examination data and original English Reddit/ELI5 data across 15 topics, adding domains such as engineering, biology, physics, and mathematics. The human–human, human–model, and model–model comparison families remain.

E2.justification: v2 adds Qwen/Llama/DeepSeek judges, reasoning models, Skywork and RM-R1 reward models, Prometheus, FineSurE, and a separately measured human baseline. Several earlier comparators, including BLEU, BLEURT, CritiqueLLM, TIGERScore, and ReFeR, disappear. G-Eval and ChatEval remain in Appendix B.4, Table 13.

E3.justification: v2 adds macro-F1 alongside accuracy and changes scalar tie-rounding from two to three decimal places. The reported annotation pool increases from five to ten, fluency is explicitly excluded from judging, and three additional PhD annotators provide a human baseline. Temperature-zero controls and TTRL training/validation settings introduce further experimental protocols.

E4.justification: v2 adds temperature sensitivity, contamination checks, efficiency comparisons, TTRL/clipping ablations, and quantified error categories with new case studies. Domain, response-origin, CoT, and tie-exclusion analyses are retained but revised. v1's five-vote consistency analysis and analyses conditioned on human annotator disagreement are removed.

E5.justification: Annotation reliability reporting changes from raw agreement rates by subject and comparison mode in v1 Table 2 to chance-corrected Cohen's kappa in v2: 0.78 for reference validation and approximately 0.65 for preference annotation. Neither version reports confidence intervals, significance tests, or seed-based variability for evaluator performance.

E6.justification: Results are substantially replaced and expanded. GPT-4o's average accuracy is 0.532 in v1 Table 3 versus 57.5% in v2 Table 2, but changed data and protocols prevent interpreting this as a same-setting gain. v2 adds bilingual F1 scores, human accuracy averaging 79.9%, and TTRL results, including 63.9 versus 66.5 with higher clipping for Qwen2.5-3B (Table 7).

M1.justification: The described construction pipeline adds question filtering and expert reference rejection, while text transformation shifts from expanding references to paraphrasing human responses. v2 also introduces evaluator adaptation using structured outputs, TTRL, and DAPO-style higher clipping (Section 5.7); v1 contains no corresponding evaluator-training procedure.

P1.justification: Beyond renaming, the abstract, introduction, methodology, and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten. A broad Analysis section replaces the dedicated agent section, Discussion moves to Appendix C, and the appendices are reorganized around additional results, discussion, cases, instructions, and annotation.

P2.justification: The overview figure is redesigned, the main results table changes from subject-level accuracy columns to bilingual accuracy/F1 columns, and agreement displays become paired kappa heatmaps. New analysis tables and an error-type chart appear; many earlier full-page diagrams are removed or replaced. The annotation screenshot is retained and relocated.

R1.justification: v2 substantially extends positioning toward reasoning models, reward modeling, and reinforcement learning, adding work on Prometheus, Skywork, RM-R1, FActScore, contamination detection, TTRL, and DAPO. Section 5.6 explicitly positions LFQA-E against Expert, Feedback-Bench, RM-Bench, and Reward-Bench. Several earlier agent/planning references and discussions disappear.

T1.justification: Neither version develops substantive mathematical theory, formal assumptions, or proofs. v2's standard accuracy and macro-F1 formulas explain empirical scoring; they do not introduce new mathematical reasoning.

improvement.justification: The broader language/domain coverage, separately measured human baseline, and focused sensitivity/error analyses substantially address v1's narrow coverage and limited support for human comparisons. These gains strengthen the paper's empirical foundation. Reporting weaknesses remain: the overview gives 1618 questions/7323 comparisons while the conclusion gives 1625/7649, and Appendix B.4's agent-leadership claim exceeds Table 13's average results. These weaknesses do not outweigh the substantial evidential improvements.

A1.justification: Both PDFs are complete, readable versions of the same reference-based LFQA benchmarking work, renamed from CALF to LFQA-E and substantially expanded. Their text, tables, figures, equations, and appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original bilingual evaluator experiments, a human baseline, sensitivity analyses, contamination checks, and reinforcement-learning results in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluator experiments, annotation agreement, agent comparisons, and supplementary analyses, including Tables 2–5 and 15–17.

results.title: LFQA-E: Carefully Benchmarking Long-form QA Evaluation

C1.justification: The principal generation claim strengthens from O(L^(3/2) sqrt(log L)) to O(L log^2 L). Prompted generation improves from O(L log L + K^2) to O(L log L + K log^2 K). v3 also claims demonstrated efficiency in deep convolutional and hybrid models. Exactness, applicability to convolutional models and the O(K) prompt-cache claim are retained.

C2.justification: Beyond v1's hardware caveat, v3 discusses runtime–memory trade-offs, near-optimality up to logarithmic factors, unsupported quantization, and long-prompt GPU memory failures. Appendix A.1 explicitly qualifies that STU-T's approximation loses the original LDS learning guarantees. Section 5.2 adds explanations linking practical speedups to model scale and avoided prompt recomputation.

D1.justification: v1 discloses little beyond a single-layer CPU loop. v3 documents H100 and TPUv2 hardware, PyTorch and JAX implementations, precision choices, tokenizer, initialization, 48 filters, STU-T factorization, attention configuration, FFT padding and casting, and separate prefill timing. Appendices A.1 and B.1 also provide dependency source and licensing information, substantially improving reproducibility documentation.

E1.justification: Coverage expands within autoregressive generation timing: v1 evaluates generation from scratch, while v3 also evaluates prompt-conditioned decoding, including prompts longer and shorter than the generated continuation (Section 5.2; Appendix A.3). Neither version reports a named language corpus or downstream accuracy benchmark. Larger and hybrid architectures primarily change model configurations.

E2.justification: Naive convolution remains the principal empirical baseline. v3 Appendix B and Figure 4 additionally evaluate a two-layer Transformer with a standard KV cache. Attention appears only in theoretical complexity comparisons in v1. Flash Inference and approximate inference methods are discussed in v3 but are not reported empirical comparators.

E3.justification: Beyond v1's single-layer CPU experiment, v3 introduces complete-forward-pass H100 timing protocols across model depths, widths and precisions, with prefill and decoding measured separately. Appendix B adds matched two-layer convolutional and Transformer configurations on TPUv2. The controlled timing plots also use a revised sequence-length sweep. These are new evaluation designs, not established reruns of v1 under identical conditions.

E4.justification: v1 mainly examines runtime scaling with sequence length. v3 Section 5.2 and Appendix A add systematic depth, width and prompt-length analyses, comparisons of fully convolutional and hybrid configurations, and a cache-length sweep testing the runtime trade-off at fixed generation length. Figure 2b and Table 15 directly examine the choice of epoch length K.

E5.justification: v1 provides no run counts or quantified timing uncertainty. v3 Section 5.2 and Appendix A.1 specify three timings per configuration, discard the first, and report the mean and sample standard deviation of the remaining two, omitting deviations below 0.01 seconds. This introduces systematic uncertainty reporting without establishing increased runs for the earlier experiments.

E6.justification: v3 adds Continuous-FutureFill timings and extensive model, prompt and cache-sweep results. For the 670.75M STU-only model, Table 3 reports 1009.36 seconds versus 1731.67 for naive convolution at 126,976 tokens, but 17.07 versus 14.72 at 4096 tokens. These newly reported settings establish both gains and short-sequence slowdowns; they are not same-setting performance improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The earlier periodic FFT-cache scheme becomes Epoched-FutureFill. v3 additionally introduces Continuous-FutureFill, which accumulates future contributions through power-of-two blocks. This new procedure is incorporated into prompted generation and offered as an online-convolution module for spectral filtering in Algorithms 3–4; it is more than a renaming or expanded explanation.

P1.justification: The exposition is substantially reorganized around an explicit online-convolution problem and FutureFill primitive. Online algorithms now precede prompted generation; experiments become a standalone section; conclusions and limitations are added. Existing model background, related work and the spectral-filtering discussion move into appendices, alongside extensive rewriting of the introductory and technical narrative.

P2.justification: The complexity tables gain memory information and separate algorithm variants. Earlier timing plots are reworked into v3 Figure 1, while new model and cache plots, an architecture diagram and numerical tables expand the presentation. The earlier FutureFill schematic is redrawn and relocated, and Figure 7 adds a multiscale execution diagram. Typography and page layout also change substantially.

R1.justification: v3 acknowledges independent Flash Inference work obtaining the same quasilinear bound and distinguishes FutureFill through its formulation, memory trade-offs and implementation (Section 1.1; Appendix C.1).
