It also positions exact inference against approximate cache compression and sparse attention, and adds FlashSTU and implementation-related references. Much of v1's related work is retained in Appendix C.

T1.justification: The periodic-cache runtime analysis is retained, but v3 adds the formal FutureFill decomposition in Proposition 1, the O(L log^2 L) runtime and O(L) additional-memory result in Theorem 3, and correctness arguments using binary decompositions in Appendix E. Prompt-generation and spectral-filtering corollaries are strengthened accordingly; the underlying spectral-filtering regret guarantee remains unchanged.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens both the theoretical contribution and its empirical support: it adds a quasilinear algorithm with correctness/runtime arguments and replaces v1's largely unsupported assertion of large-model benefits with accelerator measurements, ablations and uncertainty reporting for Epoched-FutureFill. Detailed implementation documentation further improves assessability. Reporting weaknesses remain, including conflicting baseline prefill times in Tables 2 and 6 (37.20 versus 32.70 seconds) and broad speedup wording despite short-sequence slowdowns. These defects qualify, but do not outweigh, the substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe FutureFill and are fully readable, including equations, figures and tables. v1 ends with references and has no appendix; v3 includes complete Appendices A–E. The substantial revision supports reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 Section 5 and Appendices A–B report original controlled timings, GPU model experiments, Transformer comparisons and sensitivity analyses.

before.justification: v1 Section 4.2 and Figures 3–4 report original CPU timing experiments comparing FutureFill with naive convolutional generation.

results.title: FutureFill: Fast Generation from Convolutional Sequence Models

C1.justification: The central claims of training-free visualization up to 100 frames, improved consistency, and better interactions remain. V2 explicitly elevates the curated long-story benchmark to a main contribution and removes v1's abstract-level characterization of the framework as computationally efficient, qualifying efficiency elsewhere.

C2.justification: V2 substantially expands explanations involving embedding convergence, content-adaptive attention, and suppression of irrelevant references. It adds interpretations of editing-model failures and explicit diversity and runtime limitations. Appendix F changes v1's conclusion that ten iterations are optimal to suggesting fewer than ten suffice, and discusses adaptive stopping and weighting as future work.

D1.justification: V2 documents Grounding-DINO cropping and first-occurrence reference selection for the existing metrics, identifies NVIDIA RTX A6000 hardware, and specifies StoryDiffusion's four reference frames. It updates code-access instructions to a repository and supplementary material. Most original hyperparameters and the pseudocode are retained, with their relocation alone constituting no reproducibility addition.

E1.justification: StorySalon, the twenty GPT-4o-generated 50/100-frame stories, and the 2,000 subject-consistency prompts are retained. V2 adds pose-conditioned visualization examples in Figure 9 and additional comic, film, and monochrome style scenarios in Appendix H.3, modestly broadening evaluation coverage.

E2.justification: V2 Table 1 adds IP-Adapter and IP-AdapterXL to the regular-length comparison. Table 2 adds FLUX.1.Kontext, Nano Banana, DALL·E 3, SEED-LLaMA, ConsiStory, and 1prompt1story to the long-story comparison. The original subject-consistent generation comparator set is retained.

E3.justification: V2 adds four-step LCM evaluation, pose-conditioned testing, embedding Jensen-Shannon divergence tracking, and full-story time/memory comparisons. The original model's 50-step sampling, guidance 7.5, and ten iterations remain unchanged. Appendix C also changes the reported human-evaluation rubric from five criteria to four by dropping image quality; this does not establish that the study was rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds attention maps and embedding-convergence analysis, four additional linear-weight ranges in Table 5, and sliding-window, random-reference, and mean-pooled aggregation ablations in Table 7. It also adds editing-model failure cases and a third-iteration result. The original GRCA-versus-CSA analysis is retained and expanded in Appendix A.5, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: V2 Section 4.1 newly states that experiments use a fixed random seed by default, while Appendix H.3 mentions examples spanning different seeds. Neither version supplies repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests; the added disclosure does not demonstrate increased replication.

E6.justification: The proposed models' main benchmark scores are unchanged, but v2 adds extensive comparator, variant, efficiency, and ablation results. AR-LDM's StorySalon CLIP-T/aCCS/aFID changes from 0.237/0.683/40.25 to 0.239/0.684/42.55 in Table 1. Human image-quality scores are removed from v1 Table 5's counterpart, v2 Table 8, while the remaining ratings are retained.

M1.justification: The original initialization, GRCA, and linearly weighted external iteration remain substantively unchanged. However, v2 Section 4.4 adds an SDXL-LCM Fast variant using four diffusion steps and a ControlNet variant accepting pose maps. These introduce substantial extensions to inference and conditioning, beyond the method's renaming.

P1.justification: V2 rewrites the abstract and substantial introduction and method prose, consistently distinguishes external iterations from diffusion steps, and adds an explicit contribution list. Related work is reorganized, pseudocode and implementation details move to the appendix, and dedicated variants, reproducibility, limitations, and disclosure sections reshape the narrative.

P2.justification: V2 adds attention, convergence, pose-control, metric-extraction, and editing-failure displays, and replaces the main long-story comparison with a different illustrated comparison. The original combined ablation table is split and extended, while the human-evaluation table loses its image-quality column. Numerous retained figures and tables are also relocated or reformatted.

R1.justification: The broad diffusion-model survey is replaced by substantially expanded story-visualization positioning, including DreamStory, StoryGPT-V, MovieDreamer, and interactive-generation literature. Appendix E expands subject-consistency coverage, while the introduction and Appendix D develop distinctions from IP-Adapter and reference-image editing models. These exceed citation or bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: Equations 1–4 retain the same mathematical procedure. The explicit linear-weight formula restates the existing schedule, and Appendix B explains the previously used evaluation metrics. The new convergence discussion is empirical interpretation, without added formal assumptions, theorems, derivations, or proofs.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens support for GRCA through controlled aggregation and weighting ablations and comparisons with relevant additional methods. Full-story timing and Fast-variant results expose the practical speed-quality tradeoff missing from v1's per-image efficiency analysis, while metric documentation improves transparency. These gains outweigh the removal of human image-quality ratings and unclear per-image versus per-story FLOP accounting in Table 6, although those issues limit the revision's quality.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same iterative story-visualization work, renamed from Story-Adapter to Story-Iter. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds baseline comparisons, variant evaluations, attention analyses, and further ablations.

before.justification: V1 reports original story-visualization and subject-consistency experiments, component ablations, computational measurements, and human evaluations in the main text and appendices.

results.title: Story-Iter: A Training-free Iterative Paradigm for Long Story Visualization

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central claims: explicit DiT scaling laws, compute-optimal model/data allocation, successful large-budget extrapolation, predictable generation quality and transfer, and inexpensive design assessment. The additional experiments principally support these existing contributions.

C2.justification: Section 4 corrects the cross-attention model-exponent interpretation from 'larger' to 'smaller,' matching Table 1's 0.54 versus 0.56. New Appendices I–J substantially expand applicability limits and explain why the simplified architecture comparison does not establish intrinsic conditioning-mechanism superiority. However, Appendix I's claim that all experiments are compute-limited conflicts with the new data-constrained ImageNet experiment in H.9.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents maintaining and saving model-EMA weights with coefficient 0.99 and supplies settings for added experiments. It drops v1's explicit identification of Euler as the image-generation sampler, although the 25-step, CFG-10 defaults remain in Appendix H.3. Most existing implementation details are retained.

E1.justification: Coverage expands beyond the original LAION-derived training data, COCO transfer evaluation, and JourneyDB ablations. v2 adds Flickr30k transfer, JourneyDB as an additional transfer target, data-constrained ImageNet experiments, and GenEval compositional-generation tasks (Appendices H.7, H.9, and H.10).

E2.justification: The in-context versus PixArt-style cross-attention comparison retains the same participants, as does the diffusion-formulation comparison in Table 5. Flux and SiT appear in separate scaling-law tests, rather than as added comparators in the retained comparisons.

E3.justification: v2 introduces GenEval and HPSv2.1/ImageReward evaluation, 512-by-512 training, model-EMA evaluation, and guidance/sampling-step controls across compute budgets. It also replaces v1's stated 1B-model learning-rate schedule of 1e-4, 3.16e-5, then 1e-5 with a constant 1e-4 description. This establishes a reported protocol revision, without establishing that the original experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: The original formulation, aspect-ratio, loss-smoothing, and sampling ablations remain. v2 substantially expands tests of scaling stability across guidance scales, sampling steps, model-weight averaging, architectures, resolution, and transfer domains. It also adds a sparse-versus-dense caption comparison and qualitative samples controlled by fixed prompts and seeds.

E5.justification: Appendix H.8 newly states that qualitative samples use fixed sampling seeds. Neither version reports repeated-training-run counts, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty across seeds; the addition is limited seed-control information.

E6.justification: The original fitted scaling equations and numerical entries in Tables 1 and 5 are retained. Figures 10–23 add extensive numerical and qualitative results, including additional architecture, transfer, ImageNet, GenEval, and preference-reward curves. The new caption experiment reports a FID scaling exponent of -0.216 for sparse captions versus -0.234 for the retained dense-caption setting.

M1.justification: The central rectified-flow velocity objective, transformer designs, isoFLOP optimization, and power-law fitting procedure are retained. Additional architecture and model-EMA experiments do not establish a redesign of the proposed method.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main narrative are retained. v2 creates dedicated scaling-metric subsections, moves diffusion-transformer background and limitations into appendices, clarifies 'vanilla in-context' terminology, and updates affiliations and publication information while adding acknowledgments and an LLM-use disclosure.

P2.justification: v2 adds Figures 10–23, including scaling comparisons, new evaluation curves, and a generated-image grid. Retained figures and tables receive panel labels, formatting changes, and relocation. The original guidance and sampling-step plots survive with their contents exchanged between Figures 8 and 9, leaving captions and textual references mismatched.

R1.justification: v2 adds Hu et al.'s statistical DiT theory, Fan et al.'s generative-model work, and references supporting the new datasets and evaluation metrics. Discussion of Flux and SD3/MMDiT expands architectural context, while the central novelty positioning and most related-work coverage remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The velocity objective, likelihood derivations, power-law formulation, and FLOP-counting mathematics are retained. v2 makes the loss's data expectation and minibatch indexing explicit and numbers more equations, without introducing a substantive new mathematical result or derivation.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for the paper's existing claims. Appendix H.6 directly tests the data-quality application that v1 illustrated mainly through architecture comparisons; additional transfer, ImageNet, compositional-alignment, preference-reward, and robustness experiments address important gaps in generality and generation-quality validation. Appendix J also limits architectural overgeneralization. These gains outweigh the learning-rate reporting ambiguity, swapped figure captions, and contradictory finite-data limitation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same scaling-law study. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched despite reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds architecture, dataset-transfer, caption-quality, ImageNet, GenEval, and preference-reward evaluations in Appendix H.

before.justification: v1 reports original compute-budget training sweeps, approximately 1B-parameter extrapolation experiments, architecture comparisons, and diffusion-formulation and sampling ablations.

results.title: Scaling Laws for Diffusion Transformers

C1.justification: The central claims remain that SimpleToM tests explicit and applied ToM across diverse everyday scenarios and exposes a substantial capability gap. v2 foregrounds scenario diversity and generic-intervention failures, but retains the successful task-specific combined intervention in Appendix F. This changes emphasis rather than the underlying claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations of human consistency, small-model judgment anomalies, and persona effects, plus a hypothesis involving backtracking or self-questioning for o1-preview (Appendices H, N, P). Appendices A–B also develop concrete deployment implications and explain the false-belief-only evaluation scope.

D1.justification: v1 already supplies dataset access, evaluation outputs, and detailed prompts. v2 additionally reports generation/inference code availability, documents added model identifiers and temperature requirements, and provides exact persona descriptions. Table 4 nevertheless lists the Qwen-2.5-14B full name as Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, leaving that identifier inconsistent.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same 1,147 stories, ten information-asymmetry scenarios, and three question types, with identical dataset statistics. The human study samples existing stories, while persona prompts change model conditions rather than the represented story domains or tasks.

E2.justification: Table 2 expands from ten to 21 named LLMs, adding models including GPT-5, DeepSeek-R1, GPT-4.5-preview, o1, o3-mini, and smaller Llama, Qwen, and Ministral models. Appendix H adds a human comparator. The original intervention comparison sets remain in Appendix F.

E3.justification: v2 introduces a human evaluation using five stories per scenario, totaling 50 stories and 150 responses; five persona conditions for two LLMs; and an additional high-reasoning-effort o1 configuration. It also specifies temperature exceptions for added reasoning models. The original full-dataset accuracy evaluation is retained.

E4.justification: Appendix P adds a systematic persona sensitivity study, Table 2 adds an o1 reasoning-effort comparison, and Appendix N quantifies Llama-3.1-8B's inconsistent behavior-versus-judgment answers. These extend the original prompt-variation and scenario analyses, which remain available.

E5.justification: v1 reports point estimates without uncertainty intervals. v2 adds 95% Wald intervals, paired task-gap bootstrap intervals and p-values using 10,000 resamples, and scenario-level intervals using 5,000 resamples (Appendix Q). These concern sampling uncertainty; they do not establish additional independent model runs.

E6.justification: Original Table 2 point estimates are retained, but substantial results are added for new models, personas, humans, and reasoning effort. Figure 10 reports human accuracies of 88%, 86%, and 70% on the sampled stories. A retained Llama-3.1-405B baseline entry changes from 58.3 to 58.2 in the reminder table (v1 Table 3; v2 Table 5).

M1.justification: v2 adds persona-conditioned inference by inserting role descriptions into system prompts (Appendix P). This is a limited prompting extension; benchmark construction, filtering, and the original mental-state reminder, system-prompt, chain-of-thought, and combined interventions remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The abstract, opening motivation, contribution list, intervention narrative, and conclusion are substantially rewritten. Detailed intervention discussion moves into Appendix F, while the appendices are reorganized and expanded with applications, psychological grounding, human evaluation, model interpretations, personas, and statistics.

P2.justification: v2 restructures Table 2 with uncertainty annotations and a reasoning-model block, creates a consolidated intervention Table 3, and relocates the original intervention tables. It adds human, persona, and statistical displays and scenario plots with error bars. Main-text Figure 5 excerpts an existing appendix example rather than introducing a new case.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands psychological grounding through Appendix D, connecting benchmark choices to work on explicit versus applied competence, perspective use, and conceptual versus procedural knowledge. It also adds research on social deployment failures and reasoning limitations. Publication updates to previously cited works are separate from these substantive additions.

T1.justification: Neither version develops formal mathematical theory or proofs. The new psychological framework in Appendix D is conceptual, while Appendix Q adds statistical estimation rather than new theoretical results or derivations.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of the central capability gap through newer-model evaluations, a human reference, persona sensitivity tests, and paired confidence intervals, addressing v1's lack of human calibration and uncertainty analysis. Reported code availability also helps reproducibility. The human comparison uses only 50 stories versus full-dataset model scores, and Table 12's chance-comparison p-values conflict with the stated positive-gap testing direction. These limitations constrain parts of the added evidence but do not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SimpleToM and retain the same benchmark and experimental core. The main text, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial expansion and reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains these experiments and adds evaluations of further LLMs, a human baseline, persona interventions, and statistical analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of ten LLMs, including task accuracies, scenario analyses, and prompting interventions in Tables 2–5.

results.title: SimpleToM: Exposing the Gap between Explicit ToM Inference and Implicit ToM Application in LLMs

C1.justification: The central claims of last-iterate Nash convergence and compatibility with existing optimization methods remain. The abstract and introduction expand the empirical contribution from Qwen2-1.5B to larger models, explicitly claiming controlled win rates above 60.2% and 56.8% for Llama-3 and Qwen2.5, respectively.

C2.justification: New Appendix L explicitly acknowledges that nonconvex LLM optimization lacks guarantees of achieving the required prox solutions and discusses unresolved convergence-rate limitations. Section 5.2 adds interpretations of post-training instability, capability retention, and benchmark-objective mismatch, including COMAL's failure to outperform Iter-IPO on Arena-Hard. These materially qualify practical applicability.

D1.justification: Appendix G adds actionable solver pseudocode, while Sections 5.1 and J document the new oracle identities, training schedules, regularization settings, reference-update intervals, and compute requirements. Conversely, v2 omits v1's code-and-trained-model access footnote and detailed hyperparameter-search reporting; this establishes lost documentation, not that the resources became unavailable.

E1.justification: v2 adds Tulu3 SFT training data and evaluation on GSM8K, MMLU, BBH, HumanEval, and Arena-Hard, substantially extending coverage to mathematical reasoning, knowledge, coding, and additional alignment tasks. UltraFeedback, AlpacaEval, UltraChat, and the original synthetic game remain represented.

E2.justification: The evaluated comparison methods remain the initial/SFT policy, DPO, IPO, iterative IPO, and INPO for LLMs, and MD, iterative DPO, iterative IPO, SPPO, and INPO for synthetic experiments. Iter-IPO-L is a regularization configuration; newly described GRPO, DRO, and REBEL integrations are not new empirical comparators.

E3.justification: v2 adds 7B/8B experiments with 18 training iterations, a Skywork/ArmoRM mixture preference oracle, one-epoch cosine-schedule training, and reference updates every six iterations. It also introduces GPT-4 evaluations and best-versus-final checkpoint comparisons for the new experiments. The original 42-iteration Qwen2-1.5B protocol remains in Appendix K rather than being replaced.

E4.justification: v2 extends regularization-sensitivity testing to iterative IPO on Llama-3, comparing strengths 0.002 and 0.1 to examine training collapse and stability. The original synthetic and output-length analyses remain, but v1's detailed DPO/IPO hyperparameter sweep in Appendix G and Table 3 is omitted.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates and training trajectories without repeated-run or seed counts, confidence intervals, error bars, or formal significance tests. The additional results retain the same uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results in Tables 1–3 and Figure 2: COMAL beats Iter-IPO by win rates of 60.25% on Llama-3 and 56.89% on Qwen2.5, while standard-benchmark rankings are mixed. These are new experimental settings, not improvements to the original scores. v1 Tables 2 and 4 are numerically preserved as v2 Tables 5 and 6; the hyperparameter-sweep results are removed.

M1.justification: The COMAL outer loop and INPO solver remain unchanged. Appendix G.1 adds a GRPO-based instantiation using group-sampled win-rate rewards and relative advantages. The expanded SPPO/DRO/REBEL pseudocode largely documents integrations already described generically in v1.

P1.justification: The introduction and method motivation are substantially rewritten and expanded. Related work, Bradley-Terry background, prox details, detailed synthetic discussion, and the original small-model experiments move into reorganized appendices. This is extensive narrative restructuring beyond the addition of new scientific content.

P2.justification: v2 adds an overview figure, larger-model training plots, and three main results tables; it redraws and relocates existing synthetic figures and moves the original LLM displays into Appendix K. The hyperparameter table disappears. The property comparison also loses its robust-alignment column and incorrectly merges DPO/IPO and SPPO/Nash-MD into shared rows.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning against Magnetic Preference Optimization and concurrent or subsequent extragradient, Mirror-Prox, and optimistic alignment methods. It distinguishes its approximate-solver guarantee from exact-solver assumptions and connects COMAL to GRPO and clairvoyant prox methods. The INPO citation's change from 2024 to 2025b is a publication update to the same work.

T1.justification: The full-support assumption, Theorems 1–3, and exact- and approximate-solver convergence proofs are retained from v1. Section 3.2 newly states that choosing tau = O(epsilon) yields an epsilon-approximate equilibrium in O-tilde(1/epsilon squared) iterations. This is a limited additional rate statement, not a new approximate-solver convergence proof.

improvement.justification: v1's practical validation relied on one 1.5B model and its training oracle. v2 substantially strengthens validation through two larger models, capability-retention tests, and GPT-4 evaluations that reveal both transfer and limits to superiority. Appendix L also clarifies the theory-to-practice gap. These address important evidential and qualification gaps, outweighing the omitted access information and hyperparameter results and the misleading merged rows in Table 4.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same COMAL research, with matching core algorithms, convergence proofs, and original experiments. All pages, including appendices, are readable, and relocated material can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 retains the original experiments in Appendices I and K and adds Llama-3-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B experiments, including preference comparisons and standard-benchmark results.

before.justification: v1 reports original three-action preference-game simulations and Qwen2-1.5B fine-tuning experiments, including training trajectories, pairwise comparisons, and hyperparameter-search results.

results.title: COMAL: A Convergent Meta-Algorithm for Aligning LLMs with General Preferences

C1.justification: The central contribution remains fast, entirely latent-space assimilation combining LDNets, historical LSTM observations and joint state/parameter estimation. v2 adds reconstruction-architecture improvements to its explicit contribution claims and advertises handling irregularly located observations. These extend the retained contribution without redefining its central purpose.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantial applicability qualifications and mechanism explanations: different sensor sets require encoder retraining, rapidly varying parameters require an additional dynamics model, and atmospheric parameter recovery is difficult because observations weakly constrain forcing. Appendices E–G discuss distribution-shift degradation, latent-dimension failure modes, surrogate-error propagation and why filtering improves noisy LSTM reconstructions. Appendix C.2 additionally discusses offline training costs versus online savings.

D1.justification: v2 substantially extends v1's training appendix with a repository pointer for data generation, training and inference; fine-tuning settings of 1,000 epochs at learning rate 0.0001; the diffusion parameter value 0.01; and explicit latent-noise estimation. It also documents atmospheric data generation, parallel simulation hardware and LDNet training times on an RTX A6000 (Appendices A–C and E.1).

E1.justification: v2 adds a spherical atmospheric simulation initialized from ERA5, alongside the retained Kolmogorov and shallow-water examples. It also evaluates irregular sensor locations, non-Gaussian and heteroskedastic observations, and initial conditions outside the training region. The shallow-water example is renamed tsunami modeling, with a revised reported equation and quarter-domain initial-position sampling.

E2.justification: v1 primarily compares assimilation against EnSF and Latent-EnSF. v2 adds LETKF, Latent-EnSF-dyn and, for tsunami modeling, 4DEnVar (Figure 4); atmospheric LETKF divergence is explicitly reported. Surrogate comparisons add VAE-dyn and original LDNet (Table 1), while Appendix G introduces CNN-encoder and LSTM-only controls.

E3.justification: Reported configurations and budgets change for retained examples: the tsunami reconstruction network changes from 7 layers of width 180 to 10 layers of width 300, and LSTM training changes from 30,000 epochs to 20,000 for tsunami and 75,000 for Kolmogorov (training tables). v2 also introduces atmospheric evaluation settings, controlled sensitivity protocols and CRPS evaluation in Appendix F.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's noise-level tests, smoothness comparisons and reconstruction retraining analysis, v2 adds temporal-interpolation testing, distribution-shift and structured-noise experiments, and sensitivity to latent dimension, ensemble size, training duration, observation density and latent-noise misspecification. Appendix G isolates reconstruction architecture, encoder choice, joint versus separate training, and the benefit of filtering beyond direct LSTM reconstruction.

E5.justification: v1 provides error curves without reported repeated-experiment counts or uncertainty bands. v2 reports means and uncertainty across 20 different ground-truth trajectories in Appendices E.4–E.5 and adds uncertainty displays in comparison and ablation figures. Appendix E.1 specifies a standard-deviation estimator for latent observation noise. This establishes expanded statistical reporting, not an explicit increase over v1's unknown run count.

E6.justification: v1 Section 4.2 reports final LDNet reconstruction errors of 1.2% for shallow water and 2.0% for Kolmogorov; v2 Table 1 reports 1.68% and 1.23%, respectively, under revised configurations. v2 adds a 6.56% atmospheric surrogate error, approximately 5% atmospheric assimilation error with 10% observation noise, numerous new baseline and ablation outcomes, and revised timings. These are updated and expanded results, not controlled same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: v2 introduces residual reconstruction blocks and trainable Fourier coordinate encoding, materially extending v1's plain MLP reconstruction architecture (Section 3.1; Appendix G.1). The shifted initialization, two-stage LDNet training, historical LSTM encoder and latent EnSF assimilation loop were already present in v1.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, methodology and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten and condensed. v2 introduces an explicit contribution list, moves detailed filtering background and simulation specifications into appendices, relocates related work from the introduction to Section 5, and reorganizes the supplement into Appendices A–H. This substantially changes the document's narrative structure.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn from a full-page vertical pipeline into a compact horizontal framework. Reconstruction and latent-trajectory plots are reorganized, full-field visualizations move to Appendix H and gain irregular-observation rows, and new atmospheric maps, uncertainty bands and diagnostic plots are introduced. Comparison and training tables gain methods, datasets and settings, alongside a changed document template.

R1.justification: The introduction and expanded Section 5 position LD-EnSF against additional research families and specific methods, including FlowDAS, DiffDA, deep Bayesian filtering, Koopman-based assimilation and learned variational systems such as Tensor-Var, 4DVarNets and LEVDA. These additions include substantive distinctions concerning latent dynamics, score training and filtering architecture, beyond bibliographic updates to retained references.

T1.justification: Most filtering mathematics is retained and relocated to Appendix A, but v2 omits v1's explicit prior-score integral and normalized-weight derivation in Equations 11–12. It adds the Fourier-feature definition and atmospheric model equations, and revises the shallow-water equation to include Coriolis forcing. Neither version supplies a convergence theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: v1's evidence rests mainly on two examples and EnSF-family comparisons. v2 substantially strengthens validation through LETKF/4DEnVar comparisons, component-isolating ablations, distribution-shift and sensitivity tests, and uncertainty reporting across 20 trajectories. The atmospheric example and expanded implementation documentation further improve applicability and reproducibility. These additions resolve important validation gaps. Unclear break-even accounting in Appendix C.2 and conflicting tsunami initial-region descriptions limit individual conclusions, but do not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical support and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LD-EnSF work. The complete main texts and appendices are readable, including equations, tables and figures. Renamed shallow-water/tsunami experiments and relocated background, training details and visualizations can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 Section 4 and Appendices D–H report original results for three dynamical systems, including atmospheric simulations, additional comparisons, robustness tests and component ablations.

before.justification: v1 Section 4 reports original shallow-water and Kolmogorov-flow experiments, including surrogate accuracy, assimilation results, noise sensitivity and computational timings.

results.title: LD-EnSF: Synergizing Latent Dynamics with Ensemble Score Filters for Fast Data Assimilation with Sparse Observations

C1.justification: V2 makes applicability across world-model backbones and segmentation extractors an explicit contribution. It also narrows the novelty wording from successful object-centric learning on these games to integrating few-shot pretrained segmentation into world models. The central sample-efficiency claims for Atari and Hollow Knight remain.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations for Cutie's advantage over SAM2 features, the effects of omitting particular objects, and the inadequacy of unconditional SAM segmentation. Atari subgroup interpretation shifts toward detection completeness. It also shortens the limitations and removes v1 Appendix B's explanation that useful latent distinctions may support control despite poor pixel reconstruction.

D1.justification: V2 newly identifies the Cutie and SAM2 checkpoints, explains SAM2 integration, specifies six annotations for Meta-world, and supplies hardware, training-time, and component-latency information. It adds a project-page link without establishing its contents locally. The shared hyperparameter table remains, but v1's explicit selection of Cutie's first eight foreground features is no longer documented.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same 26 Atari games, six Hollow Knight bosses, and four Meta-world tasks. Meta-world evaluation moves from v1 Appendix J to v2 Section 5.3. Added object-omission and computational tests vary configurations within retained coverage.

E2.justification: V2 Table 1 adds SAM2-OC-STORM and Cutie-OC-DreamerV3 comparisons and extends the existing mask-based, FOCUS-like comparison across Atari. Its external comparison adds SPR, TWM, and Delta-IRIS. The published STORM column from v1 Table 1 disappears, while the lightweight STORM* baseline survives under the name STORM.

E3.justification: V2 expands the controlled backbone/extractor comparisons and introduces systematic object-omission and runtime-measurement protocols, including a synthetic ten-object timing configuration. It also replaces v1's 15/11-game representability partition with a 13/13-game detection-completeness partition. The retained experiments preserve their principal training budgets, evaluation episode counts, and shared hyperparameters.

E4.justification: V2 adds targeted annotation-object removal, unconditional SAM segmentation examples, computational scaling analyses, and comparisons involving SAM2 features. Existing random feature-zeroing, annotation-count, policy-network, reward-shaping, and Meta-world studies are retained or moved. The Breakout panel from the input-representation ablation and the STORM latent-probability visualization are removed.

E5.justification: V2 Figure 4a omits v1 Figure 4's explicit statement that curves show five-seed means and standard deviations. The main five-seed Atari and three-seed Hollow Knight reporting remains. This is a loss of reporting detail, not evidence that run counts changed.

E6.justification: V2 adds extensive comparison and runtime results, including HNS means of 119.4% for Cutie-OC-DreamerV3 versus 106.6% for lightweight DreamerV3, and 124.6% for SAM2-OC-STORM. It also adds object-omission findings and revises external baseline entries, including IRIS CrazyClimber from 59234 to 59324. Core OC-STORM Atari aggregates and Hollow Knight scores remain unchanged; revised subgroup scores use different group definitions.

M1.justification: V1 uses Cutie with the STORM backbone and explicitly leaves SAM2 integration to future work. V2 adds SAM2 features with occlusion-based feature zeroing and a DreamerV3 adaptation incorporating spatial attention into recurrent dynamics (Sections 3.1–3.3 and Appendix G). These substantially extend the supported procedures; the original Cutie/STORM architecture and losses remain.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and method exposition are extensively rewritten. Related work moves behind the experiments, detailed architecture moves into an appendix, and existing continuous-control and segmentation-failure studies enter the main analysis. Author information, affiliations, acknowledgements, and an LLM-use disclosure also change.

P2.justification: V2 introduces a pipeline overview combined with reused reconstruction examples, restructures the Atari tables, and adds runtime tables and analysis figures. The detailed architecture and Hollow Knight results table move to appendices, while training curves move into the main text. Several existing figures are merged or resized, and the standalone Cutie diagram and latent-probability panels disappear.

R1.justification: V2 adds citations including Schwarzer et al. (2021) and Feng et al. (2026), while removing background references including Spelke (1990) and Zhang et al. (2021). SAM2 changes from a prospective alternative to an evaluated component. The principal positioning against FOCUS and the two-stage/end-to-end taxonomy remain.

T1.justification: V2 Section 2 adds an explicit finite-horizon MDP definition and discounted expected-return objective. The substantive VAE, KL-loss, actor-critic, and action-factorization mathematics is retained in the reorganized appendices; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: V1 evaluates the proposed approach principally through Cutie/STORM and lacks computational measurements. V2's controlled alternative-backbone/extractor comparisons, targeted object-omission study, and runtime breakdown substantially strengthen evidence about generality, failure conditions, and practical cost. These gains improve validation despite unchanged headline OC-STORM scores. Lost feature-selection detail, uncertainty-caption information, and reconstruction caveats weaken documentation, but do not outweigh the stronger empirical basis.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe OC-STORM. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite the changed title and substantial reorganization.

after.justification: V2 retains original reinforcement-learning results and reports additional model comparisons, object-omission experiments, and computational measurements.

before.justification: V1 reports original Atari and Hollow Knight experiments, with additional Meta-world results and ablations in its appendices.

results.title: Object-Centric World Models from Few-Shot Annotations for Sample-Efficient Reinforcement Learning

C1.justification: v1 emphasizes similarly interpretable latents and suggests SAEs provide limited insight into learned computation. v2 substantially narrows the central claim to the insufficiency of aggregate evaluation metrics, qualifies similarity as occurring under certain conditions, and explicitly allows trained-model SAEs to recover meaningful computational features.

C2.justification: v2 adds the interpretation that SAEs may faithfully describe simple computation in random networks and explains how aggregate scores obscure feature-level differences (Introduction and Appendix H). Its new Limitations section identifies dependence on Pythia, RedPajama-V2 and one explanation model, while explicitly limiting conclusions about SAE capabilities.

D1.justification: Appendix K newly discloses use of a single NVIDIA A100 80GB GPU and approximate runtimes by model and variant, totaling 435 hours for final experiments, with preliminary/failed experiments estimated to cost roughly as much. Existing toy implementation and training details are retained.

E1.justification: v2 actually evaluates detection classification alongside fuzzing: the evaluator identifies examples containing activating tokens, rather than judging marked tokens (Section 3 and Appendix B). The underlying RedPajama, Pythia, GloVe and synthetic-data coverage is retained.

E2.justification: The evaluated transformer comparisons retain Trained, Step-0, re-randomized variants including/excluding embeddings, and the inconsistent Gaussian-embedding Control. Toy experiments retain Gaussian-input controls; newly discussed prior methods are not added as evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: The default 100M-token, R=64, k=32 setup remains, but substantial additional protocols are evaluated. These include 1B-token training for Pythia-70M/410M, 1M- and 1B-token training for Pythia-1B, R=2 with k=4 or 256, and detection scoring (Appendices B–D and G).

E4.justification: v2 retains the earlier Pythia-160M sweep and toy analyses, while adding tests of training-data sufficiency, severe undertraining and extreme SAE capacity/sparsity settings. Appendix H adds per-latent entropy-versus-interpretability analysis, and Appendix L adds 80 detailed feature dashboards beyond the retained examples.

E5.justification: v2 adds uncertainty plots over five random seeds for Pythia-70M (Appendix E), extending uncertainty reporting beyond v1's toy experiments. The toy study's ten-seed count remains, but v1 Figure 6's explicit SEM description is omitted from v2 Figure 5; the new transformer error-bar statistic is also unspecified.

E6.justification: v2 adds detection results across the Pythia sizes and substantial results from the new budget, hyperparameter and feature analyses. Figure 19 shows that reduced reconstruction quality can coexist with similar auto-interpretability scores; Figure 20 reveals high-entropy, high-scoring latents in trained models. These extend v1's evidence rather than establish a same-setting performance improvement.

M1.justification: The TopK SAE procedure, transformer randomization constructions, and ReLU/L1 toy autoencoders remain unchanged. Additional scoring procedures and hyperparameter experiments do not introduce a new SAE algorithm or architecture.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, substantial introductory passages and conclusion are rewritten around evaluation-metric validity. Results subsections become paragraph headings, a dedicated Limitations section is introduced, and the appendices are reorganized into a more extensive topical structure.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one, ROC plots are redrawn with numerical AUC legends, and the summary figure gains a detection row. The 410M ROC display moves to the appendix, the main Pareto figures are merged, and new analysis plots, a compute table and activation-colored dashboards are added.

R1.justification: v2 adds focused positioning against Karvonen et al.'s board-game findings and Bricken et al.'s random one-layer transformer results, plus Adebayo et al.'s randomization sanity checks and several newer references. Most of the earlier related-work framework remains.

T1.justification: The Lomax/Gaussian construction, linear-transformation argument for preserving superposition, and synthetic-data generation mathematics are retained. Moving displayed equations inline and relocating Appendix C to Appendix I do not change the mathematical substance.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially improves claim calibration and empirical support. It replaces v1's broader implications about SAE limitations with a more defensible conclusion about aggregate metrics, supported by training-budget and capacity controls, detection evaluation and feature-level analysis. Explicit limitations and compute disclosure further improve assessability. Uncertainty reporting remains incompletely specified, but the gains address important weaknesses in the earlier argument.

A1.justification: The PDFs describe the same Pythia/SAE study despite the changed title. Their main text, equations, figures and appendices are readable and support reliable matching across versions.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds detection scoring, training-budget and hyperparameter experiments, seed-based uncertainty plots, and feature-level analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original SAE experiments on trained and randomized Pythia models, feature analyses, and toy-model and embedding experiments.

results.title: Automated Interpretability Metrics Do Not Distinguish Trained and Random Transformers

C1.justification: The efficient-selection and 8.9×–11.6× savings claims remain. However, v2 replaces the abstract's claim of discovering VLMs outperforming state-of-the-art counterparts with approximately 69% higher average weighted Kendall correlation than an existing selector, making comparative ranking quality a headline contribution. It also removes the explicit first-time problem-formulation claim.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations of task-dependent encoder/LLM importance, persistent component differences after fine-tuning, distribution-shift applicability and less stable predictions for smaller models. Appendix E expands projector and similarity-metric applicability discussions and explicitly qualifies top-1 guarantees and hyperparameter sensitivity, beyond v1's model-size and multiple-request limitations.

D1.justification: v2 adds Cornstarch implementation information, CKA batch sizes and dataset-pass counts, baseline feature/label encoding procedures, and Q-former checkpoint details. Most original training and search settings remain. A repository link is newly provided, although the reproducibility statement still promises future code release.

E1.justification: v2 retains the LLaVA-1.5 alignment data and all six original evaluation benchmarks, adding MMMU for multidisciplinary multimodal understanding and reasoning. The other new experiments predominantly reuse existing task coverage with different training or model settings.

E2.justification: v1 evaluates against grid search and reports a fixed CLIP-Vicuna reference. v2 adds actual comparisons with EMMS, LogME, LEEP and NLEEP under matched compute budgets in Table 3 and without alignment in Table 8. LogME's citation in v1 was not an evaluated comparison.

E3.justification: v2 introduces equal-total-budget baseline evaluation, target-specific fine-tuning of four combinations on three datasets, smaller LLM configurations, unaligned controls and Q-former experiments using pretrained projectors and 20% of the alignment data. These are new experimental designs; the original main training defaults are largely retained.

E4.justification: New analyses examine persistence of model differences after fine-tuning, vision-encoder versus LLM contributions, smaller-model robustness, removal of alignment/warmup, Q-former compatibility and clustering overhead. The original CKA validation, scaling curves, component ablations and GQA sensitivity analysis are retained or relocated, not newly added.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-seed variability, confidence intervals or significance tests. The 12 fine-tuning runs in v2 Appendix A represent four model combinations across three tasks, not repeated trials for uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: The original six-task top-1 scores and search times remain unchanged. New results include MMMU at 36.6% with 503 GPU hours and 10.8× speedup, comparative ranking scores such as ScienceQA's 0.960 for Mordal versus 0.770 for EMMS, and the new appendix experiments. These expand reported evidence rather than demonstrate improved performance under the original settings.

M1.justification: The core CKA clustering, successive halving and scaling-prediction procedures remain unchanged. Appendix D.4 adds a zero-warmup variant described as using similarity-based inter-/intra-cluster evaluation without alignment, although its ranking mechanics are underspecified. This is a limited procedural extension.

P1.justification: The introduction, existing-solutions discussion, evaluation narrative and conclusion are substantially revised. CKA validation moves into method motivation, appendix sensitivity analysis becomes Section 4.4, and the appendices are reorganized and expanded. Ethics, reproducibility and LLM-usage statements are added.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to predominantly single-column layout. Existing evaluation diagrams and result plots are merged, recolored and rearranged; the CKA table and heatmaps become one figure. New architecture diagrams, baseline tables and appendix displays substantially change the visual presentation beyond renumbering.

R1.justification: v2 substantially develops positioning against transferability selectors, including newly cited EMMS, LEEP and NLEEP, and distinguishes CLIP-based, encoder-decoder and LLM-based VLM selection. It also adds literature on CCA alternatives, projector architectures and fine-tuning behavior, while dropping the explicit first-time novelty assertion.

T1.justification: The CKA/HSIC, scaling-law and ranking equations remain unchanged. Appendix E adds mathematical justification for preferring CKA: quadratic covariance-matrix costs and a cited degeneracy result for transformation-invariant similarity measures when representation width exceeds sample count. No new original theorem or proof is supplied.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses an important weakness of v1: reliance on grid search without evaluated competing selectors. Budget-matched comparisons in Table 3 substantiate the approximately 69% gain in mean weighted correlation over EMMS, while new fine-tuning, scale and projector analyses strengthen scrutiny of applicability. These gains outweigh remaining weaknesses: absent statistical uncertainty, an underspecified training-free variant and broad top-1 wording despite the retained ChartQA miss.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Mordal framework. Their main texts, equations, algorithms, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across substantial reformatting and relocation.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds baseline comparisons, MMMU evaluation, task-specific fine-tuning, smaller-model experiments and alignment/projector analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original six-benchmark model-selection results, GPU search costs, ranking comparisons, component ablations and appendix sensitivity analyses.

results.title: Mordal: Automated Pretrained Model Selection for Vision Language Models

C1.justification: V1 acknowledges lower utility than RHO and suggests further tuning. V2 asserts full preservation of loss-only filtering's utility and presents a specialized attention backward kernel as an explicit algorithmic contribution. Its headline efficiency claims also concern 50% filtering and models up to 40B, replacing the earlier small-model, 40%-filtering claims.

C2.justification: V1's explanation of utility loss through reduced gradients and unsuitable hyperparameters is removed. V2 explains strawman non-convergence through damaged query gradients, discusses model-size-dependent graph-update overhead, and introduces MoE load-balancing and long-context forward-filtering considerations. The reference-model cost caveat and compression/n-gram discussion disappear; most distributed-communication reasoning survives in Appendix D.

D1.justification: V2 adds a code-hosting statement, identifies FlashAttention plus a cuDNN attention-bias kernel, and documents LoRA rank 64/projections, updated software and H20 hardware. It newly specifies two warmup iterations but omits v1's explicit 15B-token, one-epoch training budget. Most graph-generation code and integration instructions are retained in Appendices B-C rather than newly supplied.

E1.justification: Both retain OpenWebMath mathematical adaptation and the same nine downstream benchmarks, including GSM8K, MATH and MAWPS. No additional dataset, domain or downstream task is reported. Larger models, alternate reference models, tensor parallelism and LoRA change configurations within the retained coverage.

E2.justification: RHO, renamed loss-only filtering, is removed from the downstream accuracy and timing tables and the context-length comparison. It remains in v2's new convergence comparisons, which also introduce a naive activation-filtering strawman in Figure 4(a). The filtering-ratio comparison switches its reference from RHO to regular training, substantially revising the principal comparisons.

E3.justification: Main comparisons change from 40% to 50% token filtering. V2 drops Phi-1.5 and adds configurations up to 40B parameters, four-GPU data parallelism, tensor parallelism and single-GPU LoRA. Timing changes from a 512-sample iteration to processing one million tokens; Qwen2.5-1.5B context changes from 3K to 2K. The largest models use an additional H20/NVLink testbed.

E4.justification: V2 Figure 4 adds convergence tests under two reference-model choices and tests whether naive activation filtering causes failure. V1's n-gram versus transformer correlation/token-overlap analysis and operator-overhead sensitivity plot are removed. Context-length and filtering-ratio analyses remain but are revised, including different model configurations and a filtering-ratio sweep ending at 60% instead of 70%.

E5.justification: Both average efficiency measurements over ten iterations. Neither reports independent training-run counts, experimental seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests or uncertainty bands. V2's newly stated warmup procedure does not change uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: V1 Table 2's 40%-filtering result, averaging 20.7, is replaced by v2 Table 1's 50%-filtering result averaging 27.3; the regular-training average remains 17.8. V2 adds convergence findings and system results reaching 49.9% backward and 34.7% total time reductions. Old timing entries, full-training day estimates and n-gram results disappear. Changed methods and settings prevent interpreting these as matched-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: V1 Section 3.1 filters softmax activations, or Q/K activations for FlashAttention. V2 Section 4.1 introduces separate backward computations: key/value gradients use retained-token activations, while query gradients also incorporate discarded-token key/value contributions. This substantively changes gradient computation to avoid interference. The dimension-reduced GEMM and automatic graph-update mechanisms are retained.

P1.justification: Beyond the title and system rename, v2 extensively rewrites the motivation and attention explanation, separates observations from preliminary material, moves related work forward and places discussion after evaluation. Much of v1's graph-update, implementation and communication discussion moves into Appendices B-D, substantially reorganizing the narrative.

P2.justification: V2 changes the document from two columns to one, combines v1 Figures 3-4 into Figure 2, adds convergence plots and redesigns the efficiency plots. Result tables change comparator rows and columns, including removal of the full-training-time column. Several illustrations and analysis plots disappear, while graph attributes, implementation diagrams and code listings move to appendices.

R1.justification: V2 Section 2.2 substantially expands data-selection and parameter-efficient training coverage, adding works such as DoReMi, QuRating, RegMix, QLoRA and Compacter. It emphasizes model-adaptive token selection and complementarity with parameter-efficient methods, whereas v1 mainly describes parameter reduction as an alternative that may harm utility. Several earlier freezing/pruning references are removed.

T1.justification: V2 Section 4.1 replaces v1's shared activation-filtering rationale with distinct sparsity arguments for query versus key/value gradients. Equations 3-4 partition retained and discarded activations and derive their separate gradient contributions. This substantially revises the mathematical justification underlying the method; the token-selection objective remains unchanged.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses an important weakness in v1's activation-filtering procedure with an explicit split-gradient kernel and targeted convergence evidence, rather than leaving utility loss to future tuning. Actual tensor-parallel, LoRA and large-model measurements substantially strengthen practical validation. Removing the direct RHO downstream comparison and reference-model cost discussion weakens support for complete utility preservation and total-cost claims, but these reporting losses do not outweigh the gains in the central method and its validation.

A1.justification: The PDFs describe successive versions of the same token-filtering system, renamed from Collider to CENTRIFUGE. Both are readable, including equations, figures and tables. V1 has no appendix; v2's Appendices A-D were included in the comparison.

after.justification: V2 reports original downstream-task results, convergence experiments and efficiency measurements across model sizes and training configurations in Tables 1-2 and Figures 4-5.

before.justification: V1 reports original downstream-task results, training-time measurements, sensitivity experiments and an n-gram reference-model analysis, including Tables 2-3 and Figures 9 and 11-13.

results.title: Unlocking Full Efficiency of Token Filtering in Large Language Model Training

C1.justification: The central contribution and qualitative superiority claim remain. The abstract and introduction reduce the advertised maximum worst-language/average error reductions from 65.9%/47.7% to 47.1%/32.9%. The conclusion also broadens suggested applicability from other sequence tasks to settings with group-level losses, while presenting these extensions as possibilities.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive explanations of normalization's effects on relative gradients, CER–WER disagreement, batch-duration sensitivity, and scalability tradeoffs. It newly interprets statistical tests as showing no significant best-language degradation. Conversely, the relocated impact statement removes v1's specific warning that CER may not reflect transcript usefulness, although general deployment cautions remain.

D1.justification: v3 supplies selected hyperparameters, the learning rate of 10^-4, per-set batch durations, A6000 hardware, training times, and an approximate overall compute budget. These substantially expand reproducibility information. Its introduction supplies a repository link and states that code and models are public, replacing v1's release promise, although Appendix B still contains future-release wording.

E1.justification: The original five six-language sets and their balanced/unbalanced coverage remain. v3 adds an 18-language evaluation under both data regimes, including Bashkort, Burmese, French, Guarani, and Swati, which were absent from v1's evaluated sets (Appendix H, Table 17). This substantially extends joint multilingual coverage within the same ASR benchmark.

E2.justification: The main comparator identities remain the CTC baseline and group DRO, abbreviated Base and GDRO in v3. Appendix G, Table 16 additionally evaluates frame-normalized and target-normalized group DRO alternatives. v1 mentions unsuccessful normalization experiments but does not report these comparator results.

E3.justification: v3 Section 4 explicitly adds length-matched batching to the stated baseline recipe while retaining the original sampler for group DRO. New evaluation designs include WER scoring on set 4 and a 23-versus-46-second batch-duration comparison on set 5. The main data splits, 40-epoch budget, and 16-batch gradient accumulation remain; the PDFs do not identify which earlier experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained component ablation and XLS-R group-weight analysis, v3 adds normalization comparisons, batch-duration sensitivity, four-seed robustness, best-language tradeoff analysis, and scalability tests. Additional MMS weight trajectories test whether the stability finding extends across models and language sets (Appendices F–H).

E5.justification: v1 provides performance point estimates without run-count or performance-uncertainty reporting; its standard deviations describe dataset statistics. v3 Table 15 reports four-seed means, standard deviations, differences, and win counts for sets 1 and 3. Appendix F.5 additionally introduces paired t-tests and p-values for best-language comparisons across settings.

E6.justification: Main results change substantially: balanced set 1 XLS-R baseline/CTC-DRO worst-language CER changes from 187.9/64.0 in v1 Table 2 to 64.9/57.6 in v3 Table 1. These revised results do not establish a controlled cross-version performance gain given the differing procedure descriptions. Numerous results are added, including Table 15's worse mean worst-language CER for set 3 XLS-R with CTC-DRO: 34.7 versus baseline 33.2.

M1.justification: The core length-matched batching and smoothed group-weight update remain. However, line 21 changes from a weighted average batch loss in v1 Algorithm 2 to a weighted sum in v3 Algorithm 1, removing division by batch size. This changes the stated loss used for model-parameter updates; the PDFs do not establish whether it corrects documentation or changes implementation.

P1.justification: The main section sequence remains, but supporting material is substantially reorganized: the group DRO algorithm, dataset overview, CER definition, and impact statement move into dedicated appendices. The objective/update exposition is reordered, motivation and related-work prose expand, and the former compact appendices become a structured development-results, test-results, and analysis narrative.

P2.justification: v3 changes the main text from two columns to one, rearranges retained tables into side-by-side blocks, and adds hyperparameter columns to the main result tables. It retains the original plots while adding two MMS weight-trajectory figures and numerous development, robustness, normalization, scaling, and timing tables. These are substantial display and layout changes beyond numerical updates.

R1.justification: v3 substantially expands positioning through comparisons with auxiliary CTC objectives, conditional adapters, other DRO variants, and reinforcement-learning approaches, citing Chen et al. (2023), Lu et al. (2024), Lokhande et al. (2022), and Tjandra et al. (2018). It also adds motivation concerning CTC versus autoregressive ASR. The original first-successful-robust-optimization novelty claim remains.

T1.justification: v3 Section 3.2 extends the existing Lagrangian argument rather than introducing a new theory. It replaces v1's abbreviated proportionality step with equalities, explicitly assumes positive group weights, invokes complementary slackness, and derives the normalized interior solution in Equations 14–17. This is a substantive but localized mathematical revision.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens evidence for the method's reliability and limits: normalization comparisons, batch-duration tests, four-seed results, broader language coverage, and measured training costs address questions left unresolved by v1's basic comparisons and ablations. Reproducibility details also improve considerably. The added evidence exposes mixed outcomes, including the set 3 XLS-R seed reversal. Some overstatement remains—the conclusion still describes LID improvements in almost all cases despite Section 5 reporting seven of fourteen—but the gains in evaluability and empirical support outweigh these residual weaknesses.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CTC-DRO research, with readable text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices. Content can be matched across relocation and renumbering. Differences in reported experimental settings require caution when comparing scores directly.

after.justification: v3 reports original ASR results, including revised main comparisons and additional normalization, batch-duration, four-seed, WER, and 18-language experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original multilingual ASR experiments with MMS and XLS-R, including balanced and unbalanced training, component ablations, and language-specific appendix results.

results.title: CTC-DRO: Robust Optimization for Reducing Language Disparities in Speech Recognition

C1.justification: v1's principal claims concern granularity-aware representation and task-agnostic generative modeling. v2 retains these while extending its headline claims to classification with minimal adaptation, model/data scaling behavior, and cost-effective industrial applicability. These materially broaden the claimed capabilities and contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations of scaling, transfer and computational efficiency, including the qualification that widening shallow models may not help. Appendix B.5 newly limits established applicability to clearer periodic/trend structure and identifies unresolved robustness on noisy or irregular series. It also discusses biased anomaly metrics while retaining v1's benchmark-comparability concerns.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-repository link, Algorithm 1, tensor dimensions, and explicit tail-masking probability and fraction, both 0.3. It also documents classification and profiling details. The original optimizer, training budget, backbone configuration and six-A100 training setup remain unchanged; these are principally additions to documentation.

E1.justification: v2 adds classification on ten UEA datasets, forecasting on PhotoVoltaic and Lead-to-cash data, and anomaly detection on TSB-AD-U. These substantially broaden task and data coverage beyond v1's generative benchmarks. GIFT/GIFT-Eval appears only as future work.

E2.justification: The original comparison sets are retained, while v2 adds Time-MOE-Base and Sundial-Small forecasting comparisons (Table 20). New comparisons include iTransformer and UniTS variants for classification, five foundation models for zero-shot forecasting, and MOMENT, TimesFM, Lag-Llama, Chronos, FITS and AnomalyTransformer on TSB-AD-U.

E3.justification: New protocols include zero-shot forecasting at horizon 96, ETTm1 few-shot evaluation using 10% fine-tuning data, classification accuracy, and nine TSB-AD-U metrics. Additional experiments vary model depth/width, pre-training sample volume, patch/look-back lengths and profiling configurations. The original forecasting horizons, imputation ratios and principal pre-training settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds model/data scaling studies, patch-length and look-back sensitivity tests, and latency analyses across hardware, channel counts, frequency-module counts and sequence lengths (Sections 4.8–4.9; Appendices B.3.6–B.3.8). The original frequency/granularity ablations and qualitative case studies are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: v1 provides no repeated-run uncertainty reporting. v2 reports ten independent forecasting trials and Student-t-based 95% confidence intervals for MSE and MAE on ETTh1, ETTm1 and Weather (Appendix B.3.1, Table 19). This introduces substantial uncertainty reporting, although v1's unspecified run count prevents inferring a numerical increase in runs.

E6.justification: Matched original benchmark and component-ablation scores are retained. v2 adds extensive results, including 69.9% FaceDetection accuracy and leading scores on eight of nine TSB-AD-U metrics. New comparisons also show mixed outcomes: Table 20 reports ETTh1 average MSE of 0.379 for Time-MOE-Base versus GTM's 0.404. Transfer, scaling, sensitivity, timing and repeated-run estimates are newly reported.

M1.justification: v2 adds classification adaptation through a replacement projection head and cross-entropy fine-tuning (Section 4.5; Appendix B.2.3). The backbone, Fourier attention, span shuffling, 2D positions and random/tail masking already appear in v1. Appendix B.3.8's parallel-inference description conflicts with retained autoregressive wording, so it does not reliably establish another procedural change.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, related work and method exposition are extensively rewritten and reorganized. v2 uses more structured method descriptions, expands the experimental narrative, reorganizes the technical appendices, and adds acknowledgements and an LLM-use disclosure. These changes extend well beyond inserting new results.

P2.justification: v2 redraws the architecture diagram with tensor dimensions, merges v1's amplitude and appendix phase plots into Figure 1, replaces the main full forecasting table with an average-results table, and redisplays ablation averages as bars. It also adds transfer/scaling plots and numerous experimental tables within a substantially revised layout.

R1.justification: v2 removes v1 Appendix A.1.1's substantial deep-learning and frequency-domain survey, including discussion of Fredformer, FreTS and TimeMixer++. It adds literature on MOMENT, Chronos, Sundial, scaling laws and newer benchmarks, and explicitly characterizes TimesNet/PatchTST as precursors falling short of full foundation-model requirements. This changes the substantive research positioning.

T1.justification: The attention, reconstruction-loss and KDE mathematics are retained apart from notation and expanded specification. The explicit masking-probability equation formalizes the previously described procedure. Neither version provides new theoretical guarantees, theorems or proofs; the confidence-interval formula is statistical reporting.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for GTM's generality and reliability through classification, zero/few-shot transfer, broader forecasting tests, multi-metric anomaly evaluation and ten-trial confidence intervals, addressing important gaps in v1's validation. Updated comparators and sensitivity/scaling analyses make its strengths and limits more assessable. These gains outweigh the unresolved conflict between autoregressive generation in Section 3 and parallel inference in Appendix B.3.8, although that ambiguity limits reproducibility.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GTM research, with matching core architecture and original benchmark results. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial rewriting and reformatting.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds classification, transfer, expanded benchmark, scaling, sensitivity and efficiency experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original forecasting, imputation, anomaly-detection, pre-training and ablation results, alongside empirical frequency-distribution analysis.

results.title: GTM: A General Time-series Model for Enhanced Representation Learning of Time-Series data

C1.justification: The contribution is reframed from an exploratory diffusion policy supplying rewards and downstream initialization to a diffusion-model framework supporting both Gaussian and diffusion adaptation. Performance claims broaden from beating exploration methods and competing with skill-based methods to outperforming URL and diffusion fine-tuning baselines, with particular emphasis on complicated mazes.

C2.justification: v2 Section 5.4 newly reports that diffusion-policy fine-tuning underperforms Gaussian-policy fine-tuning and tentatively attributes this to limited online interactions, qualifying the earlier emphasis on diffusion-policy initialization. Section 5.6 adds explicit limitations concerning discrete actions and computational costs. The pre-training explanation also shifts toward maximizing state entropy.

D1.justification: v2 Appendix C.3 and Table 2 newly disclose extensive DDPG and diffusion hyperparameters, architectures and optimization details. Appendices C.1 and C.7 add episode limits, hardware and training times; C.2 adds implementation sources for new baselines. These are substantial documentation additions, not evidence that previously unspecified settings changed. Both versions state that code is in supplementary material.

E1.justification: Maze coverage expands from Square-b, Square-c and Square-tree to include Square-a, Square-d, Square-bottleneck and Square-large. This extends evaluation to bottlenecked and substantially more complex maze geometries. The four URLB domains and their sixteen downstream tasks remain unchanged.

E2.justification: The maze comparison expands beyond RND, DIAYN and BeCL to include ICM, Disagreement, LBS, SMM, LSD, CIC and CeSD. URLB adds CeSD and a separate diffusion fine-tuning comparison against DQL, IDQL, QSM and DIPO. CeSD was already cited in v1 but was not evaluated there.

E3.justification: Maze pre-training changes from 500k to 100k steps. v2 separately evaluates Gaussian-policy fine-tuning with DDPG and diffusion-policy fine-tuning, and introduces pre-training budgets of 100k, 500k, 1M and 2M steps for sensitivity analysis. Standard URLB budgets of 2M pre-training and 100k fine-tuning steps remain.

E4.justification: v2 adds aggregate and per-domain pre-training-duration analyses in Figures 6(a) and 11. It removes v1's score-reward ablation and the direct comparison between replay-buffer trajectories and samples from pre-trained policies in Figures 3, 8 and 9. Q-learning and diffusion sampling-step analyses are retained in v2 Figures 6(b–c).

E5.justification: v2 explicitly reports Maze2d means and standard deviations over ten seeds in Table 1; v1's maze plots show bands without specifying the maze seed count or uncertainty definition. URLB retains ten seeds per task and stratified bootstrap confidence intervals. The added disclosure does not establish an increase in runs.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive maze results and separate Gaussian/diffusion fine-tuning results; Table 4 reports Gaussian-policy IQM of 0.80 for ExDM versus 0.71 for CeSD. Retained baseline values also change: CIC's Jaco top-right score changes from 168.9 to 167.6, and BeCL's Quadruped walk score from 640.3 to 694.9. Proposed-method scores involve changed methods and policy settings, so they are not direct same-setting gains over v1.

M1.justification: In v1, the conditional action diffusion policy supplies the intrinsic reward Rscore(s,a). v2 Section 3.1 and Algorithm 1 add a separate state diffusion model and derive Rscore(s) from state modeling while retaining action modeling. Section 3.2 also introduces Gaussian-policy fine-tuning alongside the retained IQL/CEP diffusion procedure.

P1.justification: The EDP-to-ExDM renaming accompanies extensive rewriting of the abstract, introduction, pre-training explanation and experimental narrative. Experiments now distinguish Gaussian and diffusion fine-tuning, appendices are reorganized, and Broader Impact moves from the main text to Appendix D.

P2.justification: The main text switches from two columns to one. Conceptual diagrams are redrawn and combined into v2 Figure 1; maze plots and trajectory panels are substantially reorganized; ablations are combined into Figure 6. New coverage, hyperparameter and aggregate-results tables and URLB task illustrations materially expand the displays.

R1.justification: The URL and diffusion-RL literature framing remains, with expanded citations including DIME, Soft Diffusion Actor-Critic, EUCLID and geometric-probability work. General language-model and vision pre-training references are removed. The novelty positioning is broadened from diffusion policies for unsupervised exploration to diffusion models in URL, without replacing the central research positioning.

T1.justification: v2 adds Theorem 3.1 and Appendix A.1, deriving a geometric-probability bound concerning nondeterministic maximum-state-entropy policies under an assumption of independent, uniformly distributed deterministic-policy state occupancies. The earlier policy-improvement and convergence theorem is retained as Theorem 3.2 with its proof in Appendix A.2.

improvement.justification: v2 separates Gaussian-policy/DDPG evaluation from diffusion-policy fine-tuning comparisons, reducing v1's confounding of exploration and policy-class advantages. Relevant new comparators and challenging maze evaluations strengthen the evidence, while explicit hyperparameters and computing details substantially improve reproducibility. Removing the score-reward and direct policy-diversity ablations weakens component attribution, and the new theorem relies on idealized assumptions, but the evaluation and reproducibility gains provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work, renamed from EDP to ExDM. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison despite substantial revisions.

after.justification: Section 5 and Appendix C report original seven-maze exploration, Gaussian and diffusion policy fine-tuning, and ablation results.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendix C report original Maze2d exploration, URLB fine-tuning and ablation results.

results.title: Exploratory Diffusion Model for Unsupervised Reinforcement Learning

C1.justification: The central contribution remains training-free, model-independent retrieval of references for missing concepts to improve rare and fine-grained generation. The third backbone and expanded evaluations support this existing claim. Calling the retained VLM stages guided chain-of-thought does not establish a different core contribution.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations of why embedding metrics can miss fine-grained improvements and why CLIP retrieval can succeed when generation fails. It also discusses ambiguous prompts, hypothesizes why unrelated references are ignored, and characterizes model-dependent diversity versus faithfulness tradeoffs. Existing limitations concerning retrieval coverage, counting and text generation are retained and illustrated.
