D1.justification: Appendix A adds FLUX-schnell/OminiControl settings, 50 inference steps, retrieval-threshold disclosure, and VLM timing and API-cost estimates. Section 8 promises code release, without establishing availability. Existing prompts and retry details are relocated, while v1's explicit 1024×1024 resolution and comparative-study decision-bypass disclosure are omitted.

E1.justification: v2 Appendix E.1 adds fine-grained generation using Stanford Dogs, Oxford Flowers and Stanford Cars, including their images in retrieval. It also adds a VLM concept-identification task and explicit mismatched-retrieval scenarios. ImageNet, iNaturalist, CUB, Aircraft and personalization remain covered; Aircraft results survive in Appendix E.

E2.justification: FLUX joins the comparative human study in v2 Figure 4, having previously appeared only in automatic comparisons. The new diagnostic experiment compares GPT-4o with Gemini, Qwen2.5-VL-7B and LLaVA. Most generation comparators remain, but Aircraft loses its original full baseline comparison, including Pixart-Σ and GraPE-O.

E3.justification: v2 adds GPTScore, CLIP-I evaluation on additional datasets, and evaluation of ImageRAG with FLUX/OminiControl. Human evaluation expands from 46 participants and 767 comparisons to 67 participants, 977 comparisons and 231 absolute judgments. The absolute study selects cases where the VLM triggered retrieval. Appendix E.5 introduces a controlled diagnostic protocol with 20 classes and 780 prompts.

E4.justification: v2 adds controlled tests of VLM concept recognition, seed-based diversity comparisons, concrete retrieval/counting/text failure cases, and qualitative component-ablation examples. The original prompt-rephrasing, retrieval-caption, retriever-choice and retrieval-dataset-size ablations are retained, sometimes relocated, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Appendix E.6 newly reports generation with different seeds, showing five outputs per prompt in Figures 17–19. It does not provide seed identities or aggregate repeated-run uncertainty. Existing mean-plus-standard-error tables and comparative-study error bars remain; no new significance-testing procedure is specified.

E6.justification: Most retained OmniGen/SDXL scores and original ablation values are unchanged. v2 adds ImageRAG-F, GPTScore, additional-dataset, VLM-diagnostic and absolute-study results; the latter reports 92%, 90% and 84% concept presence for OmniGen, SDXL and FLUX on selected cases. FLUX baseline values also change, such as ImageNet CLIP from 0.262 to 0.271, but configuration equivalence is insufficiently documented to interpret this as a same-setting gain.

M1.justification: The core VLM diagnosis, caption generation, retrieval and reference-conditioning workflow remains unchanged, including the prompts and error fallback. v2 Section 3.2 adds optional similarity-threshold filtering and repeated generation until VLM-confirmed alignment. These are proposed procedural options; Appendix A explicitly states that experiments use no retrieval threshold.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, method and experimental narrative are extensively revised. Method exposition is reorganized around guided chain-of-thought; implementation, error handling, personalization and proprietary-data experiments move into appendices. Related-work subsections are consolidated, and reproducibility and LLM-usage statements are added.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column layout, with extensive figure and table restructuring. The teaser and qualitative comparison grids are revised, the user-study figure gains FLUX and absolute-evaluation panels, and new failure, ablation and diversity figures appear. Existing ablation and proprietary-result tables are split or regrouped, alongside new GPTScore and dataset tables.

R1.justification: v2 substantially updates positioning against close alternatives: RealRAG's trained retrieval module and FineRAG's retrieval of all concepts with layout construction. These comparisons sharpen the distinction of training-free, gap-directed retrieval beyond v1's contrast with RAG-trained generators. It also adds relevant chain-of-thought, editing, conditioning and evaluation references; RealRAG and FineRAG are discussed rather than directly benchmarked.

T1.justification: Neither version presents theoretical proofs or formal guarantees. The prompt template is restated for the already-used one-image-per-concept setting. The added chain-of-thought and retrieval explanations introduce no substantive mathematical derivation.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation beyond v1's similarity metrics and relative preferences: the absolute human study checks concept presence on retrieval-triggered cases, while the controlled VLM experiment tests a central diagnostic assumption. Additional backbone coverage and explicit failure and diversity analyses strengthen applicability assessment. Unexplained FLUX reporting inconsistencies—the LAION-F rows in Tables 6–7 repeat base-FLUX values rather than Table 2's ImageRAG-F values—and some omitted protocol details limit parts of the evidence, but do not outweigh these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ImageRAG by the same authors. Their text, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable and support comparison despite extensive reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds FLUX-based results, additional datasets, VLM diagnostic tests and expanded human evaluations.

before.justification: v1 reports original image-generation benchmarks, ablations, proprietary-retrieval experiments and a user study with 46 participants and 767 comparisons.

results.title: ImageRAG: Dynamic Image Retrieval for Reference-Guided Image Generation

C1.justification: The main representation claim expands from approximate binary first-order smoothing to exact smoothing for arbitrary finite-state first-order processes. The introduction replaces the claim of introducing a novel Markov-ICL framework with applying an existing framework to Mamba, and emphasizes convolution together with selectivity and recurrence. The empirical higher-order learning claim remains.

C2.justification: V2 substantially qualifies convolution's importance: additional layers can compensate for its removal, gating matters strongly in language modeling, and convolution's relative effect decreases in deeper models. It proposes that other layers approximate convolution, explains held-out behavior through asymptotic minimax optimality, and contrasts recurrent exponential memory requirements with transformer scaling. Learning dynamics are explicitly left outside scope.

D1.justification: Appendix F newly reports a single Nvidia A100 and 10-60 minutes per experiment. However, v1's explicit WikiText sequence length of 256, two-layer transformer with dimension 256, and four-layer Mamba configuration disappear; the replacement reference to Appendix F does not recover them. The code link and original Markov hyperparameter tables are retained.

E1.justification: V2 adds PG-19 language modeling, first-order Markov evaluation with 4, 6, and 8 states, and fifth-order binary Markov evaluation. Appendix E.5 also tests generalization between disjoint transition-probability ranges. These substantially broaden the binary Markov, switching Markov, and WikiText-103 coverage in v1.

E2.justification: Figure 7 adds one- and two-layer linear-attention transformers to the Markov comparisons. Figure 11 adds a one-layer transformer with convolution on its query, key, and value representations, an important control for Mamba's apparent advantage. Convolution-augmented transformers already appeared in v1's WikiText experiment, but not its Markov comparisons.

E3.justification: New protocols include training on transition probabilities in [0, 0.5] and testing on [0.5, 1], depth comparisons through four layers, convolution-free widths of 10, 100, and 1000, and 12-layer language models with 110M or 200M parameters. Figure 8 also adds relative loss-gap evaluation. The original Markov hyperparameter grids remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 adds checks of learned count-selection inner products and smoothing constants, hidden-dimension scaling, depth and overparameterization, and held-out-distribution generalization. Appendix E.6 tests whether convolution or additional layers explain Markov performance; E.8 separately ablates convolution, gating, and nonlinearities in language models. These substantially extend v1's convolution-focused analyses.

E5.justification: Both versions already specify five repetitions and display error bars or shaded intervals. V2's Figure 1 caption newly identifies its intervals as standard deviations across five runs. This clarifies uncertainty reporting without establishing any increase in runs; the additional tables also report plus-minus values without consistently defining them.

E6.justification: Numerous results are added: convolution enables a one-layer transformer to solve the Markov task, and two-layer Mamba succeeds without convolution. Table 4 adds WikiText perplexities of 32.16 without gating and 28.98 without nonlinearities. Table 5 adds deeper-model and PG-19 results. Original Table 1 scores remain unchanged; the deeper-model scores are new settings, not same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The proposed MambaZero retains the same selective recurrence, convolutions, residual embedding, linear output, and L1 normalization. The finite-state parameter construction extends the representation analysis without introducing a new learning or inference procedure. Additional architectural variants serve as experimental controls.

P1.justification: The introduction, related work, and theoretical narrative are substantially rewritten and condensed. V2 removes the contents page, moves detailed language-model equations into Appendix B, relocates the switching-process procedure and lower-bound intuition, and reorganizes the proofs around the general theorem and retained binary theorem. These are substantial structural changes beyond added experiments.

P2.justification: V2 adopts the ICLR layout, resizes and repositions existing displays, and adds Figures 5-12 and Tables 2-5. The switching result moves from main-text Figure 4 to appendix Figure 13, while the original transition-factor plot becomes Figure 4. Figure 1 receives a more informative caption, and existing hyperparameter tables are repacked.

R1.justification: V2 explicitly credits Edelman et al. for the Markov-ICL framework and positions its novelty as applying that framework to Mamba. Related work is substantively reframed around representation power rather than architectural superiority, adding work on ICL, transformer-recurrent separations, and SSM expressivity, including Park et al., Ekbote et al., and Wang and Xue.

T1.justification: V2 adds an exact finite-state representation theorem with N=S and d=2S and a new constructive argument in Appendix C.2. V1's binary approximation theorem survives as Theorem 4 with d=N=2. The explicit higher-order Conjecture 1 is removed, while the exponential-memory lower bound remains. The new construction contains inconsistent stated projection dimensions.

improvement.justification: The new controls substantially strengthen the central explanation: convolution-augmented transformers, deeper convolution-free Mamba, and language ablations establish clearer boundaries for v1's convolution-focused claims. Broader state-space and distribution-shift evidence, together with more careful research positioning, improve support and interpretation. Missing WikiText setup details and dimensional inconsistencies in the new proof are drawbacks, but the empirical and interpretive gains are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Mamba and Markov-chain study. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: The original empirical results remain, supplemented by experiments on larger state spaces, additional comparators, distribution shift, model capacity, and language-model ablations in Appendices C-E.

before.justification: Sections 3 and 5 report original training and evaluation results on random Markov chains, switching Markov sequences, and WikiText-103, including prediction plots, ablations, and perplexities.

results.title: From Markov to Laplace: How Mamba In-Context Learns Markov Chains

C1.justification: v1 principally contributes a particular recurrent Transformer derived from dual hyperspherical energies. v3's abstract, introduction, and conclusion broaden this to a general MLE-grounded design principle supporting multiple attention/feedforward operators and depth-wise adaptation. Parameter efficiency and competitive performance remain central claims, but architectural generality becomes an explicit contribution.

C2.justification: v3 develops the mode-seeking/mass-covering interpretation and interprets the new shared-QKV controls as evidence about the architectural mechanism. Its new limitations discussion identifies potentially restrictive uniformity assumptions, heuristic subspace choices, modulation-network overhead, validation below 20 million parameters, and the absence of causal structure. These substantially extend v1's narrower scalability caveats.

D1.justification: v3 newly tabulates the adaptive-step network's matrix dimensions, separates CIFAR and ImageNet training/configuration recipes, and supplies ImageNet-specific hardware and sample counts. It documents learning-rate bounds and warmup, revises existing hyperparameters, and specifies adapter dimensions, Gaussian initialization with standard deviation 0.02, scaling factor 4, and joint training. These are substantial changes to the reproducibility information; the existing code/data links remain.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate Sudoku with 17–34 given digits, CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet-100 classification, and ImageNet-100 masked reconstruction at the same masking ratios. The new ablations and scaling studies use existing datasets. Moving the layer-iteration analysis from CIFAR-10 to CIFAR-100 does not expand the paper's overall coverage.

E2.justification: v3 adds Energy Transformer to the classification comparison and evaluates both Energy Transformer and CRATE on Sudoku, where v1 compared only against Transformer. Appendix F.3 also introduces shared-QKV Transformer controls with ordinary and reversed attention-update signs. These are reported comparisons, not merely new citations.

E3.justification: The classification protocol is substantially revised: CIFAR input/patch sizes change from 224/16 to 32/8, Adam betas from (0, 0.95) to (0.9, 0.999), learning rate from 1e-4 to a 1e-3 maximum, and weight decay from zero to 5e-5. v3's ImageNet table specifies batch size 256 versus v1's blanket 128. Sudoku and reconstruction recipes also change AdamW beta1 from 0 to 0.9; retained scores do not establish reruns. New rank and width sweeps extend the evaluation design.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's energy, rank, angle, masking-ratio, and layer-iteration analyses, v3 tests alternative attention/feedforward operators and learned versus fixed step sizes in Table 3. Appendix F.3 examines shared-QKV projections and attention-sign reversal. LoRA-rank and larger-width studies add scalability evidence, while the layer-iteration study is revised to CIFAR-100.

E5.justification: v3 Figure 4 adds error bars explicitly defined as standard deviations over five runs for the layer-iteration comparison; v1 Figure 6 provides neither these bars nor that specification. Five-run averaging for Sudoku was already reported in v1 and remains unchanged. An increase in runs for retained experiments is not established.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces classification scores under revised settings: scaled Hyper-SET's ImageNet-100 accuracy changes from 55.98 to 70.16, and Transformer's from 57.82 to 69.44. These are not same-setting gains. v3 adds baseline failures on Sudoku, operator/control results, and scaling results, including 72.20 accuracy with rank-32 LoRA versus 70.16 without adapters. The Sudoku extrapolation values and all masked-reconstruction table values are retained.

M1.justification: The original symmetric attention, ReLU feedforward, and adaptive-step updates remain. However, v3 Section 5.5 and Appendix G introduce sigmoid and linear attention variants, softmax and gated feedforward variants, and iteration-specific low-rank adapters trained jointly with shared parameters. These extend the actual procedures beyond v1's architecture.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and substantial method prose are rewritten around the new conceptual framework. Hopfield preliminaries move from Section 3 to Appendix B, metric definitions move to Appendix D.5, and previously distributed representation analyses become Section 5.4. The new limitations and discussion sections substantially reorganize the narrative.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one, with extensively restyled and rearranged plots. Figure 1 gains an alignment sequence, Figure 3 gains Sudoku training curves, and new tables and shared-QKV plots present added studies. The original appendix reconstruction grid is retained as v3 Figure 8, while v1's separate main-text reconstruction panel is removed.

R1.justification: Energy Transformer changes from a briefly cited related method into a central comparison, with detailed distinctions in the introduction, related work, and Appendix H. v3 also positions its principle against contrastive alignment/uniformity and expands discussion of Hopfield memory capacity, shared projections, and recursive LoRA. Added references support these substantive positioning changes.

T1.justification: v3 introduces the MLE/KL objective in Section 3 and derives it in Appendix A using explicit independence, uniform-prior, and conditional-independence assumptions, followed by a von Mises–Fisher mixture interpretation. Appendix G adds generalized energy definitions and induced operators. The original Hopfield background, core gradient derivations, and rank/angle definitions are retained or relocated.

improvement.justification: The direct Energy Transformer comparisons, component ablations, and shared-QKV/sign controls address important gaps in v1's evidence for its design rationale. Explicit assumptions and concrete applicability limitations also make the claims substantially easier to assess. These gains are tempered by changed classification protocols and apparent negative-gradient sign and beta-scaling inconsistencies in the new Table 18 formulas. The revision nevertheless provides substantially stronger empirical scrutiny and clearer boundaries, without fully establishing its broader theoretical or large-scale claims.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Hyper-SET research, retaining the core architecture and experiments despite the changed title and expanded scope. Text extraction and visual inspection support comparison of the main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and reports additional baseline comparisons, component ablations, shared-QKV analyses, and scaling experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original Sudoku, image-classification, and masked-image reconstruction experiments, including numerical results and analyses of energy and token representations.

results.title: Hyper-SET: Designing Transformers via Hyperspherical Energy Minimization

C1.justification: The three principal contributions and abstract/conclusion claims about interpretable, category-agnostic multilayer prompts remain. v2 additionally asserts in the introduction that cross-layer alignment emulates human visual reasoning. Renaming hierarchical concepts otherwise leaves the central contribution intact.

C2.justification: v2 retains the in-domain-prototype limitation but adds concrete explanations of background confusion, occlusion failures and degradation from prompting too many layers. It also develops interpretations concerning monosemanticity, human reasoning and transferable concepts, including domain-dependent concept priorities observed in separately fine-tuned VLCS models.

D1.justification: Appendices A–C add optimizer, learning rates, batch size, epochs, scheduling, initialization, trainable-parameter exceptions, hardware, timing and parameter accounting. Appendix B details the adopted loss implementation. The abstract also supplies a code-repository link absent from v1; these are substantial documentation additions, without independently establishing implementation changes.

E1.justification: v2 adds quantitative PartImageNet and PASCAL-Part evaluation, FGVC-Aircraft visualizations, broader CIFAR-100/ImageNet examples, VLCS domain studies and unseen-category CUB evaluation. It also introduces human concept-interpretation evaluation. CUB, Stanford Cars and Gleason-2019 coverage is retained.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains all twelve comparator rows. The added dataset comparisons reuse ProtoPool, Huang et al. and VPT-Deep, and the computational comparison uses existing VPT. Prompt-CAM receives related-work discussion but is not evaluated.

E3.justification: New protocols include extracting representative part points for PartImageNet/PASCAL-Part, layer/prototype configuration sweeps, validation-set alignment IoU, and a 20-participant study using 100 regions and five-point ratings. Appendix A also reports unfrozen backbone tokens and position embeddings despite the frozen-backbone description retained from v1; this changes the reported setting without establishing a rerun.

E4.justification: The existing component ablation gains a spatial-bias row. Appendices C–G add computational-cost analysis, layer/prototype sensitivity, cross-layer alignment measurements, domain and unseen-class analyses, concrete failure cases, grade-dependent pathology scores, and visual comparisons across prototype counts and backbones.

E5.justification: v1 supplies point estimates without uncertainty reporting. v2 Table 5 introduces ± values for alignment IoUs, including an overall 99.0% ± 0.6, but does not define the uncertainty measure or sampling unit. Neither version specifies repeated-run counts, seeds or significance tests.

E6.justification: All 195 Table 1 scores and the original component-ablation scores are unchanged. New results include IVPT consistency/stability/accuracy of 63.2/71.5/74.2% on PartImageNet and 72.6/77.4/86.4% on PASCAL-Part, 97.5% human annotation accuracy, alignment IoUs, overhead measurements and additional ablation and qualitative findings. These expand the evidence rather than demonstrate same-setting gains over v1.

M1.justification: CRD with spatial bias, region-based feature aggregation, Gumbel-Softmax grouping, KL alignment and prompt-score averaging are retained. The cross-layer terminology, explicit loss coefficients still set to one, and fuller descriptions of existing part-shaping losses do not establish a changed algorithm.

P1.justification: The introduction, related work and method explanations undergo substantial rewriting, with cross-layer terminology replacing hierarchical terminology throughout much of the paper. The VPT preliminary is condensed into prompt construction, qualitative discussions are reordered, the original region-map comparison moves to Appendix G.1, and the expanded material receives a new appendix structure.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column presentation. v1's introductory illustration is removed, the fusion diagram is redrawn, pathology and car displays are combined with aircraft examples, and the original qualitative comparison moves to v2 Figure 8. Additional tables and figures present alignment, sensitivity, generalization and failure analyses.

R1.justification: v2 adds a direct discussion of Prompt-CAM and references for aircraft, VLCS and newer prompt-learning work, while removing LPT, PW-Net and S-Prompts references. Comparisons with prior approaches become more explicit, but the principal positioning around region grounding, shared concepts and multilayer interpretation is retained.

T1.justification: Appendix B supplies explicit mathematical definitions for the previously referenced part-shaping losses and radial background mask (Equations 11–17), expanding their formal specification. The core aggregation and fusion mathematics remains equivalent, and no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially reduces v1's reliance on one quantitative benchmark and sparse training documentation through additional benchmark comparisons, targeted ablations, human evaluation, explicit failure analysis and detailed implementation information. Human-study scoring and IoU uncertainty remain under-specified, and backbone-freezing descriptions conflict. Nevertheless, the broader testable evidence and improved reproducibility provide a substantial net quality gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe IVPT, with matching authors, core pipeline and retained experiments. Text, equations, tables and figures are readable throughout. v1 ends with references; v2 includes Appendices A–G, which were included in the comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds benchmark comparisons, human evaluation, alignment measurements, sensitivity experiments and additional qualitative analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original CUB-200-2011 comparisons, component ablations and qualitative experiments on birds, Stanford Cars and Gleason-2019.

results.title: Exploring Interpretability for Visual Prompt Tuning with Cross-layer Concepts

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central contributions: SD2.1-VAE16, SR-specific CiD/CiDA, and a simplified one-step pipeline offering a favorable quality-efficiency tradeoff. Additional evidence and appendix extensions do not materially redefine these main claims.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive limitations concerning unexplored larger latent spaces and CiDA's memory requirements restricting DiT extensions (Section 5). It qualifies SD2.1-VAE16's T2I performance and adds interpretations of semantic prompts, CFG's fidelity-quality tradeoff, and adversarial loss improving no-reference scores while worsening LPIPS (Appendix A.4). v1 provides substantially less qualification and component-level interpretation.

D1.justification: v3 adds training pseudocode and staged-training documentation, guidance and weighting parameters, the 19.2% data-selection retention rate, user-study sampling details, complete prompt alternatives, and TensorRT deployment information. These greatly expand reproducibility documentation without establishing that the original training procedure changed. However, v1's explicit LAION-5B/FLUX data-generation description and project-page pointer disappear.

E1.justification: The principal SR and text-to-image coverage is retained. v3 adds qualitative evaluation on KwaiSR user-generated content (Figure 17) and targeted tests with extremely degraded faces (Figure 10). These provide limited additional domain and degradation-scenario coverage.

E2.justification: The main SR benchmark comparator set is unchanged. v3 adds HYPIR and SD3.5-large with ControlNeXt in Figure 15, and additional VAE comparators including SD3.5 and FLUX in Table 5. DALL-E is removed from the retained text-to-image comparison, matching v1 Table 1 to v3 Table 11.

E3.justification: The main SR protocol is retained, but v3 substantially extends evaluation settings. It adds DeQA scoring while retaining DepictQA in the appendix, and reports an expanded GenEval/FID comparison on 20k COCO prompts, whereas v1's T2I table specified 30k. New protocols include prompt and CFG sweeps, batch-size-8 training-cost measurements, multiple deployment precisions and resolutions, and the 10k-iteration SDXL extension.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's distillation, VAE-channel and prompt-extractor comparisons, v3 separately examines adversarial and representation-alignment losses (Table 8), positive/negative prompt combinations and CFG sensitivity (Tables 6-7), VAE reconstruction and latent distributions (Table 5; Figures 11-12), and difficult face-restoration cases. These substantially expand evidence about individual design choices.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates and preference percentages without repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. v3's disclosure of ten user-study images concerns sample selection, not repeated-run uncertainty.

E6.justification: Most headline SR scores and the 77 ms runtime remain unchanged. v3 adds DeQA results, including GenDR's 4.1289 on RealSet80, detailed GenEval scores, VAE/component/prompt/CFG results, computational measurements and SDXL-variant examples. Conversely, v1's RealLR200 benchmark table and VAE-specific 36.25%/63.75% human-preference results are removed. The DepictQA heatmap is retained unchanged in the appendix.

M1.justification: The original SD2.1-based GenDR and CiDA objectives remain essentially unchanged. However, Appendix A.5 introduces GenDR-1.3B: a pruned SDXL generator adapted to SD3.5's 16-channel VAE and flow-matching scheduler, with SD3.5 score networks and an adapted CiD objective. This is a substantive architecture and distillation extension.

P1.justification: The title, abstract and selected explanatory passages are revised. Preliminaries is integrated into Related Work, T2I and DepictQA material is reorganized, and limitations and appendices receive explicit sections. Most existing methodology and conclusion prose remains closely matched; the expansion is primarily additional scientific documentation.

P2.justification: v3 switches to a single-column ICLR layout, redesigns the opening comparison, expands the VAE/distillation visual comparison, and introduces algorithm boxes, diagnostic tables and extensive qualitative panels. The earlier T2I gallery/table and DepictQA heatmap are relocated and reformatted, while the RealLR200 comparison table is removed.

R1.justification: v3 adds discussion of Transfer VAE Training as a related fidelity solution with the same compression rate, plus references supporting HYPIR, ControlNeXt, KwaiSR and DeQA. Several earlier references, including DALL-E, LAION-5B and DepictQA, are removed. The broader positioning around GAN priors, diffusion restoration and score distillation remains stable.

T1.justification: v1 asserts the generated-to-ground-truth latent substitution underlying CiD without a formal proof. v3 Appendix A.1 adds Equations 12-15, characterizing an optimal MSE predictor through conditional expectation and deriving the corresponding expected-inner-product identity. This adds formal reasoning for a central step under an optimal-predictor assumption; the main equations remain essentially unchanged.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially improves support for the central design choices through separate loss-component ablations, VAE/prompt/CFG analyses, an idealized CiD derivation, and measured training and deployment costs. Pseudocode and explicit limitations make the method more assessable. Removing the RealLR200 comparison and some data-provenance details weakens completeness, and the new warm-up prose specifies L1 while Algorithm 2 shows squared-L2 loss. These shortcomings temper but do not outweigh the substantial gains in diagnostic evidence and technical transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GenDR research, with readable text, equations, tables and figures. v1 ends after its references; v3 includes Appendices A and B. Material relocated into those appendices can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and additionally reports component ablations, reconstruction tests, computational measurements and preliminary SDXL-based GenDR results.

before.justification: v1 reports original GenDR benchmark results, distillation ablations, human and MLLM preference evaluations, and SD2.1-VAE16 generation results.

results.title: GenDR: Lighten Generative Detail Restoration

C1.justification: The principal claims about robust inference-time alignment, convex weight optimization, analytic best responses and efficient blockwise decoding remain. v2 adds an abstract-level effectiveness claim for the distilled policy and extends its headline empirical claims to LLM-as-Judge evaluation, without redefining the central contribution.

C2.justification: v2 argues that RMOD also works with positively correlated objectives, attributes high-K deterioration of some best-of-K baselines to reward overoptimization, and interprets distillation performance alongside policy divergence. Its qualitative explanations shift from conciseness to helpfulness and safety. It also removes v1's explicit concluding limitation about reward bias and value-function accuracy.

D1.justification: v2 documents distillation using 16000 HH prompts and three training epochs, the MAXMIN-GRPO implementation, approximate training/evaluation times, and additional hardware settings. Appendix C.5 supplies complete separate GPT-4o judging prompts and evaluation instructions. These materially expand reproducibility information; the repository URL itself is unchanged.

E1.justification: The same three datasets remain. Within UltraFeedback, v2 replaces the conciseness objective with safety and adds a four-objective scenario excluding safety to examine positively correlated objectives. Coverage changes are confined to task variants within an existing dataset.

E2.justification: v2 Figure 2 adds MAXMIN-GRPO, shown as the Maxmin GRPO bar, providing a robust fine-tuning comparator. UltraFeedback's CONCISENESS comparator is replaced by INSTRUCTION-FOLLOWING and SAFETY. Table 3 adds direct-reward best-of-K comparisons, including WORSTCASE selection. The CD- prefixes merely rename existing controlled-decoding baselines.

E3.justification: Reported UltraFeedback settings change from four to sixteen training responses per prompt and from 956 to 1000 test prompts; Figure 4 changes from worst-case win rate to reward improvement. v2 also introduces separate GPT-4o grading for helpfulness and harmlessness, KL estimation protocols, and length-normalized HH latency measurements on a 40GB A100. The original UltraFeedback latency protocol remains.

E4.justification: v2 adds the correlated-objective ablation, KL-divergence analysis, and direct-reward best-of-K sweeps examining reward overoptimization. It updates weight-trajectory examples and replaces the UltraFeedback conciseness case study with two HH cases. Existing block-size, lambda, ValuePrism reverse-order and UltraFeedback latency analyses are retained, sometimes relocated.

E5.justification: Both versions display error bars without explaining their construction and retain the same unelaborated latency-significance statement. v2's additional error bars accompany revised or new results; it does not document new repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence-interval procedures or significance tests.

E6.justification: v2 replaces UltraFeedback results under changed objectives and settings, so these do not establish a same-setting improvement over v1. It adds substantial results: Table 1 reports GPT-4o worst-case win rates of 59.1% for RMOD, 57.9% for DISTILL-RMOD and 57.6% for CD-UNIFORM. Tables 2-4 add latency, direct-reward best-of-K and KL results, alongside new ablation and qualitative findings.

M1.justification: The central maxmin decoding procedure remains, but v2 introduces DISTILL-RMOD, a policy trained by supervised fine-tuning on RMOD-generated responses. Appendix C.1 also changes UltraFeedback's value architecture from five separately trained models to one model with five outputs. These are substantive procedural and architectural changes.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are substantially rewritten around balancing critical objectives. Related Work becomes a separate section, the method exposition centers on one practical algorithm, blockwise decoding moves earlier, and the experimental appendix is extensively reorganized. Acknowledgement and reproducibility statements are added.

P2.justification: v2 changes document typography and page layout, condenses two algorithm displays into one, adds four tables, expands Figure 2 and redraws UltraFeedback plots with different axes and legends. v1's paired ValuePrism figure is split between the main text and appendix, and judging prompts and response examples receive boxed displays.

R1.justification: The main positioning within robust multi-objective alignment remains. v2 adds discussion of Transfer Q-star, Chehade et al.'s constrained inference-time alignment and Yoon et al.'s robust best-of-K work, and distinguishes objective robustness from MAXMIN-RLHF's user-group robustness. References supporting the removed preference-history motivation and no-regret discussion are dropped.

T1.justification: v1 Appendix D's alternative Hedge-BR treatment is removed, including payoff definitions, update derivations, an O(1/sqrt(I)) approximate-equilibrium guarantee and comparisons with gradient descent. The central RMOD proofs and KKT analysis remain in Appendices A-B. v2 additionally formalizes the MAXMIN-GRPO objective and updates in Appendix C.1.

improvement.justification: v1 primarily assesses alignment using the reward models driving optimization. v2 substantially strengthens validation through separate GPT-4o judging, direct investigation of reward overoptimization and a robust fine-tuning comparator. Distillation, latency and KL analyses also make practical tradeoffs more assessable, with fuller implementation and judging details. These gains outweigh removal of the optional Hedge-BR discussion and explicit concluding caveat, while the central proofs remain. The added judge comparisons still lack uncertainty estimates, and revised UltraFeedback results cannot establish gains over v1 under identical conditions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RMOD research. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original benchmark experiments and reports additional distillation, GPT-4o evaluation, KL-divergence and latency results.

before.justification: v1 reports original RMOD experiments on HH, UltraFeedback and ValuePrism, including reward comparisons, ablations, latency measurements and generated examples.

results.title: Robust Multi-Objective Controlled Decoding of Large Language Models

C1.justification: The central contributions remain the four-role agent and efficient Chain-of-LoRA integration. v3 explicitly positions Chain-of-LoRA as a test-time scaling mechanism and extends the introduction's headline comparison to both GPT-4o and Gemini-1.5-Pro on long-video benchmarks. These refine the contribution claims without replacing the central research proposition.

C2.justification: Beyond v1's brief component explanations, v3 discusses why continuous timestamp regression helps, identifies grounding as the dominant failure source, and distinguishes grounding/QA correlations across datasets. It acknowledges sequential error accumulation and unmatched settings in imported API comparisons, interprets prompt-only transfer, and adds joint optimization and audio integration as future directions (Appendix B.2–B.3 and Section 5).

D1.justification: Most training hyperparameters and prompt templates are retained. v3 adds runtime hardware and controlled-API settings, and explicitly states that code, checkpoints, data, and training logs are released; v1 only supplies the project link. Conversely, v3 omits v1's general 2-FPS sampling specification with a 1-FPS grounder exception, and removes the explicit QVHighlights test-split label.

E1.justification: v3 adds MultiHop-EgoQA, requiring grounded reasoning across multiple relevant moments, and introduces egocentric training through 67K NaQ samples for VideoMind-Ego (Tables 10 and 12). These extend coverage within the existing video grounding and question-answering domains; the original 14 benchmarks remain.

E2.justification: Comparison sets change substantially. v3 Table 5 adds Grounded-VideoLLM, TRACE, LLaVA-ST, and UniTime while dropping several earlier grounding comparators, including the fine-tuned specialist rows. Table 17 adds LongVILA-R1 and Video-R1. CG-Bench loses GPT-4o-mini, Gemini-1.5-Flash, Qwen-VL-Chat, and MiniCPM-v2.6; NExT-GQA loses VIOLETv2. These are comparator changes within corresponding experiments, beyond renamed methods.

E3.justification: v3 introduces controlled 300-question MLVU/LVBench subsets with matched frame and decoding settings, an 80/20 held-out planner retraining experiment, and GPU latency evaluation. Additional configurations include Qwen2.5-VL, InternVL3, and the NaQ-trained variant. The Charades-STA VTimeLLM comparison also switches from 13B to 7B. These constitute substantial additions to evaluation design, without establishing that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v3 adds alternative timestamp-modeling comparisons, planner input ablations, expanded verifier evaluation, error attribution, grounding-versus-answering correlation, runtime analysis, and transfer across backbones and prompted APIs (Appendix B.3). The original pyramid and verifier-style ablations remain, while v1's auxiliary decoding-loss ablation and its results are removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or formal significance tests. The new random splits, sampled subsets, and error proportions do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Reported VideoMind-2B Video-MME All/Long scores change from 53.6/45.4 to 55.4/46.3; MVBench average changes from 61.9 to 62.5; QVHighlights R1@0.7 changes from 55.77 to 59.35. v3 also adds QVHighlights-7B, MultiHop-EgoQA, adapted-backbone, controlled-API, and diagnostic results. Main CG-Bench, ReXTime, and NExT-GQA scores remain unchanged. Results under newly introduced conditions are additional evidence, not same-setting improvements.

M1.justification: The principal four-role architecture, timestamp decoder, losses, and Algorithm 1 remain intact. Appendix B.3 adds a limited procedural adaptation: simulating the multi-role pipeline through successive prompts on closed-source models without role-specific architecture or training. The expanded Chain-of-LoRA section otherwise explains the existing mechanism.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and method explanations are extensively rewritten. v3 creates a dedicated Chain-of-LoRA subsection, reorders the experimental questions, moves benchmark exposition into the appendix, places references before the appendix, and adds an appendix contents list plus ethics, reproducibility, and LLM-use statements.

P2.justification: The document changes from a two-column layout to the single-column ICLR format. Figure 1 is substantially redrawn around a shared backbone; separate Charades-STA and ActivityNet tables are merged. New error-distribution and correlation plots accompany numerous new analysis tables, while retained figures and tables are resized, restyled, and relocated.

R1.justification: v3 substantially updates positioning through recent video reasoning, temporal grounding, and backbone literature, including explicit comparisons with LongVILA-R1 and Video-R1. It replaces v1's characterization of its own procedure as moment-level MCTS with moment-level searching, prunes older search references, and adds neuroscience references supporting the human-reasoning analogy. These exceed citation-style or publication-metadata updates.

T1.justification: v3 removes v1 Section 3.2's inconsistent pyramid-level shape expression T/n^2, retaining the explicitly specified lengths T, T/2, T/4, and T/8. This is a limited correction to the mathematical description. The numbered equations and inference algorithm otherwise remain, with no new theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens validation of the central design and efficiency claims through alternative timestamp implementations, held-out planner evaluation, measured latency, failure analysis, and matched-setting API comparisons. These address important gaps in v1. The benefits outweigh the removed loss ablation and documentation omissions, although reporting inconsistencies remain: Table 5 gives UniTime higher Charades-STA mIoU despite blanket superiority language, and Figure 7 shows 6.6% planning errors despite the text claiming less than 5%.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same VideoMind research. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite the revised title, organization, and expanded experiments.

after.justification: v3 retains original evaluations and adds MultiHop-EgoQA results, controlled comparisons, planner tests, runtime measurements, and error analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original VideoMind evaluations across 14 benchmarks, component ablations, and qualitative analysis in the main text and appendix.

results.title: VideoMind: A Chain-of-LoRA Agent for Temporal-Grounded Video Reasoning

C1.justification: v3 retains the central target-aware generation, curated-dataset and two-application contributions. It reframes the loss contribution from proposing a novel cross-attention loss to utilizing cross-attention supervision, and adds an explicit introductory claim of robustness to mask quality. Motion-planning motivation receives greater emphasis but already existed in v1.

C2.justification: v3 adds explanations linking noisy captions to preservation of pretrained priors and grounding to the target token rather than the object noun. It identifies channel-scaling, multi-object-mask and temporal-switching limitations, and explains the hand detector's inapplicability to non-human agents. Appendix C.3 also discusses false positives and undercounting under the original and extended metrics.

D1.justification: Most training and inference details are retained. v3 adds parameter-count and VRAM-saving information, evaluation-mask selection instructions, automatic-mask hardware/timing details and more precise inference timing. It adds a project-page pointer while omitting v1's future code/data-release statement; the PDFs do not establish actual release availability.

E1.justification: The 1,290-clip BEHAVE/Ego-Exo4D training collection remains. v3 adds EgoIT-99 training for egocentric generation, explicit outdoor human-interaction tests, corrupted or automatically generated conditioning inputs, and multiple-object and temporal target-switching scenarios. These substantially broaden viewpoint, environment and input-condition coverage.

E2.justification: The CogVideoX, data-fine-tuned CogVideoX and adapted Direct-a-video attention-modulation baselines remain, as do DragDiffusion, Go-with-the-Flow and inpainting comparisons. The CogVideoX-Ego experiment extends the existing backbone-versus-target-aware comparison through domain fine-tuning; it does not introduce a distinct competing method.

E3.justification: The principal benchmark grows from 50 to 80 images, yielding 250 versus 400 videos. v3 introduces stricter temporal/contact-plus-motion metrics, 50-image mask experiments, egocentric adaptation and additional ablation settings. Its Section 4.3 specifies every fifth supervised block, conflicting with Appendix A.1's retained every-third setting; the actual block schedule therefore remains unresolved.

E4.justification: v3 adds mask dilation, erosion, circular-mask and automatic-segmentation tests; caption-removal training ablations and corrupted-prompt inference tests; and explicit multiple-object and target-switching failures. It also expands loss-weight sensitivity and domain-transfer/action-diversity analyses. The original block-selection, attention-region and attention-modulation analyses are retained.

E5.justification: v3 newly specifies that the five videos per test image use random seeds; v1 already reported five videos per image. This adds seed information without establishing increased repetition. Neither version supplies confidence intervals, variability estimates or significance tests.

E6.justification: Table 1 and the original ablation tables contain revised scores: the proposed method's Contact Score changes from 0.896 to 0.878, and data-fine-tuned CogVideoX changes from 0.692 to 0.638. These concern different benchmark sizes, not demonstrated same-setting declines. New Table 9 reports 0.770, 0.693 and 0.783 for the proposed method's two-frame, three-frame and Interaction Scores. Numerous robustness and qualitative findings are added; user-study scores remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The core mask-channel architecture, target token, attention loss and LoRA training remain. v3 adds an automated GPT-4o/Grounded-SAM mask-acquisition pipeline and an egocentric adaptation procedure that transfers the target-aware LoRA onto a separately fine-tuned backbone (Appendices B and C.1).

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are substantially rewritten around target awareness and motion planning. Application order is reversed, the video-creation account is condensed, attention-region and block discussions are reordered, and the main discussion becomes a conclusion. The appendix is reorganized into thematic discussions, including relocated and expanded limitations.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column presentation. The opening teaser is removed, method diagrams and attention visualizations are merged into paired figures, and the video-creation pipeline moves to the appendix. New robustness tables and extensive qualitative and failure-case figures substantially change the visual presentation beyond renumbering or numerical updates.

R1.justification: v3 explicitly connects the planning motivation to World Models, Navigation World Models and Dexterous World Models, and adds references supporting new components, including Grounded-SAM, CoTracker and EgoLife. The established controllable-video and human-scene positioning remains. Publication-year and venue updates to retained works do not constitute additional research.

T1.justification: Appendix C.3 introduces precise definitions for consecutive-frame Contact Score and Interaction Score, which combines contact with a target-displacement threshold. The diffusion objectives and attention equations remain substantively equivalent; the downsampled-mask notation is clarified. Neither version contains theoretical propositions or proofs.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens validation of the central claim. Unlike v1, it tests dependence on mask precision and caption quality, checks whether the advantage survives stricter temporal/contact-plus-motion criteria, and documents concrete failure boundaries (Tables 5–9 and Appendix C). These address important weaknesses in v1's reliance on single-frame contact and limited robustness evidence. The new block-selection inconsistency harms reproducibility, and statistical uncertainty remains unreported, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in evidential depth and qualification.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Target-Aware Video Diffusion Models work. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable, and retained content can be matched across the substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds mask and caption robustness experiments, stricter interaction measurements, domain-transfer demonstrations and failure cases.

before.justification: v1 reports original video-generation comparisons, two user studies, ablations, qualitative demonstrations and physics-based imitation results in the main text and appendices.

results.title: Target-Aware Video Diffusion Models

C1.justification: V1 claims discovery and first proof-of-concept evidence of hidden semantic backdoors in deployed LLMs. V2 redefines the contribution as auditing concept-conditioned semantic divergence, explicitly treating flags as triage signals without causal or intent attribution. Controlled stance implantation and the twelve-topic screening remain central contributions.

C2.justification: V2 introduces benign explanations such as prescriptive pull and survey-like response tendencies, and states that flags establish neither malicious intent nor normative correctness. It explains that attribution requires independent provenance or mechanistic evidence. New appendix interpretations address judge-dependent misses, parameter sensitivity, and the effects of bias proportion.

D1.justification: V2 supplies the full question-generation prompt, topic-selection criteria, LLaMA-Factory identification, CPU/RAM information, judge-decoding settings, and supplementary-artifact instructions. The advertised repository changes from RAVEN to RAVEN-AI. Conversely, v1's detailed Algorithm 3 scoring pseudocode is removed, so reproducibility documentation gains substantial detail while losing one explicit procedural specification.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same twelve topics, conceptual relationships, and public-figure target/control task. Entity-X replaces the XXX XXX pseudonym. Added bias proportions, controls, and judge configurations operate within the retained data and task coverage.

E2.justification: V2 adds a shuffled-label Null-adapter comparator in RQ1 and compares RAVEN implementations using Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, and Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct judges against GPT-4o-mini in Table 9. These are controls and component variants; neither version benchmarks a competing backdoor detector.

E3.justification: The stated default alpha changes from 0.5 to 0.4. V2 distinguishes a 60% peer-disagreement gate from score-based reporting at 85, whereas v1 specifies divergence threshold 0.5 and Algorithm 3 filters scores above 50. New designs include shuffled-label controls, fixed-size 25%/75% biased training sets, parameter sweeps, and alternative judges. The original six samples, temperature 0.7, and 360-prompt audit remain.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's preliminary sampling check and brief examples, v2 adds threshold, weighting, and temperature sensitivity analyses in Appendix C.5, bias-proportion experiments in Appendix D, and judge ablations and manual cluster inspection in Appendix E. Appendix F expands the existing vaccination example with all five models' responses.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-training-run statistics, confidence intervals, error bars, or formal significance tests. V2 adds point estimates and qualitative statements about reduced variance, without a new statistical uncertainty procedure. The ten-sample check was already mentioned in v1.

E6.justification: The main suspicion scores and implantation sentiment averages carry over, but v2 removes Table 2's contradiction-strength values and several individual LoRA example scores. New outcomes include control drift of at most two percentage points, 14–25 flags across entropy thresholds, and judge totals of 17, 15, 14, and 17 in Table 9. These are additional results under specified configurations, not demonstrated same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The four-stage framework remains, but Algorithm 2 changes from all-pairs entailment-matrix cluster merging to sequential representative-based assignment. V2 also specifies low entropy plus majority disagreement for flagging, replacing the description of separate multiple-confident, confident-pair, and single-confident cases in v1's Algorithm 3. These materially revise the documented operational components, although v2's flagging descriptions are not fully consistent.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, threat-model exposition, research-question narratives, related work, discussion, and conclusion undergo extensive rewriting. Backdoor terminology is systematically replaced with divergence and triage language. Ethics material is moved and shortened, and reproducibility, acknowledgement, and expanded appendix sections reorganize the supporting narrative.

P2.justification: V2 adds Tables 5–9 for sensitivity and judge comparisons, regroups Tables 1–2 by model, removes Table 2's Avg. Strength column, and reformats Tables 3–4. Figure 1's labeling and caption change, algorithm displays are revised or removed, and the document adopts the ICLR layout. These substantially alter evidence presentation.

R1.justification: V2 substantially repositions the work as complementary behavioral triage rather than first-of-its-kind backdoor identification. It adds framing, agenda-setting, social-desirability, survey-response, and prescriptive-sampling literature, alongside BadChain and LLaMA-Factory, while removing several attack references. This changes the intellectual context beyond citation formatting.

T1.justification: Equation 1 replaces the qualitative large conditional-probability gap defining a semantic backdoor with an explicit probability-difference estimand over a paraphrase-controlled prompt distribution. V2 distinguishes this estimand from operational flagging. The entropy and bidirectional-entailment definitions remain, and no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: V2 resolves a central inferential overclaim by replacing asserted discovery of hidden backdoors with explicitly non-causal behavioral triage. Added controls and sensitivity analyses substantially strengthen validation. Reproducibility remains imperfect: detailed scoring pseudocode disappears, flagging descriptions conflict, and Table 9's 17-case baseline is not reconciled with Table 5's 14 cases at the default entropy threshold. These limitations qualify but do not outweigh the substantial gains in claim validity and supporting evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RAVEN framework, controlled LoRA study, and twelve-topic audit. All pages, including figures, tables, equations, and appendices, are readable. The substantial reframing and appendix expansion do not prevent comparison.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and adds control outcomes, parameter sweeps, bias-proportion experiments, and entailment-judge comparisons.

before.justification: V1 reports original LoRA implantation experiments, sentiment measurements, and RAVEN audit results across five LLMs in Sections 3–4.

results.title: Propaganda AI: An Analysis of Semantic Divergence in Large Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution summary now acknowledge benefits from budget-aware TALE-EP, qualifying the earlier inference-time message centered on self-refinement and majority voting. Claims about model-family niches, temporal cost reductions and the importance of model-level innovation remain substantially unchanged.

C2.justification: Appendix D substantially expands applicability boundaries, covering provider variability, prompt sensitivity, benchmark contamination, model-selection bias, hybrid human-AI workflows and costly errors. C.6 interprets cheaper human labor as reducing the penalty for model failure, while C.8 identifies benchmark gaming and proposes mitigations. Existing verification, variance and human-reliability caveats are retained and developed.

D1.justification: v2 explicitly documents original-provider access for proprietary models and TogetherAI access for open models, supplementing provider links already present in v1. It clarifies averaging and supplies technical cost inputs for new analyses, including regional rates and the INR88:$1 conversion. The original prompt, decoding settings, token prices and repository link remain.

E1.justification: Appendix C.2 adds Tau-bench airline and retail tasks involving tool use and multi-turn agent-user interaction, substantially extending the original mathematical and question-answering coverage. All six original datasets remain. The India analysis changes labor-cost assumptions, not the evaluated problem population.

E2.justification: TALE-EP, previously only cited, joins the retained self-refinement and majority-voting comparisons in Table 2. Appendix C.8/Table 13 also compares a random-answer Llama-3.1-8B configuration against the original leading models. The original ten-model comparison panel remains unchanged.

E3.justification: New protocols include 16 Tau-bench tasks, costs aggregated across interaction rounds, a $2.06 human baseline, and a separate India labor-cost calibration. Section 3.4 also changes the essentialness denominator from the full-model frontier to the frontier excluding the tested family. Figure 3 retains its values, so this reported metric revision does not establish that the original experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New analyses test human-baseline essentialness (C.4), sensitivity to regional labor costs (C.6), ranking stability under bootstrap estimation (C.7), and exploitation by cheap random guessing (C.8). These directly examine assumptions and failure conditions previously untested. The earlier model-release and individual-model counterfactual analyses remain in C.3 and C.5.

E5.justification: v1 reports eight repetitions per model-instance pair without confidence intervals. v2 retains that sampling budget and adds 95% bootstrap percentile intervals for all Table 1 estimates using 10,000 resamples (C.7/Table 12). The new Tau-bench experiment separately reports four independent trials; this is not a reduction in the original experiments' repetitions.

E6.justification: Substantial new results include TALE-EP frontier-cost reductions of 66.6% on GSM8K and 50% on GPQA-Diamond, Tau-bench costs, regional estimates and human-essentialness findings. Table 13 reports random-guesser costs of $0.000079 on BBQ and $0.00021 on GPQA-Diamond. The original Table 1, accuracy/cost tables and Figures 2-5 retain their numerical results.

M1.justification: The proposed cost-of-pass calculation C/R, minimum frontier over model and human strategies, and estimation procedure remain intact. TALE-EP and random guessing are additional evaluated strategies. Richer cost functions and success criteria are discussed as extensions rather than implemented replacements.

P1.justification: The main five-section narrative remains, with localized rewrites to the introduction, economic setup and inference-time discussion. Appendix D reorganizes its explanations into modeling extensions, interpretability and limitations, while Appendix C accommodates additional analyses. Terminology, cross-references, acknowledgments and the author block are also edited.

P2.justification: The paper changes from a two-column layout to a single-column conference format, extensively resizing and relocating existing displays. Table 2 gains a TALE-EP row, and Tables 7-13 introduce displays for Tau-bench, regional costs, confidence intervals and adversarial comparisons. All five original figures retain their plotted content.

R1.justification: Related work adds connections to inference-price studies by Cottier et al. and Gundlach et al., and economics research on automation, expertise, R&D and compute allocation. Additional references support Tau-bench, provider variability, hybrid workflows and revised labor-cost sources. The central positioning as an adaptation of production theory remains.

T1.justification: Section 3.4 revises the formal normalization of family essentialness. Section 2.5 replaces population-expectation equalities with explicit approximations using an i.i.d. empirical distribution. Appendix C.8 adds a short mathematical counterexample showing that random guessing among k options can achieve cost-of-pass approximately k times its inference cost. The foundational C/R and frontier definitions remain.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens scrutiny of assumptions left untested in v1: TALE-EP supplies a missing cost-oriented comparison, regional sensitivity tests the human-cost reference, and the random-guesser experiment exposes a fundamental failure mode. Expanded limitations make the conclusions better calibrated. Tau-bench remains small at 16 tasks, and bootstrap-midpoint ranking agreement does not establish the claimed statistical significance, but these weaknesses do not outweigh the substantial gains in critical validation and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Cost-of-Pass framework. All 16 pages of v1 and 25 pages of v2, including Appendices A-D, are readable. The original equations, experiments, tables and figures can be matched reliably despite additions and substantial layout changes.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds TALE-EP comparisons, Tau-bench evaluations, regional cost sensitivity, bootstrap intervals and a random-guessing experiment.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of ten language models across six datasets, including accuracy, inference costs, temporal and counterfactual analyses, and inference-time technique comparisons.

results.title: Cost-of-Pass: An Economic Framework for Evaluating Language Models

C1.justification: The ViMo and STR novelty claims remain intact, but v2 broadens the introduction and conclusion to claim generalisation to unseen apps and successful online task completion. This extends v1's empirical contribution beyond offline action prediction and qualitative compositional generalisation; the contribution summary also adds a human-evaluation advantage.

C2.justification: v2 explains discrepancies between human and automatic ratings and discusses accumulated prediction errors at longer horizons. It also justifies one-step lookahead as an accuracy–cost tradeoff despite two steps scoring highest. The malformed-placeholder limitation is relocated into a dedicated section rather than newly discovered.

D1.justification: v2 specifies GPT-4o as the default LLM, explicitly documents IP2P fine-tuning, and supplies human-study instructions. It adds deployment information including 16 GB GPU memory, V100 timings, three-action requests, and API integration. Appendix F newly describes a user-commitment requirement for the planned checkpoint release; these disclosures do not establish changed training.

E1.justification: v2 adds online navigation on AndroidWorld's 116 tasks and zero-shot evaluation on Android Control apps excluded from training. These extend coverage beyond v1's offline evaluation on the retained 19-app dataset and qualitative examples of unusual action combinations.

E2.justification: SeeAct is newly included in the zero-shot and online comparisons in v2 Tables 4–5. Existing GUI, trajectory, and agent comparators remain present after matching appendix relocations. IP2P becomes IP2P* with explicit fine-tuning disclosure; its retained scores do not establish a new comparator.

E3.justification: v2 introduces a 70-participant study of 80 generated samples, including normalized 1–5 visual ratings, and online evaluation using task success. New Gemini-2.0-Flash experiments test rollout depths with only the final predicted state informing selection. The original data splits and 57-episode evaluation remain; Table 6 also clarifies the first control as no ViMo, without establishing a rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds quantitative unseen-app robustness testing, a one-/two-/three-step lookahead ablation in Table 7, and inference-time/accuracy analysis in Table 12. The original trajectory evaluation is retained as Table 10 and reframed as error analysis; the original component ablations and qualitative failure examples are also retained.

E5.justification: v2 Table 11 adds standard deviations across the same three runs already listed in v1 Table 9. The run count and individual run results remain unchanged; no additional runs, confidence intervals, or significance tests are established.

E6.justification: v2 adds human, unseen-app, online, rollout-depth, timing, and some category-level results. Its new online experiment reports 33.19% task success for Gemini-2.0-Flash T3A versus 40.95% with ViMo, not a cross-version performance gain. The retained full-test harmonic score changes from 0.7583 to 0.7578, while original trajectory and main agent scores remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The proposed default STR construction, diffusion predictor, GUI-text predictor, and one-step action-selection pipeline remain unchanged. The expanded two-stage selector explanation already appears in v1 Appendix B. v2 tests deeper rollout variants as an ablation while retaining the original one-step default.

P1.justification: v2 reorganizes the experimental narrative around three evaluation settings, moves trajectory and qualitative analyses into Appendix B, and brings existing action-selection explanation into the main text. Earlier implementation appendices are consolidated under Experimental Details, with deployment and limitations separated. The title changes, although much method and related-work prose is retained.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column layout and substantially reorganizes its displays. v2 expands the introductory comparison and GUI-quality table, restructures agent-comparison tables, merges and relocates qualitative ablation figures, and adds rollout, deployment, and survey displays. Many original screenshots and numerical tables are retained through these moves.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for the GPT-4o system card, Gemini 2.0, and a deepfake survey. The related-work discussion and positioning against language-based world models and pixel-based GUI generators otherwise remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Equations 1–6, including the diffusion objective and prediction/selection formulations, retain their mathematical content. Neither version adds distinct theorems, proofs, formal assumptions, or derivations in its appendices.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's reliance on offline proxies for practical usefulness by adding unseen-app and online task-completion evaluations, complemented by human assessment and horizon/cost analysis. These strengthen validation of the paper's central application claims. Reporting weaknesses remain: the unseen-app sample size is unspecified, and some human-study harmonic scores in Table 1 are inconsistent with their listed components. These issues limit precise quantitative claims but do not outweigh the broader validation gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ViMo/STR research despite the revised title and formatting. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds human evaluation, unseen-app and online-navigation results, rollout-depth experiments, and inference-time measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original GUI-generation evaluations, trajectory-synthesis results, agent comparisons, component ablations, and repeated-run experiments.

results.title: ViMo: A Generative Visual GUI World Model for App Agents

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion retain the same central claims: optimal convergence when p is known, the best-known centralized rate when p is unknown, topology independence and node-count speedup in the stated regime, and empirical robustness. The qualified Transformer interpretation appears in Section 5.2 without a corresponding revision of the broad main claims.

C2.justification: Section 5.2 replaces v1's interpretation that GT-NSGDm is the only successful Transformer optimizer with the finding that it nearly matches DSGD-GClip, emphasizing competitive performance together with theoretical guarantees. New Remarks 7–8 also explain required parameter knowledge, finite-horizon topology and node-count effects, and tradeoffs against bounded-variance theory. These substantially qualify the method's practical and theoretical advantages.

D1.justification: Appendix C adds update equations and Transformer hyperparameter-search ranges for the four new baselines, including GT-Adam's stabilization parameter and QG-DSGDm's momentum choices. Existing model architecture, hardware, reported runtime and original methods' search grids are retained. No new code or data access resource is supplied.

E1.justification: Both versions cover synthetic token-like regression and Multi30k language modeling, including the same noise families, graph topologies and node-count scenarios. The revised synthetic feature allocation changes the reported generation setting within existing coverage, rather than adding a dataset or task.

E2.justification: The Transformer comparison expands from four to eight baselines by adding DSGD-GClip, DSGD-CClip, GT-Adam and QG-DSGDm. All four have reported results in v2 Table 1; the original baselines remain. These additions substantially strengthen the comparison, while the synthetic comparator set is unchanged.

E3.justification: Section 5.1 revises the synthetic feature specification: v1 states two frequent and eight rare features despite declaring d=20; v2 specifies four frequent and sixteen rare features. This is a reported data-generation correction, without evidence establishing a rerun. The retained Transformer experiments still use the same model, 12 epochs, batch size 64, validation metric and graph settings.

E4.justification: The gradient-noise investigation, comparisons across noise distributions, and sensitivity studies varying connectivity, noise level and node count are retained in Figures 1–3. No distinct ablation, robustness scenario or case study is added. The removed Transformer learning curves report the existing benchmark experiment rather than a separate supplementary analysis.

E5.justification: Both versions report Transformer means and standard deviations over five independent runs. v2 presents this information in Table 1 and extends the same practice to additional baselines; it does not introduce a different run count, confidence interval or significance-testing procedure.

E6.justification: v2 adds results for four Transformer comparators, changing the empirical ranking. DSGD-GClip reports losses of 0.253, 0.249 and 0.267 on ring, exponential and complete graphs, below GT-NSGDm's retained means of 0.258, 0.261 and 0.282. v1's validation and training trajectories are removed, including its reported training endpoints of 0.100, 0.096 and 0.091. The synthetic findings remain unchanged.

M1.justification: GT-NSGDm's momentum, gradient-tracking and normalized update equations remain unchanged. However, its theoretical step-size prescription in Equation (5) changes from min(1, max{three candidates}) to the minimum of all four quantities, and replaces 1+2.5L with 3.5L in one candidate. This changes parameter selection without introducing a new optimizer component.

P1.justification: v2 makes localized grammatical corrections, condenses the experimental prose, removes the paper-outline paragraph, and adds a proof roadmap and acknowledgments. The principal section organization is retained. A small new inconsistency remains: Section 5.2 says three additional baselines while listing four.

P2.justification: The Transformer evidence is substantially reformatted: v1 Figure 4's validation curves are replaced by a numerical table grouped by theoretical guarantees, and Figure 5's training curves are removed. Baseline-description and Transformer-search tables expand and move to separate appendix pages. Figures 1–3 retain their plotted content, with placement changes.

R1.justification: Section 1.2 adds discussion of adaptive federated optimization and earlier gradient tracking with normalization for deterministic max-margin learning. Additional references support the new baselines, spectral and bounded-variance comparisons, and related divergence examples in Appendix A; some general optimization references disappear. The overall research positioning remains unchanged.

T1.justification: The mathematical support for both main theorems is materially revised. Equation (5) corrects the min/max step-size choice; the final derivation restores a missing smoothness factor L and propagates revised constants. Lemmas 6–8 separate unconditional martingale bounds from subsequent conditional-expectation calculations. Remarks 7–8 add parameter-selection and finite-horizon derivations. These changes affect the reasoning supporting the guarantees, although the assumptions and principal convergence exponents remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important weaknesses in both central forms of evidence: it repairs the step-size prescription and proof arguments supporting convergence, and introduces stronger Transformer baselines that produce a more credible, qualified empirical interpretation. These gains outweigh the loss of learning-curve detail. The unchanged broad superiority wording in the abstract remains a limitation, but the theoretical support and comparative evaluation are substantially improved.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GT-NSGDm research, with matching algorithms, theoretical results and experimental tasks. Text, equations, figures, tables and Appendices A–C are readable, and relocated material can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 retains original synthetic experiments and gradient-noise measurements and reports Transformer validation results for an expanded comparator set in Table 1.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic regression experiments, empirical gradient-noise distributions and decentralized Transformer training results, including validation and training losses in Figures 1–5.

results.title: Decentralized Nonconvex Optimization under Heavy-Tailed Noise: Normalization and Optimal Convergence

C1.justification: The abstract is unchanged apart from formatting. The introduction and conclusion retain the same central contributions: the retrieve-and-rerank framework, SWELOC training data, state-of-the-art localization on the two main benchmarks, and favorable efficiency relative to agentic methods.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations of retrieval and repair bottlenecks, failure on complex issues, semantic matching beyond lexical overlap, and transfer beyond Python. It attributes reranking gains to cross-function dependencies and discusses agents confusing symptom locations with underlying causes. These substantially extend v1's discussion of data quality, model choice, and cost.

D1.justification: V1 promises future code, data, and model releases; v2 reports code and models available through a repository. V2 also documents file/module score aggregation and latency hardware. Appendix A is unchanged, while the token-pricing footnote and agent-result provenance notes in Tables 1–2 are removed.

E1.justification: V2 adds downstream issue resolution using SWE-Fixer on SWE-Bench-Lite, extending evaluation beyond localization. Appendix F adds SWE-Bench Multilingual, covering 234 tasks across nine non-Python programming languages. The existing SWELOC training data and two main localization benchmarks remain.
